summary: This episode recounts Martin Luther's dramatic summons to the Diet of Worms (April 1521), his confrontation with imperial and ecclesiastical authorities, and his famous refusal to recant—summarised by the oft‑quoted line "Here I stand". The hosts set the political scene: Charles V's recent election, Frederick the Wise's patronage, and fears of schism amid Ottoman pressure. After Worms, Luther is given safe conduct but is abducted by agents of Frederick and hidden at the Wartburg Castle, where he adopts the alias Junker Georg. While in hiding he translates the New Testament from Greek into German, and his image and pamphlets—helped by Lucas Cranach and Melanchthon—circulate widely. Back in Wittenberg, radical reformers led by Andreas Karlstadt instigate iconoclasm and liturgical changes; on his return Luther reins in the excesses, protecting some church practices and opposing more radical reformers. The episode closes by previewing the violent consequences to come, notably the German Peasants' War, and noting bonus content available to club members.
title: Luther: Showdown with the Emperor (Part 4)

description:
Three years on from Martin Luther’s publication of the Ninety-Five Theses - an assault on the Catholic Church and the selling of indulgences - his radical new ideas and brilliant use of the printing press had unleashed chaos in western Christendom. Still in Wittenberg, under the Protection of the powerful Frederick III, Luther’s increasingly radical beliefs were slowly beginning to undermine the entire fabric of the Catholic Church, and the theology that has shaped the Latin West for centuries. All the while, support for his outrageous ideas was swelling, and Luther’s own celebrity grew hand in hand with the ever-looming threat of excommunication. At last, in August 1518, Luther was summoned to have his beliefs examined at the Imperial court in Augsburg - would he survive this reckoning?

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the growing radicalism of Luther’s doctrine, his seminal Reformation moment, and the great debate in Augsburg which would see his fervour put to the test.

summary: This episode (episode three of a series on Martin Luther) traces Luther’s escalation from disputant to revolutionary reformer. Holland and Sandbrook open with the dramatic burning of the papal bull and use that scene to explore the threefold nature of the crisis Luther provoked: institutional challenge to papal authority, radical theological claims (notably justification by faith and Sola Scriptura), and mastery of print and public spectacle. They discuss Luther’s ‘reformation moment’ in reading Saint Paul, his public confrontations with Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg, the Leipzig disputation with Johann Eck, and the growing popular fervour—students, pamphlets and book-burnings—that amplified his message. Themes include the rise of individual conscience, proto-nationalist resentment of Rome, apocalyptic fears about Ottoman advances, and the modern parallels in media and populist rhetoric. The episode closes with Luther’s excommunication and the cliffhanger of how Charles V will respond at the forthcoming Diet of Worms.
title: Luther: The Battle Against Satan (Part 3)

description:
Martin Luther is one of the few people to have genuinely changed the world, igniting a religious revolution that tore Christendom in two, and undermined European tradition in ways that still reverberate today. But along with Luther’s uniquely tortured psyche, three events contributed to his extreme transformation from young lawyer to fervent monk: the loss of a dear friend, a near fatal accident, and a cataclysmic thunderstorm. It was at the University of Wittenberg that Luther’s truly revolutionary understanding of God, theology and scripture began to evolve. His scorn for the state of the Church bubbled underneath the surface, until one day, a friar called Johann Tetzel rolled into Saxony, claiming to sell awesome indulgences, which would allow sinful locals to shorten their stay in purgatory. Such staggering corruption drove Luther to take drastic action, and, marching to Wittenberg Castle’s Church, he legendarily nailed his Ninety-Five Theses to the door. Or did he?

Join Tom and Dominic as they describe Luther’s tormented journey to priesthood, the events that lead up to the apocryphal nailing of the Ninety-Five theses, and the truly radical nature of his newfound relationship with God and Christianity.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Martin Luther's transformation from a troubled student to an Augustinian monk and then to a university professor whose reading of Scripture and use of print set Europe on a new course. They recount the near-fatal sword wound and the thunderstorm vow to Saint Anne that propelled Luther into monastic life, his anxieties and confessions to Johann von Staupitz, and his move to Wittenberg under the patronage of Frederick, Elector of Saxony. The hosts discuss the cultural context—relic culture, indulgences, the role of the Fuggers and the papal campaign to rebuild St. Peter's—and the crucial technological impact of printing. Luther's solo engagement with the Bible, his 97 theses and the better-known 95 Theses, and his explosive response to Johann Tetzel’s indulgence campaign are covered, culminating in the printing and dissemination of his theses in 1517. The episode ends with a tease to Rest Is History Club for continuation.

description:
The Reformation, launched in 1517, stands as one of the most convulsive and transformative events of all time, shattering Christendom and dividing Europe for centuries. Its outcome determined the fates of Kings and Emperors, and saw the souls of millions consigned to the fiery pit of heresy. The man behind it all was Martin Luther, a humble monk of obscure origins. Bold, intellectually arrogant, and a master of spin, the assault he unleashed on the medieval Church had him excommunicated by the Pope. But what was it about Luther’s humble upbringing in Saxony and his strained relationship with his intimidating father that led him down a path of insolence? And was the religious revolution that he sparked inevitable?

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the early life of Martin Luther, the apocalyptic environment from which he and his radical ideas emerged, and the Catholic Church he would come to take on…

summary: This episode is an introductory survey of Martin Luther and the wider Reformation, led by hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook. Using Richard Rex's The Making of Martin Luther as a springboard, the hosts outline the famous 31 October 1517 moment in Wittenberg and place Luther in his provincial Saxon context. They explore Luther’s upbringing, family background and education, and situate his ideas amid late-medieval anxieties — Ottoman expansion, the Italian wars, apocalyptic prophecy — and the intellectual currents of Renaissance humanism. description:
"Then it is I drown again, with all those dim lost faces I never understood… Include me in your lamentations.”
The aftermath of the Titanic’s sinking saw different reactions erupt across the Atlantic, and the responses of both mourners and onlookers were visceral. Guilt-ridden survivors were both ostracised and lauded. Heroes became legends - the unsinkable Molly Brown and the band that played on till the frozen end - while villains were condemned forever more. Reputations were splintered and characters blackened as the investigation went on. None more so than J. Bruce Ismay, the head of White Star, whose survival was viewed as a weakness of character. But the key question needed answering: was anyone really to blame, and if yes, who? 

Join Dominic and Tom, as they discuss the terrible aftershocks of the sinking of the Titanic, as they unpick truth from legend, and analyse James Cameron’s 1995 film, which famously immortalised this extraordinary story.

summary: This episode (the sixth in the podcast's Titanic series) examines the immediate aftermath, public reaction and long-term cultural meanings of the sinking of the RMS Titanic on 15 April 1912. The hosts recount the Carpathia rescue under Arthur Rostran, casualty figures and survival patterns by class and gender, and how news spread via Marconi stations and newspapers. Political and social responses are surveyed — from President Taft's mourning to Herbert Henry Asquith's emotional reaction — and the divergent US and British inquiries (and their populist or conciliatory tones). The episode traces the vilification and private decline of Bruce Ismay, survivor trauma and suicides, and transnational reactions such as Masabumi Hosono's ostracism in Japan. Finally they review the Titanic in culture: early films, Walter Lord's A Night to Remember, Derek Mahon's poem, and James Cameron's blockbuster, discussing metaphors of hubris, empire and chance that have kept the story resonant.

description:
“A story of horror unparalleled in the annals of the Sea.”
On the 14th of April 1912, Titanic, a floating palace sailing through the North Atlantic, found itself hurtling towards a formidable iceberg. Contrary to the panicked reactions of her crew who, fatefully, pulled the hulking vessel to starboard, the ship's passengers slept, laughed and played on, unaware of the danger ahead. Then came a terrible grinding sound, as the side of the ship grated against the iceberg, followed by a long, dead silence. At 12.15am a distress call went out, and the order went out to begin filling the lifeboats, women and children first. But, with far fewer lifeboats than passengers, who would be allowed to board them, and who would be left behind? What leverage did gender, class, and age provide when so many lives hung in the balance? By 1.55am, the lifeboats were scarce, and the panic of those still aboard the ship spiralled out of control, as the Titanic entered her death throes… 

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss Titanic’s collision with the iceberg, the reactions of her doomed passengers and crew, and the stories of courage, incompetence, and tragedy.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-part examination of the Titanic, focusing on the collision, the ship's progressive flooding and the chaotic lifeboat evacuations. Drawing on accounts in Walter Lord's A Night to Remember and Richard Davenport Hines' Titanic Lives, they reconstruct the timeline from impact through the two hours and forty minutes to sinking. The episode explores watertight compartment design, Marconi distress calls, and the confused rescue response (including the Carpathia and the nearby but ineffective Californian and Mount Temple). The hosts emphasise how gender, class, social codes and officer interpretations of “women and children first” shaped survival rates, and relay moving individual stories—Isidor and Ida Strauss, Ben Guggenheim, Wallace Hartley and the band, the Duff-Gordons, and numerous third-class passengers. They discuss controversial moments (Murdoch, Ismay, Lightoller/Lytholler) and why many lifeboats left underfilled. The episode ends by promising a final installment about aftermath, myth-making and cultural responses.

description:
It is Sunday the 14th of April 1912, and the passengers of the Titanic, from the tycoons in first class to the migrants in third class, have been enjoying a journey incomparable in its modernity. The weather, up until that point exceptionally clement, suddenly grew colder, stiller, calmer, and the ice warnings that had been coming through the ship’s sophisticated communications machine since Friday were growing evermore urgent. Ominously, they were left beneath piles of competing letters, unread. Then, at 11.40pm that night, a night of dancing and laughter, a cry came from the crow’s nest: “Iceberg ahead!”

Join Dominic and Tom as they unpack the captivating lives and stories of the Titanic’s third class passengers, and recount the days and moments building up to the ship’s final hours.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-episode examination of the Titanic, focusing on third-class passengers, the ship's final hours before impact, and the social and technological context of 1912. They profile the demographics of third class — Scandinavians, Lebanese Maronite Christians, Armenians, Croats, Greeks and others — and outline the reasons for emigration to the United States (noting peak immigration in 1907). The episode highlights specific passengers (the Goldsmith family, Alfred Rush, Nikola Lulic) and broader tragedies that frame their stories, including violence in the Ottoman Empire and the later Armenian genocide. The hosts discuss shipboard life for third-class passengers, White Star marketing, Marconi wireless operations and message backlogs, and the sequence of iceberg warnings. They describe the bridge officers on watch (Murdoch, Lightoller), lookouts (Frederick Fleet), and the actions that led to the fatal contact with an iceberg on the night of 14 April 1912, setting up a follow-up episode on the sinking and its aftermath.
title: Titanic: The Iceberg Strikes (Part 4)

description:
The drama and tragedy of the Titanic’s sinking has spawned all manner of myths about those who left Southampton on the 10th of April 1912, and for four days luxuriated in the ship’s modern facilities, extravagant interiors, and plush cabins. Among them were many magnates and tycoons, such as J.J. Astor, the richest man onboard, and the American businessman Ben Guggenheim. Conspicuously absent, however, was J. P. Morgan, who cancelled his booking at the last minute, and five days later would find his greatest business competitors eliminated… Just as intriguing though, and often overlooked, were the Titanic’s second class passengers: middle-aged men with their teenage mistresses, a father who had his kidnapped his children, excited migrant families, and Joseph Laroche, a brilliant engineer and the only black man on board, for whom the Titanic provided the chance to start a new life- the same was true for many others.
Join Tom and Dominic as they explore the dazzling, eccentric and endlessly fascinating First and Second Class passengers of the Titanic, whose extraordinary lives shine all the brighter for the terrible danger and tragedy waiting for them on the icy horizon…

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey the passengers aboard RMS Titanic, focusing on the social range from gilded millionaires to respectable second-class travellers. They profile prominent first-class figures — John Jacob Astor IV, Benjamin Guggenheim, Isidor Straus, the Widener family, W.T. Stead, financiers like John Pierpont Morgan (who ultimately cancelled), and cultural figures such as Francis Davis Millet and Archibald Gracie IV — and discuss the ship’s hotel-like luxury. The hosts emphasise complexity beyond the popular rich/poor narrative, highlighting second-class passengers (clergy, clerks, Cornish miners, immigrants like Masabumi Hosono and Joseph Laroche) and quirky human details (dogs aboard, lingerie entrepreneur Lucy Duff-Gordon, kidnappings, spiritualism). They reference Richard Davenport-Hines’s Titanic Lives for biographical colour and preview a subsequent episode on third-class steerage and the iceberg collision. The tone mixes historical analysis with anecdote, correcting myths about class segregation (driven by US immigration rules) and preparing listeners for the disaster to come.
title: Titanic: Countdown to Disaster (Part 3)

description:
The Titanic was a product of the furious competition of the late Gilded Age, and no expenses were spared to make her the most extraordinary and luxurious ship ever built. The height of an eleven-story building, fully electric, and with first class suites designed for the world’s wealthiest, the Titanic embodied the Edwardian obsessions with grandeur and greatness. But the ship was also designed to accommodate immigrants, who made up the majority of its passengers, in third class, or “steerage”. But is their any truth behind the myths surrounding class-based mistreatment of the poorer passengers, in contrast to the over-pampered rich? Was safety sacrificed in favour of a hubristic lust for luxury and grandeur? 

Join Dominic and Tom as they discuss the Titanic’s sumptuous, modern interiors, her gargantuan proportions, and the stories of builders who brought her to life. They dive into a world of butlers, stewards, maids and crewmen, and look into the man whose name would later become synonymous with disaster: the Titanic’s captain, Edward Smith.

summary: This episode (the second in the podcast’s Titanic series) examines the construction, design and early operational life of RMS Titanic. Holland and Sandbrook discuss the ship’s Belfast origins at Harland and Wolff, the role of designer Thomas Andrews and the White Star directors (including J. Bruce Ismay and Lord Pirrie), and the blend of extreme luxury and mass emigration that defined Titanic’s layout. They challenge simple narratives of negligence by explaining advanced safety features (double bottoms, 15 watertight bulkheads) while also addressing the lifeboat shortfall in the regulatory context of the time. The hosts trace the ship’s build timeline (keel, launch, fitting out, sea trials), the move to Southampton as the Atlantic hub, and the charged political backdrop of the 1912 Home Rule crisis. Key crew and officers (Captain Edward Smith, Charles Herbert Lightoller), the experiences of stewards and firemen, and small acts of chance that affected who sailed are covered. The episode ends by teasing the next installment on the passengers.
title: Titanic: Kings of the World (Part 2)

description:
"There is no danger that Titanic will sink. The boat is unsinkable and nothing but inconvenience will be suffered by the passengers."
The sinking of the Titanic, on a freezing Sunday night in April 1912, claimed more than 1500 lives. But how this state-of-the-art ocean liner came to be is also a story full of drama, encapsulating the turn of the century’s spirit of competition and drive for modernity. The booming financial world of the 1900s, rising immigration, the excitement of speed and steam, and an ever-growing transatlantic rivalry between Britain and the U.S. all played a part in the liner’s inception. And from this era emerged three men who would shape the Titanic’s journey: J.P. Morgan, an American titan of business; Thomas Ismay, the English magnate who owned the ship’s parent company; and William Pirrie, a leading British shipbuilder. Between these three men and two pivotal cities - New York and Belfast - the origins of the disaster that defined a generation can be traced… 
Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the context behind the building of RMS Titanic. From the rivalries of the transatlantic liner industry, to the tensions surrounding the Irish Home Rule movement, the story of the “unsinkable” began in a tumultuous age.

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the origins and broader historical context of the RMS Titanic. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the story to three central men — John Pierpont Morgan, J. Bruce Ismay, and William Pirrie — and to two cities, New York and Belfast. They situate the Titanic within early-20th-century themes: the rise of American capitalism, Anglo-German naval rivalry, the cult of speed and technological modernity, luxury competition among shipping lines (White Star, Cunard, German lines), and mass emigration to America. The discussion moves to Belfast and Harland and Wolff, detailing industrial scale, sectarian tensions, and the shipbuilding workforce. The episode references contemporary commentary and historiography (including Richard Davenport Hines) and frames the Titanic as both a product of industrial ambition and a prelude to larger geopolitical shifts leading into the First World War. The hosts indicate the story will continue in subsequent episodes focused on the ship, its fittings, passengers, crew and the sinking itself.
title: Titanic: The Tragedy Begins (Part 1)

description:
Man in his arrogance thinks himself a great work, worthy the interposition of a deity. More humble, and I believe truer, to consider him created from animals.
A military grave from the 5th century BC was found to contain something extraordinary; a macaque monkey dressed as a roman legionary. Did he fight alongside his human fellows, or merely serve as their mascot? Whatever the case, it demonstrates the role of monkeys and chimps throughout human history. From antiquity, when to possess a monkey signified status, to the the east where they symbolised corruption and vice, to the fighting pits of regency London where the ape Jacco Macacco had fortunes lost and won on his violent exploits. So too the monkey accused of treason during the Napoleonic Wars, the noble Corporal Jackie, a South African baboon who nursed injured human soldiers during WWII, and Jenny; the orangutan who in her commonality with man influenced Darwin's theory of evolution. Less earnest but just as dazzling was the role of monkeys and chips in art and culture. From starring roles on television amidst the glitz and glamor of Hollywood, to the diva-like personalities of Elvis’ erratic Scatter and Michael Jackson’s infamous Bubbles.
Join Dominic and Tom as they reveal history’s greatest apes, orangutans and monkeys, and the extraordinary lives they lead. From Roman legionaries, war veterans and train conductors, to superstars, football mascots and artists, these remarkable creatures have featured in every corner of human life, imitating us, befriending us and even influencing us.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a themed episode, "History's Greatest Monkeys," surveying notable primates in history and their cultural roles. They open with macaques in the Roman world — including a buried pet found in a late-5th-century Pyrenean grave — and anecdotes from early Islamic courts (Yazid I’s monkey Abu Qais). The episode moves to 19th-century Britain to recount Jaco Macaco, a famed pit-fighter at the Westminster Pit, and the outrage that helped spur animal-cruelty campaigns. They examine apes in entertainment and celebrity: early film apes, Elvis’s Scatter, Michael Jackson’s Bubbles, and Hollywood chimps. South African cases include Jack the Signalman and Corporal Jackie, baboon mascots and wartime companions. The Hartlepool monkey-hanging legend and the later Hartlepool football mascot Hangus (Stuart Drummond) that led to an elected mayoralty are discussed. They close with artistic and scientific encounters — a chimpanzee painting hoax, Desmond Morris’s The Naked Ape, and Charles Darwin’s observations of Jenny the orangutan and how they influenced his thinking on human origins.
title: History's Greatest Monkeys

description:
‘For if a person fatigued with long and hard labour, or with a violent agitation of the mind, takes a good dish of chocolate, he shall perceive almost instantly that his faintness shall cease, and his strength shall be recovered’
The Cacao tree was first domesticated by the Olmecs in Mesoamerica, possibly as early as 1500 BC, and was then first encountered by Europeans in the 16th century, when it is said that the Aztec Emperor Montezuma welcomed Hernan Cortes into his dominion with a mysterious dark drink. Indeed, Chocolate was originally consumed as a drink, and was a cornerstone of Aztec life, whether used as currency or as part of religious rituals. Brought back by the conquistadors to Europe, Chocolate slowly spread through the continent, particularly among the ruling classes, up until the industrial revolution of the 19th century, when technical advancements allowed for chocolate to be made into a food, at a far lower cost. This paved the way for Quaker families, such as the Cadburys or the Frys, keen to find an alternative to alcohol, to make the snack available to the masses…
Tom and Dominic have partnered with Cadbury, in celebration of their 200th year anniversary, to explore the story of how chocolate, from its Mesoamerican origins, became a British favourite.

Over the coming months, Cadbury will be announcing more plans for its 200th anniversary year, including ways that fans nationwide can get involved in the celebrations. For more information, visit: https://www.cadbury.co.uk/about/anniversary/200-years-of-cadbury/

summary: This episode traces the long history of chocolate from its Mesoamerican origins to its central place in modern British life. Holland and Sandbrook discuss early use by the Olmecs, Maya and Aztecs—where cacao functioned as a ritual, medicinal and social drink—and the Spanish transmission of cacao to Europe (first recorded presentation to Philip II in 1544). They survey European religious debates over chocolate, seventeenth-century adoption in coffee- and chocolate-houses, and early recipes. The hosts then turn to industrial transformation: Quaker entrepreneurs (the Frys and Cadburys), Dutch innovations (the Van Houtens' press) and mechanisation that made chocolate an edible bar. The episode highlights Cadbury’s development, Bournville model village, wartime provisioning in WWI, and the democratization of chocolate consumption between the wars. The discussion links chocolate’s history to broader themes—religion, empire, industrialisation and social reform—while noting cultural myths and memorable advertising and product developments (Dairy Milk, Fruit & Nut, Flake).
title: The History Of Chocolate

description:
In the third century BC, a clash which had been brewing for centuries finally erupted: Rome, the ruthless imperialist upstart dominating Italy, against Carthage, the ancient but sinister apex predator of the Mediterranean. The conflict sparked in Messina in 263 BC, and went on for over two decades, as the fortunes of both powers rose and fell. Rome’s superior, land-based army proved the perfect match to the Carthaginians’ maritime might, though both forces rapidly adapted to the expertise of their foe. By 250 BC, Carthage was embattled and flailing, and in need of a hero, to restore the fate of Carthage, and ensure her survival…
Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the outbreak of the First Punic War, in which history’s greatest rivalry, Rome vs Carthage, finally came to blows. As the established power of Carthage was challenged by the rise of a new contender in Rome, but could either live in a world where the other survived?

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate the course of the First Punic War and its brutal aftermath. Using Polybius and later classical sources, they trace the conflict’s origins in Sicily — Messina and the seizure by Campanian mercenaries — through major engagements at Akragas and the sea victory at Mylae, to Rome’s risky invention of the corvus and decisive naval campaigns culminating in the Roman invasion of Africa. They describe Roman political dynamics, Claudian actions, and catastrophic Roman losses to storms. After Rome forces Carthage from Sicily, the podcast moves to the vicious mercenary rebellion against Carthage, recounting atrocities on both sides, Hamilcar Barca’s guerrilla resistance, his eventual victories, and the crushing of the mercenaries at the Defile of the Saur. The episode closes with Hamilcar’s expedition to Spain and the oath of his young son Hannibal Barca, setting up the narrative for Hannibal’s later campaigns against Rome.
title: Carthage vs. Rome: Total War (Part 4)

description:
“Every man is the architect of his own destiny”
Long before Rome reigned over the Mediterranean, there was Carthage: the supreme predator of Antiquity. But how did Rome rise to become one of the most ruthless powers of all time, united in cold, disciplined violence? And what was it about the Roman people that made them the greatest threat Carthage would ever face? Whilst the Carthaginians depended upon foreign mercenaries, Rome’s legions were formed of Romans, all committed to protecting and furthering the interests of Rome. And unlike anyone before, the Roman people shared a collective sense of destiny, with Roman citizenship generously offered to all conquered peoples. But following the Sack of Rome by Gauls in 390 BC, the Romans would become even more ruthless, disciplined and bent on total victory…
Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the rise of Rome, history’s most famous superpower. By 285 BC her dominion of Italy was almost complete. Only one thing stood in her way: the formidable military leader Pyrrhus. He alone foresaw the destruction to come, and the “beautiful killing ground” that would emerge when, ten years later, Rome and Carthage would finally go to war…

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine early Roman–Carthaginian relations, starting with a Bronze-age treaty recorded by Polybius (dated 509 BC) that constrained Roman and Carthaginian naval and commercial activity. They discuss Rome's transition from monarchy to republic, Roman institutions like consuls, and the civic values (honor, virtus, and shared citizenship) that shaped Roman military conduct. The hosts contrast Rome’s manpower-based, integrative model with Carthage’s mercenary, trade-focused system. Key turning points covered include the Sack of Rome by the Gauls (390 BC), the Latin revolt (340s BC), the prolonged wars with the Samnites (including the Caudine Forks), and Rome’s consolidation of the Italian peninsula. They conclude with Rome’s clash with Pyrrhus of Epirus (the Pyrrhic War, 280–275 BC), his use of elephants, and his eventual withdrawal — setting the stage for the coming Roman–Carthaginian wars. The episode weaves military, social, and diplomatic developments to explain Rome’s rise toward rivalry with Carthage.
title: Carthage vs. Rome: The Wolf at the Gates (Part 3)

description:
“An aristocratic republic, secret and well-ordered, where individuals are subject to the harsh laws of the austere and disciplined rich…”
The mysterious, wealthy and glamorous city of Carthage flourished between the ninth and second centuries BC, becoming one of the greatest naval and mercantile powers in the world. By the sixth century BC the Carthaginians were a force to be reckoned with, holding off assaults from various Greek rivals, and starting to colonise larger parts of the Mediterranean. Where once there had been a barren wasteland, now stood glittering villas and temples, bustling marketplaces, and vast walls stretching down to the sea. Yet Carthage also had a reputation for violence and cruelty. Bloody human offerings were made to the gods, with hundreds of Carthaginian children cast into the flames, whilst crucifixion was often inflicted on generals who fell short of Carthage’s exacting standards…
Join Tom and Dominic as they explore the extraordinary rise of Carthage, a city of blazing innovation and sinister mystique. By the third century BC it seemed that no power could ever rival it. But little did the Carthaginians know that another city, a minnow from an Italian backwater, was on the rise. A city that may even one day challenge her supremacy: Rome.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-part series on Carthage, surveying the city's origins, growth and geopolitical role in the western Mediterranean. They discuss primary ancient sources — especially Polybius and Herodotus — and the Roman and Greek framing that gives Carthage a dark, exotic reputation. The episode covers Carthage's Phoenician roots, its advantageous site near modern Tunis, rapid urban and commercial expansion, agricultural expertise attributed to Mago, and maritime empire-building through trading posts across Sardinia, Sicily and Spain. The hosts trace Carthage's rivalries with Greek city-states (notably Syracuse and Gelon), key engagements such as the Battle of Himera (480 BC), and episodic leaders and dynasties including the Magonids, Hamilcar, Hanno and Himilco. They explore Carthaginian institutions — suffets, a senate-like council and the Tribunal of 104 — and compare Carthage’s mercantile, naval-focused empire to later maritime powers. The episode ends by setting up the forthcoming confrontation with Rome, and mentions additional club-only episodes available to Rest Is History Club members.
title: Ancient Carthage: Rise of a Superpower (Part 2)

description:
“Carthago delenda est.”
Carthage must be destroyed: this was the rallying cry of Cato the Elder, the senator endlessly pushing for war against Rome’s sworn enemy, Carthage. But what are the origins of this supposedly decadent and sinister city, and did the Carthaginians really sacrifice their children? Starting as a crafty, seafaring people called the Phoenicians, a mighty mercantile civilisation emerged, who would eventually come to be know as the Carthaginians. But who were the Phoenicians, and why are they so mysterious? From the Bible, the Iliad and the Odyssey, to Herodotus’ account of the Persian Wars, and the conquests of Alexander the Great, their shadow haunts Antiquity…
Join Tom and Dominic as they investigate the Phoenicians, the first masters of the Mediterranean. Pioneers of seafaring, craftsmanship and writing, these were the people who gave birth to Rome’s most feared enemy, Carthage. Myths, legends, child-sacrifice, and the rise and fall of civilisations abound.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the origins and reputation of Carthage by tracing its roots to the Phoenician city of Tyre. Beginning with Gustave Flaubert's lurid depiction of child sacrifice in Salombeau, they unpack how Greek and Roman authors, the Bible, and later writers shaped Carthage’s exotic and brutal image. The hosts examine archaeological and textual evidence: Phoenician maritime prowess, the production of Tyrian purple, the spread of a Phoenician-derived alphabet, and the establishment of colonies including Carthage (traditional 814 BC). They review modern scholarly debates—Josephine Quinn’s skepticism about a unified “Phoenician” identity and Carolina Lopez-Ries’s defense of a shared culture—and consider the Tophet burials and inscriptions that suggest child offerings at Carthaginian sanctuaries. The episode ends by setting the next installment’s task: to view Carthage from Carthaginian perspectives and continue the series toward its great rivalry with Rome.

description:
The horrific Guildford Pub Bombings of Saturday 5th October 1974 sent shockwaves through Britain, worsening the sense of crisis sweeping through the nation. It cast a dark shadow over the election campaign due to take place five days later. The future had rarely seemed grimmer, with a general sense of moral and economic panic, weariness and depression. For the fourth time, Labour’s Harold Wilson and the Conservative’s Edward Heath faced off, with Wilson able to scrape a three-seat majority. But could Wilson really revive the nation? Or would it be up to the new figure emerging from the Conservative Party, a certain Margaret Thatcher…
Join Dominic and Tom for the conclusion to their series on one of the maddest years in British history, 1974. With dysfunctional governments, dark conspiracies, economic meltdown and ongoing terrorist attacks, can Britain survive the year?

summary: This episode is the concluding part of a four-part Rest Is History series on the year 1974 in Britain. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook open with the Guildford pub bombing (5 October 1974), describing victims and the later wrongful convictions associated with the case, and place it in the context of Northern Ireland violence seeping into Britain. They review the October 1974 general election, Harold Wilson's narrow victory and chaotic team dynamics (Marcia Williams, Bernard Donoghue), Tony Benn's policy role, and Edward Heath's faltering Tory campaign and personal misfortunes. The hosts discuss Jeremy Thorpe's ill-fated hovercraft tour and the Birmingham pub bombings and the subsequent Prevention of Terrorism Act and miscarriages of justice (the Birmingham Six). They assess economic deterioration, mass emigration, and the political consequences that opened space for figures such as Margaret Thatcher and Keith Joseph. The episode closes by tracing the immediate political aftermath, the trajectory toward the 1976 IMF crisis, and the longer-term choices facing Britain in the late 1970s.
title: Britain in 1974: Thatcher Enters the Ring (Part 4)

description:
Following a tumultuous election in February 1974, Labour’s Harold Wilson has been re-elected Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. Wilson, an unpretentious, kind man, has inherited a nation in crisis: train strikes in Norfolk, students fighting in Oxford, inflation, an ongoing oil crisis, a terrible cost of living crisis, striking miners, and weekly IRA terrorist attacks. He’s further hindered by his divided minority government, and the dysfunctional environment in Downing Street, in part due to his strange relationship with his private secretary and “political wife”, the frenzied Marcia Williams. What’s more, Wilson is suspected of being a KGB agent by the security services, and increasingly succumbs to paranoia. Is a right wing coup brewing, to put an end to industrial action? Will Wilson really be the man to drag Britain out of these trying circumstances? 
Join Dominic and Tom as they discuss the first Wilson government of 1974, featuring imploding economies, psycho-sexual dramas, communist conspiracies, madness-inspired nudity, baying unions, and attempted murder…

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the chaotic opening months of Harold Wilson's first 1974 government. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the political and social landscape: a fragile minority administration, rampant inflation amplified by the 1973 oil shock, a recent miners' strike and the ending of the three-day week, and lavish pay settlements that fuelled rising prices. The hosts trace the soap-opera dynamics inside Number 10 — especially Wilson's fraught relationship with his private secretary Marcia Williams and the role of aides such as Bernard Donahue and Joe Haynes — and reveal extreme reactions within the establishment, including talk of right-wing vigilante groups and even suggestions of murder. They explore wider national anxieties — press speculation about Wilson’s alleged communist links, MI5 interest, fears of a coup, and the Ulster Workers' Council strike that brought down the power-sharing executive — closing on Wilson's decision to call another general election to secure a decisive mandate.
title: Britain in 1974: Countdown to a Coup (Part 3)

description:
Three days after one of the most devastating IRA attacks launched upon British soil, the Conservative Prime Minister Edward Heath called an election, in circumstances that had never been more dire. Running against him was the veteran Labour leader, Harold Wilson, now as tired and beleaguered as his rival, and whose party was increasingly divided by internal conflict. Jeremy Thorpe, the charming but reckless leader of the liberal party had also thrown his hat into the ring. As the election drew closer, the parties were neck and neck, and with the sense of national hysteria and economic chaos rising, escalated by a baying press and the likes of Enoch Powell, the stakes had never been higher. Could the longstanding Labour and Conservative duopoly finally be broken? 
Join Dominic and Tom for the second part of their series on 1974, one of the most disastrous years in British history, as they discuss the terrible circumstances surrounding the seismic February election, and its momentous outcome.

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, examines Britain in early 1974, focusing on the M62 coach bombing and the broader Provisional IRA bombing campaign that brought Northern Irish violence to the British mainland. Sandbrook situates the violence within the gloomy domestic context: high inflation, banking and property crises, the Three-Day Week and industrial strife. The discussion turns to the February 1974 general election, contrasting Edward Heath's beleaguered Conservative leadership and campaign strategy with a fatigued Harold Wilson and a Labour manifesto heavily influenced by its left wing (notably Tony Benn). The unexpected surge of the Liberal Party under Jeremy Thorpe (around 19% of the vote) breaks the traditional two-party mould, producing a hung result—Conservatives slightly ahead in vote share but Labour ahead in seats—leading to days of uncertainty and aborted coalition talks. The episode previews further episodes and a club-only extra about the eccentricities of Downing Street during the transfer of power.

description:
“Who governs Britain?”
Britain in the early 1970’s was a state in crisis, and by 1974, things had never seemed bleaker. Held hostage by the Trade Unions, British industry was flailing. England’s sporting record was atrocious, the economy was tanking and the prospect of a miners’ strike loomed large. Violence was surging in Northern Ireland, as the IRA escalated its bombing campaigns, and the outbreak of the Yom Kippur War would send oil prices soaring, with the miners on the verge on plunging Britain into darkness. By the end of the year, the British people had voted in two general elections, had a three-day week enforced on them, and the Conservative party were on the cusp of electing their first female leader…
Join Dominic and Tom for the first episode of their four-part epic on 1974, undoubtedly one of the darkest and most dramatic years in British political history…

summary: This episode examines Britain in 1973–74 under Prime Minister Edward "Ted" Heath, exploring how economic distress, industrial conflict and international shocks combined to produce a political crisis. Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss Heath’s technocratic style, his drive to modernise (including entry into the European Common Market and county reorganisation), and his fraught relations with trade unions — notably the National Union of Mineworkers. They trace the escalation from incomes policies and the Barber boom to the miners’ overtime bans, and show how the Yom Kippur War and the 1973 oil shock turbocharged inflation, empowering the miners. The government’s emergency measures culminated in the Three-Day Week and severe social unease, punctuated by IRA bombings and the attempted kidnapping of Princess Anne. Sandbrook references his books State of Emergency and Seasons in the Sun. The episode ends as Heath calls a February 1974 election, setting up the next instalment to cover the poll and its consequences.
title: Britain in 1974: State of Emergency (Part 1)

description:
Geoffrey Chaucer stands as a founding father of English literature, and ‘The Canterbury Tales’ is an enthralling account of his age, holding a mirror up to the traditional hierarchies of 14th century England. Chaucer’s own life was spent navigating the rapids of a particularly tumultuous period, from fighting in the Hundred Years’ War alongside Edward III, to working for the infamous John of Gaunt, becoming embroiled in London politics, and surviving the gruesome Black Death. Chaucer even lived through the explosive Peasants’ Revolt, during which his own life hung in the balance…

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the turbulent life and seminal work of Geoffrey Chaucer, a titan of English history and trailblazer of social change.

summary: This episode examines Geoffrey Chaucer and The Canterbury Tales as both a literary masterpiece and a vivid window onto late 14th-century England. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Chaucer’s biography—his London mercantile background, survival of the Black Death, service at court, continental travel, capture and ransom in 1360, and patronage connections to John of Gaunt. They explain how The Canterbury Tales uses the pilgrimage framing device to present a panoramic, socially mixed cast (knight, miller, Wife of Bath, parson, ploughman) and how Chaucer’s mixture of humour, moral complexity and vernacular English reflects social upheavals: endemic plague, the Peasants’ Revolt, and changing labour relations after the Statute of Labourers. The hosts highlight standout tales and figures (the Pardoner, the Wife of Bath) and mention modern scholarship and translations, including Neville Coghill and a biography by Marian/Marion Turner. They argue Chaucer’s work helped legitimize English literary culture and capture the newfangled social mobility of the age.
title: The Canterbury Tales (Ep 4)

description:
“For within the hollow crown that rounds the hollow temple of a king…”
Richard II, son of the dashing Black Prince and grandson of Edward III, became King of England at only ten years old. By the age of fifteen he had overcome one of the most terrifying threats to the English Crown up to that point: the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381. In the ensuing years, Richard’s rule became increasingly autocratic. This, coupled with the threat of foreign invasion and his dangerous proclivity for favourites, increasingly alienated Richard’s subjects, with rebel lords eventually taking up arms against the king. As the storm-clouds of civil war loomed large, King Richard II clung to his hollow crown….

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the events that resulted in Richard’s deposition and mysterious death, and what his reign tells us the English monarchy in the 15th century.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate the rise and fall of Richard II, tracing how his personality, favourites and political choices—set against the backdrop of the Hundred Years' War and the Peasants' Revolt—led to his deposition in 1399. They examine Richard's spectacular court, reliance on non-noble favourites (Michael de la Pole, Robert de Vere, Sir Simon Burley), clashes with magnates and parliaments (the Wonderful Parliament and the Merciless Parliament), and the role of the Lords Appellant. The episode follows Richard's temporary recovery, his punitive actions in 1397, and how the exile and return of Henry Bolingbroke (later Henry IV) capitalized on Richard's weaknesses and John of Gaunt's death. The narrative ends with Richard's surrender, deposition, Henry's coronation, and Richard's subsequent death, linking these events to long-term instability culminating in later civil wars. The hosts read Shakespeare's famous passage from Richard II and preview the series' concluding club episode on Chaucer and The Canterbury Tales.
title: The Murder of Richard II (Ep 3)

description:
On the 13th of June 1381, the rebel army of English peasants, led by Wat Tyler, entered London and brought chaos, death and destruction upon some of the city’s most important buildings and figures, among them the Archbishop of Canterbury and his home at Lambeth Palace. Within the Tower of London, the 14 year-old Richard II and his government still cowered, with the rebels demanding that Richard’s treacherous advisors be handed over. Desperate, the charismatic young King was convinced by his advisors to ride out and meet the rebels. A meeting ensued, upon which the whole course of English history depended, as the radicals demanded terms that would mean the abolition of serfdom, and the transformation of the English social order forever. 

Join Tom and Dominic as they describe the gory and unprecedented events of the Peasants' Revolt, and discuss the stories of mob violence, murder and vandalism…

summary: This episode examines the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, focusing on the dramatic events around Blackheath, Mile End, London and the Tower of London. Tom and Dominic describe the rebels’ grievances—especially against poll taxes, feudal exactions and monopolies—and profiles key actors such as Wat Tyler, John Ball and John of Gaunt. They recount the rebels’ entry into London, the sacking of Savoy Palace and other targeted attacks on records and hated officials, and the storming of the Tower where leading ministers (including Simon Sudbury and Robert Hales) were executed. The hosts narrate Richard II’s risky negotiations with the rebels at Mile End and Smithfield, Wat Tyler’s killing and beheading, and the subsequent surrounding and dispersal of rebel forces. The episode assesses the revolt’s suppression, the mixed legacy (including the end of poll taxes and the revolt’s ambiguous political meanings), and the formative effect these events had on the young Richard II. They close by previewing further episodes on Richard’s deposition and Geoffrey Chaucer.
title: The Peasants’ Revolt: London’s Burning (Ep 2)

description:
By the late 14th century, England was in decline. Already weakened by the Hundred Years’ War, both Edward III and his son, the Black Prince, had died, leaving the country in a perilous state. Richard II, the new king, was only a child. With the poor facing increasingly harsh poll taxes, and distrust of the nobility growing among them, an uprising broke out in southern England in 1381. It was led for the first time by peasants, a class of person invisible on the historical stage up to this point. The Peasants’ Revolt would prove to be one of the most iconic events of English history, altering not only England’s society and the fate of her monarchy, but also generating a new kind of grassroots radicalism. 

Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss the outbreak of this landmark moment in the history of English socialism, building up to the climactic moment when Richard II and his men find themselves besieged in London by the rebel army surrounding her walls, under the leadership of the elusive Wat Tyler…


*The Rest Is History LIVE in 2024*

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the causes and early outbreak of the 1381 Peasants' Revolt. Placing the uprising in the wider context of the waning fortunes of Edward III's England and the ongoing Hundred Years' War, they explain how repeated poll taxes, military failures, and resentment toward conspicuous elite wealth (notably John of Gaunt and his Savoy Palace) provoked popular anger. The hosts emphasize structural pressures from the Black Death and the Statute of Labourers, which created upwardly mobile rural communities in East Anglia and Kent. They detail the coordinated beginning of unrest in Essex and Kent, targeted attacks on tax collectors and legal record repositories, and the role of radical preachers such as John Ball alongside the charismatic leader Wat Tyler. The episode ends with the rebels massing outside London and a cliffhanger promising the outcome in a following episode — with a paywalled continuation for Rest Is History Club members.
title: The Peasants’ Revolt: England Erupts (Ep 1)

description:
Extolling his love for democracy, the Senator took on autocratic powers, during a time of emergency, to save the Republic. The Republic was then abolished, and in its place rose an Empire… This is not the story of Julius Caesar or Augustus, but of ‘Star Wars’, the blockbuster movie series telling the story of a struggle between good and evil, a battle for the revival of the old Republic. 
But is the world of ‘Star Wars’ really inspired by Roman history? How does ‘Dune’ reflect the birth and growth of Islam? Why does ‘The Hunger Games’ use Roman iconography and names? Does Isaac Asimov’s ‘Foundation’ reflect the fall of the Roman Empire?
Join Tom and Dominic in today’s episode, as they look at how the Roman myth has seeped into popular culture, inspiring quests, stories and entire worlds, from ‘Star Wars’ to ‘Dune’, ‘Star Trek’, ‘The Hunger Games’, and many more sci-fi bestsellers.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the surprising ways Star Wars and other science-fiction/fantasy works draw on Roman imagery and wider historical themes. They trace George Lucas’s cultural influences — from contemporary 1970s anxieties (Vietnam, Watergate, Nixon) and Joseph Campbell’s mythic templates to classical visual cues (togas, senates, Roman-style iconography). The conversation highlights echoes linking Palpatine to imperial Rome/Augustus, the Senate’s decline, and the Nazi and Cold War resonances encoded in the films. They discuss tie-in literature (the Alan Dean Foster Star Wars novelization), and show how Isaac Asimov’s Foundation (explicitly modelled on Gibbon) and Frank Herbert’s Dune rework Roman and late-antique motifs — including analogies to the rise of Islam and the role of resource politics. The hosts broaden the theme to gladiatorial spectacle in Star Trek and The Hunger Games, consider why Rome rather than Greece dominates the Western political imagination, and note scholarship by Michael Charles and Martin Winkler. The episode closes with a preview of the next show on Richard II and the Peasants’ Revolt.
title: Romans in Space: Star Wars, Dune and Beyond...

description:
In the late 17th century, during the glorious reign of Louis XIV, the Sun King, France was at its apogee, with royal absolutism at its zenith. But, beneath the gold and glamour of Louis’ reign, there lay a terrifying darkness: a prison system into which people could be disappeared without a trace. And at the very heart of this darkness there lurked an excruciating secret…a prisoner, his terrible crime unknown, moved from prison to prison, forbidden to speak, and whose face was encased at all times in a mask of steel. Who was he, if he even existed at all? An English spy? Louis’ long-lost father, driven into obscurity? Or, even more threateningly, his twin brother? 


Join Tom and Dominic as they explore one of the greatest mysteries of all time: the Man in the Iron Mask. Following in the footsteps of Voltaire and Alexandre Dumas, they definitively solve the case and reveal, once and for all, the identity of this enigmatic figure…

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the long-running mystery of the Man in the Iron Mask. They review contemporaneous evidence: a 1687 Gazette report of a masked prisoner brought to Île Sainte-Marguerite by the jailer Saint-Mars, Bastille register entries noting a masked, unnamed inmate arriving in 1698 and dying in 1703, and later descriptions (notably by Voltaire) that popularised the iron-mask image. The hosts lay out historical context under Louis XIV and the lettre de cachet system, then survey major identity theories — a secret royal brother or twin (Voltaire/Dumas), a father-substitute story proposed in the 20th century, various foreign candidates, the Italian Count Mattioli, and finally documentary-backed scholarship identifying the documented prisoner named in original orders (transcribed in the episode as Eustache de Gea / Doget). They argue the best-supported conclusion is that the masked man was a lower-status valet kept under extreme secrecy, while sensational royal theories stem largely from later exaggeration. The mystery endures due to deliberate secrecy and embellished retellings.
title: The Man in the Iron Mask

description:
By November 1938 the scene in Germany was at its darkest yet, as the full scale of Hitler’s intentions for the Jewish population of the German Reich was becoming evermore apparent. As the threat of another world war increased, so the Nazi anti-semitism machine went up a gear. Synagogues were destroyed, Jewish businessmen, bureaucrats, lawyers and doctors disbarred, plans were made for a mass expulsion of Jews from Europe. But the worst was yet to come, as the assassination of a German official in Paris in late 1938 instigated the most savage wave of Jewish persecution in Germany so far…

Join Dominic and Tom as they discuss the build up to Krystallnacht - the Night of Broken Glass - and the diabolical destruction, brutality and violence that ensued. By the end of 1938, Hitler’s two dearest ambitions, an apocalyptic victory over the Jewish people and the conquest of Europe itself, seemed terrifyingly within reach.

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook chart the escalation of Nazi anti‑Semitism from the relative calm after the 1936 Berlin Olympics to the violence of Kristallnacht in November 1938. They trace how Nazi racial policy, driven by Hitler and implemented by figures such as Goebbels, Himmler and the SS, moved from legal and economic exclusion (professional bans, Aryanisation of businesses, J-stamped passports) toward organised violence. The hosts discuss symbolic acts — demolition of major synagogues, public renaming — and the complicity of German society and major firms. They recount the assassination of Ernst von Rath in Paris by Herschel Grinchman (as given in the transcript) and how the regime used that incident to stage a nationwide pogrom, arresting tens of thousands and imposing punitive fines. The episode links Kristallnacht to subsequent bureaucratic measures (a central office for Jewish emigration under Heydrich) and situates these developments in the wider context of Nazi preparations for war and the path to industrialised genocide.
title: The Nazis in Power: The Night of Broken Glass (Ep 7)

description:
As Hitler ramps up the German war machine, he remains obsessed with one idea: uprooting Jews from the Reich. The Nazis embark on a campaign of totalitarian oppression against them, persecuting Jewish people in every aspect of life. They are excluded from most professions, forbidden from intermarrying, Jewish children are bullied and excluded from schools, all Jews have a “J” stamped in their passport, to name but a few measures. Worst of all, the brainwashing of the German people has become apparent, and many are willing participants in the various forms of persecution; plenty of German towns have put up signs by this point saying “Jews not wanted here”. Hitler may tone down the oppression to whitewash the 1936 Berlin Olympics, but this does not last. One terrifying truth is clear: he is fully set on the destruction of European Jewry.

Join Tom and Dominic in the fifth part of our series on the Nazis in power, as they look at how the persecution of Jewish people in the Reich increased in the lead-up to the Second World War.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the escalation of Nazi anti-Semitism from early rhetorical extremism to formal legal persecution in the 1930s. They open with a 1922 quotation from Adolf Hitler and show how violent street actions, local boycotts and SA intimidation in 1933–35 progressively isolated Jewish Germans. The hosts discuss early discriminatory laws such as the April 1933 civil service purges, local and national boycotts (notably 1 April 1933), and the conceptual difficulty Nazis faced defining who was Jewish. They explain the tactical oscillation between unleashing activists and then regularizing repression, culminating in the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 (citizenship and racial protection statutes) and the SS/Gestapo’s intrusion into private life. They note limited emigration patterns, the temporary public easing around the 1936 Olympics, and how social complicity and institutional enforcement made persecution increasingly normalised—setting the scene for the later violence of Kristallnacht.
title: The Nazis in Power: The War on the Jews (Ep 6)

description:
“We must have a healthy people to dominate in the world”.
In July 1933, Hitler’s Nazi party passed a new law for the compulsory sterilisation of anyone with a physical disability, or “congenital feeble-mindedness”. They claimed this was scientifically sound, and for the moral and biological good of the Aryan race. The measure darkly foreshadowed the tragedies to come, as Nazi Germany ratcheted up its horrific program of racial sterilisation, euthanasia and extermination. But why did the Nazis see their horrific crimes as beneficial to the fatherland, and consider themselves on the right side of History? What motivated Hitler, the figurehead behind these terrifying ideologies, to act on them? And how many of these ideas, propagated by Hitler and his generals, were shared and accepted by the German people?

Join Tom and Dominic as they delve into the roots of the Nazis’ pseudo-science: from the glorification of ancient Greece, Rome, and the “Nordic” race, to the intellectual ideals of the 19th century, in which Darwinism and the survival of the fittest flourished. They attempt to unravel one of the darkest ideologies in all world history, and their uniquely hideous brand of anti-semitism.

summary: This episode examines Nazi morality and ideology: how Nazism construed race, history and biology into an internally coherent ethical system that justified persecution and violence. Holland and Sandbrook discuss Hitler's early speeches and reading habits, Himmler's legal-racial vision, and the Nazis' appropriation of classical Greece and Rome as racial precedent. They trace intellectual roots in late 19th-century racial science and social Darwinism, and show how propaganda and institutions disseminated these ideas through schools, youth organisations, physicians and civil servants. The hosts analyse concrete policies: the 1933 sterilisation law and the escalation to involuntary euthanasia in 1939, and they preview forthcoming episodes on Nazi antisemitic policies. Throughout, the discussion emphasises the chilling normalisation of policies presented as scientific and moral for the 'health of the race', and how ordinary professional and civic actors became implicated in persecution.
title: The Nazis in Power: Hitler's Dream (Ep 5)

summary: This episode examines the Anschluss — the German annexation of Austria in 1938 — tracing the political manoeuvres, key personalities and immediate consequences. Holland and Sandbrook open with cultural touchpoints (The Sound of Music) before reviewing Hitler’s strategic aims laid out to his generals in late 1937, and the purge of senior army figures that left him unopposed. They chart the tensions in Austria under Engelbert Dolfuss and Kurt von Schuschnig, Franz von Papen’s ambassadorship in Vienna, and Hitler’s diplomatic pressure, culminating in the Berchtesgaden meeting and a German ultimatum. The Wehrmacht enters; mass public enthusiasm and manufactured plebiscites follow, but the hosts stress the rapid repression that accompanied annexation — mass arrests, plunder of Austrian assets and brutal persecution of Jews in Vienna. The episode closes by showing how Anschluss emboldened Hitler toward further expansion (Czechoslovakia) and how early Nazi policies in Austria prefigured later, more catastrophic, developments across Europe.
title: The Nazis in Power: The Conquest of Austria (Ep 4)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Adolf Hitler’s ideology and the calculated gambles that transformed Germany’s international position between 1933 and 1936. They open with a passage from Mein Kampf to show how struggle and war were central to Hitler’s thinking, then trace his domestic and foreign-policy moves: walking out of League disarmament talks, courting the army and elites, signing a Polish non-aggression pact (1934), reintroducing conscription (1935), securing naval concessions from Britain, the Saar plebiscite (1935), and finally remilitarizing the Rhineland (1936). They discuss economic drivers—Adam Tooze’s argument that rearmament was tied to predatory economic aims—and the social response in Germany as foreign-policy triumphs outweighed shortages at home. The hosts assess Allied weakness, intelligence failures, and the tactical performance of Nazi propaganda and spectacle, and they outline how 1936 consolidated Hitler’s sense of providence and set the stage for further expansion (Spain, Axis diplomacy and the planned Anschluss), material the next episode will continue.
title: The Nazis in Power: Hitler’s Road to War (Ep 3)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, examines the Nazis' use of mass spectacle, propaganda and social policy to forge public consent in the 1930s. Focusing on the Nuremberg Rally of 1934 and its theatrical staging, the hosts describe how Hitler and Goebbels combined atavistic imagery with modern technology, including film and radio, to create ritualized mass politics. They discuss Leni Riefenstahl's films (Triumph of the Will and Olympia) and the regime's control of cinema and broadcasting, plus the spread of Nazi symbolism and rituals across Germany. The episode then moves into domestic policy: the gendered role the regime enforced for women, natalist incentives, restrictions on education and professional life for girls, and the militarized youth organizations. It closes by linking cultural manipulation and spectacle to broader foreign-policy developments and previews forthcoming episodes on Hitler's war plans and the Anschluss.
title: The Nazis in Power: The Nuremberg Rallies (Ep 2)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) examines the Night of the Long Knives (late June–early July 1934) and situates it within the Nazis' consolidation of power. After a brief recap of Nazism's roots, the hosts describe intra-party tensions between Ernst Röhm's SA (Stormtroopers) and Germany's conservative elites and army. Hitler, anxious to secure the army and curb SA lawlessness, coordinates with rivals such as Göring, Himmler and the SS and uses fabricated evidence of a Röhm coup to justify a purge. The episode narrates Hitler's confrontations in spa towns, the arrest and murder of SA leaders and other opponents (including Kurt von Schleicher), the post-facto legal cover via a cabinet law, and the subsequent binding of the army to Hitler through an oath and a plebiscite after Hindenburg's death. The hosts reflect on winners (SS, army acquiescence), public reaction, and the event's role in transforming the regime into a Führer-state, previewing later episodes on propaganda, Nuremberg and Kristallnacht.
title: The Nazis in Power: The Night of the Long Knives (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the legend of Pope Joan — a purported female pope said to have reigned disguised as a man and to have died in childbirth. They trace the story’s earliest attestations (Jean de Mailly and Martin of Poland), its adoption into lists of popes, and later scholarly demolition by David Blondel and the papal repudiation under Clement VIII. The hosts survey possible origins and analogues: the pornocratic period in Rome and powerful women like Marozia, the scandalous pontificate of John XII, and institutional changes from the Gregorian Reform that created a pan-European College of Cardinals. They discuss rituals (twin curule chairs with holes) later associated with verifying a pope’s sex, and explore medieval anxieties about gender and clerical masculinity shaped by Aristotelian and Christian thought. The episode also covers the Guglielma/Mare Frada episode in Milan, Joachimite expectations of a new age of the Spirit, and concludes with reflections on why the Catholic Church excludes women from priesthood and papacy today.
title: The Mystery of the Pregnant Pope

summary: On this Christmas-morning episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook investigate the claim that Christmas is fundamentally a pagan festival stolen from rival cults. They examine Dan Brown's fictional Lee Teabing’s assertions — that Mithras, Osiris, Adonis, Dionysus and Krishna share December 25 birthdays and Christian motifs — and find little ancient evidence for most of those parallels. The hosts distinguish Mithras from Sol Invictus, discuss the Calendar of 354 entry noting a natalis invicti on December 25, and overview Emperor Aurelian’s promotion of sun-cult festivals. They then explore Saturnalia (17–23 December) — its customs, social inversion, gift-giving and possible echoes in later medieval customs — and argue that many alleged direct links between Saturnalia and Christmas derive from nineteenth-century scholarship or convergent evolution. Finally they explain the Christian reasoning for dating the incarnation to March 25 (leading to December 25 nine months later) and close with a Roman-era hymn by Saint Ambrose.
title: Christmas: Pagan or Christian?

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Trevor Phillips about the arrival and legacy of the Empire Windrush (1948). Phillips — drawing on his original 1998 Windrush project and a later updated book with his brother Mike — frames Windrush as a powerful but not exclusive origin story for postwar Caribbean migration to Britain. Discussion covers who the Windrush passengers were (many wartime veterans and young adventurers), official British attitudes in 1948, the transition from temporary migration to permanent settlement driven by family formation in the 1950s–60s, and the lived experience of the first British-born Caribbean generation. They also address cultural touchstones (the West Indies cricket tour of 1950), later demographic shifts (migration from Africa and a growing mixed‑race population), and the modern Windrush scandal. Phillips argues for treating these communities as subjects with their own histories rather than symbols in others’ narratives.
title: Windrush: The Story of Black Britain

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook speak with novelist Zadie Smith about the Victorian Titchborne case and her novel The Fraud, which revisits the extraordinary trial of a man claiming to be Sir Roger Titchborne. Smith summarises the saga: a presumed-drowned heir, a large claimant (Arthur Orton), a devoted Jamaican servant-witness (Andrew Bogle), and an eccentric legal defence led by Edward Kenealy. The conversation traces the family curse, the overseas search for the missing heir, the claimant’s return and dramatic courtroom scenes that blurred law and theatre. They discuss how the case galvanised working-class populism, spawned fundraising and associations, exposed legal dysfunction (huge numbers of witnesses, protracted summings-up), and eventually collapsed on small evidential points (tattoo testimony), leading to conviction and imprisonment. Smith explains her fidelity to historical sources, the book’s Victorian-novel influences, and how the episode illuminates race, class, media-driven spectacle and legal reform in 19th-century Britain.
title: Victorian Britain's Maddest Mystery

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the Allied invasion of Italy in 1943 and the early consequences through the end of that year. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by guest James Holland, author of The Savage Storm: The Battle for Italy, 1943, who explains the strategic context—decisions taken at Casablanca and Trident, prioritisation of Overlord and the resulting shortages of landing craft and materiel. They discuss the fall of Benito Mussolini, the Italian armistice of 3 September 1943, and the successive amphibious operations (Baytown and Avalanche) including the hard fighting at Salerno. James Holland emphasizes the harsh conditions—mountainous terrain, ruined towns, scorched-earth measures around Naples, the seizure of Foggia airfields, and the looming catastrophe at Monte Cassino. The conversation weaves military detail with civilian experience, referencing diaries (including Norman Lewis's Naples '44 and the monk Dom Eusebio) and classical echoes such as Cannae and Alaric. The episode foregrounds the campaign's brutality, strategic trade-offs, and cultural damage to Italy's ancient monuments.
title: The Savage Storm: World War II and The Battle for Italy

description:
On the 27th of September 1964 the Warren Commission, established by President Lyndon B. Johnson a year earlier to investigate the assassination of President Kennedy, concluded that he had been killed by Lee Harvey Oswald, acting entirely alone. But who was Lee Harvey Oswald? And why, if at all, might he have wanted Kennedy dead?  

Born in Louisiana in 1939, Oswald was a bitter loner with communist inclinations and an overactive sense of his own destiny. During the course of his life before the arrest, Oswald joined the Marines, defected to and from Russia, and caught the attention of both the CIA and the KGB… 

Join Tom and Dominic for the grand finale of their investigation into the assassination of JFK, where they give their verdict on this murkiest of mysteries. And, by delving into the past, politics and personality of his alleged murderer, conclusively reveal whether Lee Harvey Oswald did in fact kill President Kennedy.


*Dominic’s book The Fall of the Aztecs is available now from bookshops across the UK - the perfect Christmas present!*

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook conclude a multi-part examination of the assassination of John F. Kennedy, arguing that the strongest explanation is that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone. The hosts build a psychological profile of Oswald from his troubled childhood, ideological drift to Marxism, service in the US Marines, time in the Soviet Union (including marriage to Marina Prusakova), and post‑return life in Dallas. They review concrete elements: Oswald's purchase of a mail‑order rifle, his employment at the Texas School Book Depository, witness reports of a shooter on the sixth floor, flight from the scene, the killing of officer J.D. Tippitt, inconsistent statements at interrogation, and reactions of family and wife. The episode contrasts Occam's razor with sprawling conspiracy theories (CIA, mafia, LBJ), places the killing in Cold War and 1960s cultural context, and reflects on the assassination's enduring role in American conspiratorial politics and popular culture.
title: JFK: The Mystery is Solved (Part 7)

description:
“We can’t accept very comfortably that two nobodies, two nothings - Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby - were able to change the course of world history.”

The murder of Lee Harvey Oswald, JFK’s apparent assassin, by the night club owner Jack Ruby on 24th November 1963 changed everything. Right from the start, rumours had circulated that Oswald had not been acting alone, building on the deep anxieties of American society in the 1950s and 1960s. Some blamed Communist states such as Cuba or the Soviet Union; others anti-Castro exiles, or the Ku Klux Klan. As the years passed, the CIA and FBI came under suspicion. Did Lyndon Johnson know more about the conspiracy than he pretended? Just what was Richard Nixon doing on that fateful day? And how did Frank Sinatra’s drummer fit in?

Join Tom and Dominic as they explore the background to the Kennedy conspiracy theories, from umbrella men to grassy knolls, discussing the wider context and investigating every last clue in their tireless search for the truth.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the history and persistence of conspiracy theories surrounding the assassination of John F. Kennedy. They review the immediate investigations (Dallas Police, FBI) and the creation and work of the Warren Commission, stressing its large documentary record and conclusion that Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone and Jack Ruby acted alone in killing Oswald. The discussion surveys early conspiracy literature and media — Mark Lane, Thomas Buchanan, Vincent Bugliosi and Oliver Stone’s film JFK — and how cultural shifts (Vietnam, Watergate) amplified distrust. Key theories are evaluated — Soviet or Cuban involvement, CIA/FBI/military-industrial complex, the Mafia, right-wing groups, Lyndon Johnson — with hosts weighing plausibility and practical objections (motive, capability, risk, forensic evidence like the Zapruder film and the grassy knoll). They note the House Select Committee’s later acoustic evidence (debated and disputed) and defer a final judgement to a concluding episode, encouraging listeners to join their community for early access.
title: JFK: A Conspiracy Unmasked (Part 6)

description:
“Jack, you son of a bitch, don’t do it!”

Just hours after President Kennedy’s assassination, in the full glare of the world’s media, the Dallas police are confident they have solved the case. They have found the murder weapon, and are poised to charge their chief suspect, a strange loner called Lee Harvey Oswald. But as they prepare to move him to the county jail, one local businessman has other ideas. As they are leading Oswald into the station garage, an eccentric nightclub owner Jack Ruby steps forward. And as he aims his pistol at Oswald’s chest, the course of American history is about to take another dizzying turn …

Join Dominic and Tom as they trace the footsteps of two erratic nobodies, Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby, in the days before Kennedy’s assassination, leading up to the critical moment on 24th November when the two men finally came face to face, changing both of their lives and the course of the investigation forever…

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (episode five of the hosts' multi-part survey of JFK) recounts the immediate aftermath of John F. Kennedy's assassination. Holland and Sandbrook narrate the Dallas police's rapid case against Lee Harvey Oswald, his movements on 22–23 November 1963, and evidence compiled by investigators. They discuss Oswald's demeanor in custody, family visits, and the discovery of a rifle photograph and mail-order paperwork. The hosts then describe Jack Ruby's emotional state, his motivations as he claimed them, and the chaotic transfer of Oswald that allowed Ruby to enter the basement and fatally shoot him in front of worldwide media. The episode covers Oswald's death at Parkland Hospital, Kennedy's funeral in Washington and burial at Arlington, and the smaller funerals of Oswald and policeman J. D. Tippett. The pair close by framing the outstanding questions about whether Oswald acted alone or as part of a conspiracy and promise further episodes to address the theories.
title: JFK: The Second Assassin Strikes (Part 5)

description:
It’s 12:31pm on Friday 22nd November 1963, and in Dallas, Texas, President John F. Kennedy lies slumped against his screaming wife, half of his head cradled in her hands and his blood spattered across her elegant pink suit and the seats of their car. 

Just moments earlier, three shots had rung out from the direction of the Texas Book Depository. Or had they? Who had fired the shots? A single gunman - or more? Just who was the oddly detached, vacant-looking man whom left the building minutes later? Why did he murder a Dallas policeman shortly after the shooting? Was he really Kennedy’s killer, or a red herring, planted by a wider conspiracy? And was he working for the Cubans, the Communists - or the CIA?

Join Tom and Dominic as they plunge into the extraordinary drama of 22 November 1963, from the national shock after the president’s assassination to the thrilling hunt to track down his assassin.
