summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-episode examination of the assassination of John Fitzgerald Kennedy on 22 November 1963. They recount the immediate aftermath: the chaotic arrival at Parkland Hospital, Jackie Kennedy’s anguish, the rapid police search of the Texas Book Depository and the discovery of cartridge casings and a rifle. The episode follows eyewitness reports and the separate killing of Dallas officer J. D. Tippett, the arrest of Lee Harvey Oswald, and the swift tracing of the Mannlicher–Carcano rifle to a Chicago mail-order purchase. The programme contrasts the human drama — Jackie, the Kennedys, and the shocked LBJ administration — with the speedy police response and early conspiratorial speculation from senior officials such as J. Edgar Hoover. They profile Jack Ruby’s background and behaviour, and note the role of media and Cold War context (including Oswald’s Soviet links) in shaping public reactions and later conspiracy theories. The episode closes by setting up the next instalments covering 23–24 November and the growing swirl of controversy.

description:
“It wouldn't be very difficult to kill the president of the United States, you just have to be in a high building with a high powered rifle, telescopic sight and there's nothing anyone could do about it….”

On the morning of Friday, 22nd November 1963, John F. Kennedy awoke with just hours to live. Ahead was a flight to Love Field, Dallas; then a motorcade into the heart of the city’s business district. But as the president and his glamorous wife, Jacqueline, settled back in their limousine for the journey towards destiny, they had no idea of the horror to come …

By 12:22pm the motorcade had reached Dealey Plaza in downtown Dallas, passing the nondescript Texas Book Depository and slowing for the unexpectedly large and enthusiastic crowds gathered to greet the President. At 12:25 bystanders spotted the figure of a man on the sixth floor of the Book Depository, staring strangely away from the motorcade. Then, at exactly 12.30 pm, the first shot rang out around the square….

Join Dominic and Tom as they break down the events of the day of the assassination of President Kennedy moment by moment, from the night before the murder to its traumatic aftermath, poring over the evidence in order to solve this supremely fascinating historical mystery.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook give a detailed, play-by-play account of President John F. Kennedy's trip to Texas and his assassination in Dallas on 22 November 1963. The episode reconstructs the motorcade route, the Texas School Book Depository, eyewitness accounts, the sequence of shots as captured in the Zapruder film, immediate reactions in the motorcade, and the rush to Parkland Memorial Hospital. summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey John F. Kennedy’s life, politics and foreign policy to explain possible motives behind his assassination. They profile Kennedy the man — his charm, health problems, private life and family background, notably his father Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. — and his political rise through the 1960 primaries and narrow election victory over Richard Nixon. The discussion covers Kennedy’s centrist domestic record, evolving stance on civil rights (including federal interventions and his June 1963 speech), and economic policy. Foreign-policy crises dominate: the Bay of Pigs, Operation Mongoose, the Vienna Summit, the erection of the Berlin Wall, and especially the Cuban Missile Crisis, where Kennedy’s deliberative approach averted nuclear escalation. Vietnam’s growing involvement and the 1963 South Vietnam coup are examined. They close by explaining Kennedy’s late‑November 1963 Texas tour plans and set up the next episode on the assassination day and competing theories about culpability.
title: JFK: Cuba, Camelot and the Cold War (Part 2)

description:
“There were a lot of people who wanted Kennedy dead, a lot of powerful people. There are secrets still being held and I never bought for a minute that Oswald operated alone.”

The assassination of President John F. Kennedy in Dallas on 22nd November 1963 is one of history’s most iconic stories, a moment of terrible innocence lost and a foundational myth for modern America. The tragedy of the murder, coupled with the mystery surrounding it and the glamour of Kennedy himself, have only heightened the enduring fascination with the event. But what really happened in the days before, during and after the assassination? Did Lee Harvey Oswald really act alone? Or was he just a tool for darker forces at play in American politics - or for an international conspiracy at the terrifying height of the Cold War?

Join Dominic and Tom as they launch their epic investigation into the life and death of JFK, beginning with the controversial Kennedy clan, the young ‘Jack’s’ upbringing and the personality of the victim himself. Along the way they discuss his battle with crippling illness, his sexual escapades and his romance with the woman who became his wife, Jacqueline Bouvier.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook open a multi-episode series examining John F. Kennedy by focusing on his origins, character and early career. They trace Kennedy's Irish-Catholic Boston upbringing, the towering influence of his father Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., and the family’s social ambitions. The discussion covers Kennedy’s education, anglophilia and voracious reading (including Churchill), his father’s ambassadorship in London, and Jack’s formative travels in Europe. Dominic and Tom recount Kennedy’s wartime heroism in the South Pacific (the August 1943 boat incident and subsequent rescue), his persistent and debilitating health problems, relationships including Inge Arvad, and his marriage to Jacqueline Bouvier. They outline his postwar political rise from Congressman to Senator, near-selection as Adlai Stevenson’s 1956 running mate, and the role of family ambition in his career. description:
Tenochtitlan, once the glittering jewel at the heart of the mighty Aztec Empire, has fallen. Hernán Cortés stands triumphant, the master of this New Spain. Or so it seems. For the last Aztec emperor, Cuauhtemoc, is still alive and well. And in the jungles of Mexico and Honduras, a dark and bloody story is only just beginning …

In the final episode of this astonishing journey, Dominic and Tom discuss the aftermath of the fall of Tenochtitlan, the fates of Cuauhtemoc, Cortés and Malinche, the experiences of the local population and the story of Mexico in the decades after the Spanish conquest. As this mighty epic draws to a close, they also explore the Black Legend of Spanish imperialism, and discuss the long-term repercussions of the conquest and its status in the context of world history and politics today.

summary: This episode is the eighth and final instalment of an eight-part series on the fall of the Aztecs. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the immediate aftermath of Tenochtitlan's fall (August 1521): Cortés's frustrations searching for hidden gold, the brutal treatment and torture of Cuauhtémoc, the social and legal remaking of the city into Ciudad de México, and the establishment of encomiendas. They discuss cultural and religious change — including the apparition narrative of the Virgin of Guadalupe at Tepeyac and syncretic conversion practices — and the pivotal demographic impact of smallpox. The hosts survey the fates of principal actors (Cortés, Malinche/Doña Marina, Cristóbal de Olid, Catalina Suárez, Martín Cortés) and broader consequences: the template the conquest provided for European expansion and debates among historians about narrative framing (they reference Miguel León Portillo's Broken Spears, Camila Townsend's Fifth Sun, and contemporary scholarship). The episode balances the drama of the conquest with its horrors, emphasizing complexity and multiple perspectives rather than a single moral verdict.
title: The Fall of the Aztecs: The Last Emperor (Part 8)

description:
"Conquer or die indeed, Cortes thought… The hour of decision was at hand…"

It is the spring of 1521 and the fate of Mexico hangs by a thread. Smallpox has ripped through the local population, while the ruthless Spanish commander, Hernán Cortés, has cut off the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, from its surrounding provinces. 

So begins one of the bloodiest and most dramatic struggles in all history - an extraordinary clash between the Old World and the New, as the Spanish tighten their grip on the island city of the Mexica. But can the new Aztec emperor, Cuauhtemoc, save his people? For he has a secret weapon - the terrifying Quetzal-Owl …

In today’s episode, Dominic and Tom tell the story of the Siege of Tenochtitlan - the last stand of the Aztec warriors, as the Spanish and their allies close in for the kill.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate and analyse the climactic stages of the Spanish conquest of the Aztec capital. They recount Cortés's construction and launching of brigantines on Lake Texcoco (28 April 1521), the strategic blockade of Tenochtitlan, and the attritional fighting along the causeways led by captains including Pedro de Alvarado, Cristóbal de Olid and Gonzalo de Sandoval. The episode covers key figures (Cortés, Cuauhtémoc, Montezuma, the Tlaxcalan allies), Nahuatl and Spanish eyewitness testimony (Bernal Díaz), ritual elements such as the Quetzal Owl warrior, mass sacrifice, famine and disease, and the final capture of Cuauhtémoc. They discuss sources and modern histories including Tom Holland’s children's book The Fall of the Aztecs and Camilla Tansen’s The Fifth Sun, reflecting on cultural loss, brutality, and the mixed motives of the conquerors. The episode ends by setting up a final instalment on consequences for Cortés, Mexico and early modern colonisation.

description:
Things have never looked bleaker for Hernán Cortés and his band of Spaniards. They are trapped, starving and terrified in the heart of the Aztec city of Tenochtitlan, surrounded by an enraged people bent on revenge. And with their imperial hostage Montezuma dead, they only have one option left - a desperate escape in the dead of night. 
Can they make it across the lake with their gold? Or will the Aztecs intercept them before it’s too late?
In today’s episode of this epic series, Tom and Dominic tell the story of one of the most dramatic moments in all history - the night of 30th June 1520, La Noche Triste, when the Spanish tried to break out of Tenochtitlan. They also explore the aftermath of this hellish episode, and the arrival of another, even greater threat to the survival of the Aztecs - disease …

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, recounts the aftermath of Hernán Cortés's captivity in Tenochtitlan and the dramatic escape known as La Noche Triste (30 June–1 July 1520). The hosts describe the chaotic retreat across causeways, heavy Spanish losses and the collapse of makeshift bridges, and the subsequent strategic and political consequences: Cortés's battered force withdraws to Tlaxcala, where the Tlaxcalan decision to continue their alliance proves decisive. The episode then shifts to the catastrophic arrival of smallpox in central Mexico, its demographic and social effects (including the deaths of successive Aztec rulers), and how disease reshaped alliances and warfare. Cortés's adaptation to a European-style, attritional campaign is detailed—cutting supply routes, brutal reprisals, and the construction of brigantines by Martín López—culminating in the sacking of Texcoco and preparations for the final assault on Tenochtitlan. The hosts reflect on violence, historiography, and the role of indigenous allies and epidemics in the conquest.

description:
“The blood flowed like water…”

It is 1520 and word has reached Hernán Cortés in Tenochtitlan that another group of Spaniards led by the ferocious Pánfilo de Narváez, have landed on the coast to hunt him down. Taking drastic action, he decides to leave the city with his wily mistress Malinche to pursue the newcomers, but not before taking the Emperor of the Aztecs, Montezuma, as his hostage. 
But can Cortés really overcome a much larger force commanded by such a formidable rival? And can his lieutenant, the dashing, violent and reckless Pedro de Alvarado, keep his cool in the heart of the capital? For one of the most hallowed Aztec festivals is fast approaching. The tension is mounting, and the Spaniards’ swords are thirsty for blood …
In today’s episode in this unmissable series, Dominic and Tom lead us deeper into the heart of darkness, as the story of the Fall of the Aztecs takes a shocking and nightmarish turn …

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-part series on Hernán Cortés and the fall of the Aztec Empire. The episode recounts Cortés’s risky return to the Gulf coast, his defeat of Pánfilo de Nárvaez (winning over Narváez’s men), and his reinforced march back to Tenochtitlan in 1520. Left in charge, Pedro de Alvarado grows paranoid and violent; during the Tóxcatl festival he orders a brutal attack on unarmed worshippers inside the temple precinct, triggering a wider uprising. The Spaniards fall back to the palace with Montezuma (Montezuma II) held as a hostage. Sources—Spanish memoirists like Bernal Díaz, later chroniclers such as Gomara, indigenous accounts collected in the Florentine Codex, and Diego Durán—offer conflicting details about events and Montezuma’s eventual death. The hosts discuss motives, source biases, and the desperate conditions that lead to the Spaniards being trapped and the subsequent decision to attempt escape (to be covered in the next episode, including the Noche Triste).

description:
The year is 1519. Hernán Cortés and his Spanish comrades have arrived in Tenochtitlan, the capital city of the Aztecs, and have been welcomed by their Emperor Montezuma. But what is Montezuma planning? Are the Spaniards his guests - or his prisoners? Has he really acknowledged them as his overlords? Or are they destined for a rather darker fate, as the latest inmates in his mysterious zoo?

In today’s episode, Tom and Dominic follow the Spaniards as they explore the magnificent city of Tenochtitlan, from the crowds in the markets to the blood-drenched shrines atop the temple pyramids.
 
The days pass, the smiles fade and the tension rises. And then Cortés hears news from the coast that changes everything, and must roll the dice one more time in the greatest gamble of all …

summary: This episode (episode four of the hosts' Aztec series) follows Hernán Cortés and his men while based in Tenochtitlan, exploring the culture shock of the Spaniards, their encounters with Moctezuma (Montezuma), and the ambiguous balance of power. Using primary accounts (notably Bernal Díaz) and recent scholarship, the hosts debate interpretations: whether the Spaniards were prisoners, guests, or exhibits in Moctezuma’s reputed zoo, and whether the Mexica planned to eliminate them during the spring festival of the flaying of men. description:
“Conquer or die! Conquer or die! Conquer or die!”

Making a decision that will change the course of history, Hernán Cortés chooses to disobey his orders and head inland in search of the gold-rich empire of the mysterious Montezuma. Ahead lie the mountain passes that will lead him down into the Valley of Mexico, a vast lake shimmering at its heart. 

In the middle of the lake lies the island city of Tenochtitlan, a vision of bustling marketplaces and soaring pyramids. But are the Spaniards advancing as conquerors - or are they walking into a trap? And just what is Montezuma planning? 

Join Dominic and Tom to explore perhaps the most astonishing encounter in all human history - not just the meeting of two extraordinary characters, but a collision of cultures that will have dark and bloody consequences …

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-part narrative of Hernán Cortés's expedition into the Basin of Mexico. They discuss Cortés's decision to march inland, the crucial role of Malinche as interpreter and political broker, and the Spaniards' encounters en route — from the valley of Zautla and the hostile but pivotal Tlaxcalan territory to the massacre at Cholula. The hosts examine the mixed messages the Spaniards received from Mexica emissaries, the psychological and cultural disorientation of the Europeans on seeing Tenochtitlan, and the ambiguous interaction between Cortés and Moctezuma (Moctezuma Xucayotzin) when the Spaniards enter the capital on 7–8 November 1519. description:
Hernán Cortés has set sail from Cuba, eager to find the truth behind the rumours of gold on the coast of Mexico. Ahead lies a world he can barely imagine - a land of pyramid temples, terrifying gods and unknown peoples - the empire of the Aztecs. But Cortés has a secret weapon: a woman whose very name has become a byword for treachery …

In today’s episode, Dominic and Tom explore the extraordinary story of Malinche, the slave-girl given by the Mayans to the Spanish, who becomes Cortés’s translator, guide, lover and adviser. As the expedition moves north along the Mexican coast, is she really doing the Spaniards’ bidding? Or has she secretly taken control, leading them ever closer to a tumultuous and bloody showdown? For all the time, Montezuma is waiting …
Don’t miss the second episode in this thrilling account of the Fall of the Aztecs!

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, narrates Hernán Cortés's 1519 expedition from Cuba to the Mexican mainland and the early stages of contact with Maya and Mexica peoples. The hosts discuss Cortés's ambiguous motives (religious, legalistic and commercial), his tense relationship with Diego Velázquez of Cuba, and the composition of his force. Key advantages — swords, horses, dogs, ships and unwitting diseases such as smallpox — are examined alongside the critical role of interpreters: Jerónimo de Aguilar and the Nahua woman known as La Malinche, who became essential to Cortés's diplomacy. The episode covers encounters at Cozumel, Potonchán, and Tabasco, the gifting of women (including La Malinche) and Cortés's decision to found Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz before marching inland. Legal practices like the Requerimiento and the litigious, bureaucratic mindset of Spaniards are emphasized, and historians and books (Fernando Cervantes, Camilla Townsend, Hugh Thomas) are cited. title: The Fall of the Aztecs: The Woman Who Changed The World (Part 2)

description:
The meeting of the controversial Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés and the formidable Emperor Montezuma in 1519 was one of the great hinge moments of world history, and the beginning of the end for the mightiest of the New World empires: the realm of the Aztecs. 

The build-up to this extraordinary encounter is at once a thrilling adventure story and a tragic tale of violence, brutality and loss. It’s a story of temples and sacrifices, exploration and imperialism, with cataclysmic consequences for human history.

Join Tom and Dominic in the first episode of this sensational saga, as they follow the young Cortés across the Atlantic to the Caribbean islands of Hispaniola and Cuba, where the search for gold comes at a terrible price …

summary: This episode (the first of a multi-part series) examines the opening phase of the Spanish encounter with the Mexica/Aztecs, focusing on Hernán Cortés's background, motivations and early career in the Caribbean before his expedition to the Mexican mainland. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Cortés's upbringing in Extremadura, his education, his time on Hispaniola and Cuba, and the island-hopping process by which Spanish armed entrepreneurs reached the Gulf coast of Mexico. They chart early voyages by Hernández de Córdova and Juan de Grijalva, encounters with Totonacs, reports of a great city and gold, and the environment of violence and religious militancy shaped by the Reconquista. The episode situates the famous 8 November 1519 meeting between Cortés and the Aztec emperor (Moctezuma) within wider themes: chivalric influences on conquistadors, disputed sources, and the political and moral complexity of colonization. summary: This episode follows Napoleon's transition from Corsican outsider to rising French military and political figure. After returning to a chaotic Corsica and experiencing early humiliation during an attempted Sardinia operation, Napoleon and his family flee to France. The hosts cover Napoleon's decisiveness and technical skill during the Siege of Toulon (1793), his promotion, and the patronage networks that shaped his career. They discuss the Thermidorian turn, the volatile Parisian atmosphere, and Paul Barras's role in recruiting Napoleon to suppress the royalist 13 Vendémiaire uprising in October 1795 — the famous 'whiff of grapeshot' moment that secures the Directory and gives Napoleon the command of the interior. The episode also examines Napoleon's courting and marriage to Josephine, his literary attempts (Clisson et Eugénie), his Italian ambitions, and the symbolic shedding of his Corsican identity as he signs 'Bonaparte.' The hosts set this as part two of their short Napoleon series and sketch the political and personal forces that propel him toward command in Italy.
title: Young Napoleon: The Shadow of the Guillotine (Ep 2)

description:
“I would plunge the avenging dagger, up to the hilt, in the breast of the tyrant!”
Born in Corsica a year after the island was given to France by the Genoese, Napoleon Bonaparte grew up in a world of political and civil unrest. His father had close ties with the leader of the Corsican resistance movement, Pasquale Paoli, who would leave a lasting impression on young Napoleon. However, sent to study at a military academy in France, the future Emperor would begin to shed his Corsican roots, and start to embrace more revolutionary, universalist ideals... Join Tom and Dominic in the first part of our series on Young Napoleon, as they discuss the tumultuous island he grew up on, his enthusiasm for the French Revolution, the effect on him of his military schooling, and his complicated relationship with France.

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, examines the origins and youth of Napoleon Bonaparte. The hosts situate Napoleon in 18th-century Corsica — its Ligurian dialect, Genoese rule, Pasquale Paoli’s nationalism, and the 1768 transfer to France — and outline his family background (Carlo Maria Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino). They trace young Napoleon’s austere military education, his struggles with French language and culture, his autodidactic appetite for classical authors (Plutarch, Caesar, Cicero, Tacitus) and Ossianic romance, and his early political oscillations between Corsican nationalism and support for the French Revolution. Key revolutionary moments (the Bastille, Varennes, the Tuileries assault) are discussed for their impact on his developing authoritarian republicanism and career prospects. The hosts emphasize mythmaking around his youth (snowball fight, gothic writings) and set up a follow-up episode continuing Napoleon’s rise amid revolutionary turmoil.
title: Young Napoleon: Teenage Revolutionary (Ep 1)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History continues the hosts' narrative of Captain James Cook's first voyage. After observing the 1769 transit of Venus at Tahiti, Cook follows sealed Admiralty orders to search for Terra Australis, encountering complex interactions with Tahitians—trade, sexual economies, tattooing (tatau → "tattoo"), and the recruitment of the Tahitian Tupia as interpreter. The voyage then proceeds to New Zealand (October 1769), where violent clashes with Māori occur alongside Cook's evident admiration for Māori skill and culture. Cook charts New Zealand's coasts before pressing on to the eastern coast of New Holland (Australia) in April 1770, landing at Botany Bay, recording the kangaroo and dingo, and suffering hull damage on the Great Barrier Reef. The episode ends with the Endeavour's return to England in 1771 and the wide public reception—celebrity for crew and even the ship's goat—while reflecting on Cook's ambiguous legacy as an enlightened scientist and an agent of imperial claim-making.
title: Captain Cook: To the Ends of the Earth (Ep2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook introduce a multi-episode focus on Captain James Cook’s first Pacific voyage. They trace Cook’s humble Yorkshire origins, apprenticeship, skill as a navigator and chartmaker, and rapid rise in the Royal Navy, including his surveying work on the St. Lawrence and Newfoundland. The hosts explain why Cook was chosen to command HMS Endeavour: the Royal Society and Admiralty wanted precise observations of the 1769 Transit of Venus and—secretly—geographical intelligence about Terra Australis. They introduce the expedition’s scientific dimension through Joseph Banks and his team (including Dr. Solander and artist Sydney Parkinson), the odd cargo (animals, cheeses, beer) and efforts to prevent scurvy. Early encounters — crossing the equator, stops at Rio and Tierra del Fuego and first contact with the Fuegians — are described, with discussion of Cook’s evolving view of indigenous peoples and the broader Enlightenment context. The episode sets up the next instalment covering Tahiti, New Zealand and Australia.
title: Captain Cook: History's Greatest Explorer (Ep1)

summary: This episode — the fourth in the hosts' series on Baghdad and the Islamic Golden Age — examines how medieval Baghdad became both an Islamic legal and intellectual centre and a global cultural crossroads. The hosts discuss the rise of jurisprudence (fiqh), the role of hadith, and competing Sunni legal schools (Abu Hanifa, Malik ibn Anas, Al-Shafi, Ibn Hanbal), and how scholars constrained caliphal power. They outline the House of Wisdom and the Abbasid translation movement that preserved and transformed Greek, Persian and other learning, noting Dmitri Goutas's work. The conversation then turns to the Arabian Nights: Antoine Galon’s influential European translations, later Victorian and Burtonian additions, and the stories’ mixed origins in Persian, Indian, Greek and oral street traditions. The hosts highlight how the Nights reflect Baghdad’s low-life, criminals and cosmopolitan imagination (Sinbad, Ali Baba, Aladdin, Al-Uqab), and emphasize the long-term impact of Baghdad’s intellectual achievements on both the Islamic world and medieval/modern Europe.
title: Baghdad: The Arabian Nights (Ep 4)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Harun al-Rashid and Baghdad at the height of the early Abbasid Caliphate. They contrast the mythic Baghdad of the Arabian Nights with surviving historical sources (Al-Yakoubi, Ibn Sarapion, Al-Tabari), sketch Harun's family and court — the powerful queen-mother (Al-Kaiziran), the influential Zubaydah, and the Barmakid vizier family (Yahya, Jafar) — and discuss themes of succession, patronage and court violence. The hosts describe Baghdad as a vast, global metropolis with extensive trade links, canals, gardens, markets and extreme social inequality, noting key developments like Harun's military activity against Byzantium, the establishment of Raqqa as a seat, and the later catastrophic succession crisis between Al-Amin and Al-Ma'mun. They trace the city's long-term fragility — slave armies, revolts (including the Zanj uprising) and eventual decline culminating in the Mongol destruction — and set up a following episode on Baghdad's cultural legacy and the Arabian Nights for Rest Is History Club members.
title: Baghdad: The Golden Age (Ep 3)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History traces the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate and the rise of the Abbasids, focusing on the revolutionary movement in Khorasan, the role of charismatic agents like Abu Muslim, and the violent consolidation under Abu al-'Abbās al‑Saffāḥ and his successor Abu Ja'far al‑Mansur. The hosts recount key episodes: the black flag raised outside Merv, rapid Abbasid gains through Iran and Iraq, the decisive defeat of Marwan II at the Great Zab, and the near-extermination of Umayyad rivals (with Abd al-Rahman escaping to Spain). The conversation then turns to Al‑Mansur’s foundation of a new capital at Baghdad (founded 762), its Persian architectural influences, urban design (the round city and central mosque/palace), demographic mix, and its symbolic role as a crossroads synthesizing Roman, Sasanian and Islamic traditions. The episode ends by previewing a forthcoming show on Baghdad’s golden age and noting sources and books listeners might consult.
title: Baghdad: Crossroads of the Universe (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook set the scene for a four-episode series on Baghdad by surveying the late Umayyad world and the forces that produced the Abbasid revolution. They outline the extraordinary rapidity and scale of the early Arab conquests, the demise of the Sasanian empire, and the complex, multi-religious populations (Christians, Zoroastrians, Jews) living under Arab rule. The hosts discuss internal pressures on the Umayyads: frontier defeats (notably in 717 and 732), sectarian movements such as the Kharijites and Shia, and the rise of urban legal and religious scholars who produce hadiths and a Sunnah drawing on Jewish and Zoroastrian precedents. Tom explains how these currents undermine Umayyad legitimacy and how the Abbasids exploit Sunni and Shia grievances. The episode stops before Baghdad’s foundation, teasing a club-only installment covering the Abbasid Revolution and promising subsequent episodes on the city’s founding and golden age.
title: Baghdad: The Forging of Islam (Ep 1)

summary: This episode examines the life and notoriety of Unity Valkyrie Mitford, one of the famous Mitford sisters, and her intimate association with Nazi Germany and Adolf Hitler. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Unity’s aristocratic background, family connections (including links to Winston Churchill), and early social life. They discuss her descent from posh dilettantism into committed pro-Nazi activism: attending Nuremberg rallies, living in Munich, cultivating contacts like Julius Streicher, and receiving personal favours from Hitler. The hosts contrast Unity’s frivolous, celebrity-like devotion with the more ideological commitments of other figures, place her actions in the context of British fascism and interwar Anglo-German attitudes, and recount her dramatic 1939 suicide attempt in Munich, repatriation, and subsequent cognitive decline and death in 1948. They also review scholarship and biographies (Laura Thompson; a 1977 David Price-Jones work) and address persistent rumours—debated in the press—that she might have returned to Britain pregnant by Hitler, which the hosts judge unlikely.
title: Hitler and the Mitford Sisters (Ep 4)

description:
“You will never catch Sir Oswald admitting to anti-semitism - all he does is embody it!”
Following the violent scenes at Kensington Olympia, the British fascist movement is in decline. Britain is swirling with unemployment, having just come out of a decade of general strikes, and as the country suffers, changes and becomes more urbanised, the fascists seek a scapegoat to pin Britain’s downfall on. On the 6th of October 1936, Mosley gathers with 3000 of his blackshirts to march through London’s East End, an area with a large Jewish population; they are met by 100,000 anti-fascist demonstrators blocking the streets… Join Tom and Dominic in the third episode of our series on British fascism, as they look at the Battle of Cable Street, fascism in the pre-war years, Oswald’s role in the anti-war movement, his eventual arrest and detainment, and much more.

*The Rest Is History Live Tour 2023*:

Tom and Dominic are back on tour this autumn! See them live in London, New Zealand, and Australia!

summary: This episode — the third in The Rest Is History's series on British fascism — examines the lead-up to and fallout from the Battle of Cable Street (4 October 1936) and situates Oswald Mosley and the British Union of Fascists in the political, economic and social context of 1920s–1930s Britain. The hosts discuss Mosley’s shift toward anti-capitalism and opportunistic antisemitism, the localised nature of East End conflicts, and how Cable Street’s mythology (often claiming a decisive defeat of fascism) differs from the historical record. The conversation moves to the late 1930s: Mosley’s peace campaigning during appeasement, the abdication crisis of Edward VIII, the impact of Germany’s actions on British attitudes to antisemitism, and the start of the war. They close with the internment of fascists under Regulation 18B, Mosley’s imprisonment, and a preview of the next episode focused on the Mitford sisters and pro-Nazi sympathies in Britain.
title: The Battle of Cable Street: Fascism Defeated (Ep 3)

summary: This episode (the second in a short series on British fascism) examines the life and political trajectory of Sir Oswald Mosley. Holland and Sandbrook trace Mosley from an aristocratic, war-scarred youth to a charismatic MP who moved from the Conservatives to Labour, authored demand-management proposals foreshadowing Keynesian policies, and ultimately founded first the New Party and then the British Union of Fascists (BUF). The hosts discuss Mosley's theatricalism, adoption of uniforms and paramilitary stewards, his attempts to appeal across classes (including women and ex-servicemen), and early establishment sympathy (notably from Lord Rothermere). They identify the turning point in 1934 — the violent Olympia meeting — and the close timing of Germany's Night of the Long Knives, arguing these events precipitated the withdrawal of elite support and rapid membership decline. The episode previews the next instalments (Cable Street and the Mitfords) and notes some primary sources and secondary literature referenced during the discussion.
title: Oswald Mosley: Fascist Leader (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook introduce a multi-episode series on British fascism, arguing that while Britain never became fascist, many cultural and political ingredients existed from the late 19th century into the interwar years. They discuss precursors including imperial nostalgia, fears of national degeneracy after the Boer War, eugenics, anti-Semitism, and anxieties about women voters. They cite Martin Pugh's Hurrah for the Blackshirts and literary figures such as Henry Williamson and J.R.R. Tolkien to show how similar themes circulated in Britain. The hosts trace paramilitary traditions, post‑war demobilisation and the appeal of Mussolini in the 1920s as galvanising models; they describe early British fascist groups (including female-led movements), the Imperial Fascist League, and colourful characters such as William Joyce and Valerie Arkell Smith (Sir Victor Barker). They conclude that contingent factors—British victory in 1918, a less severe Depression, and resilient parliamentary politics—kept fascism marginal, while teasing Oswald Mosley as the future focal figure for the movement.
title: The Birth of British Fascism (Ep 1)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, continues their examination of Chile in 1973 and the events that led to the overthrow of Salvador Allende and the rise of Augusto José Ramón Pinochet Ugarte. The hosts review political polarisation, economic turmoil, congressional conflict and US involvement during the Cold War. They recount the failed June tanquetazo, the resignation of General Carlos Prats after a public scandal, and the late‑summer plotting by Chilean military factions. On 11 September 1973 the navy, air force and army seized key locations; La Moneda was attacked, Allende delivered a final radio address and died in the palace. The aftermath included mass arrests, killings (notably Victor Jara), detention in the national stadium, the Caravan of Death, establishment of DINA, and Pinochet’s consolidation of power. The episode also discusses international reactions, including praise from Margaret Thatcher and wider debates about Cold War ethics and the regime’s economic and repressive legacy.
title: The 1973 Chilean Coup: General Pinochet Seizes Power (Ep 2)

summary: Recorded on 11 September (the 50th anniversary of the 1973 coup), this episode traces Salvador Allende's rise from a medical student and socialist organiser to his 1970 election as Chile's president. Holland and Sandbrook outline Allende's reformist, parliamentary Marxism and the repeated American efforts to prevent his victory — covert CIA spending, business lobbying (notably US copper companies and ITT), and Nixon administration plans captured in declassified documents (including Richard Helms's note to "make the economy scream"). The hosts recount the failed 1970 attempts to neutralise commander-in-chief René Schneider, Schneider's death, Allende's confirmation by Congress, and the ambitious social and economic programme Allende launched. They discuss the combined impact of Chile's economic troubles, commodity price falls, US economic pressure, and domestic opposition (truckers, conservative press) that polarised politics and set the stage for the coup. The episode ends by setting up the next instalment detailing the 1973 coup and Augusto Pinochet's takeover.
title: The 1973 Chilean Coup: Allende, Nixon and the CIA (Ep 1)

summary: This episode is an introduction/read-through by Tom Holland of his book Pax, exploring the heyday of the Roman Empire under emperors such as Hadrian. Holland uses Hadrian's visit to the Tyne and the building of Hadrian's Wall as a starting point to discuss the scale and meaning of the Pax Romana, its material achievements, and the darker aspects of Roman rule (slavery, spectacles, repression). He surveys how Rome has been remembered and reimagined—from Edward Gibbon's praise of the second century to George R. R. Martin's fictional appropriation in A Game of Thrones—and examines the competing legacies of Christianity and Jewish memory, including the Jewish revolts and the rebuilt Roman city of Jerusalem. Holland explains his methodological caution about anachronism, assesses the unevenness of ancient evidence (archaeology, inscriptions, Josephus, Tacitus), and situates Pax as the third volume in a sequence following Rubicon and Dynasty, framing the narrative balance between peace and the wars that enforced it.
title: PAX: War and Peace in Rome’s Golden Age (Extract)

description:
“Are you not entertained?!” 
The emblem of Rome, the Colosseum was the unsettling but glamorous home of Roman violence, used for gladiatorial bouts, naval reenactments, and by the emperors to re-stage popular myths. Built by the Flavian dynasty in the first century AD, it is both an awe-inspiring monument to the grandeur of antiquity, and a blood-spattered arena of death. But why was it built? What was the deeper meaning of the cruelty it celebrated? In today’s episode Tom and Dominic delve into the gory roots of the Colosseum, and the stories of the gladiators who fought and died there.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Colosseum and Roman spectacles, using the film Gladiator as an entry point. They trace the origins of gladiatorial games from funerary rites to mass entertainment and civic ritual, and explain how spectacles served social cohesion and imperial propaganda. The episode examines the Flavian dynasty—Vespasian and Titus—who built the Flavian Amphitheatre on Nero’s drained lake to assert dynastic legitimacy after the chaos of AD 69. Seating arrangements, the ritual and mythic framing of executions, exotic animals, and gladiators’ celebrity status are analysed as elements that fused spectacle, religion and power. The hosts consider literary witnesses (Tertullian, Martial, Suetonius, Petronius, Augustine) and later perceptions of the arena, and touch on the Colosseum’s changing uses through late antiquity and the medieval period. Holland’s book Pax is recommended for further reading.
title: The Colosseum: Rome's Arena of Death

description:
“To be a boy at one of these schools was to be alternately tyrant and slave.”
More gruesome even than the Battle of Hogwarts, 18th century British Public schools were hotbeds for violence and uproar, despite their deeply Christian origins. From raucous rebellions featuring students fighting militias and building barricades, hostage-taking and pistol-firing, to animal assassinations, abysmal teaching and gruesome hazing rituals, their organised brutality was mis-sold as “character-building”. Join Tom and Dominic in the second part of our series, as they explore the schools which inspired Hogwarts, their pupils, stories and legacies.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-episode examination of the origins and cultural resonances of Harry Potter by focusing on the model of British public schools that inspired Hogwarts. They interweave close readings from J.K. Rowling's novels with historical survey: the medieval foundation of feeder grammar schools (William of Wickham and Winchester College, New College Oxford), the royal establishment of Eton by Henry VI, and the evolution of other notable schools (Merchant Taylors', Westminster, St Paul's). The episode traces recurring tensions—charitable pretence vs. elite patronage—and exposes chronic problems: poor funding, corruption, brutal hazing, and pupil revolts from the late 18th to mid-19th centuries. They discuss how classical curricula and violent initiation rituals shaped character and empire-building, survey famous alumni, and compare reforming figures such as Thomas Arnold to Rowling's Dumbledore. The show closes by placing Hogwarts within a broader imperial and cultural legacy and previews upcoming episodes on gladiators and the 1973 Chilean coup.
title: The History Behind Hogwarts: Ancient Schools and Revolting Students (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Harry Potter as a continuation of a long British boarding-school tradition. Using Tom Brown's School Days (Thomas Hughes) as the central exemplar, they trace how Victorian public-school culture — Dr Thomas Arnold's character-forming pedagogy, house systems, prefects, sport (notably cricket and codified games), fagging, rites, punishments and a classical curriculum — shaped narratives later echoed by J. K. Rowling. They survey children's literature predecessors (Enid Blyton, T. H. White, Susan Cooper, Diana Wynne-Jones, Terry Pratchett), the Boys' Papers (The Magnet, The Gem, Boy's Own Paper), and global impacts (Pierre de Coubertin, C. L. R. James). The discussion covers gender, co-education, erotic and disciplinary aspects of Victorian schooling, and how Hogwarts blends medievalism, secrecy, competition and moral instruction. The episode is presented as part one of a series on the origins of Harry Potter; a second episode and bonus club material are available for Rest Is History Club members.
title: The Real Harry Potter: Magic, Empire and Beastly Bullies (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Rana Mitter about Deng Xiaoping and China’s “opening up” after Mao. Mitter outlines Deng’s background—his Sichuan origins, time in France and Moscow, participation in the Long March and the civil war—and his political resurrection after Mao’s death. The conversation traces the late-1970s factional struggle (including Hua Guofeng and the Gang of Four), Deng’s pragmatic turn away from ideological “book worship,” and the economic experiments that combined authoritarian politics with market mechanisms. They discuss influences on reformers (Eastern European reformers, Milton Friedman, and others), the role of Zhao Ziyang and Hu Yaobang, and grassroots as well as state-driven elements of growth (special economic zones, female labor). The episode also covers cultural signifiers like the TV series River Elegy and the crisis of 1989, culminating in Tiananmen and Deng’s subsequent southern tour to reassert economic reform. Mitter’s books and other scholarship are referenced throughout.
title: The Architect of Modern China

summary: This episode examines the life, works and long shadow of the Marquis de Sade. Holland and Sandbrook narrate Sade’s biography: his aristocratic background, military service in the Seven Years’ War, serial scandals and repeated imprisonments under the Ancien Régime, his prolific prison-writing (notably The Hundred and Twenty Days of Sodom written in the Bastille), and his turbulent role during the French Revolution and its aftermath. They explore Sade’s philosophical materialism and radical sexual ethics, arguing he anticipated and influenced later intellectual currents — the bastardisations of Darwinism and Nietzschean critique, psychoanalytic readings (Krafft-Ebing, Freud), and twentieth-century thinkers (Foucault, Beauvoir). The hosts discuss the paradox of Sade as both an advocate of certain progressive causes (women’s sexual equality, tolerance) and a thinker who pushed those principles toward extreme, violent conclusions that later readers linked to totalitarian atrocities. They consider his posthumous reception, censorship, cinematic adaptations (Pasolini) and continuing controversial legacy within literature, philosophy and political thought.
title: Le Marquis de Sade: Sex and Violence

summary: This episode examines 1960s British fashion and youth culture, tracing the emergence and international impact of trends such as the shift dress, miniskirt and the cult of youth. The hosts open with Jean Shrimpton’s notorious appearance at Melbourne Derby Day (October 1965) and discuss Mary Quant’s influence, the rise of Twiggy (Leslie Hornby) as the face of 1966, and the aesthetic of The Avengers (Diana Rigg). They chart Carnaby Street’s evolution—John Stephen and other boutiques—alongside the Beatles’ cultural export and the broader British Invasion. The program explores the infantilization and sexualization of female fashion, Germaine Greer’s critique in The Female Eunuch, and the shift toward hippie aesthetics by 1967: Eastern influences, Sergeant Pepper’s Victorian revival, and the later commercial collapse exemplified by Biba. The hosts conclude by reflecting on how 1960s styles recycled into later decades (punk, new romantics) and on the lasting cultural legacy of the era’s youth-driven fashion revolutions.
title: Sixties Fashion: Swinging London (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the rise of British fashion from wartime austerity to the global prominence of Swinging London in the 1960s. They explain how the monochrome, utilitarian clothes of the Second World War and postwar rationing (1941–1949) set the scene for reactions such as Christian Dior's New Look in 1947 and subsequent shifts. The discussion surveys subcultures (Teddy Boys, Mods and Rockers), the influence of American and Italian styles, and the economic power of teenagers as consumers. They profile key figures: Mary Quant and her Kings Road boutique, photographers (David Bailey, Terence Donovan, Brian Duffy), and supermodel Jean Shrimpton, and explain how boutiques, magazines (Honey, Queen) and the new colour supplements (notably the Sunday Times from 1962) helped diffuse styles nationwide. The episode ends on a cliffhanger about Shrimpton's notorious Melbourne appearance in October 1965, teasing extra detail for Rest Is History Club members and a promised continuation in the next episode.
title: Sixties Fashion: The Teenage Revolution (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook speak with Dr. Mehreen Chidurazvi (also referenced as Maureen Cheeda-Razvi) about the history, construction and symbolism of the Taj Mahal. The conversation traces Mughal origins from Babur through Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan, explains Persian and Timurid artistic influences, and examines the relationship between Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal that prompted the mausoleum. They cover construction chronology (mausoleum 1632–1636; full complex by 1643), architectural symbolism (paradisiacal gardens, Qur'anic inscriptions), European contemporary reactions (Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, François Bernier), and British-era conservation led by George Nathaniel Curzon. The episode also addresses later politicization and legal claims about the site's origins, recent attempts to recast the Taj's past in communal terms, and its enduring status as a global symbol of India and of romantic devotion.
title: The Taj Mahal: Love and Death

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the reality and mythology of the Library of Alexandria. Opening with a pop-culture depiction in Assassin’s Creed Origins, they trace the deeper antecedents of libraries in the Near East, the Assyrian collections (notably Ashurbanipal) and Greek intellectual institutions such as Aristotle’s Lyceum and the Museion in Alexandria. They discuss Ptolemaic motivations for assembling texts—status, preservation of Greek literature and genuine scholarly aims—citing agents, book acquisition stories and the production of standard editions (Iliad, Odyssey). The hosts dispel grand myths: the library’s focus was largely Greek and literary, not a universal scientific Silicon Valley. They survey competing destruction narratives (Caesar’s fire, imperial civil wars, Aurelian, later Christian mob action at the Serapeum, and later Muslim conquest), concluding loss was likely gradual through neglect, decay of papyrus and episodic damage. They reference scholarship including Luciano Canfora’s The Vanished Library and close by celebrating surviving libraries and the British Library.
title: The Lost Library of Alexandria

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook record from Central Park and examine New York City in the 1970s, centring on the dramatic blackout of 13 July 1977. They describe the technical failure that plunged all five boroughs into darkness and the rapid descent into looting and arson—especially in neighborhoods such as Bushwick—contrasting civil scenes in parts of Manhattan with devastation elsewhere. The discussion places the blackout in the wider context of 1970s urban decline: deindustrialization, suburbanization, soaring unemployment among Black and Hispanic New Yorkers, cuts to public services, police corruption exposed by the Knapp Commission (Frank Serpico), and the Son of Sam killings. They trace media and political reactions—from sensationalist tabloid coverage under Rupert Murdoch to debates over crime, welfare and law-and-order politics—and follow consequences including the 1977 mayoral turnover and early redevelopment deals that presaged 1980s transformation (including the Commodore/Hyatt redevelopment associated with Donald J. Trump). Films and books that reflected and shaped perceptions of the era are also discussed.
title: Fear City: New York in the 1970s

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook record on location at the Lincoln Memorial to examine Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream" speech and the 28 August 1963 March on Washington. They set the speech in context: Jim Crow segregation, post‑war change, Brown v. Board of Education, the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the Birmingham campaign (and King’s Letter from Birmingham Jail). The episode details the march’s organization (A. Philip Randolph, Bayard Rustin), controversy over leadership and the exclusion of women from speaking roles. Holland and Sandbrook analyze King’s rhetorical methods—slow cadence, biblical allusion, anaphora—and the famous improvised “I have a dream” section (possibly prompted by Mahalia Jackson). They discuss contemporary reactions, limited immediate conversion of opponents, and longer‑term memory that often sanitizes King by privileging this speech over his later, more radical anti‑war and economic justice work. The episode concludes by reflecting on the speech’s enduring resonance and the complexities of King’s legacy.
title: Martin Luther King's Dream

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview archaeologist and scholar Neil Price about Norse religion, magic (seiðr), and the cultural complexity of the Viking Age. Price discusses his influential books The Viking Way and Children of Ash and Elm, arguing that Viking belief was embedded in everyday life rather than compartmentalized as a separate “religion.” He emphasises Sami and circumpolar shamanistic influences, the centrality of magic and altered states, and Odin’s ambiguous, often unsettling character. The conversation covers sources from the Poetic Edda to Ibn Fadlan’s eyewitness account of a 922 Volga ship burial, and a medieval poem, The Tale of Valsi, linking sexualized ritual practices and preserved horse phalli to magic (and possibly to Sleipnir and Valkyrie imagery). Price challenges romantic and simplified stereotypes — including berserker myths — and traces continuities into medieval Christian-era folklore and law. The episode is presented as the first part of a multi-part discussion, continuing after a break.
title: Viking Sorcery

summary: In this special "Historical Love Island" episode of The Rest Is History, hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Dominic's daughter, Katie, who acts as the Love Island expert. The episode maps Love Island archetypes onto historical figures — from jesters and minxes to devoted partners and accidental heartbreakers — and sketches eight contestants (male and female) from a wide chronological range. Notable pairings discussed include Charles II of England, Catherine Howard, Peter the Great, Poppaea Sabina, Sir William and Emma Hamilton, Horatio Nelson, Empress Zoe, Mary Fisher, and Tony Benn. The hosts recount relevant biographical episodes (exile, the Restoration, adultery scandals, executions, Nelson’s naval victories, and Peter’s Grand Embassy), cite David Loades’ History of the Tudors on Catherine Howard, and stage a mock public vote. After bombshell entrants and deliberation, Katie predicts the public would favour the pairing of Tony Benn and Mary Fisher. The episode is a humorous, anachronistic exercise blending popular culture and historical anecdote to illuminate personalities and scandals across eras.
title: Historical Love Island: The Sequel

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) examines the life, mystical experiences, and political influence of Saint Catherine of Siena (born 25 March 1347). The hosts set her life against the turbulent 14th century — climate failure, famine, the Hundred Years' War, the Avignon Papacy, and the Black Death that struck Siena in 1348. They trace Catherine’s childhood, visions, ascetic practices (extreme fasting, hair-cutting, mortification), alleged miracles and stigmata, and her mystical “marriage” to Christ. The discussion considers modern readings (medical/psychological interpretations such as anorexia) versus medieval religious frameworks (Eucharistic devotion, female spiritual roles). Catherine’s public role is highlighted: healing, peacemaking in Siena, letters to Pope Gregory XI, her journey to Avignon, persuading Gregory to return to Rome (1377), and her involvement in the events that contributed to the Great Schism. The hosts recommend Caroline Walker Bynum’s Holy Feast and Holy Fast to understand medieval attitudes to food and female sanctity.
title: The Blood-Drinking Bride of Christ

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, examines Mount Vesuvius and the destruction of Pompeii and Herculaneum. Drawing on the eyewitness letters of Pliny the Younger, archaeological evidence and volcanology, the hosts reconstruct the two-day catastrophe: precursory earthquakes, the enormous ash column described as a pine-like/mushroom cloud, heavy pumice fall that darkened midday skies, and subsequent deadly pyroclastic surges that obliterated Herculaneum and buried Pompeii. The discussion covers individual experiences (Pliny the Elder's abortive evacuation and death; Pliny the Younger's survival), the visible aftermath across the Bay of Naples, and social and religious reactions in Rome. They place the eruption in the reign of Emperor Titus and link its cultural resonances to subsequent acts, such as the Colosseum's inauguration. The episode references modern and literary works (Tom Holland's Pax, Robert Harris's novel Pompeii) and considers ongoing volcanic risk and archaeological legacy in the Bay of Naples.
title: Roman Apocalypse: Pompeii 79 AD

summary: This episode — the second part of the hosts' examination of May 1968 — focuses on how the Paris student occupations and nationwide strikes escalated into a constitutional crisis. Holland and Sandbrook trace Charles de Gaulle's reaction: initial contempt, paralysis, a dramatic move to consult General Jacques Massu and French forces in Baden‑Baden, then a decisive radio address dissolving the National Assembly and threatening emergency powers. The Grenelle Accords, union negotiations, and large Gaullist counter-demonstrations are discussed alongside key figures (Pompidou, Chirac, Georges Séguy, Daniel Cohn‑Bendit). The hosts assess the short‑term political failure of the left in the subsequent elections but explore longer cultural legacies — notably the intellectual responses of Michel Foucault and others, and how 1968’s spirit resonated differently abroad. They place May 1968 among other 1968 crises (Prague Spring, Mexico City, US unrest) and debate whether the events were revolutionary or ultimately a cul‑de‑sac for political change while reshaping cultural discourse.
title: Paris 1968: The Return of De Gaulle (Ep2)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook report from Paris to tell the story of May 1968. They set the scene—postwar France, rapid expansion of university education, grim suburban overspill campuses (notably Nanterre), and a hierarchical, paternalistic society under Charles de Gaulle. A local student occupation at Nanterre, led in part by Daniel Cohn-Bendit, met heavy-handed disciplinary responses, drawing protests into central Paris and provoking violent confrontations with the police. Media (radio and television) spread events nationally; students erected barricades, chucked cobbles, and staged situationist/absurdist happenings. The movement expanded as workers initiated widespread strikes: within days millions were on strike and factories were occupied. The hosts discuss intellectual currents (mentions of Michel Foucault, Antonin Artaud), police figures like Maurice Papon, and the difficulty of aligning student demands with workers' grievances. The episode ends by promising a second instalment focused on de Gaulle’s response and the dramatic late-May developments.
title: Paris 1968: The Students' Revolt (Ep1)

summary: This episode is a guided historical tour of Amsterdam, tracing its rise in the 17th-century Dutch Golden Age — the building of the ring canals, merchant townhouses and civic pride — and the political tensions between republican city elites (the De Graeffs and the De Witts) and the stadtholders of the House of Orange. The hosts discuss cultural achievements (Rembrandt, Vermeer), Amsterdam’s role as a publishing and intellectual refuge (Spinoza, Menasseh ben Israel), and the global reach of Dutch trade (New Amsterdam). They cover later upheavals: the Rampjaar (1672), the Batavian Republic (1795), Napoleonic rule, 19th-century changes and the loss of Belgium. The episode then turns to the 20th century — Nazi occupation, the Rotterdam bombing, the Hunger Winter, the deportation of Dutch Jews and Anne Frank’s story — and Amsterdam’s postwar transformation into a model of liberalism (gay rights, drugs policy, legalized prostitution). Finally, they examine contemporary tensions around immigration, Islam, and a reassessment of hyper-liberal policies.
title: Amsterdam: Kings, Canals and Coffee Houses (Ep2)

summary: This Rest Is History Club episode is a walking tour of Amsterdam that traces the city’s rise from a 13th‑century fishing and peat settlement to a global commercial and financial powerhouse. The hosts discuss the Miracle of Amsterdam (1345) and its later suppression during the Reformation, the city’s distinctive mixture of civic tolerance and legalism (illustrated by the Begijnhof and hidden Catholic chapels), and the transition from a Catholic pilgrimage centre to a Protestant stronghold during the Alteration of 1578. They then move to Amsterdam’s Golden Age: the arrival of refugees from Antwerp, the founding of the Dutch East India Company (VOC) in 1602, the birth of modern finance in the Amsterdam bourse, and early stock‑market behaviours and scandals. The episode closes by touching on tulip mania and the city’s broader contribution to globalization, consumer culture, and financial innovation, promising a second episode to continue the architectural and economic tour.
title: Amsterdam: Miracles, Money and Mud (Ep1)

summary: This is the fourth and final episode of a four-part Rest Is History mini-series on the American Revolution. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Professor Adam Smith to trace the conflict’s climax from French and Spanish intervention through the British strategic collapse in North America. They discuss Valley Forge, the role of women, Native Americans, Black loyalists (including the Ethiopian Regiment and Harry Washington), and contentious figures such as Benedict Arnold, John André and Bernastre Tarleton. Cornwallis’s entrapment at Yorktown and the delayed diplomacy leading to the Treaty of Paris (1783) are covered, alongside naval and Caribbean theaters. The conversation turns to the Revolution’s consequences: the creation of a fragile United States under the Articles, debates that produced the Constitution, Washington’s symbolic role, and broader international effects—especially on France and abolitionist currents. Contemporary historiographical disputes, including references to the 1619 Project and debates over founding myths and slavery, close the episode.
title: The Triumph of George Washington (Part 4)

summary: This episode — the third in The Rest Is History's American Revolution series — features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Adam Smith. They discuss the impact of Thomas Paine's Common Sense (January 1776) and his later pamphlet The American Crisis, and situate Paine's rhetoric in wider transatlantic debates. The hosts examine the Continental Congress's move toward a formal Declaration of Independence (Thomas Jefferson's draft), internal divisions among revolutionaries (e.g., John Adams's reservations), and the document's intellectual roots in Locke, Enlightenment thinkers and earlier English traditions. Militarily, they follow the British shift from Boston to New York, the 1776 campaigns (Long Island, evacuation, Washington's crossing of the Delaware, Trenton/Princeton) and the Saratoga campaign (1777), showing how those battles and Parisian support (Beaumarchais, Louis XVI; Lafayette's involvement) altered the conflict. The episode notes broader geopolitical pressures on Britain and ends by directing members to a club-only continuation covering Yorktown and the peace settlement.
title: The Birth of the United States (Part 3)

summary: This episode (the second in The Rest Is History's series on the American War of Independence) explores the escalation from colonial protest to open rebellion. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Oxford historian Adam Smith to discuss the Tea Act of 1773, the Boston Tea Party (16 December 1773) and British motives behind the policy favoring the East India Company. The conversation covers colonial arguments of "no taxation without representation," varied Loyalist and Patriot sympathies, and British reactions including the Coercive/Intolerable Acts and the Quebec Act. Smith outlines how the First Continental Congress and the Suffolk Resolves prepared colonies for armed resistance, leading to Lexington and Concord, Bunker Hill, and the creation of the Continental Army under George Washington. The episode also debates slavery's role in the crisis (including Lord Dunmore's proclamation), guerrilla tactics versus conventional warfare, and wider imperial concerns that shaped British strategy. The hosts preview the next episode on the Declaration of Independence and the war's course.
title: The Boston Tea Party (Part 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome Professor Adam Smith (Edward Osborne Professor of History, Oxford) for a scene-setting episode on the American War of Independence. They survey the prosperous, self-governing nature of the thirteen mainland colonies, the impact of the Seven Years' War (and its North American theatre, the French and Indian War), and the new British military and fiscal presence after 1763. Smith explains metropolitan concerns — frontier order, Native American alliances and heavy war debt — and London reforms under George Grenville (Sugar Act, Stamp Act) that sought revenue and tighter enforcement. Colonial reactions — boycotts, mobs, the homespun movement, and legal resistance to vice-admiralty courts — inflamed tensions, culminating in incidents such as the Boston Massacre. Religious differences, the Great Awakening, and divergent constitutional understandings (parliamentary sovereignty vs. colonial rights) are highlighted as drivers of mistrust. Smith argues independence was not inevitable in 1770; much depended on subsequent political choices. The episode is labeled the first part of a short series covering the road to open war and independence.
title: The American Revolution (Part 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the origins, meanings and later receptions of the Holy Grail legend. Tracing the motif from a mundane medieval term for a serving platter to Chrétien de Troyes' 12th-century Perceval — where the grail first acquires sacral overtones — they chart subsequent retellings by Robert de Boron and Wolfram von Eschenbach that transform the grail into a Christian relic tied to Joseph of Arimathea, the Passion and a sacred bloodline. The discussion evaluates 20th-century interpretations (J. L. Weston, T. S. Eliot, Jung/Campbell, Holy Blood/Da Vinci Code) and rejects diffuse Jungian, prehistoric pagan or purely psychological origins in favour of a historically specific late 12th–early 13th-century Latin Christendom context: crusading fervour, the Albigensian Crusade, Cistercian influence, debates over Eucharistic doctrine and the sacralization of knighthood. They argue the grail narratives functioned as recruiting, doctrinal and cultural tools for militant Christendom, while later reinterpretations attempt to supply 'software' to meanings now obscured by historical distance.
title: The Mystery of the Holy Grail (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the history, biblical traditions, and later mythologies surrounding the Ark of the Covenant, framing the discussion through Raiders of the Lost Ark and popular culture. They outline the Ark's description in Exodus and its paradoxical role across biblical texts — as a divine throne/footstool, a container for the tablets of law, and a weapon-like manifestation of God’s presence. The hosts recount episodes in Judges and the Ark’s capture by the Philistines, its return, David’s triumphal entry in Jerusalem, and the later disappearance before the post-exilic and Roman periods. The episode surveys competing theories about the Ark’s origin and fate — Egyptian or Phoenician influences, hiding before the Babylonian conquest, relocation traditions (notably Ethiopian Kebra Nagast claims), and modern sensational claims popularized by writers such as Graham Hancock. They reflect on how the Ark’s physical absence transformed its theological role in Judaism and Christianity and close by situating the episode as part one of an Indiana Jones double bill with the Grail to follow.
title: Raiders of the Lost Ark (Ep 1)

summary: This episode (the second part of a two-part survey) examines J. Robert Oppenheimer's life after the Trinity test and the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Oppenheimer's mixed responses—public acclaim, private anguish, and a turn toward internationalism—his fraught meeting with President Truman, and the growing Cold War context that shaped US policy. They trace debates over the hydrogen bomb (with Edward Teller as a prominent advocate), the rise of anti-communist paranoia, FBI surveillance, and the escalating feud with Lewis Strauss. The hosts detail the suspension and public review of Oppenheimer's security clearance, Teller's controversial testimony, and the verdict that effectively removed him from policy influence while transforming him into a martyr figure. The episode closes with Oppenheimer's partial rehabilitation in later years, his declining health, and reflections on his complex legacy as a scientist who both shaped and agonized over the nuclear age.
title: Oppenheimer: The Witch Hunt (Ep 2)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (part one of a multi-part look at Oppenheimer) traces Julius Robert "J. Robert" Oppenheimer’s life from his privileged New York upbringing through his intellectual development and central role in the Manhattan Project. Holland and Sandbrook discuss Oppenheimer’s character, early studies in chemistry and physics, time at Cambridge and Göttingen, and his eccentric personal life (including relationships with Jean Tatlock and Kitty Harrison). The hosts outline his political associations in 1930s California, resulting FBI scrutiny, and the sequence of events that led Colonel Leslie R. Groves to appoint Oppenheimer director of the Los Alamos laboratory. Scientific developments (Hahn and Strassmann’s fission discovery, uranium isotope U-235) and allied projects (Tube Alloys, Uranium Committee) are covered, culminating in the selection of the Trinity test site and the first detonation on 16 July 1945. The episode sets up the second part, which will examine the bombings of Japan and Oppenheimer’s later downfall and partial rehabilitation.
title: Oppenheimer: The Father of the Atom Bomb (Ep 1)

summary: This episode (the second in the programme's Oscar Wilde series) recounts the collapse of Wilde's libel suit, the subsequent committal proceedings at Bow Street and the two criminal trials in 1895 that ended with his conviction and a two-year sentence with hard labour. The hosts review witness testimony compiled against Wilde, the contrasting behavior of judges and barristers, and the political pressure that drove further prosecution. They describe Wilde's treatment in prison — solitary confinement, enforced regimen, illness — and his later transfer to Reading Gaol where kinder governors and fellow inmates allowed him to write, producing De Profundis. The episode addresses public reaction, the roles of Lord Alfred Douglas (Bosie) and the Marquess of Queensberry, contemporaneous debates about homosexuality and morality, and campaigns such as W. T. Stead's age-of-consent crusade. Finally, they consider Wilde's tragic post-prison decline and his complex legacy as both martyr and emblem of emerging ideas about homosexuality in Britain.
title: The Trials of Oscar Wilde: Downfall and Prison (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Oscar Wilde's literary brilliance and the circumstances that led to his public downfall. They outline Wilde's rise — Oxford education, editorship, Dorian Gray, Salome and comic plays — and his increasingly public same-sex relationships from the mid-1880s, especially with Robbie Ross and Alfred Lord Douglas ("Bosie"). The discussion situates Wilde's behaviour within changing legal and medical frameworks: the Buggery Act legacy, the 1885 criminalization of "gross indecency," and contemporary German sexology (Richard von Kraft-Ebbing). The episode narrates the escalating feud with the Marquis of Queensbury, Wilde's libel suit, the unravelling of his case at the Old Bailey (with Edward Carson and Sir Edward Clark prominent), and the transfer of evidence to Crown prosecutors that resulted in Wilde's arrest. The hosts debate interpretations of Wilde as martyr versus exploiter, and close with John Betjeman's poetic account of the arrest.
title: The Trials of Oscar Wilde: Sex and Scandal (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life, death and posthumous cult of Antinous, the exceptionally beautiful young Greek associated with Emperor Hadrian. They outline Antinous’s origins in Bithynia, his education and travels with Hadrian, and the circumstances of his drowning on the Nile during the festival of Osiris around 130 CE. The episode examines Roman and Greek sexual norms, the role of delicati and eunuchs, and why Antinous’s Greek identity and mythic resonances (Ganymede, Hylas) made him a powerful symbol. The hosts explore competing explanations for Antinous’s death — accident, sacrifice, suicide, murder or flight — and describe Hadrian’s extraordinary reaction: visions, a star, the founding of Antinopolis, and the establishment of a syncretic cult that spread across the eastern empire. They consider archaeological evidence (many surviving statues), Christian reactions, and cultural afterlives (including Oscar Wilde’s interest). The episode frames Antinous as both a product of ancient erotic culture and a figure whose story resonates in modern discussions of love, power and identity.
title: Hadrian and Antinous

summary: Recorded in the GPO in Dublin, this episode (the fourth and final in the series on Ireland and its relations with Britain) features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Paul Rouse, Professor of History at University College Dublin. The discussion traces the causes, participants and course of the Easter Rising (Easter Monday, 24 April 1916): the role of the Irish Republican Brotherhood, the Irish Citizen Army, cultural nationalism and figures such as Patrick Pearse, Tom Clarke, James Connolly and Roger Casement. Rouse explains the failed German arms shipment, the split in the Volunteers, the improvised seizure of key Dublin sites, the British military response (artillery, gunboats) and the destruction of Sackville/O'Connell Street. The episode examines the immediate political impact — the executions, internments and the rapid rise of Sinn Féin as a political vehicle — and reflects on counterfactuals and the Rising's longer-term role in leading to guerrilla warfare, the War of Independence and the Free State.
title: Ireland: The Easter Rising, 1916 (Ep 4)

summary: This episode examines the British side of the Home Rule crisis of 1912–1914, arguing that Edwardian Britain was poised on the brink of civil conflict over Irish Home Rule. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by historian Dan Jackson, whose work on popular opposition to Home Rule foregrounds how unionist sentiment in places such as Liverpool, Glasgow and the industrial north coalesced behind leaders like Sir Edward Carson and political figures including Andrew Bonar Law and F.E. Smith. They trace how parliamentary developments (the Parliament Act 1911), mass mobilisation (the Ulster Covenant and formation of the Ulster Volunteers), gun-running, and army unwillingness to act (Curragh Mutiny) created a stalemate that was only forestalled by the outbreak of the First World War. The episode situates anti-Catholic and imperial anxieties within broader Edwardian politics and shows how wartime suspension of Home Rule postponed, but did not erase, the conflict that would culminate in the Easter Rising and later Irish independence struggles.
title: Ireland: Home Rule, Mutiny - and Civil War? (Ep 3)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (a multi-part sweep of the interwoven histories of Ireland, England and Britain) features hosts Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland with guest Paul Rouse of University College Dublin. They continue from the previous episode by tracing Irish political and social developments from Wolfe Tone and the 1798 rebellion through the Act of Union, Catholic Emancipation under Daniel O'Connell, and the ambivalent Anglo-Irish loyalties exemplified by figures like the Duke of Wellington. The discussion focuses on the demographic and economic pressures that produced the Great Famine (1845–1849), British government responses and contested culpability, and the long-term political consequences including mass emigration. They chart later nineteenth-century movements: land agitation, the Land War, the rise of Charles Stewart Parnell and the Irish Parliamentary Party, the Home Rule campaigns, the constitutional changes around the Parliament Act of 1911, and the tense lead-up to 1914 when civil war in Britain/ Ireland seemed possible. The episode closes by previewing a follow-up about the Home Rule crisis and the Easter Rising.
title: Ireland: Union, Famine and Parnell (Ep 2)

summary: Recorded at the GPO in Dublin with guest Professor Paul Rouse, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace roughly 800 years of Anglo‑Irish history as a preface to a future episode on the Easter Rising itself. The discussion moves from Viking Dublin and the Norman arrival (Strongbow, Richard Fitzgillbert, Henry II) through the uneven English lordship, the Tudor reformation and Henry VIII’s assumption of the Irish kingship, to plantations, the Ulster settlement and the deepening link between land, religion and identity. They examine the seventeenth‑century crises — the 1641 rebellion, Cromwell’s 1649 campaign and the transplantation of populations — then the consolidation of the Protestant ascendancy after the Battle of the Boyne and the penal laws. The episode covers late‑eighteenth‑century radicalism (the United Irishmen and 1798), the Act of Union and the cultural currents (romantic nationalism, language revival) that feed into republicanism and ultimately the 1916 proclamation. Recurring themes are land dispossession, religious division, myth‑making and how competing histories shaped modern Ireland.
title: Ireland: Celts, Conquest and Cromwell (Ep 1)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host John Dickey to discuss his book The Craft: How the Freemasons Made the Modern World. The episode traces Freemasonry's transformation from medieval stonemason lore into an eighteenth-century club and then a global institution: key moments include the court of James VI, the foundation of the Grand Lodge in 1717 and the Anderson's Constitutions (1723). Dickey and the hosts examine Masonic rituals, their intentionally banal "secrets," and how those practices provided civic ceremony useful to the founding of the United States. They cover the long history of anti‑Masonic conspiracy theories — notably the Léo Taxil hoax and Catholic hostility culminating in papal condemnations — and the diverse political afterlives of Masonry, from imperial networks in India to brutal repression under Franco, Nazi bans, and the P2 scandal in Italy. The conversation also addresses Prince Hall Freemasonry and African American civil‑rights links, plus popular and celebrity Freemasons, showing how the movement intersects with broader modern history.
title: The Freemasons: History's Greatest Conspiracy Theory

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the origins and character of Athenian democracy.
