Using myth (Athena, Erechtheus, Theseus) and constitutional history, they trace social tensions in Archaic Athens — Solon's reforms, the rival aristocratic families, the rise and rule of Peisistratos and his sons, and the Spartan intervention — leading to Cleisthenes' radical restructuring (demes, tribes, thirds) around 507–506 BC. They emphasise that Athenian democracy was not rights-based in a modern sense but embedded in religion, autochthony and communal ritual, including distinctive roles for women and cult practices. The episode argues Cleisthenes framed reform as ancestral restoration to legitimate novelty and shows how later readers reinvented Athens as a modern model. They also discuss how the Athenians' uses of democracy (and its collapse in later wars) shaped subsequent perceptions in the Renaissance, English Civil War and French Revolution. The conversation touches on historiography and how modern assumptions (materialism and Christian-derived ideas of rights) distort understanding of the ancient political mindset.
title: Athens and the Birth of Democracy

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines England's tumultuous 1650s after the 1649 execution of Charles I. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by historian Anna Kay, author of The Restless Republic, Written Without a Crown. They discuss the immediate constitutional confusion after the king's death, the abolition of the House of Lords and establishment of the Commonwealth, tensions between Parliament and the army, and radical movements such as the Diggers led by Gerard Winstanley. Case studies include Charlotte, Countess of Derby's holdout on the Isle of Man, the opportunistic newspaperman Marchmont Needham, and the role of William Petty in mapping and redistributing Irish land after Cromwell's campaigns. The conversation covers Cromwell's actions — both administrative and brutal in Ireland — his 1653 coup, the Major-Generals, and the weak succession of Richard Cromwell that culminated in General George Monk's intervention and the 1660 Restoration. The episode weighs the decade's failures and its longer-term constitutional and cultural legacies.
title: The Republic of Britain: Life Under Cromwell

summary: This episode examines H. Rider Haggard and his formative influence on late-Victorian popular culture, focusing on King Solomon's Mines (1885) and its thematic siblings, notably She. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook outline Haggard's life — his years in South Africa, fascination with the Zulus, brief ostrich-farming interlude, and rapid literary success after reading Treasure Island — then parse the novels' plot devices, racial assumptions and masculine fellowship. They situate Haggard in the wider imperial moment (Berlin Conference; Scramble for Africa), link the myth of Ophir/Great Zimbabwe to contemporary archaeological claims, and discuss how Haggard's tropes (lost civilizations, the quest map, dangerous sorceresses) seeded later popular culture from Tolkien and early cinema to Wilbur Smith, Indiana Jones and even Black Panther. The hosts also confront Haggard's racism, social-Darwinist rhetoric and anxieties about racial degeneration while noting the narrative complexity that prevents his work from being mere propaganda. The episode closes by tracing Haggard's enduring legacy in adventure fiction and film.
title: King Solomon's Mines

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Malcolm Gaskell about witchcraft and early colonial life in 17th-century New England, centring on his book The Ruin of All Witches. The conversation opens with a vivid account from Springfield, Connecticut, and follows the lives of William Pynchon (founder), and the married couple Mary Lewis (later Mary Parsons) and Hugh Parsons. Gaskell explains Puritan beliefs, the economic drivers (land, fur trade) and social pressures that shaped accusations of witchcraft. He highlights the role of childbirth anxieties and midwives—citing the 1648 hanging of midwife Margaret Jones—and discusses how local rumors escalated into formal slander and court cases. The episode emphasizes that many accusations failed in court, noting low conviction rates, and links the darker mood to news of unrest in England. It also situates Springfield within later conflicts with Native Americans in the 1670s and reflects on continuities between colonial social dynamics and later American life.
title: American Witches

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Herodotus — his life, methods and enduring appeal — drawing on Tom Holland's Penguin translation and his children's book The Wolf Girl, The Greeks and The Gods. They situate Herodotus in fifth-century BC Halicarnassus, emphasize his cosmopolitan perspective on the Persian Empire and his role as the first major prose historian, travel writer and ethnographer. The episode examines Herodotus' method of recording oral testimony, his famous digressions (Egypt, odd customs, “giant ants”), and debates over his reliability. Key figures and episodes are discussed: Xerxes, Darius, Cambyses, Themistocles, Leonidas and the major encounters of the Greco-Persian Wars (Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea). Themes include cultural relativism, the rise and fall of empires, and Herodotus' mix of admiration and critique for both Greeks and Persians. The episode ends by placing Herodotus' warnings about power and empire in a longer historical framework and promoting Holland's translations and related works.
title: Herodotus: The Birth of History

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook conclude their multi-episode tour of British coronations, tracing the shift from sacral rite to public spectacle across the Hanoverian, Victorian and modern eras. They recount chaotic and extravagant episodes — George I's Latin coronation amid riots (1714–15), Handel composing Zadok the Priest for George II (1727), the shambolic George III banquet (1761), George IV's ludicrously lavish 1821 coronation and the removal of many medieval trappings under William IV. They discuss Victorian and Edwardian spectacles, imperial displays (including the Delhi Durbar and an Imperial Crown of India), and the 20th-century transition to mass media: George VI's radio coronation and Elizabeth II's televised 1953 event, which coincided with news of Everest's conquest. Recurrent themes are the tension between religious sacrality and popular theatrics, riots and picnics at banquets, and evolving public engagement with coronations. The episode closes by reflecting on Charles's upcoming coronation and whether modern Britain views these rituals as meaningful, entertaining or obsolete.
title: Coronations: Chaos, Ceremony and Empire (Ep 3)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the political, religious and performative history of English coronations from the Anglo-Saxon period through the Stuarts. Using anecdotes — Edwy’s scandal after his 956 coronation, William the Conqueror’s troubled Christmas Day investiture, Tudor pageantry (Henry VIII, Anne Boleyn, Elizabeth I), and Stuart-era upheavals — they show how coronations reflect legitimacy anxieties: usurpers beef up ritual, reformers trim it, and restored rulers amplify spectacle. They discuss medieval sources and coronation oils, Shakespeare’s treatment of anointing (Richard II, Henry V, Macbeth), and key episodes such as Henry VI’s French coronation, Cromwell’s protectorate investiture, the Restoration, and the Glorious Revolution oath for William and Mary. Pepys’s eyewitness account and the evolution of regalia, rituals and public pageantry underline how coronations serve propaganda, religion and national identity. The episode sets up a continuation into Georgian and modern coronations.
title: Coronations: Sex, Holy Oil and Civil War (Ep 2)

summary: This episode is the first of a three-part series on coronations. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the British coronation ceremony back to ancient roots — from Bronze Age and Near Eastern precedents through Old Testament anointing traditions, Roman and Byzantine ceremonial models, and the Carolingian adoption of anointing. They discuss physical elements (regalia, the coronation chair, Cosmati pavement, the Stone of Scone) and liturgical continuity (the Liber Regalis, the 10th-century ordo and Edgar's 973 coronation in Bath). The episode explains how figures such as Dunstan shaped the medieval English rite, how anointing connects kings to biblical models (Saul, David, Solomon), and how later events (Charles I's execution, Charles II's 1661 coronation, Edward I's removal of the Stone) affected the material tradition. Holland and Sandbrook set out the plan for future episodes to examine medieval and modern coronations and reflect on public responses to such a profoundly ancient ritual in the 21st century.
title: Coronations: The Deep History (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Sir Christopher Clark about his wide-ranging book Revolutionary Spring: Fighting for a New World, 1848–1849. The conversation situates the 1848 revolutions in their social, economic and communicative contexts—bad harvests of 1846–47, urban discontent, political plurality (many competing socialisms and liberalisms), and the accelerating spread of news across Europe. Clark emphasises the contingent, multi-intentioned nature of the revolutions, their rapid contagion from Sicily and Paris across the continent, and the dramatic arc from spring euphoria to summer fracturing and autumnal repression (notably in Vienna). Personal stories such as Robert Blum’s trajectory and execution illustrate human costs. The discussion also addresses why Britain largely avoided revolution (policing, colonial transportation of agitators, economic measures) and the longer-term legacies: surviving constitutions (Switzerland, Denmark, Netherlands, Piedmont), the remaking of Catholicism, and the rise of managed nationalism under statesmen like Bismarck. The episode ends with a sung translation of Burns’ “For All That.”
title: The Year of Revolutions: 1848

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) recounts the chaotic final days of Saigon in April 1975 and examines the immediate and long-term consequences for Vietnam and the United States. Using contemporary eyewitness accounts (notably a Chicago Daily News correspondent) the hosts vividly describe the U.S. embassy evacuation, helicopters lifting off, Marines’ last departures, and the desperate crowds outside the compound. They discuss the fate of South Vietnamese—re-education camps, economic collapse, the boat people exodus—and wider regional fallout including Vietnam’s intervention in Cambodia and subsequent conflicts. The episode also surveys American cultural responses (films like Apocalypse Now and The Deer Hunter, Born on the Fourth of July) and political lessons drawn thereafter, contrasting narratives of victimhood, humiliation, and later interventionist tendencies. Comparisons to earlier imperial withdrawals (e.g., Kabul 1842) and debates over whether Vietnam offered any coherent foreign-policy lesson conclude the discussion.
title: Fall of Saigon: Apocalypse Now (Ep 2)

summary: This episode (part one of a two-part series) analyzes the lead-up to the Fall of Saigon in April 1975. Holland and Sandbrook sketch the geopolitical and domestic context: the legacy of French colonialism, the defeat at Dien Bien Phu, the Paris Peace Accords (1973), Nixon-era bombing and Cambodian incursions, and the political effects of Watergate that constrained later US responses (Case–Church Amendment and the War Powers Resolution). They track the North Vietnamese and Viet Cong offensives of 1974–75, the collapse of South Vietnamese defenses, President Nguyễn Văn Thiệu's resignation, and the agonized deliberations in Washington (Gerald R. Ford, Henry Kissinger) over aid and evacuation. The hosts recount chaotic evacuation scenes (Da Nang, private airlifts, Operation Babylift) and the simultaneous catastrophe unfolding in Cambodia with the Khmer Rouge’s advance and Phnom Penh’s fall. Throughout, they emphasize moral and practical dilemmas—abandonment vs. intervention—and set up the climactic events (rooftop helicopter evacuations, embassy scenes) to be covered in part two.
title: Fall of Saigon: The Nightmare Begins  (Ep 1)

description:
Rin Tin Tin, born on the Western Front in 1918, became one of the biggest movie stars of the silent film era. Greyfriars Bobby gained his fame for guarding his masters' grave for 14 years, until the day he died. 
Bounce, Admiral Collingwood’s loyal companion, would hide below deck during the Napoleonic Wars, and Collingwood would sing to him after battle, to calm his nerves. Nixon's dog Checkers saved his political career, but never lived to see the White House.
The wolfhound Gelert, who died protecting his master's infant son, and Blondi, Hitler's German Shepherd, were both put to death by their owners. 
Join Tom and Dominic as they discuss history's most famous dogs.


*The Rest Is History Live Tour 2023*:

Tom and Dominic are going on an international tour in 2023 and performing in London, Edinburgh, Salford, Dublin, Washington D.C. and New York! 

Buy your tickets here: restishistorypod.com

Twitter: 

@TheRestHistory

@holland_tom

@dcsandbrook
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a whimsical but informative episode listing their seven greatest dogs in history. They open with Boson, Lord Byron's dog, then discuss Checkers, Richard Nixon’s famous cocker spaniel and the 1952 “Checkers speech.” They examine Greyfriars Bobby and the mixture of legend and later embellishment surrounding the Edinburgh terrier, and touch on Eleanor Atkinson’s novel that popularized the tale. The episode covers Adolf Hitler’s dogs (including Blondie) and how canine devotion complicates perceptions of historical villains. Mythic and semi-legendary dogs such as Gellert (associated with Llewelyn the Great) are considered, followed by Lootie, a Pekingese taken to Queen Victoria after the Sack of the Summer Palace, and Bounce, Admiral Cuthbert Collingwood’s ship dog at Trafalgar. They finish with Rin Tin Tin, rescued in WWI and turned into a Hollywood star. The conversation mixes cultural context, anecdotes, occasional skepticism, and reflections on how animals shape human stories.
title: History's Greatest Dogs

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Katja Heuer about her new book Beyond the Wall: East Germany, 1949–1990. The conversation traces the GDR's origins in the Second World War aftermath, the contested decision to create a separate East German state, and the influence of German communists who lived through Stalinist exile and purges. Heuer outlines early postwar violence and looting, land reforms, refugee pressures, and the mass exodus to the West that culminated in the 1953 uprising and Soviet intervention. The discussion covers Ulbricht’s and Honecker’s contrasting leaderships, cultural life (music, the Puhdys, Dean Reed), consumer features like the Trabant and fridges, East German sports programmes and doping, the pervasive but uneven reach of the Stasi, and daily lived experience. Heuer closes by describing 1989’s events, the sudden collapse of the regime, and the long social and cultural legacies that continue to distinguish east and west Germany.
title: East Germany: Life Behind the Iron Curtain

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) examines the aftermath of the English victories at Crécy and Poitiers and the consequences of John II of France's capture and ransom. The Treaty of Bretigny initially seems to secure vast territories for Edward III and the Black Prince, but French collapse, peasant revolt (the Jacquerie), and roaming free companies create lasting disorder. The Black Prince’s rule in an expanded Aquitaine is destabilised by taxation, the free companies, and his costly Castilian adventure, which leaves him ill and indebted. Edward III’s final expedition fails to secure total conquest; negotiations at Bretigny and Lancaster’s counsel lead to temporary settlements. Charles V (the former Dauphin) and his constable (named in the episode) rebuild French strength through attrition and strategic recovery, retaking most English gains except Calais. The episode concludes with the decline and deaths of key leaders (Black Prince, Edward III), the fragile succession of young monarchs, and a preview of the later phases of the Hundred Years' War culminating in figures like Henry V and Joan of Arc.
title: Hundred Years' War: A Storm of Swords (Ep 4)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their series on the Hundred Years' War, examining how chivalric culture and the Black Death shaped mid-14th century Anglo-French conflict. They open with readings from Arthur Conan Doyle's Sir Nigel and reference Barbara Tuckman's A Distant Mirror to set the plague-strewn backdrop. The hosts contrast English military innovation and prestige under Edward III with French attempts to restore martial honor through Geoffrey de Charny's Order of the Star. Edward's creation of the Order of the Garter and its Arthurian spectacle is discussed as propaganda and noble cohesion. The episode follows the Black Prince (Edward of Woodstock) on his 1355 chevauchée through rich southern France, and culminates in a detailed narrative of the 1356 campaign and the Battle of Poitiers, where the English win a decisive victory and capture John II of France. Throughout, they emphasize the tension between chivalric ideals and brutal practical warfare, and set up the consequences to be explored in the next episode.
title: Hundred Year's War: The Black Prince (Ep 3)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the early campaigns of the Hundred Years' War, focusing on Edward III's strategy of taking the war to France, the use of alliances (notably with cities in Flanders), and the military technologies that transformed medieval warfare. They trace economic and political pressures — including English wool export bans, loans from Italian bankers, and the resulting financial collapse — that shaped Edward's campaigns. Key battles covered include the naval victory at Sluys (1340) and the decisive land victory at Crécy (1346), where longbowmen and early field cannon played a central role. The episode follows Edward's subsequent operations: raids through Normandy, the crossing of the Somme, the march toward Paris, and the lengthy siege and capture of Calais (1346–1347). It closes by noting concurrent events — Scottish defeats at Neville's Cross and the sudden arrival of the Black Death in 1347 — which will dramatically alter the course of the war in future episodes.
title: Hundred Years' War: Triumph of the Longbow (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts discuss the cultural and political background to the outbreak of the Hundred Years' War, opening with a reading from Arthur Conan Doyle's Sir Nigel and contrasting literary and scholarly views (Conan Doyle vs Barbara Tuchman). They outline France's dominance in the early 14th century, the expansion of the Capetian royal domain, and the diminished Angevin holdings of the English crown (Gascony, Aquitaine). The episode traces the dynastic crisis after Philip IV of France, the rapid succession and deaths of his sons, and the accession of Philip VI of Valois. The hosts narrate English domestic turbulence — the reign and fall of Edward II, Isabella and Roger Mortimer's intervention, and Edward III's assumption of power — and explain how the Scottish–French alliance and disputes over Gascony produced escalating tensions. The episode ends with Edward III's 1337 manifesto and the strategic importance of the longbow, setting up subsequent episodes on key battles such as Sluys and Crécy.
title: Hundred Years' War: A Game of Thrones (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by anthropologist and historian Luke Pepperer to survey female military and political leadership across African history. The conversation opens with the Dahomey Agoji (the so-called "Amazons") and their contested portrayal in popular culture, then moves to an extended profile of Njinga of Ndongo (a seventeenth-century ruler who negotiated with and fought the Portuguese, allied with the Dutch, and reconstituted her realm). Pepperer also discusses Ashanti Queen Mothers — especially Yaa Santewa and her role in resisting British demands over the Golden Stool — and the controversial reign of Ranavalona (Madagascar) and her anti-Christian policies. Themes include the relationship between gender, ritual, and military institutions; the role of European observers and propaganda in shaping reputations; and slavery, diplomacy and warfare in West and Central Africa. Pepperer’s forthcoming book Motherland is mentioned as ongoing work that frames many of these episodes in long-term African history.
title: African Amazons

summary: This episode examines the life and activism of Benjamin Lay (1681–1759), an eccentric Quaker activist whose experiences in Barbados and later in Pennsylvania drove him to radical early abolitionism. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Lay’s background in Essex, his move with his wife Sarah to Barbados, and the brutal, industrialized system of Caribbean slavery that transformed both their consciences. The hosts discuss Lay’s vegetarianism, his pamphlet All Slave Keepers That Keep the Innocent in Bondage Apostates (printed by Benjamin Franklin), and his theatrical protests — including a famous stunt involving a blood-like pokeberry display inside a Quaker meeting. The episode situates Lay within wider Quaker radicalism, earlier critics like Bartolomé de las Casas, and the evolving Anglo-American abolitionist tradition. It covers graphic plantation violence (citing Thomas Thistlewood’s journal), Lay’s later life in Pennsylvania, and his role in shifting Quaker opinion toward opposing slavery.
title: The First Abolitionist

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue a multi-part exploration of the Atlantis myth, tracing its origins in Plato's Timaeus and how the story was reworked across the Renaissance, early modern utopian literature, 19th-century popularizers and 20th-century esoteric and political movements. They discuss early modern readings that equated Atlantean survivors with peoples encountered during the Age of Discovery, and the rise of influential figures such as Ignatius Donnelly, whose 1882 Atlantis book popularized the idea of a prehistoric antediluvian civilization seeding world cultures. The episode examines later occult and clairvoyant contributions (Edgar Cayce), the Nazi appropriation of Atlantean ideas, and academically-grounded archaeological theories linking Minoan Crete and the Thera eruption to aspects of the myth. They critique modern pseudo-archaeology (e.g., Graham Hancock) while acknowledging its cultural appeal and thematic resonance with Plato’s warnings about hubris and environmental catastrophe.
title: Atlantis: Legacy of the Lost Empire (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the origins and afterlife of the Atlantis story, contrasting Graham Hancock’s modern cataclysmic thesis (as presented in his book Magicians of the Gods and Netflix's Ancient Apocalypse) with Plato’s original account. They trace Atlantis to Plato’s dialogues—the Timaeus and Critias—contextualising the tale within Plato’s life, Athenian politics and classical historiography. The hosts argue Plato likely crafted Atlantis as a literary-political parable, blending elements from Herodotus and Thucydides and drawing on contemporary memories of earthquakes and tsunamis, rather than preserving an 11,000+ year-old cataclysmic history. They discuss how later receptions transformed Atlantis—sometimes read literally, sometimes allegorically—and preview a second episode that will explore the revival of Atlantis in later centuries and modern pseudo-historical claims.
title: Atlantis: The Legend (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook speak with historian Peter Frankopan about the long relationship between climate (and the wider natural world) and human history. Using examples from the Curse of Akkad (~2250 BC) through the Roman Warm Period, the Justinianic Plague (6th century), volcanic episodes such as Santorini and Tambora, the Little Ice Age and the Industrial Revolution, Frankopan argues that climate and environmental shifts have repeatedly reshaped societies — sometimes triggering disease, migration and political change, sometimes reinforcing elites. The conversation stresses new scientific tools (ice cores, tree rings, pollen, genomics, satellite imagery) that let historians test and nuance old narratives. They cover modern consequences: fossil-fuel driven warming since the 20th century, biodiversity loss, unequal responsibilities between rich and poor regions, and the political challenges of adaptation. Frankopan is cautiously optimistic about human resilience but warns of cascading ecological risks and governance failures if mitigation and adaptation are neglected.
title: Climate Apocalypse

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Ronald Reagan's presidency across his first and second terms, emphasising image, policy and pivotal episodes. They open with the iconic 'Morning in America' ad and analyse Reagan's talent for performance and parable, his inauguration style and recovery after the 1981 assassination attempt. Domestically they trace Reaganomics — supply-side tax cuts, David Stockman's role, rising defence spending and ballooning deficits — and decisive moves like the firing of air traffic controllers. They criticise the administration's slow response to AIDS and narrate the complex Iran–Contra scandal: secret arms-for-hostages dealings and covert funding of the Contras. Internationally they map Reagan's hardline Cold War rhetoric alongside his intense concern about nuclear weapons, STAR WARS/SDI, and the summits with Mikhail Gorbachev that led to de‑escalation and the INF Treaty. The hosts weigh Reagan's legacy as a master of presidential image who reshaped Republican politics while leaving contested economic and ethical records.
title: Reagan, Iran-Contra and the Cold War (Ep 3)

summary: This episode traces Ronald Wilson Reagan's transition from mid‑century Hollywood actor to national political figure. Holland and Sandbrook examine Reagan's 1964 alignment with Barry Goldwater that raised his political profile, his role as General Electric's television ambassador and plant tourer (which radicalised and honed his political rhetoric), and his marriage to Nancy Davis Reagan. They discuss the sources that shaped his politics (Reader's Digest, Human Events), his appeal to suburban Sun Belt voters and businessmen, and his pragmatic record as governor of California after the 1966 campaign. The hosts cover Reagan's failed 1976 primary challenge to Gerald Ford, the political environment of the 1970s (oil shock, Watergate, Panama Canal debate), and how Carter-era crises (economic malaise, the Iran hostage crisis) opened the path for Reagan's successful 1980 run. The episode addresses controversies—welfare parables and the Neshoba County Fair “states’ rights” speech—and sets up the concluding episode on Reagan's presidency.
title: Reagan: The Road to the White House (Ep 2)

summary: This episode is the first of a multi-part series surveying the life of Ronald Reagan. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Reagan's origins in Tampico, Illinois (born 1911), his Midwestern small-town upbringing, family dynamics, faith, and early love of sport and performance. They follow his career from college at Eureka, to radio sportscasting in the Midwest, to a Warner Brothers acting contract and B-film career (including King’s Row and Knute Rockne, All American). The discussion covers Reagan's wartime propaganda work, his leadership in the Screen Actors Guild, his evolving anti-communism amid Hollywood union disputes and HUAC pressures, and the personal shifts—divorce from Jane Wyman, later marriage to Nancy Davis—that shaped his politics. Themes include Reagan’s performative sincerity, his blending of fantasy and reality, and how cultural touchstones (movies, Reader’s Digest, faith) forged his worldview. The hosts preview forthcoming episodes covering General Electric, the Goldwater campaign, his governorship, and the presidency.
title: Ronald Reagan and the American Dream (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Christopher Columbus's later voyages, his declining health and reputation, and the immediate administrative and moral fallout of his governorship in Hispaniola. They recount the third and fourth voyages (including his near-arrival at South America, the Orinoco estuary, navigation of the Caribbean, shipwreck on Jamaica, and rescue), the emergence of the encomienda system, and the Spanish crown's intervention (Bobadilla). The episode then moves to Columbus’s posthumous reputation: early Spanish criticism (notably Bartolomé de las Casas), the later mythologizing of Columbus in the United States (manifest destiny, Knights of Columbus, Columbus Day), and the 1992 quincentenary debates. They weigh arguments about culpability for slavery and indigenous demographic collapse, emphasize historical context, and recommend Carlos Fuentes's Terra Nostra as a literary way to engage the subject. The hosts conclude that Columbus was a complex figure whose achievements and atrocities resist simple moral categorization.
title: Columbus: Villain or Hero? (Ep 4)

summary: This episode (part three of the podcast’s series on Christopher Columbus) follows Columbus’s return to Spain and his rushed second voyage to the Caribbean. Holland and Sandbrook discuss the political and religious context — Ferdinand II and Isabella I, papal intervention in May 1493 that divided territorial claims, and the Treaty of Tordesillas — and the Spanish desire for gold, conversion and colonists. They narrate the second expedition’s scale, the capture and shipment of indigenous people, accusations of cannibalism, sexual violence, and the collapse of the settlement La Navidad. The hosts explore early Spanish debates over slavery and conversion (including figures such as Bartolomé de las Casas), the beginnings of tribute/encomienda practices, disease, and ecological impacts that foreshadow the Columbian Exchange. They cite historians and books (Hugh Thomas’s Rivers of Gold; Fernando Cervantes’s Conquistadores; Tom Holland’s Dominion), note contemporary controversies over Columbus’s legacy, and preview subsequent episodes covering the third and fourth voyages and broader historical assessment.
title: Columbus: Death in the Caribbean (Ep 3)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate the preparation, voyage and immediate aftermath of Christopher Columbus's first Atlantic expedition (1492). They cover recruitment at Palos, the three ships (Niña, Pinta, Santa María) and key crew figures — notably the Pinzón brothers — and discuss navigation, instruments and the decision to sail with prevailing winds. The hosts describe growing tension aboard, Columbus's dual ship logs and his leadership tussle with Martín Pinzón, culminating in landfall (likely Guanahani) on 12 October 1492. They examine first encounters with Taíno peoples, Columbus's immediate claims for the Crown, taking captives and the search for gold, and the wrecking of the Santa María leading to the foundation of La Navidad. The episode closes with Columbus's return to Spain, royal reception, contemporary reactions and the seeds of later controversy over enslavement, exploitation and European expansion. The hosts reference Hugh Thomas's Rivers of Gold and preview further voyages and debates to come.
title: Columbus: A New World? (Ep 2)

summary: This episode examines Christopher Columbus's origins, character and the political and maritime context that produced his voyages. Holland and Sandbrook discuss the strong Genoese roots of Columbus, his early maritime career in the Mediterranean and Portugal, and the intellectual milieu — printing, travel accounts (Marco Polo), and theorists like Toscanelli and Pierre Dailly — that convinced him a westward route to Asia was possible. They trace Columbus's persistent efforts to secure royal backing, his contacts with the Franciscan monastery of La Rábida, and repeated rejections by Portuguese and Spanish authorities before Ferdinand and Isabella finally commissioned him in April 1492. The hosts stress Columbus's personal ambitions for titles and status, the financial and crusading motives of the Spanish crown (including the recent conquest of Granada and the impending expulsion of Jews), and the preexisting Iberian Atlantic expansion (Canary Islands, Madeira) that framed his enterprise. The episode ends by situating Columbus as both visionary and crank and previewing further episodes covering his voyages.
title: Columbus: The Adventure Begins (Ep 1)

summary: This episode continues the hosts' multi-part examination of Julius Caesar's assassination and its aftermath. Picking up from the killing, Tom and Dominic describe the chaotic days in Rome: Antony's shrewd manipulation of Caesar's funeral, the public reaction, and the conspirators' failure to secure political control. They follow the shifting alignments — Cicero's efforts to rally the Senate, Octavian's arrival as Caesar's heir and his rapid political and military ascent, Antony's campaigning in northern Italy, and the eventual formation of the Second Triumvirate with Lepidus. The hosts recount the brutal proscriptions, the hunt for the assassins, and the eastern campaign culminating in the twin battles at Philippi where Brutus and Cassius fall. The episode closes by reflecting on the Republic's end, Octavian's survival and eventual transformation into Augustus, and the historiographical debate about whether the Republic was already doomed by Rome's imperial expansion.
title: The Fall of the Roman Republic

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate the rise and fall of Gaius Julius Caesar, focusing on the political tensions that culminate in his assassination on the Ides of March (44 BC). They set the scene with Caesar's Gallic command, the Triumvirate with Pompey and Crassus, the crossing of the Rubicon and the civil wars that followed, and highlight key opponents such as Cato the Younger, Cicero, Cassius and Brutus. The episode covers Caesar's clemency, his urban and constitutional reforms (including the Julian calendar), his honors and appointment as dictator for life, and moments that inflamed senatorial opinion (Lupercalia, the diadem incident). The hosts recount the conspirators' motives and the chaotic murder at the Theatre of Pompey, concluding by teasing the immediate aftermath — which they say will be continued in the next installment and in a Rest Is History Club extra.
title: The Murder of Julius Caesar

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Cathars and the Albigensian Crusade, contextualizing the movement’s later mythologization (e.g. in The Da Vinci Code) and presenting the historical reality of the war launched under Pope Innocent III. They trace Innocent’s call to armed pilgrimage in 1209, major atrocities such as the massacre at Béziers and the sieges of Carcassonne and Minerve, and the rise of Simon de Montfort as the crusader leader. The conversation follows the long, brutal campaign, noting key dates and personalities (Philip II, Louis VIII, Raymond VI/VII) and the eventual 1229 settlement that transferred territory to the French crown while continuing persecution of heresy. They examine the cultural and institutional aftermath: the role of friars (Dominicans), inquisitorial methods informed by renewed interest in Aristotle, and how persecutory logic and administrative reform (Fourth Lateran Council) reshaped medieval society. The episode closes by reflecting on modern parallels and on how later writers and historians have reshaped the Cathar story.
title: The Bloodiest Crusade (Ep 3)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the historiography behind the Cathars and the Albigensian Crusade, arguing that much of the conventional narrative is misleading. They quote Mark Gregory Pegg and R. I. Moore to show that the label "Cathar" and the idea of a unified dualist church in Languedoc were later constructions. The hosts trace how 11th–12th century papal reform, the rise of universities, and heightened anxieties about heresy produced a climate that both invented and exaggerated supposed underground heretical movements. They discuss regional politics in southern France — including rival nobles, Henry II of England's interventions, and Raymond, Count of Toulouse — and how accusations of heresy became tools in local and international power struggles. The episode ends by relating the papal campaign, Pope Innocent III's obsession with heresy, and the murder of papal legate Peter de Castelnau, setting up the impending crusade against the region and promising a continuation of the story.
title: The Mystery of the Cathars (Ep 2)

summary: The hosts mark the twentieth anniversary of Dan Brown's The Da Vinci Code and use it to trace a 20th-century lineage of myths about secret bloodlines and hidden manuscripts back to medieval history. They explain how The Da Vinci Code draws on The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail (1982) and older local legends centred on Rennes-le-Château, recounting the roles of figures such as the priest Béranger Sonnier, restauranteur Noël Corbu, hoaxer Pierre Plantard and investigator Henry Lincoln. The episode situates these modern conspiracies alongside the historical Cathars of southern France and the violent Church response in the Albigensian Crusade, and it signals scholarly debate—citing Mark Gregory Pegg's A Most Holy War—that calls into question received narratives about Catharism. The hosts frame the story as both a detective tale of forgeries and popularisation, and as an entry point to forthcoming episodes that will examine who the Cathars really were and the brutal crusade against them.
title: The Real Da Vinci Code (Ep 1)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing historian Lucy Lethbridge about her book Servants: A Downstairs View of 20th Century Britain. The conversation contrasts popular depictions of servant life (notably Downton Abbey) with primary sources and memoirs, highlighting the hierarchy, long hours, gendered nature and often harsh physical labour of domestic service. Lethbridge explains the social roots of the grand Edwardian household, the feminization of domestic labour, and how the First World War, changing opportunities for women, economic pressures and cultural shifts eroded the culture of service. They discuss cultural representations (Jeeves, The Remains of the Day, Brideshead Revisited, Upstairs, Downstairs), immigrant domestic workers fleeing Nazi Europe, and the postwar replacement of paid domestic labour by unpaid domestic labour (the housewife) aided by labour-saving devices. The episode closes by reflecting on Britain’s recurring nostalgia for hierarchical domestic order despite its decline.
title: The Real Downton Abbey

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life, career and legacy of the Egyptian pharaoh Hatshepsut. They place her in the wider context of Egypt's recovery from the Hyksos period and the consolidation of the New Kingdom, outlining key predecessors and successors (Thutmose I–III) and the royal household dynamics that allowed Hatshepsut to rise from regent to proclaimed pharaoh. The conversation covers her claims to divine birth by Amun-Ra, adoption of pharaonic symbols (crowns, false beard, throne name), monumental building programs (Karnak obelisks, mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahri), the famous expedition to Punt, and her powerful minister Senenmut. They also discuss historiographical issues — sparse source material, later attempts to deface her monuments, and modern interpretations — and reference specific works and cultural touchstones (a book on Hatshepsut and an Agatha Christie novel). The episode weighs Hatshepsut’s unprecedented rule and why she remains a compelling subject for gender and ancient-history studies.
title: The Greatest Female Pharaoh

summary: This episode examines the rapid consolidation of Nazi power in Germany across early 1933. Using primary accounts (notably Joseph Goebbels' diary) and the work of historians such as Richard J. Evans and Ian Kershaw, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the steps from Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor (30 January 1933) through the Reichstag fire (27 February) and the Reichstag Fire Decree, to the March election and the Enabling Act that allowed Hitler to rule by decree. They describe how the Nazis secured the army and police, intimidated and arrested communists and social democrats, established Dachau, organized book burnings and the April boycott of Jewish businesses, and subsumed state institutions. The hosts reflect on causes — the First World War, Versailles, the Great Depression, intellectual currents and fear of Bolshevism — and debate contingency: how other decisions might have stopped Hitler, and whether similar democratic collapses could happen today. The episode balances narrative detail with broader reflections on human nature and political responsibility.
title: The Nazis: Total Power (Ep 4)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the final phase of the Weimar Republic and the Nazi rise to power. Using the story of Horst Wessel and Nazi pageantry, they show how youthful zeal, street violence and theatrical propaganda helped expand Nazi appeal, especially after the Great Depression and the Wall Street crash. They discuss the polarization between Nazis, communists and the mainstream parties, the abuse of emergency powers under Article 48, and ill-judged decisions by Weimar elites — notably Chancellor Heinrich Brüning, President Paul von Hindenburg, and the intrigues of Franz von Papen and General Kurt von Schleicher. Electoral gains in 1930–1932, the takeover of Prussia, factionalism among conservatives, and repeated dissolutions of the Reichstag create a stalemate that the establishment hopes to manage. Backroom deals in January 1933 culminate in Papen arranging Hitler’s appointment as chancellor on 30 January 1933, setting the stage for the Nazi seizure of power. The hosts promise a follow-up on the Reichstag fire and consolidation of the regime.
title: The Nazis: Hitler's Triumph (Ep 3)

summary: This episode, the second part of a multi-episode account of the rise of the Nazis, explains the fragile political, social and economic foundations of the Weimar Republic and how they shaped Adolf Hitler's early movement. Holland and Sandbrook outline Weimar’s contested legitimacy after defeat in World War I, the role of emergency presidential powers, widespread paramilitary violence, and pervasive inflation that culminated in hyperinflation and the French occupation of the Ruhr in 1923. They narrate the Beer Hall Putsch: Hitler’s failed coup in Munich, its chaotic execution with Ludendorff, the subsequent trial that gave Hitler a platform, his prison stay at Landsberg am Lech, and the writing of Mein Kampf. The hosts track the Nazis’ reorganisation after prison, the emergence of the Führer cult, and the party’s gradual expansion northwards under figures like Gregor Strasser and Joseph Goebbels. The episode ends by noting relative Nazi electoral weakness in the late 1920s and the looming catastrophe of 1929 that would change everything.
title: The Nazis: The Beer Hall Putsch (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook open a multi-episode examination of the Nazis' rise, marking the 90th anniversary of Adolf Hitler's appointment as Chancellor on 30 January 1933. They survey competing explanations — Sonderweg, continuity from the Kaiserreich, Marxist and economic interpretations — and stress the mixture of ideas and material crises that enabled Nazism. Traces of late 19th-century racial thought, Darwinian social metaphors, eugenics, pan-Germanism and notions of Lebensraum are identified as intellectual currents. They trace relevant German developments from Bismarck’s Second Reich through the trauma of the First World War, the November 1918 collapse, and the chaotic postwar politics of Munich. The episode follows Hitler’s early life, Viennese influences, wartime experience, entry into the German Workers’ Party, and his emergence as an effective speaker and leader of what became the National Socialist German Workers’ Party. The hosts preview subsequent episodes and note club-exclusive material for subscribers.
title: The Rise of the Nazis (Ep 1)

summary: This episode — the second part of a two-part feature on Lady Jane Grey — recounts the rapid rise and fall of the teenage claimant known as the Nine Days' Queen. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook track events from Jane's proclamation and ceremonial entry into the Tower of London through the strategic errors of John Dudley, 1st Duke of Northumberland, and Jane's own constrained agency. They explain Mary I's flight to East Anglia, her shrewd use of legitimacy and networks (notably in Framlingham and the Howard affinity), the collapse of Northumberland's military plans and naval support, and the pivot of the Privy Council to Mary. The episode covers the aftermath: trials and executions (Northumberland, Henry Grey, Guildford Dudley), Jane's imprisonment and dignified Protestant witness at the scaffold, and the impact of Wyatt's Rebellion and Mary’s proposed Spanish marriage. The hosts reflect on why Jane is variably counted as a monarch, cultural memory (paintings, Protestant martyr narratives), and the alternative timelines in which Jane might have survived longer.
title: Lady Jane Grey: The Axe Falls (Ep 2)

summary: This episode is the first of a two-part examination of Lady Jane Grey and the 1553 Tudor succession crisis. Holland and Sandbrook set the scene: Edward VI’s fervent Protestantism, the insecurity of the Tudor dynasty and Henry VIII’s obsession with a male heir. They explain Edward’s “device” to alter the succession, excluding his half-sisters Mary and Elizabeth and naming Lady Jane Grey his heir, and they outline the legal and political ambiguities around that move. The hosts profile the principal actors: Jane herself (her upbringing, humanist education and reputed linguistic skills), John Dudley, Duke of Northumberland (his rise, motives and reputation), and Guilford Dudley (Jane’s young husband). The episode explores competing interpretations of who engineered the coup — Edward VI or Northumberland — and the interplay of religious conviction and self-interest. It closes on the moment Edward dies (6 July 1553) and Jane is unexpectedly presented to the Privy Council as queen, ending on a cliffhanger before part two.
title: Lady Jane Grey: The Nine Days' Queen (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Jonathan Friedland about his book The Escape Artist, which recounts the Vrba–Wetzler report and its journey into Allied and Vatican hands in 1944. The conversation examines why the report’s revelations about Auschwitz-Birkenau did not produce swifter Allied action — exploring practical objections, bureaucratic delays, antisemitism, and public-relations fears in London and Washington. They discuss how the report, once public, contributed to diplomatic pressure (including interventions by Pope Pius XII and Franklin D. Roosevelt) that helped halt the deportations from Hungary and saved roughly 200,000 people in Budapest. Friedland also reflects on the postwar life of one of the escapees — his trauma, activism, and bitter relationships — and on how individual testimony restores humanity amid mass atrocity. The episode ranges across testimony, moral culpability, the limits of comprehension of massive crimes, and the role of witnesses in shaping Holocaust memory.
title: The Shadow of the Holocaust (Ep 2)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Jonathan Friedland about his book The Escape Artist, which reconstructs the life and April 1944 escape of Rudolf Weber (born Walter Rosenberg) from Auschwitz-Birkenau. Friedland and the hosts discuss Weber's early life in Slovakia, multiple attempts to avoid deportation, his work inside Auschwitz (including the warehouse nicknamed "Canada" and the ramp), and the slow realization of the camp's killing mechanism. They examine the role of deception in the industrialised genocide, the Auschwitz underground, and Weber's decision to flee with Alfred (Fred) Wetzler. The episode follows the pair's arduous three-day concealment and flight to Slovakia and the compilation of a 32-page report (recorded by Jewish council figures Oskar Krasnianski and Oskar Neumann) that was smuggled across Europe and reached leaders including Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt. The conversation foregrounds moral dilemmas, resistance, and the challenges of communicating Auschwitz's reality.
title: The Man Who Escaped Auschwitz (Ep 1)

summary: In this year-end episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook review the major political, cultural and personal highlights of 2022. They foreground Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and its geopolitical consequences, debating whether 2022 marks the end of the post–Cold War era and noting the global resonance of Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin. They discuss energy vulnerability, comparisons to 1973's oil shock, NATO resilience, the migration crisis, and longer-term trends from the 1990s. Domestically they reflect on the death of Elizabeth II and the peculiar public mourning in the UK, and on Britain’s political turbulence—multiple prime ministers, Brexit fallout and the brief premiership of Liz Truss. The hosts also cover cultural items (modernism/1922), recent technological stories (AI, cold fusion hopes), podcast highlights and recommended exhibitions and books. They close with upcoming Rest Is History projects and an invitation to the show’s members’ club and live tour dates in 2023.
title: 2022: A History

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook record from Berry Brothers with guest Henry Jeffries to discuss the history of festive drinks, guided by Jeffries' book Empire of Booze. They trace champagne's development — including early strong glass bottles and British scientific influence on carbonation — and explain how British tastes shaped styles of claret, port and sherry. Political and commercial threads recur: claret and port carried partisan meanings after the Glorious Revolution; the Methuen Treaty bolstered Portuguese wines; the Marquis de Pombal helped formalize the Douro/port region. They cover Sherry's solera system, the rise and fall of regional wines like Marsala (linked to Nelson), and Madeira and fortification debates. The episode closes on whisky: its Scottish origins, nineteenth-century blending for London markets, and how modern global markets (US, China) reshape production and marketing. Throughout, they emphasize British consumer demand and merchant networks as central to the global history of alcoholic drinks.
title: Drink

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the historical evidence for the life, death and legacy of Jesus of Nazareth. They open by questioning elements of the Nativity narrative (Bethlehem versus Nazareth, the census and Herod stories) and consider how gospel writers may have shaped accounts to match Scripture and broader Roman-era narrative patterns. The discussion moves to John the Baptist, Jesus’s baptism, and his charismatic ministry of healings and apocalyptic preaching about the Kingdom of God. They analyze Jesus’s entry into Jerusalem, the temple cleansing, and the political-religious dynamics that led to his arrest and trial before Pontius Pilate. The hosts assess the Last Supper, crucifixion and the variety of explanations for the empty tomb and resurrection claims, noting early Christian testimony (Paul, Mark) and skeptical alternatives. Throughout they weigh the uniqueness of Jesus’s teachings and sayings as an explanation for Christianity’s rapid spread, while acknowledging continuing uncertainties and scholarly debates.
title: Jesus Christ: The History (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin a two-part examination of the life of Jesus, framing the subject as both historically crucial and theologically fraught. They read Luke's infancy narrative, then discuss why treating Jesus as a historical figure is complicated by faith claims and later Christian elaborations. The episode surveys non-Christian references (Josephus, Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius) and archaeological evidence from Galilee, arguing the macro-context of the Gospels fits the Roman provincial world. They outline Palestine's complex administration under client kings like Herod, the role of Roman prefects (Pontius Pilate), the priestly elite, and the distinctive social tensions between Galilee and Jerusalem. The hosts review Gospel authorship, dates (Mark earliest, John later), and scholarly debates about memory and sources, citing modern scholars and traditions. They close by promising part two will attempt a cautious reconstruction of the historical Jesus, while noting many uncertainties and the importance of weighing diverse lines of evidence.
title: Jesus Christ: The Mystery (Ep 1)

summary: This episode examines the cultural and political history of roast beef as an English national emblem. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace how abundant English pasture, changing agrarian practices and cheaper beef made roast meat a common staple from Tudor times into the 18th century. They discuss travel-writing observations, English roasting techniques and condiments, and the contrast with evolving French culinary fashions. The conversation covers patriotic polemics against French ‘effeminacy’ in literature and theatre (notably Henry Fielding), the formation of beef‑centred sociability (the Beefsteak Clubs and the Sublime Society of Beefsteaks), and iconic images such as Hogarth’s Gate of Calais and associated songs. The hosts link the roast‑beef image to personifications like John Bull and to later political culture, noting how the motif peaks around the mid‑18th to early 19th centuries and diminishes with industrialisation and changing tastes. The episode closes by reflecting on modern echoes of the trope and the lingering symbolic power of beef in British identity.
title: England: Beef and Liberty

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook use the Canadian beaver as a lens on Canadian history, beginning with prehistoric Castoroides (the giant beaver) and Indigenous uses of beaver resources. They trace European contact — Jacques Cartier and early traders — through the rise of the fur trade, the Beaver Wars, and English institutional control via the Hudson's Bay Company and its 1670 charter for Rupert's Land. David Thompson's mapping and the centrality of beaver pelts (especially for felt hats) drove intense trapping, intensified further by castoreum bait and Newhouse traps, pushing populations toward collapse. The hosts discuss conservation efforts culminating in the charismatic spokesman Grey Owl (Archibald Stansfeld Bellany) and 20th-century recovery to millions of beavers. They also note Eurasian beaver reintroductions in Britain and cultural echoes (place names, art). The episode situates ecological change, colonial commerce, and modern conservation within Canada’s broader historical sweep.
title: Canada: Beaver Wars

summary: This episode examines the rescue of Denmark's Jewish population during the German occupation in World War II. After the swift German invasion on 9 April 1940, Denmark was administered as a protectorate under figures such as SS general Werner Best, while King Christian X and a cooperative-but-resisting Danish political culture preserved a strong national solidarity. In August 1943 martial law and a planned roundup of Jews prompted Georg Ferdinand Duckwitz, a German diplomat with Danish ties, to warn Danish politicians and the chief rabbi Marcus Melchior. The Swedes — following intervention by Niels Bohr and others including Greta Garbo — agreed to accept refugees, and ordinary Danes (fishermen, innkeepers, civil servants and local groups like the Elsinore Sewing Club) spirited roughly 7,743 Jews across the Øresund to Sweden. Only some hundreds were captured and sent to Theresienstadt. The hosts discuss reasons for Denmark’s exceptional outcome: small, assimilated Jewish population, proximity to neutral Sweden, civic solidarity, and pragmatic choices by some German administrators.
title: Denmark: The Great Escape

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Ecuador primarily through Charles Darwin's time on the Beagle and his visit to the Galapagos Islands. Holland outlines Darwin's role as a geologist-naturalist aboard the Beagle, the ship's extended five-year survey, and the intellectual questions about species that began to intrigue Darwin. They describe the Galapagos' volcanic landscape, its tame but distinctive wildlife — iguanas, giant tortoises and numerous finches and mockingbirds — and how observations there (including notes from the penal-colony keeper Nicholas Lawson) and later analysis by John Gould helped sharpen Darwin's thinking about variation and speciation. The hosts emphasize that the islands did not instantly produce Darwin's theory of natural selection, but provided important illustrative evidence later incorporated into his writings such as The Voyage of the Beagle and ultimately On the Origin of Species. The episode situates the Galapagos in both historical and popular mythic terms and notes subsequent environmental importance.
title: Ecuador: Darwin's Adventure to the Galapagos

summary: In this World Cup Marathon episode on Morocco, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the Rif War of the early 20th century — a violent anti‑colonial conflict in the Rif Mountains of northern Morocco that peaked in the 1920s. Dominic outlines the rise of Mohammed Abdel Krim from a family once allied with Spain to leader of the Berber resistance, and the catastrophic Spanish defeat at Annual in July 1921 under General Manuel Fernández Silvestre. The hosts trace Spanish political fallout — strikes, the Tragic Week and the rise of Miguel Primo de Rivera — and the formation of the short‑lived Republic of the Rif. They describe how the conflict presaged later 20th‑century warfare: Franco and Millán‑Astray’s involvement, formation of the Spanish Army of Africa, the use of chemical agents despite the Geneva Protocol, aerial bombardment by volunteer pilots including Americans, and the large Franco‑French amphibious operation at Alhucemas in 1925. The episode argues the Rif War helped shape the military culture and personnel that later figured in the Spanish Civil War.
title: Morocco: The Rif War

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the rise, golden age and collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba. They open with the 711 crossing of Tariq bin Ziyad and the collapse of the Visigothic kingdom under Roderic, then follow the survival of an Umayyad prince, Abd al-Rahman I, who founds the emirate in al-Andalus. Tom outlines the growth of Córdoba into a wealthy cosmopolitan capital — the Mezquita, baths, vast libraries and international trade — and the transformative reign of Abd al-Rahman III who declared himself caliph in 929. The episode discusses social dynamics (jizya, conversion, slaves such as the Saqaliba), the scholarly milieu, and violent assertion of power under figures like Almanzor. Internal factionalism, Berber uprisings and the Fitna culminate in the siege and sack of Córdoba from 1010 onward, fragmenting Muslim rule and enabling the Christian Reconquista; Granada endures until 1492. The hosts nuance popular ideas of a "multicultural paradise," noting both intellectual exchange and institutional inequality and violence.
title: Spain: The Caliphate of Córdoba

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the Vinča (Vincia) culture of the central Balkans, prompted by excavations beginning with Serbian archaeologist Miloje Vasic. They describe finds from the Vinča site (Belobrdo) — advanced ceramics, thousands of figurines, and symbolic motifs — and later discoveries across Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria showing large, riverine Neolithic settlements dated c. 5700–4200 BC. They highlight evidence for early copper working (a Plocnik axe dated c. 5500 BC and copper smelting at Belovode) and discuss the controversial Tărtăria tablets (found 1961) bearing Vinča symbols that some argue represent proto-writing. The hosts review scholarly positions: early claims equating Vinča with Aegean/Greek influences, Marija Gimbutas’s hypothesis of a peaceful, goddess-centred “Old Europe,” and counter-arguments about dating, forgeries, nationalist readings and the role of Indo-European integration or environmental decline in the culture’s disappearance. They conclude the evidence is intriguing but inconclusive and note the subject’s susceptibility to academic fashion and nationalist myth-making.
title: Serbia: The Birthplace of Civilisation

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a Rest Is History World Cup special episode about Avram Petrovich Gannibal, the African-born ancestor of Alexander Pushkin. They trace Gannibal's probable origins in the region of modern Cameroon, his kidnapping and sale into slavery, and his arrival at the Ottoman court before being taken to St. Petersburg as part of Peter the Great's entourage. Peter baptizes and educates him; Gannibal studies in France, serves in the French artillery, and later becomes a celebrated military engineer and nobleman in Russia. The hosts recount his marriages, children (including descendants who helped found Kherson and Pushkin's maternal line), and debates over his precise African origin. They also discuss Pushkin's depiction of Gannibal in The More of Peter the Great, 19th- and 20th-century reinterpretations of his race and status, and Gannibal's later cultural reception in the Soviet Union and among Harlem Renaissance writers. The episode is a concise biographical sketch linking Cameroon, Russia and literary history.
title: Cameroon: The Slave General of Peter the Great

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, part of the hosts' 'World Cup marathon' series on competing countries, recounts the life and mysterious disappearance of Louis Aimé Augustin Le Prince, an early pioneer of moving-picture technology. Tom Holland tells how Le Prince, trained in photography by Louis Daguerre and later connected to the Whitley family in Leeds, combined artistic sensibility with chemical and mechanical experimentation to produce short motion sequences in 1888 (notably the Roundhay Garden Scene). Le Prince secured a US patent in January 1888 but vanished in September 1890 after boarding a train in France; his body was never found. The hosts discuss theories about his disappearance — from murder to suicide to industrial sabotage — and the subsequent rise of Thomas Edison as the public father of cinema following demonstrations in 1891 and litigation in 1898. The episode emphasizes Le Prince’s transnational career (France, Britain, the US) and argues his contributions deserve greater recognition in film history.
title: France: The Mystery of Le Prince

summary: Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland host a wide-ranging survey of Japanese history with guest Chris Harding, senior lecturer in Asian history at the University of Edinburgh and author of two books on Japan. Harding outlines key moments and figures across a millennium: the Heian court and Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji; the rise of samurai and the brutal unifier Oda Nobunaga; the Tokugawa (Edo) era's 'floating world', kabuki and Ihara Saikaku; the forced reopening of Japan, the Meiji Restoration and industrialisation embodied by Shibusawa Eichi; the Russo-Japanese War and cultural debates represented by poet Yasano Akiko; and the wartime trauma and postwar cultural revival culminating in Tezuka Osamu's manga influence. Discussion touches on sakoku isolation, encounters with Europeans (Dejima), imperial expansion, wartime atrocities and postwar economic/cultural resurgence. Harding emphasizes continuities in aesthetics and how Japan selectively adapted foreign models to create distinct institutions and cultural forms.
title: Japan: Samurai and Shoguns

summary: This episode explores the symbolic figure of the Maid of Holland that emerged during the late 16th-century Dutch Revolt against Spanish rule. Tom Holland traces the image’s roots in medieval allegory and its transformation during the revolt into a Protestant symbol combining Marian echoes, classical liberty (the Phrygian/ liberty hat) and martial Minerva-like attributes. The discussion highlights how individual exemplars — notably the Haarlem heroine Kenau during the 1573 siege — became conflated with the allegory, and how medals, prints and stained-glass imagery promoted the figure. Dominic and Tom emphasise a distinctive cultural strand: the elevation of housekeeping and cleanliness as civic virtues in Calvinist Dutch society, drawing on Simon Schama’s The Embarrassment of Riches and a period household manual. Civic order, domestic cleanliness and material prosperity were portrayed as mutually reinforcing, shaping art, politics and identity in the Dutch Republic’s Golden Age. The episode closes by situating the Republic’s later eclipse in the late 17th century under French and British pressure.
title: Netherlands: The Maid of Holland

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the little-known history of the Welsh settlement in Argentine Patagonia. They trace the episode from Ferdinand Magellan's 1520 naming of Patagonia through the 19th-century decision by Welsh nationalists, led by Michael Jones, to establish a Welsh colony (Y Wladfa) in 1865. The hosts recount the difficult early years — inadequate agricultural skills, floods and deaths — and how contact with indigenous Tehuelche people, irrigation works and later railway-building around Trelew allowed some success. They cover language and identity tensions as Argentina asserted Spanish-language and national policies, the decline of Welsh as a public tongue, and later 20th–21st century revivals tied to Welsh devolution and cultural exchanges. The episode also mentions debates over settler-colonial responsibility and literary imaginings of a larger Welsh Patagonia in novels. Overall, the discussion situates the colony within broader imperial, migratory and nationalising processes in 19th–20th century Argentina.
title: Argentina: The Welsh Colony

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook focus on Geneva in the mid-16th century, using the 1553 execution of Michael Servetus to examine the tensions at the heart of the Reformation. Holland sketches Servetus as a polymath and heterodox theologian who denied original sin and the Trinity, and describes his provocative publication The Restoration of Christianity (1553) and subsequent arrest after Calvin alerted authorities. The hosts explore John Calvin's transformation of Geneva into a model Protestant commonwealth, with its consistory, ministers, teachers, deacons and elders enforcing moral discipline while offering refuge to refugees. They place the Servetus affair in wider context — the memory of Münster's Anabaptist excesses, debates over persecution, and the emergence of both rigorous religiosity and early arguments for tolerance (citing a 1554 collection prefaced by Sebastian Castello). The discussion links these 16th-century controversies to later Enlightenment critique and to modern debates about free speech, order and liberty.
title: Switzerland: Calvin's Cancel Culture

summary: This episode continues The Rest Is History's exploration of Portugal, serving as a coda to their earlier four-part Portuguese series and as part of a World Cup-themed set of episodes. Dominic recounts the decline of the Estado Novo after António Salazar’s stroke, Marcelo Caetano’s succession, and the pressures of costly colonial wars in Angola and Mozambique. He explains how a reform to military promotion fuelled discontent among junior officers, who—guided by figures such as Otelo Sariva de Carvalho and led in the field by Salgueiro Maia—launched the largely bloodless Carnation Revolution on 24–25 April 1974. The episode traces the chaotic aftermath: occupations, land seizures in the Alentejo, competing coups (including attempts in September 1974 and 11 March 1975), the rise and fall of figures like General António Spinola and Vasco Gonçalves, Cold War anxieties involving Kissinger and allies, and the decisive 25 November 1975 counter-coup. Ultimately a moderate course prevailed, culminated in elections and Portugal’s integration into the European Community.
title: Portugal: The Carnation Revolution

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the history and modern meaning of Gorée Island and its House of Slaves in Senegal. They open with the evocative image of the 'door of no return' and trace Gorée's evolution from a marginal, disease-ravaged Atlantic outpost to a multi‑power trading hub (Portuguese, Dutch, English, French) and later a preserved symbol of the Atlantic slave trade. The hosts discuss how Gorée was repurposed as a museum and tourist pilgrimage site after Senegalese independence (1960) and its elevation to UNESCO status. They contrast the emotional/pilgrimage value of the site for African-Americans — amplified after Roots — with scholarly work (notably Philip D. Curtin) disputing claims that Gorée was a major slave-export depot. The episode explores the tension between symbolic memory and documentary history, the politics of heritage, and debates over who has authority to challenge cherished historical narratives.
title: Senegal: The Door of No Return

summary: In this episode of The Rest Is History hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome Bart van Loo to discuss Jan van Eyck and Flemish art within the Burgundian context. Van Loo situates van Eyck in Maasland (eastern present-day Belgium), outlines his role as court painter and envoy to Philip the Good, and emphasises the artist’s technical innovations in oil painting. The conversation covers van Eyck’s portraits (including the Man in a Red Turban and the Arnolfini Portrait), his inscriptions and self-representation, and his broader involvement in Burgundian court life, banquets and diplomatic missions. The Ghent Altarpiece is described in detail—its realistic detail, iconography and significance at its 1432 installation in Ghent—and listeners are directed to digital resources for close study. The episode links van Eyck’s realism to the economic and cultural dynamism of Flanders and the Burgundian state, highlighting how wealth, individualism and technical advances produced a Northern Renaissance moment.
title: Belgium: History's Greatest Artist

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a travel-style cultural and historical tour of Poland framed as its “seven wonders,” drawn from a 2007 Reszpospolita public poll. The pair open with Kraków — its founding legend (Krakus and the dragon Smok Wawelski), the vast medieval Rynek Główny (main square), the Cloth Hall and Wawel Hill with its cathedral and castle — stressing Kraków’s Renaissance and Hanseatic ties and its partial survival through WWII. They discuss Zamoszcz (a planned Renaissance town by Jan Zamoyski), the El Blanc canal with its steep-rail boat lifts, Malbork Castle (Teutonic Knights), Toruń (Copernicus’s birthplace and gingerbread tradition) and the Wieliczka salt mine with its underground chapels and salt sculptures. Alongside travel detail they weave in political history — the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, the Deluge, partitions, Nazi occupation and postwar memory — and note cultural touchstones including Copernicus and Pope John Paul II. The episode mixes historical context with anecdotes, tourism notes and reflections on national identity and preservation.
title: Poland: Copernicus, the Dragon and the Salt Mine

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the history of the Ashanti (Asante) Empire in what they frame as part of their 'World Cup Odyssey' episode on Ghana. They trace Ashanti origins and foundation myths, the role of Ose Tutu and his advisor Okomfo Anokye (creator of the Golden Stool), and the state's political and military consolidation in the 17th–18th centuries. The conversation covers the Ashanti’s wealth from gold and the slave trade, its sophisticated but non-literate bureaucracy, and contested reports of human sacrifice. The hosts contrast Ashanti power with British imperial attitudes, narrating key clashes: Sir Charles McCarthy’s 1823 defeat, 19th‑century Anglo‑Ashanti wars, Wolseley’s 1870s campaign, the 1896 exile of the king to the Seychelles, and the 1900 War of the Golden Stool. They conclude with the stool’s survival, later negotiations with British authorities, and the continuing symbolic role of the Ashanti monarchy into the 20th century and beyond.
title: Ghana: The Ashanti Empire

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History is a Brazil special focused on the Brazilian Empire and the reign of Emperor Pedro II. The hosts trace Brazil’s emergence from Portuguese rule — including the transfer of the Portuguese court to Rio — to independence in 1822 under Pedro I and the establishment of an imperial dynasty. They portrait Pedro II as a bookish, science‑loving monarch who patronized the arts and natural history, promoted Brazilian cultural identity, and sponsored scientific projects (photography, meteorite retrieval, botanical exploration). The episode examines the central contradiction of 19th‑century Brazil: a modernizing monarchy built on mass slavery, with frequent slave revolts (notably in Pernambuco and Bahia), gradual legal reforms (Law of Free Birth, 1871) and eventual abolition in 1888. The erosion of support among elites and the growth of positivist and republican ideas in the army led to the relatively bloodless coup of November 1889 and Pedro II’s exile. The hosts reflect on his legacy and Brazil’s turbulent republican era that followed.
title: Brazil: The Last Emperor

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Martin Jones about Welsh identity and the history of Wales. The discussion ranges from early claims of Roman ancestry (Magnus Maximus) and medieval Welsh polities through the Norman incursions and the creation of the Marches, to Edward I’s conquest and symbolic castle-building. Jones examines legal inequality imposed on the Welsh, Owain Glyndŵr’s rebellion, Tudor-era changes including Henry VII’s Welsh connections and the Laws in Wales (Acts of Union), and the Welsh-language Bible’s cultural impact. The Industrial Revolution’s extraction economy, demographic migration, and the consequent linguistic shift are explored, alongside cultural responses: rugby as a unifying national symbol and the cultural roots of Plaid Cymru. The episode closes by linking historical grievances — e.g., the flooding of a Welsh village for an English reservoir — to contemporary politics, Brexit, and debates over devolution versus independence.
title: Wales: The Roar of the Red Dragon

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their World Cup marathon with an episode focused on Korean culture, specifically the gisaeng (courtesan) institution and the most famous gisaeng poet, Hwang Jini (also known by the gisaeng name Myeongwol). They outline the historical background from the Goryeo period to the Joseon dynasty, explain the ambiguous social status of gisaeng — hereditary low-caste yet highly educated entertainers — and describe their roles as musicians, poets (notably composing sijo), and state-trained professionals. The episode gives biographical anecdotes about Hwang Jini: her parentage, legendary stories about a funeral-coffin episode, relationships with patrons, her riddle (Geomiligo Iribultule) and notable poems (including translations). They discuss her cultural afterlife in South Korean media and the differing attitudes in North Korea. The episode closes with readings of translated poems and reflections on how this case illuminates cultural variation in gender and social norms.
title: South Korea: The Riddle of Hwang Jini

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Kaaba’s religious significance, its rites (kiswah, tawaf, the Black Stone and Maqam Ibrahim) and the traditional Islamic narrative linking the shrine to Adam and Abraham. Holland outlines Muslim scriptural and aural traditions — miraculous heavenly prototypes, the Isra and Mi'raj vision, and the institutionalization of the Hajj — then traces the Kaaba’s contested material history: pre-Islamic idolatry, Muhammad’s cleansing of idols, subsequent destruction and rebuilding during late seventh-century civil wars, and the roles of figures such as Muawiyah I, Yazid I, Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. They note later episodes (930 theft of the Black Stone, 1626 floods, the 1979 Grand Mosque siege) and emphasize the paucity of non-Muslim contemporary references. Holland addresses historiographical debates over dating and possible later construction or consolidation of the Meccan sanctuary, reflects on the limits of secular history to resolve sacred claims, and plugs his book In the Shadow of the Sword.
title: Saudi Arabia: The Mystery of the Kaaba

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the history and modern mythology of Mexico's Day of the Dead (Día de Muertos). They challenge popular assumptions that the festival is an unbroken pre‑Columbian tradition, tracing key elements—sugar skulls, pan de muerto, altars—to post‑Conquest and especially 19th–20th century Spanish and Mexican developments. The episode highlights 19th century satirical imagery (José Guadalupe Posada's La Catrina), the influence of Spanish All Souls customs, and the politicized reinvention of indigenous symbolism during and after the Mexican Revolution, notably under Plutaco Elias Calles and Lázaro Cárdenas amid anti‑clericalism and the Cristero conflicts. Cultural references (Pixar’s Coco, James Bond’s Spectre) are used to show how contemporary media have shaped global perceptions; the Bond pre‑credit sequence even inspired a modern Mexico City parade. The hosts discuss relevant authors and works (Stanley Brands, Graham Greene, D. H. Lawrence) and emphasise how 20th century statecraft and cultural engineering remade and popularized many aspects of the festival now seen as “traditional.”
title: Mexico: Day of the Dead

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the longue durée of Anglo‑American relations in a thematic episode framed as a World Cup special on the United States. They begin with early antagonisms — the War of 1812, impressment and the 1814 burning of Washington — then move through cultural encounters: Charles Dickens’s fraught 1842 visit and publications (American Notes; Martin Chuzzlewit), the rise of American industrial power exemplified by Andrew Carnegie and his Gospel of Wealth, and political convergence in the World Wars.
