The pair then examine racial and social tensions during World War II when large numbers of American GIs arrived in Britain (including episodes of violence such as Bamber Bridge and Bristol), and the postwar cultural ascendancy of the United States followed by a British cultural comeback in the 1960s (the Beatles, British Invasion). The episode closes with late‑20th century perceptions of British decline (1970s) and recurring mutual stereotypes, mixing cultural anecdotes, literary references and political commentary to map shifting power, prestige and cultural exchange.
title: USA vs England: The 200-Year Rivalry

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook focus on Dido (Elissa), the legendary founder-queen of Carthage, using Virgil's Aeneid as the central text while comparing alternative traditions from Greek and Roman sources. They outline Virgil's tragic portrayal—Dido's love for Aeneas, his divinely mandated departure, and her subsequent suicide and curse—and contrast it with earlier versions (Trogus, Timaeus, Menander of Ephesus) that cast Elissa as a chaste, politically motivated founder. The discussion links myth to archaeology (the Carthaginian Tofet and possible child sacrifices), numismatic evidence, and the wider Phoenician origins of Carthage. They also explore Virgil's political motives and parallels with Antony and Cleopatra, and the wider consequences leading to Rome's conflicts with Carthage (Punic Wars). The episode closes with a musical coda: Juliet Pochin performs a rendition of Dido’s Lament (from Purcell’s opera), reworked by Dominic for Cleopatra.
title: Tunisia: Dido of Carthage

summary: This episode examines Uruguay's twentieth-century trajectory through the rise and impact of the urban guerrilla group the Tupamaros. After sketching Uruguay's geographic position, early prosperity and social welfare achievements (including winning the 1930 World Cup), the hosts trace post‑war economic decline and political radicalization. They discuss the Tupamaros' tactics — bank robberies, “armed propaganda” and high‑profile kidnappings — focusing on the abductions of British ambassador Jeffrey Jackson (January 1971) and US advisor Dan Mitrione (July 1970). The episode addresses contested claims about US training and alleged torture, the government crackdown and the erosion of democracy that culminated in a repressive regime (1973–1985). It closes with the story of former Tupamaro José Mujica, imprisoned and later elected president (2010–2015), and references Eduardo Galeano's The Open Veins of Latin America as emblematic of left‑wing critiques of the period.
title: Uruguay: The Tupamaros

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the rise, rule and lasting reforms of Diocletian (born Diocles in Salona) against the backdrop of the Roman Empire's third-century crisis. They explain how chaotic conditions and military prominence enabled Illyrian officers like Diocletian to ascend. Diocletian consolidates power through military success (including the eastern settlement culminating in the Treaty of Nisibis, 299), creates the tetrarchy to share imperial duties, restructures provincial administration and the tax system, and builds a more militarized, centralized bureaucracy. He attempts economic controls (the 301 edict on maximum prices) and enacts the notorious Diocletianic persecution of Christians (303). In 305 he famously abdicates and retires to his palace at Salona (modern Split). The hosts emphasize Diocletian's paradoxical blend of traditional Roman piety and far-reaching institutional innovation that laid foundations for the later Byzantine state.
title: Croatia: The Man Who Saved The Roman Empire

summary: In this episode hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook speak with historian Ali Ansari about the long, ambivalent history of Anglo–Iranian relations. Framed by England v Iran in the World Cup, the conversation traces contacts from early diplomatic exchanges through the 17th–19th century Persianate context and the East India Company, to 19th-century admiration of British institutions and the rising disappointment that followed. Key moments discussed include the Tobacco Protest, the Persian Constitutional Revolution, the 1908 oil discovery and the role of William Knox D'Arcy and the Anglo‑Iranian Oil Company, the strategic importance of Iranian oil to Britain, occupations and turmoil during both world wars, the nationalisation of oil under Mohammad Mossadegh and the 1953 coup, and the 1979 revolution and its legacies (including the 1979 hostage crisis and the 1989 fatwa against Salman Rushdie). Ansari emphasizes the paradoxical mixture of admiration and resentment in Iran toward Britain, and closes by considering contemporary public attitudes, football culture and how historical memory shapes present relations.
title: Iran: England - 'The Little Satan'

summary: In this World Cup-themed episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the history of Costa Rica, concentrating on the 1948 Civil War and its long-term consequences. Dominic narrates the lead-up: populist president Rafael Ángel Calderón, his weak successor Teodoro Picado Mikalski, allegations of electoral fraud and the murder of a newspaperman (named in the transcript as Artiglio Ularte Blanco) which triggered revolt. José Figueres Ferrer ("Don Pepe") leads a heterogeneous anti-authoritarian force to victory after weeks of fighting. Influenced by Cold War pressures and U.S. warnings, government forces collapse; Figueres governs briefly, then implements sweeping reforms: new constitution, expanded welfare and education, women’s suffrage, bank nationalization, citizenship reforms, and famously abolishes the army. The hosts discuss Figueres’s idealism (in part inspired by H. G. Wells), his later politics, and Costa Rica’s resulting stability, prosperity and environmental reputation today.
title: Costa Rica: Civil War

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the Somerton Man, an enigmatic death discovered on Somerton Park Beach near Adelaide on 1 December 1948. Tom Holland outlines the baffling physical and forensic clues: a well-dressed unidentified man with labels surgically removed from his clothing, an unused rail ticket, American items, and signs suggesting poison. A tiny scrap of paper bearing the Persian words (Tammam Shud) ripped from a copy of the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam and a book containing an undeciphered series of letters and two phone numbers (one linking to a local woman, Jessica Thompson) add to the mystery. Hosts discuss competing theories — Cold War espionage, gun-running, or a doomed personal affair — and the long modern investigation led by Derek Abbott, who used DNA from a death mask and genealogical methods (with Colleen Fitzpatrick) to identify the likely man as Charles (Carl) Webb. Many questions remain unanswered, leaving the case tantalizing and unresolved.
title: Australia: The Mystery of the Somerton Man

summary: This episode tells the story of Hans and Sophie Scholl and the White Rose resistance group in Nazi Germany. Dominic traces their upbringing in a devout, independent-minded family, their early involvement in the Hitler Youth, and how personal readings (Stefan Zweig, Thomas Mann, Augustine, Aquinas) and wartime experiences led them to oppose Nazism. In 1942–43 Hans, Sophie and their student friends produced and distributed sharply worded leaflets denouncing Nazi crimes, notably the mass murder of Jews, and calling for passive resistance and a new, federal Germany. Their increasingly ambitious campaign culminated in the Munich university leaflet drop on 18 February 1943, their arrest by a caretaker and the Gestapo, and fast trials by Judge Roland Freisler that resulted in executions. The hosts discuss the group's Christian moral impetus, methods of distribution, the subsequent spread of their message (including Allied leaflet drops), and their postwar legacy as martyrs commemorated across Germany.
title: Germany: The White Rose

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook open a World Cup themed series with a comprehensive history of Qatar, from its ancient role as a Persian Gulf peninsula notable for pearls and maritime trade to its modern emergence as a geopolitical actor. They trace classical references (Herodotus, Pliny, Ptolemy), successive regional suzerainties (Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids, Umayyads), and early modern interventions by Portuguese, Dutch and British powers. The Al Thani dynasty’s rise (1867) and British protectorate status (1916) are covered, followed by the transformative discovery of oil before WWII and full independence in 1971. The hosts recount 20th-century coups within the Al Thani family, the OPEC era, and Hamad bin Khalifa’s strategy to secure Qatar’s autonomy via soft power (Al Jazeera, Education City), sovereign investments and hosting foreign military bases. They discuss the costs of rapid development — migrant labour abuses and international criticism around the World Cup — and regional tensions culminating in the 2017 blockade and its 2021 resolution, arguing Qatar’s energy role and external partnerships underpin its survival.
title: Qatar: A History

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host former England striker and broadcaster Gary Lineker for the third episode in their World Cup series. Lineker recounts his playing experiences — notably the 1986 Mexico quarter‑final versus Argentina featuring Diego Maradona’s “Hand of God” and his celebrated solo goal — and reflects on the tournament’s power to shape careers and national memory. The conversation traces World Cup history and themes: hooliganism and its aftermath (Heysel, Hillsborough), the 1990 tournament’s cultural shift, globalization and expansion of the tournament, and recurring issues of corruption in FIFA bidding (notably the 2010 Zurich decisions leading to Russia 2018 and Qatar 2022). Lineker discusses personal anecdotes (training in heat, limited phone calls, Barcelona transfer) and addresses human‑rights and “sportwashing” concerns around hosts. The episode balances nostalgia for football’s spectacle with skepticism about commercialisation and political instrumentalisation, and ends with Lineker’s predictions for the upcoming World Cup finalists.
title: The World Cup: The Falklands, despots, and corruption (Ep 3)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their series on the history of the FIFA World Cup (this is episode two). They focus on tournaments and wider political contexts from 1954 through the 1970s: West Germany's controversial 1954 triumph (the Miracle of Bern) and its fraught reception; Hungary's decline after 1954 and the 1956 uprising; England 1966 as a cultural moment; North Korea's shock result in 1966 and its unexpected ties to Middlesbrough; Brazil's dominance in 1958–1970, Pelé's starring role, and the way successive Brazilian regimes exploited football (including the 1964 coup and later dictatorship); and the Netherlands' total football and West Germany's 1974 victory. They then examine the politicization and sportswashing of the 1978 Argentina World Cup under Videla's junta, controversies around the Peru match, and human costs of stadium- and image-building. The episode weaves footballing anecdotes with political and social analysis, and previews an upcoming guest appearance by Gary Lineker and a 32-episode country-focused series.
title: The World Cup: Post-war reconciliation, Brazilian dictatorship, and North Koreans in Middlesbrough (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the early political and cultural history of the FIFA World Cup. They argue the tournament grew from British sporting networks exported across the globe — via cricketers, sailors and expatriates — and show how South American nations (Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil) adopted and transformed football into a vehicle for national identity. The episode covers proto-World Cups at the 1924 and 1928 Olympics, the first official 1930 tournament in Uruguay, and the politicized 1934 Italian World Cup under Benito Mussolini. They discuss travel difficulties, amateurism debates, and the interwar spread of football tactics. The postwar revival leads into the traumatic 1950 Maracanã final in Brazil (Uruguay's upset) and its social consequences, notably the treatment of goalkeeper Barbosa and a young Pelé witnessing national grief. The episode previews a 32-episode World Cup marathon and upcoming guest Gary Lineker to examine later decades and the tournament's global history.
title: The World Cup: British Imperialism, South American rivalries, and Mussolini (Ep 1)

summary: This short preview episode features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook outlining a planned 32-episode Rest Is History project timed to the FIFA World Cup in Qatar. The hosts describe a daily sequence of short history episodes, each focusing on one of the 32 competing countries, ranging chronologically from 6000 BCE Serbia to 1970s Portugal. Topics will include a wide mix of smaller human stories and larger political or cultural episodes — for example, Louis Le Prince in West Yorkshire, Dom Pedro II of Brazil, the Kaaba in Saudi Arabia, Abram Petrovich Gannibal’s life and connection to Pushkin, the Rif War of the 1920s, the Ashanti, and the Costa Rican Civil War of 1948. Special World Cup–themed episodes and three preparatory episodes on the history of the football tournament are planned; guests announced for upcoming episodes include Ali Ansari, Martin Jones and Gary Lineker. The hosts highlight episode lengths and variety, and invite listeners to look forward to the series.
title: History's coming home... (preview)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life and legacy of Alfred the Great, focusing on his escape after the Viking ambush at Chippenham (January 878), the famous anecdotes (Alfred and the cakes; St Cuthbert), and his military and political recovery culminating in the Battle of Edington and Guthrum's baptism. They analyse Alfred's pragmatic statecraft: the creation and fortification of burhs (towns/boroughs), restoration of London, establishment of markets and coinage, and the administrative and educational reforms he sponsored (translations of key Latin texts, promotion of learning). The episode situates Alfred's achievements within the broader Viking impact on England — the partial settlement of Danes, the later Danelaw division (circa 886), and how these upheavals shaped the emergence of an English identity leading to later rulers like Edward and Athelstan. The hosts also touch on historiographical issues (use of the term "Anglo-Saxon") and end with a reading from Dominic Sandbrook's book Fury of the Vikings.
title: Alfred the Great: Return of the King (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the life and times of Alfred the Great and the Viking threat to ninth-century England. They open with a dramatic reading and discuss Alfred’s childhood, Roman and Frankish influences from visits to Rome and Charles the Bald’s court, and Alfred’s commitment to literacy and Christian kingship (Asser and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle are noted). The hosts place Alfred within the context of competing English kingdoms—Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria and East Anglia—and track the escalation of Viking activity from coastal raids (Lindisfarne, 793) to overwintering and the arrival of the Great Heathen Army. Key figures (Ivar the Boneless, Guthrum, Edmund, Egbert) and episodes (Ashdown, Repton, the Chippenham ambush) are highlighted. The episode ends on a cliffhanger about Alfred’s forced flight from Chippenham, setting up a subsequent instalment about his recovery and confrontation with the Vikings.
title: Alfred the Great: Fury of the Vikings (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook visit the National Archives exhibition "Treason: People, Power and Plot" with Neil Johnston, head of the early modern archives, who guides them through primary documents spanning medieval to modern treason. They examine the 1351/52 Treason Act, the parliamentary journal of the Trial of Charles I (1649), the Act of Indemnity and Oblivion and the Restoration settlement of 1660. The conversation moves to later crises: Titus Oates and the Popish Plot (1678), the Exclusion Crisis, and the political development of Whigs and Tories. They discuss transatlantic implications — the Declaration of Independence (1776), American incorporation of a treason clause, and colonial tensions over trial and taxation. Irish radicalism and republicanism are covered through Wolfe Tone, the United Irishmen and the 1798 rebellion, and the episode closes with the Easter Rising (1916) documents and the waning practical application of medieval treason laws, culminating in the twentieth-century case of William Joyce. The episode emphasises how legal definitions of treason evolved alongside shifting political sovereignty.
title: Treason in Modern Britain (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook visit the National Archives with treason expert Ewan Roger to preview the new exhibition 'Treason: People, Power and Plot'. The episode surveys the long afterlife of treason in English law—from early ideas under Alfred the Great and Roman precedents, through the Treason Act of 1351/1352, to medieval spectacles of punishment such as hanging, drawing and quartering. They examine documentary highlights: parliament rolls, indictments, attainders (including Richard III's posthumous attainder), and high-profile Tudor cases (Anne Boleyn, Thomas More, Thomas Cromwell). The conversation covers legal developments—compassing and imagining the king's death, levying war, and later Reformation-era religious treasons—and oddities like porridge-poisoning (Richard Roos) and the Monteagle letter tied to the Gunpowder Plot. The episode is the first of a two-part special, with part two promised to cover 19th–21st century cases. Listeners are invited to see the free exhibition and its accompanying book.
title: Medieval Treason (Ep 1)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Al Murray to discuss his book Command: How the Allies Learned to Win the Second World War. The conversation asks whether individual commanders matter versus institutional, comparing Titanic figures (Patton, Nelson, Alexander) with system-driven outcomes (Roman legions, Allied industrial power). Murray sketches pen portraits of commanders — Patton, Montgomery, Slim, Omar Bradley and Rommel — and examines different styles of leadership: morale-building, staff management, media projection and logistics. They use case studies (Crete, North Africa including Gazala and El Alamein, Burma and the Sittang River retreat) to show how leadership, learning, material preponderance and local conditions combined to decide campaigns. The discussion contrasts British, American and Soviet approaches to manpower, motivation and innovation, and briefly considers contemporary parallels with Ukraine. Throughout they return to the book's theme: victories required both institutional resources and commanders able to marshal men, materiel and morale in specific theaters.
title: Monty & Patton vs. the Nazis

summary: This short, timely episode responds to the resignation of UK Prime Minister Liz Truss. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook first compare Truss’s brief premiership with historical short-lived leaders (George Canning, medieval royal favourites, Roman emperors like Gordian I/II and the Crisis of the Third Century) and political churn in other countries (Australia, Italy). They discuss causes: internal party rules that empower activists, factionalism, personality politics, Brexit without coherent strategy, and recent global shocks (COVID-19, the Ukraine war and energy shocks). The hosts emphasise real economic consequences from Truss’s mini‑economic experiment — higher interest rates and risks to households and businesses — and debate whether Britain is entering a longer-term economic and political malaise reminiscent of the 1970s. They close by reflecting on changing standards and expectations of politicians and promote a related Trafalgar episode for members.
title: The Fall of Liz Truss

summary: This episode concludes the hosts' multi-part Trafalgar epic, narrating the approach, tactics and carnage of the Battle of Trafalgar (21 October 1805). The presenters reconstruct Nelson’s two-column plan, the mixed Franco-Spanish line, and key commanders and ships. They describe the slow, tense approach, the violent close-range fighting, Collingwood’s decisive raking of the Santa Ana, and Victory’s clash with Redoutable that results in Nelson being fatally shot. The programme details Nelson’s prolonged death below decks, his last requests, Hardy’s presence, and the immediate aftermath: Villeneuve’s surrender, the taking of prizes, and a subsequent storm that sank many captured ships. The episode discusses casualty figures, the behaviour of British sailors saving prisoners, national reaction at home, and the significance of Trafalgar for British naval dominance, the Continental System and wider Napoleonic strategy. It also references several historians and books used in the research and reflects on Nelson’s mythic status and its ambivalences.
title: Trafalgar: Victory (Ep 3)

summary: This episode is the second instalment in the podcast's multi-part account of Trafalgar. Holland and Sandbrook profile the principal characters — above all Horatio Nelson — exploring his personality, leadership style, charisma, personal life (notably Emma Hamilton and daughter Horatia), and his relationships with captains like Thomas Hardy and Cuthbert Collingwood. They contrast Nelson with the Franco-Spanish command under Pierre-Charles-Jean-Baptiste de Villeneuve and describe the weaknesses in the allied fleet. The hosts lay out Napoleon’s broader strategic context — plans to concentrate fleets, threaten the Channel and the Caribbean, and his eventual diversion to continental war — and trace the 1805 naval manoeuvres: Villeneuve’s escape from Toulon, the Caribbean cruise, missed rendezvous, Calder’s engagement, and Villeneuve’s return to Cadiz. The episode ends on the eve of Trafalgar (20 October 1805), describing Nelson’s final preparations and letters, and promotes a club-only fuller account scheduled for Trafalgar Day.
title: Trafalgar: Countdown to Annihilation (Ep 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook open a multi-episode series on the Battle of Trafalgar, placing the 1805 engagement in its long geopolitical, financial and naval context. They argue Trafalgar’s significance for British national survival and long-term imperial dominance, and discuss how Britain’s naval preeminence grew over the 17th–18th centuries through professionalization, bureaucratic administration, and fiscal innovations (Bank of England, navy bills). They contrast British naval practice and discipline with French and Spanish approaches, highlighting figures and institutions—Hood, Jervis, Samuel Bentham, dockyards, gunnery advances and provisioning (scurvy prevention)—that produced a highly efficient maritime fighting machine. Technical changes (carronades, better gunpowder) and tactical doctrine (aggressive initiative and decentralized command) are shown as crucial to Nelson’s methods. The episode closes by advertising club-only bonus material and promising further, more detailed installments on the battle itself.
title: Trafalgar: A World at War (Ep 1)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host film critic Muriel Zagad to present “a history of France in ten films.” Muriel discusses her ten picks spanning medieval to modern France, explaining how each film illuminates national identity and historical moments. Selections discussed include Jacques Rivette’s two-part Joan of Arc, La Reine Margot (adapted from Alexandre Dumas), Ridicule (court life under the late Ancien Régime), Abel Gance’s epic Napoleon, Les Enfants du Paradis (set in 1830s Paris), Polanski’s Dreyfus-affair film adapted from Robert Harris, Renoir’s La Grande Illusion (WWI), Clouzot’s Le Corbeau (occupation-era denunciation), the 1966 comedy La Grande Vadrouille, and Godard’s La Chinoise (pre‑May 1968). Conversation ranges from filmmaking constraints under occupation to political appropriations of historical figures, and ends with Muriel recommending Les Enfants du Paradis as a starting point for listeners wanting one essential film.
title: French History on Film

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) focuses on Winston Churchill's early imperial career and his rise to fame during the Second Boer War. The hosts recap Churchill's background, previous campaigns (including Omdurman), his early books (notably The River War and My Early Life), and his unsuccessful first run for parliament in Oldham. They set out the political and economic causes of the Boer conflict — the Great Trek, diamond and gold discoveries, and imperial ambitions led by figures like Joseph Chamberlain and Cecil Rhodes — and detail Churchill's dramatic experiences as a war correspondent: the ambushed armoured train, capture, imprisonment in Pretoria, and audacious escape via a goods train to Portuguese East Africa. His celebrated return to Durban and subsequent re-entry into uniform made him a public imperial hero, even as the war later descended into scorched-earth tactics and concentration camps. The episode situates Churchill within the complexities and controversies of British imperialism at the turn of the 20th century.
title: Young Churchill: Prisoner and Fugitive (Ep 3)

summary: This episode — part two of a multi-part survey of Winston Churchill's early life — follows Churchill from Sandhurst into his first imperial adventures. Holland and Sandbrook discuss Churchill's complex psychology after his father Lord Randolph Churchill's death, his hunger for fame and adventure, and his early work as a war correspondent. They cover his travels to Cuba (observing the Cuban insurgency), his posting to India and the Northwest Frontier (August 1897 punitive expedition), and his participation in Kitchener's 1898 Sudan campaign culminating in the Battle of Omdurman. The hosts trace how reading (Gibbon, Macaulay, Aristotle) shaped Churchill's prose and attitudes, examine his imperialist paternalism and racial assumptions, and describe his admiration of America and theatrical rhetorical style. They praise Churchill's vivid writing (My Early Life), criticise the industrial scale of imperial violence, note his disgust at Kitchener's brutality, and close with a reading of a William McGonagall poem about Omdurman. The episode sets up a subsequent part on Churchill's Boer War experience and famed escape.
title: Young Churchill: Soldier of Empire (Ep 2)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin a multipart look at the making of Winston Churchill, concentrating on his childhood and early career. They explore Churchill's conviction of destiny from adolescence, his appetite for danger and adventure, and his literary flair, noting episodes from his schooling at preparatory schools and Harrow through Sandhurst. The hosts examine the dysfunctional family background—Lord Randolph Churchill's political rise and collapse, and Jennie Jerome's social life—and the emotional neglect that shaped Winston's need for approval. They highlight formative influences: ancestry linked to John Churchill, 1st Duke of Marlborough; a beloved nanny, Elizabeth Everest; early reading (H. Rider Haggard) and war correspondence. The episode frames Churchill as a complex mixture of theatrical ambition, generosity, imperial paternalism and conspicuous courage, and sets up subsequent episodes that will follow his campaigns in Cuba, the Northwest Frontier, Sudan and South Africa. The hosts note an Andrew Roberts biography as a key modern interpretation and recommend Churchill's own My Early Life.
title: Young Churchill: Born to Lead (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by fashion historian Hilary Davidson to discuss Regency-era dress and why the period represents a genuine fashion revolution. Davidson argues that from the 1790s into the 1810s clothing changed in form and speed: women moved from structured stays to softer corsets and high, Empire-line waistlines with lightweight cottons like muslin, while men shifted toward tailored, sober cut garments that would evolve into modern suits. The episode covers cultural drivers (class, Romanticism, the French and Industrial revolutions), notable influencers (Emma Hamilton, Marie Antoinette, Beau Brummell), transmission of trends through social networks and retail infrastructure, and specific innovations — bonnets, cropped hair, riding habits, the decline of wigs, and the rise of pantaloons/trousers. Davidson situates Jane Austen’s novels within these fashion norms and highlights how military dress and tailoring reputations (Savile Row) shaped enduring male styles.
title: The Regency Revolution

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Marilyn Monroe as both a twentieth-century film star and a cultural symbol of 1950s America. Using Joyce Carol Oates' Blonde and Sarah Churchwell's The Many Lives of Marilyn Monroe as touchstones, they trace her rise from Norma Jeane Mortenson to international icon: wartime pinups, early films (Niagara; Gentlemen Prefer Blondes; How to Marry a Millionaire), advertising, and the distinctive cinematic image that outlived most of her films. They discuss her marriages to Joe DiMaggio and Arthur Miller, associations with Frank Sinatra and the Kennedys, and how her early death (1962) fed conspiracy theories and myth-making. The episode interrogates competing portrayals of Monroe as victim versus a canny self-maker, situates her in the contexts of McCarthyism, consumer culture and Cold War America, and considers her afterlife in art and popular memory (Warhol, Candle in the Wind). Ultimately they argue Monroe reveals both the difficulties of biography and the mechanics of modern celebrity.
title: Marilyn Monroe

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Rana Mitter about China’s experience in the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945). The discussion opens with the Nanjing Massacre (December 1937–January 1938) and moves to broader wartime dynamics: why brutality occurred, variation in Japanese imperial rule, and other massacres such as Suzhou. Mitter explains Chiang Kai-shek’s defensive strategy, the controversial blasting of the Yellow River dikes in 1938 and the resulting deaths and famine in Henan. The episode examines domestic fractures—Wang Jingwei’s collaborationist regime in Nanjing, internal leaks by figures like Zhou Fuhai—and the toxic US–Nationalist alliance after Pearl Harbor, focusing on Joseph Stilwell. It covers 1944’s Operation Ichigo, the U.S. Dixie Mission to the Communists in Yan’an, and debates over a possible U.S.–Communist accommodation. The conversation closes on the war’s long-term effects: the strengthening of bureaucratic and militarized governance, the Communist victory in the subsequent civil war, and how the conflict is remembered in modern China.
title: China and World War II - Part 2

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Rana Mitter about China’s war with Japan and his book China's War with Japan, 1937 to 1945: The Struggle for Survival. Mitter argues for treating 1937 (the Marco Polo Bridge/Wanping incident) as the true outbreak of the full-scale war in East Asia and discusses the deeper nineteenth- and early twentieth-century roots: the Opium Wars, Taiping Rebellion, the fall of the Qing, Sun Yat-sen, Chiang Kai-shek’s fragile nationalist state, warlordism, and the rise of Chinese communism. He outlines Japan’s rapid Meiji modernization, earlier expansion (Taiwan 1895, Korea 1910, Manchuria), the 1931 Manchurian Incident and creation of Manchukuo under Puyi. The conversation covers Chiang’s decision to resist, the Shanghai campaign, the uneasy Nationalist–Communist united front, collaborators such as Wang Jingwei, and contemporary and historiographical debates about dating the start of the global conflict. Sources cited include Chiang’s diaries and western eyewitness accounts (Auden/Isherwood).
title: China and World War II - Part 1

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Andrea Wolff about her book Magnificent Rebels, which traces the origins of Romanticism to a cluster of philosophers, poets and critics gathered in the university town of Jena in the 1790s. Wolff outlines why Jena — a small, relatively uncensored, intellectually dense place — became fertile ground for figures such as Fichte, the Schlegel brothers, Novalis, Schelling, Goethe and Schiller. She explains key ideas (the elevation of the self, imagination as a central faculty, and the unity of mind and nature), the social dynamics of the Jena set (open marriages, communes, gossip and infighting), and how their thought influenced later Romantic movements in England and America. The conversation ranges from anecdotes — Goethe and Schiller's friendship, Fichte's theatrical lectures, Caroline Schlegel's central role — to larger questions about how the Jena thinkers reshaped modern notions of selfhood and freedom.
title: Germans Behaving Badly

summary: This episode treats the Loch Ness Monster as a cultural and historical phenomenon rather than a zoological puzzle. Holland and Sandbrook trace reports back to St Columba's 6th-century encounter, note intermittent medieval and early modern mentions, and show how the 18th-century opening up of the Highlands (General Wade's roads) and 19th-century travel set the stage. The core narrative focuses on the 1933–34 Nessie mania: motorists' sightings, water bailiff Alex Campbell's plesiosaur suggestion, the Daily Mail's stunt-driven coverage, Marmaduke Weatherall's hoax footprints and the famous (later exposed) Surgeon’s Photograph (April 1934). They follow later 20th-century episodes — Tim Dinsdale's film, Sir Peter Scott's advocacy, Robert Rines's sonar/photographic claims and the 1938 coelacanth discovery that briefly made living 'living fossils' plausible — and end with modern DNA studies that find no evidence of a surviving large unknown creature in Loch Ness. The discussion situates Nessie in tourism, imperial nostalgia and conservation debates.
title: The Loch Ness Monster

description: The death of the Queen at the age of 96 brings to an end seven decades of her reign over Britain and the Commonwealth. In the first of a two-part series, Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland look back at the early years of Elizabeth’s life, leading up to her coronation.
summary: The hosts reflect on recording the episode the day after the death of Queen Elizabeth II and consider the emotional and historical weight of her long reign. They outline her early life (born April 1926), upbringing by grandparents, limited formal schooling, and how the 1936 abdication elevated her in the succession. The episode traces formative wartime experiences—evacuations, a 1940 broadcast, joining the Auxiliary Territorial Service—and the shaping influence of duty exemplified by George V and George VI. They discuss her marriage to Prince Philip, early tours (including Kenya where she learned of her father’s death), the symbolism of her coronation and anointing, and her role adapting the monarchy to a changing, increasingly multicultural Britain. Cultural references include Tom Holland’s book Dominion, T. S. Eliot’s The Waste Land, and portrayals in The Crown. The episode is presented as the first of two on the Queen’s life, ending on the tension between ancient ritual and modern media that defined her reign.
title: Queen Elizabeth II - part 1

description: In February 1952, on the death of her father King George VI, the 25-year-old Elizabeth became Queen. During her long reign she was served by 15 Prime Ministers and met an extraordinary array of people. Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland here examine her 70 years as Queen of the United Kingdom & 14 other countries, and head of the Commonwealth.
summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life and reign of Queen Elizabeth II in the second of a two-part set of episodes produced after her death and the accession of King Charles III. They trace the early smooth years of her reign, her role in facilitating decolonization and reshaping the empire into the Commonwealth, and the image-management that made the royal family seem like a model 'first family.' The hosts examine major crises: the populist tabloid culture of the 1970s, Princess Margaret's marital troubles, the Charles–Diana marriage and Diana's death in 1997, tensions with Margaret Thatcher over Commonwealth policy and apartheid, and later controversies including Harry and Meghan. They reflect on the Queen's longevity, global stature, symbolic power, popular moments (from the 1969 Royal Family documentary to Paddington at the Platinum Jubilee), and her perceived duty to serve until death. The episode ends by acknowledging the transition to King Charles III.
title: Queen Elizabeth II - part 2

description: In the final chapter of this series on the history of Portugal, Tom and Dominic explore Portugal in the 20th century, discussing the two World Wars, the Miracle of Fatima and dictator Antonio Salazar.
summary: This episode surveys modern Portugal with a focus on cultural melancholia (saudade), the rise of fado music, and the long rule of António de Oliveira Salazar. Hosts discuss 19th-century decline after the loss of Brazil, Portuguese social and economic backwardness, and cultural icons such as Amália Rodrigues and Fernando Pessoa. The conversation moves through the turbulent First Portuguese Republic, the 1917 Fátima apparitions, Portugal's participation in World War I, and the 1926 coup that opened the way for Salazar. Salazar's technocratic, Catholic, anti‑parliamentary Estado Novo is analysed: its repression, limited cult of personality, wartime neutrality, provision of the Azores to the Allies, and controversial record on refugees (including the actions of Aristides de Sousa Mendes). The pair also cover postwar politics, the 1958 Delgado challenge and 1965 murder, colonial wars in Africa, Salazar's 1968 stroke and replacement by Marcelo Caetano, and the path toward the 1970s revolution that would end the regime.
title: Portugal: Football, Fado, and Fascism? (Ep 4)

summary: This episode — the third in the hosts' multi-part history of Portugal — traces Portuguese fortunes from the late 16th century to the early 19th century. The presenters discuss the global Dutch–Portuguese conflicts over trade in the 17th century, the 1640 uprising that restored Portuguese independence and the accession of the House of Braganza, and the Anglo-Portuguese alliance (including Catherine of Braganza's marriage to Charles II). They profile Sebastião José de Carvalho e Melo (the Marquis de Pombal), his brutal reforms and the reconstruction of Lisbon after the catastrophic 1755 earthquake that provoked Voltaire's famous responses and later Candide. The episode then moves to Brazil: gold and diamond-driven demographic change, Portugal's dependence on colonial wealth, and the massive Atlantic slave trade. Finally they cover the Napoleonic crisis — the transfer of the court to Brazil in 1807, British intervention, Arthur Wellesley's campaigns and the Lines of Torres Vedras — and the path to Brazilian independence under Dom Pedro in 1822.
title: Portugal: Gold, Earthquakes, and Brazil (Ep 3)

summary: This episode continues the hosts' History of Portugal series, tracing Portuguese expansion from the death of Henry the Navigator through the first century of maritime empire. They discuss early explorers (Diogo Cão, Bartolomeu Dias) who probed Africa's coast and laid markers, and Vasco da Gama's perilous 1497–1499 voyage to India under King Manuel. The Treaty of Tordesillas and rivalry with Castile/Aragon are covered, as are the brutal methods used to secure footholds in the Indian Ocean — exemplified by Vasco da Gama and Afonso de Albuquerque's captures of Goa and Malacca. The conversation highlights Lisbon's transformation (Manueline monuments at Belém), the taking of exotic gifts to Europe, and the rise of Portuguese trading nodes that prefigure later sea empires. The episode closes with Portugal's 16th-century decline in momentum, King Sebastian's disastrous Moroccan campaign (1578), the 1580 succession crisis and union with Spain, and the emerging Dutch threat and the slave trade — setting up the next instalment.
title: Portugal: The Golden Age of Discovery (Ep 2)

summary: This episode inaugurates a multipart history of Portugal. The hosts trace Portugal's long, layered past from ancient times—Carthaginian contacts, Roman conquest and the Lusitania identity—to Visigothic and Moorish rule and the medieval Reconquista. They chart the emergence of a Portuguese kingdom under Afonso I (Alfonso Henriques) with key battles (São Mamede, Ourique) and the 1147 Siege of Lisbon aided by English crusaders. The long Anglo‑Portuguese relationship is highlighted via 14th‑century commercial treaties and the Treaty of Windsor (1386), and the marriage of Philippa of Lancaster into Portugal. The episode then follows Philippa’s sons—most notably Henry the Navigator—and Portugal’s turn outward: the capture of Ceuta (1415), Atlantic island colonisation (Madeira, Azores), advances in shipbuilding (caravel) and navigational science, voyages down the West African coast, and the grim origins of the Portuguese slave trade (Arguin 1444). The hosts set the scene for later episodes on Portugal’s expansive and ambivalent role in early globalisation.
title: Portugal: On the Edge of the World (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss J.R.R. Tolkien's The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (the episode is the second on Tolkien). They trace Tolkien's sources—Old Norse, Finnish and Anglo‑Saxon literature and imperial adventure fiction (H. Rider Haggard)—and explain the collision of the modern English domestic hobbit with archaic mythic elements. The conversation situates Tolkien in the twentieth century: the trauma of World War I, the moral dilemmas of World War II (including aerial bombing and the Blitz), and Tolkien's Catholicism as informing themes of sacrifice, corruption and redemption (the ring as a symbol). They also cover Tolkien's politics and conservatism, environmentalism, the Scouring of the Shire as postwar critique, and contemporary debates about race in his work. Cultural afterlives are noted: mid‑century American reception, the 1960s counterculture, and recent adaptations that address representation.
title: The Lord of the Rings

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin a two-part episode on J. R. R. Tolkien, situating him as both a major twentieth-century cultural figure and a scholar of medieval languages. They trace Tolkien's origins from his 1892 birth in Bloemfontein, South Africa, to childhood in Sarehole/near Birmingham, his mother's conversion to Catholicism, and his intense adolescent friendships (the TCBS). The First World War—service with the Lancashire Fusiliers, the Somme, trench horror and trench fever—looms large as a formative influence on his mythic imagination. They discuss Tolkien's linguistic scholarship, his academic career (including work on the Oxford English Dictionary), and his effort to construct an English mythology, drawing on Norse, Finnish and Anglo‑Saxon sources. Hosts link Tolkien to wider interwar myth-making (Yeats, Joyce, Eliot) and note influences on The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, ending with Tolkien’s anecdotal composition of the hobbit opening and promising a second episode to examine the books, elves and major themes in detail.
title: J.R.R. Tolkien

summary: This episode examines holidays and tourism in the ancient world, comparing Roman elite leisure — villas, spas and the Bay of Naples resorts — with modern holiday habits. Using Pliny the Younger’s villa description as a starting point, Tom and Dominic discuss Roman seaside villas, the development of pleasure architecture (e.g. Baiae), and entrepreneurs creating high-end coastal properties. They profile emperors and elites associated with retreat and spectacle: Tiberius’ seclusion on Capri, Nero’s Domus Aurea as a public pleasure complex, and Vespasian’s civic response with the Colosseum. The second half treats Roman travel abroad: generals and tourists visiting Greece and Egypt, pillaging and transporting artworks (e.g. Corinth, Athens), Paulus’ grand tour, Hadrian’s restorations in Greece, and the Memnon colossi inscriptions. The hosts end by tracing continuity into late antiquity and medieval pilgrimage (Helena in Jerusalem), arguing for long-running resonances between ancient tourism, cultural display, and pilgrimage infrastructure.
title: Roman Holidays (Ep 4)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the development of modern tourism from the First World War through the late 20th century. They discuss continued travel to the French Riviera during WWI, the rise of travel clubs and camping culture, early sunbathing fashions and sun creams (including Eugène Schueller's Ombre Solaire), and the expansion of seaside resorts and holiday camps such as Butlin's. The episode covers the appearance of overseas package flights pioneered by Vladimir Reitz's Horizon, the invention and cultural spread of the bikini (Louis Réard, Jacques Heim), and the rapid transformation of Mediterranean destinations like Majorca and Benidorm. They chart how mass package tourism peaked in the 1960s–70s and began to undermine traditional British resorts, and conclude by identifying the 1990s — internet booking and aviation deregulation — as a decisive break that reshaped how people plan holidays today.
title: Sun, Sea, and Sex (Ep 3)

summary: This episode is the second part of a mini-series on the history of holidays, concentrating on nineteenth-century tourism. The hosts discuss how travel broadened beyond the aristocratic Grand Tour into middle-class and mass tourism, drawing extensively on Lucy Lethbridge's book Tourists. They trace early package tours to Thomas Cook (1841) and the role of railways, guidebooks and phrasebooks in shaping travel expectations. The episode surveys battlefield tourism after Waterloo, spa tourism across German and Central European resorts (with often eccentric treatments), and changing attitudes toward scenery and the sublime that drove visits to places such as the Alps and Iceland. They also cover the rise of seaside resorts (Blackpool, Cape May, Florida via Henry Flagler) and class tensions around new mass tourism. The episode closes by noting how many people were on holiday as Europe slid into the July Crisis and World War I, ending with a reading of Philip Larkin’s poem “1914.”
title: Holidays: The Invention of Mass Tourism (Ep 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the history of holidays, tracing the practice from early pilgrimages and the Grand Tour through Georgian spa towns and Regency seaside resorts. They examine origins and motivations—leisure, self-improvement and status—and describe typical Grand Tour routes (Paris, Switzerland, over the Alps to Italy), tutors or "bear leaders," and the collecting impulse (e.g. Pompeii/Herculaneum finds). The hosts profile notable travellers: Thomas Howard, Inigo Jones, Milton, Boswell (with encounters with Rousseau and Voltaire), and Byron (his Mediterranean and Albanian travels and Childe Harold). They then move to domestic tourism when continental travel became difficult: Bath’s transformation into a fashionable spa (Thomas Ghidotti) and Brighton’s rise as a sea‑bathing and gambling resort (Richard Russell, the Prince Regent/George IV). The episode closes by situating these developments as precursors to 19th‑century mass tourism and promises a follow-up on rail, Thomas Cook, and the Victorian tourist industry.
title: Holidays: Byron's Grand Tour (Ep 1)

summary: This episode (the third in the Justinian and Theodora series) continues the story of Justinian I and Empress Theodora in sixth-century Constantinople. Holland and Sandbrook recount Justinian's reconquest campaigns — the swift Vandalic victory under Belisarius and the protracted, destructive Gothic War in Italy — and the mixed outcomes these produced: temporary territorial gains but severe social and infrastructure damage (notably to Rome's aqueducts). They discuss the sack of Antioch by the Sasanians and, crucially, the devastating Justinianic Plague, which undermined the empire's tax base and manpower and accelerated long-term decline. The hosts assess Procopius's conflicting portrayals (official histories vs. the scandalous Secret History), Theodora's controversial biography and reforms, and Justinian's legacy — law codification and monumental building alongside overextension. They close by situating Justinian's era as both a last flourish of Roman ambition and a turning point leading toward the Byzantine age and the later Arab conquests.
title: Justinian & Theodora: The Secret History (Ep 3)

summary: This episode is the second part of a series on Emperor Justinian I and Empress Theodora. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Justinian’s twin aims: restoring Roman territorial dominion and establishing a divinely ordered, centralized empire. They explore his legal reforms and fiscal pressures, mentioning key administrators such as John of Cappadocia and Tribonian. The hosts compare Justinian to contemporary Sasanian ruler Khosrow and outline geopolitical constraints posed by Persia. The episode focuses on the Nika riots of January 532: mob violence by the Blues and Greens devastates central Constantinople, including Hagia Sophia, and briefly elevates Hypatius as a rival claimant. Theodora’s famed refusal to flee and Justinian’s use of generals Belisarius, Mundus and the eunuch Narses to crush the rebellion are discussed. The riot’s aftermath consolidates imperial power, paves the way for the new Hagia Sophia, and diminishes the senate’s authority. The hosts reference primary and secondary sources (Procopius’ Secret History and a book titled Eternal Victory) and preview a third episode on Justinian’s wars and the plague.
title: Justinian: Making Rome Great Again (Ep 2)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook introduce listeners to the world of Constantinople and the remarkable imperial couple Justinian and Theodora. They open with a notorious passage from Procopius about Theodora’s early life in the hippodrome milieu, then situate the city geographically, politically and culturally as both a ‘new Rome’ and a distinct Christian capital. The hosts explain Constantinople’s defensive advantages, urban growth and Roman institutional continuities, discuss ecclesiastical disputes (notably Monophysitism versus the Chalcedonian settlement), and trace Theodora’s rise from performer to empress alongside Justinian’s political ascent. The episode references major contexts — currency and administration under Anastasius, frontier rivalry with the Sasanians, and later catastrophes such as the Justinianic plague and the Fourth Crusade — and ends by teasing the violent, dramatic episodes of Justinian’s reign for a future instalment.
title: Theodora: Empress of Byzantium (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome Professor Kyle Harper (University of Oklahoma) to discuss his book The Fate of Rome and the central argument that climate and infectious disease were decisive forces in the transformation of the Roman world. Harper explains how urbanization, connectivity and animal reservoirs created ecological conditions for repeated pandemics—the Antonine Plague, the Plague of Cyprian and the Justinianic Plague—and how those crises interacted with political, fiscal and military stresses. He argues disease worked alongside human factors (barbarian pressures, civil war, fiscal breakdown) to reshape demography, stature, settlement and institutions, and considers longer-term consequences including the Lombard takeover of Italy and the religious/apocalyptic climate around the emergence of Islam. The discussion highlights recent advances from ancient DNA, comparative demography and environmental history that refine how pandemics' reach and recurrence are understood.
title: Plague and the decline of the Roman Empire

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History explores the cultural, technological and military roles of pigeons across history. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by BBC security correspondent Gordon Carrera, author of Operation Columba, to discuss pigeons from sacred symbolism (Noah's dove, Christian imagery) to practical uses (ancient homing, Roman military messaging). The conversation covers pigeon-powered communications from antiquity through the 19th century (including Reuters' early pigeon service and the Siege of Paris), heroic wartime birds in WWI and WWII (Cher Ami; the Special Continental Pigeon Service/Operation Columba), and postwar intelligence uses (CIA spy pigeon experiments). They also address mass extinction via the passenger pigeon and modern pigeon fancying and breeding. The episode mixes archival anecdotes (Falcon Destruction Unit, RAF rescue pigeons such as Winky) with reflections on pigeons' PR problems, concluding that pigeons have been underestimated contributors to human history.
title: Pigeons

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Ian McGregor about the Battle of Stalingrad. They open with a passage from Vasily Grossman's Life and Fate and then discuss the micro-history of Pavlov's House, its tactical importance in the shattered city and the propaganda that turned it into a Soviet totem. McGregor explains the evolution of Soviet urban defence, the role of small assault teams, and commanders such as Chuikov and Radimtsev. The conversation moves to Operation Uranus — the Soviet pincer that encircled the German Sixth Army — and the subsequent failed German relief (Operation Winter Storm). They cover Hitler's refusal to allow breakout, the Luftwaffe airlift failure, the conditions inside the Kessel, and the eventual surrender and treatment of prisoners. The episode concludes with reflections on memory and commemoration in Russia and the continuing significance of Stalingrad, while promoting McGregor's book The Lighthouse of Stalingrad.
title: Stalingrad: Pavlov's House and the Red Army (Ep 2)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) welcomes Ian McGregor to discuss the Battle of Stalingrad. Beginning with a vivid Vasily Grossman journal excerpt, the conversation situates Stalingrad within broader WWII strategy: the aftermath of Operation Barbarossa, Hitler's Case Blue drive for Caucasian oil, and the logistical strains faced by the Wehrmacht. They examine why Stalingrad became a focal point, the Luftwaffe’s terror bombing, and the urban, house-to-house nature of the fighting. Key personalities discussed include Friedrich Paulus and his Sixth Army, Walter von Reichenau (who fell ill), and Soviet commanders such as Vasily Chuikov under orders from Yeremenko and with political oversight from Nikita Khrushchev. The hosts and guest probe Soviet measures like Order No. 227, penal battalions and blocking detachments, the ferries across the Volga (Rodimtsev’s actions), and how a flattened city provided defensive advantages. The episode closes by teasing a follow-up on Pavlov’s House and the onset of winter fighting.
title: The Battle of Stalingrad (Ep 1)

summary: This episode closes The Rest Is History's London Week with two contrasting London moments chosen by the hosts. Tom Holland recounts the Tower of London's historic menagerie: exotic royal gifts from medieval kings (a polar bear from Hakon the Young, lions from Frederick II, and an elephant from Louis IX), the menagerie's evolution through the Tudor and Stuart periods, and its eventual transfer to Regent's Park and the founding of the London Zoo in the early 19th century. Dominic Sandbrook highlights the Metropolitan Railway and the creation of 'Metro-land': the world's first underground railway (1863), its rapid suburban extensions, the railway's land-development strategy and promotional guides, and the cultural ideal of suburban Arcadia celebrated by figures such as Stanley Baldwin and John Betjeman. The discussion touches on cultural responses (Betjeman, Betjeman's 1973 film), literary parallels (The Wind in the Willows, Tolkien), and period social changes that produced modern commuting and suburban housing.
title: London: Moments (Ep 5)

description:

London: Haunted London
Join Tom and Dominic for a special live, on location episode as they walk around central London exploring the haunted remnants of the past.

Producer: Dom Johnson

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk listeners through a tightly focused ‘Hidden London’ tour around Newgate, Smithfield and the remains of St Bartholomew's. They explore concealed layers of urban history: Newgate prison and execution routes to Tyburn, the Pie Corner marker for the Great Fire of London (1666), body‑snatching links with St Bartholomew's Hospital, and the notorious Cock Lane poltergeist. They visit St Bartholomew the Great — its Romanesque and early Gothic fabric, a claimed Marian appearance, and the chapel later used as workshops where Benjamin Franklin once worked — and Smithfield, site of public tortures, the Peasants’ Revolt confrontation (Wat Tyler) and burnings in Mary I’s reign. They trace vanished elements like the River Fleet and note cultural associations (Dickens’ Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, Hogarth, Chaucer) while reflecting on how modern London’s unremarkable streets conceal violent, theatrical and devotional pasts. The episode mixes architectural description, literary connections and local anecdotes to show how history persists beneath the present city.
title: Haunted London (Ep 4)

London: People
Henry Fielding and C.L.R. James - two figures who are part of the furniture in London's history. Tom and Dominic debate and discuss their lives and legacy in the latest episode of London Week. 

Producer: Dom Johnson

summary: This London Week episode has Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook each selecting a London figure. Sandbrook profiles Henry Fielding (born 1707), covering his Eton friendship with William Pitt the Elder, early scandals, his satirical writings (including the parody Chamela and Joseph Andrews) and his masterpiece Tom Jones. They concentrate on Fielding's role as Bow Street magistrate — his reforms, the creation of an organised team of Bow Street Runners, the police gazette (Quarterly Pursuit/Public Hue and Cry) and his brother John Fielding's later innovations. Holland chooses C. L. R. James, tracing his Trinidad origins, cricket passion and writings (Beyond the Boundary, The Black Jacobins), his time in Britain and the US, meetings with Trotsky, Rivera and Kahlo, and his later life in Brixton tied to Race Today and the post‑war Caribbean community. The hosts riff on TV adaptations (joking about a Netflix series), reflect on Brixton's cultural history and signpost further London Week episodes about walks and ghosts.
title: London: People (Ep 3)

On the public feed, we'll release an episode daily, from Monday to Friday. As a friend of the show, you get them all at once!

London: Places
In the second episode of London Week, Tom and Dominic focus on two very different historical places in London's past, discussing Barking Abbey and the 2i's Coffee Bar.

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producers: Jack Davenport + Tony Pastor

summary: This episode is part of the hosts' London-themed week and focuses on two very different London places. Tom recounts a lockdown pilgrimage across South and East London to Barking, tracing its Anglo‑Saxon origins: the founding of Barking Abbey by Erkenwald (Urkenwald), the abbess Athelberg/Ethelberger as a center of female scholarship, links with All Hallows by the Tower and surviving Anglo‑Saxon fabric, and the abbey’s destruction in the Reformation leaving only the Curfew Tower. Dominic’s nomination shifts to postwar Soho in the 1950s: coffee bars and milk bars brought by Italian immigrants, the Two Eyes coffee bar on Old Compton Street and its sweaty basement scene. They discuss skiffle, early youth culture, acts and figures associated with the venue (Wally White and the Vipers, producer George Martin) and performers whose careers touched the Two Eyes—Tommy Steele, Adam Faith and Cliff Richard—illustrating a cultural moment that incubated Britain’s 1960s pop explosion. The episode contrasts ecclesiastical medieval history with mid‑20th century popular culture.
title: London: Places (Ep 2)

On the public feed, we'll release an episode daily, from Monday to Friday. However, as a friend of the show, you get them ALL at once!

Londinium:
Amid the sounds of building sites and ambulance sirens, Tom and Dominic march across the bridges and snake down the alleyways of London. In this special live episode, they uncover the Roman roots of the capital city, tracing its journey from desolate mudflats to a sprawling beacon of civilisation. 

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producers: Jack Davenport + Tony Pastor

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook lead a walking tour through Roman London (Londinium), using surviving fragments, archaeology and literary echoes to reconstruct the city's Roman past. They begin with a quotation from Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness, segue into the Roman invasion (AD 43) and why the Romans founded a bridge and port at the Thames' lowest crossing. They discuss early events including Boudicca's revolt (AD 60/61) and archaeological evidence (skulls and charred buildings) found at Poultry/Walbrook. The hosts visit the London Mithraeum and the Walbrook organic assemblage (IOU tablets and sandals), the London Stone, the basilica remains in Leadenhall Market, and stretches of the Roman wall (including preserved sections under modern structures and a fragment in a car park). They end at the grave memorial of a young Roman-era woman near the Gherkin, reflecting on Roman London’s decline, later myth-making and the intersection of developers, archaeology and civic memory.
title: Londinium (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Professor Robert Coles to discuss the life, politics and literary legacy of George Orwell (Eric Arthur Blair). The conversation follows Orwell from his imperial birth in India and upbringing in rural England, through Eton and service in the Burma police, to his essay-writing and 1930s reportage (notably The Road to Wigan Pier). They examine Orwell's experience in the Spanish Civil War and its catalytic effect on his anti‑Stalinism and subsequent books Homage to Catalonia, Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four. Coles explores Orwell's class tensions, Englishness, wartime roles (Home Guard, Ministry of Information/BBC work) and his postwar anti-communist activity, including the controversial list for the Information Research Department. The episode closes by assessing Orwell's present-day resonance — on topics from social media to Brexit and Ukraine — and recommends Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four as essential reads.
title: George Orwell

summary: This is a special “results” edition of The Rest Is History in which hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook announce the winners of their tongue-in-cheek historical Love Island contest. After recapping earlier rounds, they reveal vote shares for four couples: Stanley Baldwin and Theodora (winners, c.47%), General Custer and Lola Montes (second), Lord Byron and Sporris (third), and Jimmy Carter and Olympias (fourth). The hosts banter about contestants’ suitability, public reaction on Twitter, and cultural context—touching on issues around Byron’s reputation, Baldwin family anecdotes, and Custer’s military record. They reference Procopius’s Secret History in discussion of Theodora and propose a future episode on Justinian and Theodora. Personal asides include Dominic on holiday and Tom finishing a chapter on Parthia and Trajan. The episode mixes light-hearted parody with historical commentary and teases forthcoming episodes (including one on George Orwell).
title: Historical Love Island: THE WINNER

summary: This episode is a themed special in which hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, joined by guest Katie Holland, stage a playful thought-experiment: which historical figures would succeed on Love Island? They nominate ten archetypal contestants drawn from across history — including Lord Byron, Jimmy Carter, Judas Iscariot, General Custer, Theodora, Olympias, Lola Montez, Marcia Williams, Frances Stewart and Stanley Baldwin — discuss each figure’s biography and likely on-island behaviour, and pair them as couples for a public vote. The conversation mixes serious biographical detail (e.g. Procopius’s allegations about Theodora, Byron’s affairs, Custer at Little Bighorn) with comic asides about speedos, memes and reality-TV tropes. The episode closes by asking listeners to vote on the four couples that will go forward; the hosts promise a bonus follow-up episode to announce and analyse the result.
title: Historical Love Island

summary: Recorded on 7 July (during the July 2022 UK government crisis), this episode is a rapid-response “Boris special” in which Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook diagnose Boris Johnson’s fall from power. They begin with a comic reading from Kenneth Grahame’s The Wind in the Willows and proceed to compare Johnson to classical and modern figures — Pericles, Caesar, Otho, Reagan — exploring how his classical education and populist style shaped his premiership. They discuss key moments (sacking Michael Gove, cabinet resignations), consider whether Britain’s uncodified constitutional conventions have been damaged, and debate Johnson’s historical significance (Brexit, COVID, chaotic exit). The hosts place the crisis in longer political context — referencing Thatcher, Cameron, May, and other prime ministers — and close with light predictions about likely successors and upcoming podcast themes.
title: The Last Days of Boris Johnson

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Sarah Churchwell about her book The Wrath to Come: Gone with the Wind and the Lies America Tells. The conversation uses Margaret Mitchell's Gone with the Wind (and its 1939 film adaptation) as a lens to explore how the Lost Cause mythology shaped American memory from Reconstruction through the early 20th century. Churchwell details the novel and film's popular reception during the Great Depression and Second World War, the Atlanta premiere's segregation, and Hattie McDaniel's Oscar experience. The discussion traces Reconstruction's collapse, violent white supremacist backlash (including the Ku Klux Klan), legalized Jim Crow after the 1896 Supreme Court decision, convict leasing and chain gangs, and the entrenchment of Confederate mythology in public culture. The hosts and guest debate how cultural texts like Gone with the Wind and Birth of a Nation influenced politics and racial attitudes up to recent events such as the 2021 Capitol storming, arguing for critical engagement rather than simple suppression of problematic works.
title: Gone with the Wind

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Professor Adam Smith (Oxford), continues a multi-part exploration of the American Civil War and its long aftermath. The discussion examines Appomattox and Robert E. Lee's surrender, how immediate postwar choices and Lincoln's assassination shaped Reconstruction, and the origins and endurance of the Lost Cause myth. Adam Smith assesses the legal and political gains of Reconstruction — notably the Fourteenth Amendment — alongside the failures that permitted Jim Crow, lynching and long-term racial inequality. The episode also addresses memory and memorialisation: Confederate monuments, the naming of military assets, and changing public attitudes amid recent political polarisation. Comparisons are drawn to mid-20th-century memory and to contemporary American polarization under recent presidencies. Cultural references include Walt Whitman's verse and modern works about Lee. The hosts and guest stress that the Civil War remains a live, contested subject because its issues of race and national identity continue to reverberate in American politics today.
title: American Civil War: Aftermath & Legacy (Ep 4)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Professor Adam Smith (Oxford) about Gettysburg and the wider American Civil War. They open with a William Faulkner passage evoking Pickett's Charge, then walk listeners through Gettysburg’s three days (July 1–3, 1863): terrain, commanders, the artillery duel, and the failed Confederate assault. The discussion situates Gettysburg alongside the fall of Vicksburg (July 1863) as a turning point, examines black participation—contraband, the enlistment of roughly 186,000 Black Union soldiers, segregated units, unequal pay, and brutal treatment when captured—and the wider social reactions such as the New York Draft Riots. They cover political stakes (Lincoln’s 1864 election, McClellan, fall of Atlanta and Sherman’s campaign) and conclude by previewing the next episode on Appomattox and the war’s legacy, noting extended content available through the Rest Is History Club.
title: American Civil War: Gettysburg (Ep 3)

summary: This is part two of The Rest Is History’s examination of the American Civil War. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by scholar Adam Smith to discuss why secession became irreversible and why the North chose to fight to restore the Union. They consider the motivations of Southern elites, Robert E. Lee’s decision to side with Virginia, and the Confederacy’s early military successes under Lee and Stonewall Jackson. The conversation covers strategic dynamics — Northern advantages in manpower, industry and transport; Confederate hopes for European intervention; and key campaigns in 1862 (Peninsula Campaign, Seven Days Battles, Antietam) and operations in the Western theatre (New Orleans, Vicksburg). They also examine social dimensions: soldiers’ experience, women’s roles, and the political impact of Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation following Antietam. The episode closes by setting up 1863 as the war’s fulcrum and promising further discussion of Gettysburg and the war’s cultural aftermath.
title: American Civil War: Outbreak (Ep 2)

summary: This episode is the first of a series on the American Civil War and examines the causes of the conflict. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Professor Adam Smith (Edward Osborne Professor of Political History) to trace how slavery became the central, intractable issue in U.S. politics from the Constitution’s compromises in the 1780s through territorial expansion, cotton’s economic importance, and mid‑19th century polarisation. They discuss key flashpoints — the Fugitive Slave Act (1850), Bleeding Kansas and the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), the Dred Scott decision (1857), Anthony Burns’s arrest (1854), John Brown’s activism and Harpers Ferry (1859) — and how cultural forces (Uncle Tom’s Cabin, Frederick Douglass’s oratory) and political realignments (collapse of the Whigs, rise of the Republican Party) radicalised North and South. Lincoln’s background, beliefs, and political rise to the 1860 election are covered, and the episode closes with secession, the standoff over federal property, and the bombardment of Fort Sumter that precipitated full-scale war.
title: American Civil War: The Causes (Ep 1)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview archaeologist and author Mike Pitts about Stonehenge’s chronology, construction and meanings. Pitts outlines an extended sequence of activity beginning with a blue‑stone circle around 3,200 BC, burial activity over centuries, and a dramatic reworking of the site c. 2,500 BC when large sarsen megaliths were brought in. He rejects glacial transport for the bluestones, arguing for human movement by sledges and boats, and stresses the social and political spectacle of moving megaliths. The discussion surveys past explanations — Druids, Roman temples, astronomical 'computer' theories (Gerald Hawkins) — and highlights Mike Parker Pearson’s life/death landscape interpretation linking Durrington Walls and Stonehenge. Pitts also discusses later population change and migration around the monument’s end, cremation burials, and how Stonehenge’s role evolved. The episode promotes Pitts’s book How to Build Stonehenge and places the monument in a dynamic social and political Neolithic context.
title: Stonehenge

summary: This episode is the fourth and final part of a multi-episode examination of Mark Antony, Cleopatra VII and Octavian in the late Roman Republic. The hosts discuss Octavian's propaganda campaign (c. 33–31 BC) that portrayed Antony as effeminate and enslaved by Cleopatra, and how Roman misogyny and anti-foreign prejudice made such smears effective. They trace the literary mediation of the story through Virgil, Horace, Plutarch, Pliny and later poets (including C. P. Cavafy), and explain how Maecenas cultivated poets (Virgil, Propertius, Horace) to canonize the Augustan narrative. The conversation covers the politics and military decisions that led to the blockade at Actium, the uncertain conduct of the breakout, Antony and Cleopatra’s flight to Alexandria, Antony’s suicide and Cleopatra’s death, and Octavian’s absorption of Egypt into his personal domain. The hosts conclude with the fate of Cleopatra’s children, Egypt under Rome, and reflections on Cleopatra’s long cultural legacy and suitability as a role model.
title: Cleopatra's Downfall (Episode 4)

summary: This episode (the third in the hosts' multi-part treatment of Cleopatra/Antony) traces how Mark Antony and Cleopatra moved from political convenience to an intimate and political partnership that reshaped the eastern Mediterranean. Dominic and Tom discuss Antony's summons of Cleopatra to Tarsus and Alexandria, his winter sojourns, the division of Roman power between Antony, Octavian and Lepidus, and Antony's ambitions (including his failed Parthian expedition). The hosts cover the births of Cleopatra and Antony's children (Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene, Ptolemy Philadelphus), Antony's marriage to Octavia, and the diplomatic manoeuvres that culminate in the Donations of Antioch and the Donations of Alexandria. They analyse Roman reactions and Octavian's propaganda framing Antony as effeminate and a traitor to Rome. The episode closes with reflections on the political gamble of blending Roman and Hellenistic monarchical traditions and ends with a reading of Cavafy's poem about the Alexandrian pageant.
title: Antony & Cleopatra (Episode 3)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (part two of a Cleopatra miniseries) — hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook — examines Cleopatra VII's personality, political skill and early reign. Using Plutarch's surviving anecdotes, the hosts argue Cleopatra’s power derived from charisma and political theatre rather than conventional beauty. They recount her struggle with her brother Ptolemy XIII and his ministers, the approach of Roman civil war, and Pompey’s flight to Egypt and subsequent murder. Julius Caesar’s arrival in Alexandria, his precarious position during the Siege of Alexandria, the famous story of Cleopatra’s clandestine meeting with Caesar (the “carpet”/bag anecdote), and the political consequences — including Caesar’s relationship with Cleopatra, the birth of her son Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion), and her later return to Egypt after Caesar’s death — are explored. The episode situates Cleopatra within Mediterranean geopolitics and sets up episode three, which will follow the aftermath of Caesar’s murder and its effects on her rule.
title: Julius Caesar & Cleopatra (Episode 2)

description:

summary: This episode examines Cleopatra's place in history through a discussion between Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, drawing on Sandbrook's children’s book Cleopatra, Queen of the Nile. The hosts situate Cleopatra within the Hellenistic world founded by Alexander the Great and explain how the Ptolemaic dynasty combined Macedonian-Greek and Egyptian traditions. They outline the weak reign of Ptolemy XII Auletes, the fiscal pressures from bankers and Rome, and the Alexandrian riots that briefly deposed him. The episode highlights Cleopatra’s political skill: her use of Egyptian religious imagery (Isis), coinage and public ritual to assert authority alongside male co-rulers, and her emergence while Rome’s republic imploded into civil war. The discussion touches on key Roman figures (Pompey, Julius Caesar, Mark Antony), episodes of Roman eastern expansion, and the distorted Roman sources that shaped Cleopatra’s legend. The hosts read an evocative excerpt about Antony’s first impressions and promise a continuation of the narrative in the next installment.
title: Young Cleopatra (Episode 1)

description:
Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the 'first' fascist, Gabriele D'Annunzio, with historian Lucy Hughes-Hallett.

D'Annunzio was a key figure in Italian literature before becoming a political figure later in his life. Although never personally identifying with fascism, his ideas were hugely influential on Mussolini.
