summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Lucy Hughes-Hallett about her biography The Pike, exploring the life and influence of Italian writer and nationalist Gabriele D'Annunzio. The discussion traces D'Annunzio's rise as a celebrated poet and flamboyant celebrity, his bellicose campaigning for Italy's entry into World War I, daring aviation exploits (including a 1918 raid over Vienna), and the 1919 occupation of Fiume where he established a theatrical, quasi-revolutionary regime. Hughes-Hallett and the hosts examine his elitist, anti-parliamentary ideas, eroticized cult of violence, and how elements of his style — spectacle, uniforms, rituals and appeals to martial virility — were later adopted by Italian fascists, though D'Annunzio himself never fully embraced Mussolini. They also consider his literary reputation, influences (Flaubert, Nietzsche, Darwin), later retreat from politics, and how modern Italy remembers him. The episode situates D'Annunzio within the wider post‑war turmoil and the contested settlement after 1918.
title: The First Fascist

summary: Recorded on the evening of 6 June, this special Rest Is History episode frames the Conservative confidence vote in Boris Johnson as the latest in a long line of prime ministerial downfalls. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook compile a top-ten of dramatic exits — from Robert Walpole's 1742 forced resignation and Lord North's fall after Yorktown, to the assassination of Spencer Percival, Robert Peel's defeat over the Corn Laws, Herbert Asquith's ousting in World War I, Neville Chamberlain's Norway debacle, and modern examples such as Harold Wilson, Margaret Thatcher, Tony Blair and Theresa May. They weave historical parallels and motifs (party coups, foreign-policy disasters, personal scandal, health and intra-party rivalry), discuss the mechanics of confidence votes and by-elections, and reflect on political survival strategies. The conversation ranges across conflicts (War of Jenkins's Ear, American Revolution, Napoleonic and World Wars), political culture and illustrative biographies, and concludes by considering whether Johnson's weak confidence result will be terminal.
title: How Prime Ministers Fall

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the origins, evolution and cultural afterlife of the Robin Hood legend. They begin with early 15th-century ballads such as Robin Hood and the Monk, noting motifs — Sherwood, archery, the Sheriff, devotion to the Virgin — and the violent, trickster aspects lost in later, child-friendly retellings. They trace how Tudor, Stuart and Victorian writers (including Anthony Monday/Munday, Joseph Ritson and Sir Walter Scott) reshaped Robin into a dispossessed noble and inserted Anglo‑Saxon/Norman themes. They discuss Howard Pyle's influential late‑19th‑century children's version, 20th-century films and TV, and competing explanations for Robin's origins: a historical outlaw, a literary fusion, or a pagan/Marian-rooted figure (Lesley Coote's thesis). The episode also examines searches for medieval candidates in records, the Kirklees grave tradition, and the continuing invention of new Robin Hood folklore, ending with a poem and reflections on why the figure endures.
title: Robin Hood

description:
In today's episode, Tom and Dominic talk to Sara Read about the history of childbirth.

Sara unveils the origin of the word 'gossip' and its connection to midwifery. As well as this, they discuss how someone would qualify as a midwife; the relationship between religion and childbirth; and the average age of becoming a first time mother. They also look into the changes in the maternal mortality rate throughout history. And, finally, they touch on the authenticity of 'Call The Midwife'.  

Sara Read is the author of two works of historical fiction: The Gossips' Choice and The Midwife's Truth, available from all good bookshops.

Editor: Scarlett Murray
Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Jack Davenport

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host a wide-ranging conversation with literary historian Sarah Reed about the history of childbirth and midwifery from antiquity to the modern era. Reed discusses medieval and early modern practice: the role of gossips (female birth attendants), the emergence of printed midwifery manuals (including the translation known as The Birth of Mankind), licensing and ecclesiastical oversight in Tudor–early modern England, apprenticeship of midwives, and Jane Sharp's 1671 handbook. They examine cultural beliefs and remedies (Pliny's curious advice), Caesarean-section myths (Julius Caesar), swaddling, maternal mortality trends, and how medicalization and men’s involvement affected outcomes. Reed also appraises the representation of midwifery in Call the Midwife and contrasts community-based birthing practices with centralized, NHS-era maternity care. The episode balances technical developments (anesthesia, antisepsis) with lived experiences drawn from diaries, poems and memoirs to show continuities and cultural variation in childbirth practices.
title: Childbirth

summary: The episode surveys the history of British royal jubilees as national temperature checks, from George III's morale-boosting 1809 celebration during the Napoleonic Wars through Queen Victoria's late‑Victorian golden and diamond jubilees (1887, 1897) — which foreground empire, Indian connections (Abdul Karim) and Fenian terrorism — to George V's modest 1935 silver jubilee and Elizabeth II's more recent jubilees (1977, 2002, 2012) that reflect changing public moods and popular culture. Dominic and Tom trace how jubilees reveal Britain’s self-image: George III's 1809 pastoral patriotism; Victoria's imperial apogee and Kipling's anxious “Recessional”; George V's humdrum democratic resilience in the 1930s; the punk and economic malaise surrounding 1977; and the pop‑culture rehabilitation of the monarchy in 2002 and 2012 with palace concerts. They discuss attempts to politicize jubilees (Lord Salisbury and an 1887 counter‑terror plot), the role of imperial pageantry, and how jubilees mix spectacle, politics and identity across two centuries.
title: Jubilees

summary: This episode — the third in the hosts' short series on Australia’s wartime and post‑war prime ministers — surveys the distinctive cast and themes of late twentieth and early twenty‑first century Australian politics. Holland and Sandbrook profile major figures: Bob Hawke and his trade‑union rise and Oxford background; the Hawke–Keating reforming partnership (floating the dollar, deregulation) and Keating’s combative persona and Redfern Park speech on Aboriginal reconciliation; John Howard’s long conservative stewardship and his law‑and‑order, immigration and alliance policies; and the tumultuous 2000s–2010s of leadership “spills” involving Kevin Rudd, Julia Gillard, Tony Abbott, Malcolm Turnbull and Scott Morrison. Recurring topics are Australia’s Anglo/anti‑Anglo currents, republicanism, the influence of China and resource wealth, climate politics and the development of hardline border policies. The episode emphasizes Australia’s robust political style, international influence (on centre‑left and centre‑right reforms) and the destabilizing culture of frequent leadership challenges.
title: Australian Prime Ministers: Bob Hawke - Scott Morrison

summary: This episode (part two of a survey of Australian prime ministers) continues the hosts' rapid tour of mid-20th-century Australian leaders. They open with Harold Holt—his political career, enthusiastic support for the US in Vietnam and his mysterious 1967 disappearance off Cheviot Beach (drowning, murder or Chinese-submarine theories are discussed), and the macabre memorial swimming centre. John Gorton follows: his war injuries, larrikin persona, alcohol-fuelled anecdotes, cultural patronage and eventual party backstabbing. Briefly covered are short-term caretaker John McEwen and the widely disliked William McMahon. The bulk of the episode focuses on Gough Whitlam—his patrician background, reforming agenda (ending conscription, health and Aboriginal initiatives), bold foreign policy moves (visiting China) and the Rex Connor–Tirath Kemlani financial affair. The hosts explain the Senate blockage and Governor‑General Sir John Kerr's dismissal of Whitlam on Remembrance Day 1975, plus the subsequent Fraser landslide. They end with Malcolm Fraser's politics, anti-apartheid stance and the 1986 Memphis scandal, teasing a third episode on Bob Hawke and later politics.
title: Australian Prime Ministers: Harold Holt - Malcolm Fraser

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Australian political history, prompted by a recent Australian general election. They open with cultural observations — mateship, masculinity, egalitarianism, and the darker strains of racism and the White Australia policy — then sketch the political development from colonial divisions to federation in 1901. The hosts connect sport (especially cricket) to national identity, recount early episodes such as the Sydney cricket riot and Bodyline, and move into twentieth-century politics. They profile key prime ministers and moments: Edmund Barton, Billy Hughes and World War I/Gallipoli, Robert Gordon Menzies' leadership and postwar conservatism, John Curtin's pivot toward the United States during World War II, Ben Chifley's postwar Labour government, and episodes like the Petrov spy affair and Australia’s involvement in Vietnam. The episode is the first of a multi-part series on Australia’s prime ministers and ends promising a continuation covering later leaders including Harold Holt.
title: Australian Prime Ministers: Edmund Barton - Robert Menzies

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Frances Christie (Deputy Chairman of Sotheby's) for a Platinum Jubilee special tied to Sotheby’s exhibition Power and Image: Royal Portraiture and Iconography. Frances selects six objects to illuminate Elizabeth II's reign: Andy Warhol’s colourful portrait of the Queen, a Punch banner cartoon by E. H. Shepard for the 1953 coronation week, one of the special coronation Bibles (1953), Jamie Reid’s Sex Pistols God Save the Queen poster (1977), Frank Auerbach’s Head of Goethe Boehm (once owned by David Bowie), and Diana’s 1981 Spencer tiara. The conversation ranges over the Queen as both sacred symbol and global celebrity, her role as Head of the Commonwealth, the interplay between monarchy and popular culture (from the Beatles to punk and Bowie), and moments of crisis and continuity across her long reign. They close by reflecting on monarchy’s durability and how Elizabeth II’s long stewardship shapes expectations for her successors.
title: The New Elizabethan Age

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Agatha Christie’s life, work and enduring popularity, treating her as a mirror on twentieth‑century Britain. They consider two formative shocks in her life—early financial insecurity after her father’s death and the collapse of her first marriage, culminating in her famous 1926 disappearance—and discuss how World War I nursing taught her about poisons. They analyse recurring motives in Christie’s fiction (money, sexual jealousy, secrets), her formal innovations and famous plot twists (The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, Murder on the Orient Express, Then There Were None), and how detectives like Poirot (a Belgian refugee) and Miss Marple reflect moral frameworks and anxieties about “evil.” They also highlight Christie’s archaeology connection through marriage to Max Mallowan and settings in Egypt/Mesopotamia, and note French critical appreciation of her formal mastery. The episode argues Christie’s spare plotting, moral clarity and adaptability explain her global translations and ongoing adaptations.
title: Agatha Christie

summary: This episode is a crossover between The Rest Is History hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook and guest Dan Carlin (Hardcore History), the second installment of their mini-series. The three tackle a series of hypothetical and large-scale questions about historical choice and contingency — choosing historical identities, whether studying history makes us happier, and what inventions a ruler in AD 1000 would prefer. They debate the morality and political effects of collective memory, referencing the Spanish Civil War, Franco's legacy, the field of blackbirds/Battle of Kosovo, and the impact of historic narratives on modern conflicts (e.g., Northern Ireland, Yugoslavia, and Putin's rationale for Ukraine). Conversations move through Cold War contingencies, the potential for the West to have “lost” the Cold War, the technological pressures that affected the USSR, and contemporary geopolitics. The episode closes with discussions about the limits of knowing the past, the nature of sources, and how belief and narrative shape historical reality.
title: History's Biggest Questions with Dan Carlin (Part 2)

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome podcaster Dan Carlin for a two-part special in which they ask ten large historical questions. Across the first episode they discuss hypothetical and counterfactual scenarios (who would you least like besieged by: Assyrians, Romans or Mongols), the single most consequential 20th-century leader (arguments for Wilhelm II and discussion of WWI's domino effects), Lenin's return to Russia and the Russian Revolution, the origins and moral calculus of nuclear weapons (Truman's decision, firebombing comparisons), the relative survivability of a Confederate States of America, and which ancient empire's biographies we most wish had survived (Persian, Egyptian, Carthaginian). The conversation ranges widely through sources and historians (Plutarch, Polybius, Herodotus) and emphasizes contingency in history. The episode closes by noting there will be a second instalment available publicly on Thursday and that Rest Is History Club members have immediate access to both episodes.
title: History's Biggest Questions with Dan Carlin (Part 1)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by guest James Holland for a detailed discussion of Operation Barbarossa. The episode situates the 22 June 1941 German invasion in its 1940–41 strategic context, covering Nazi war aims, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, and Hitler’s decision-making. James outlines the planning failures and logistical shortcomings — limited mechanization, diverse vehicle types, inadequate supply lines and rail gauge problems — that undermined the German advance. The hosts examine early German successes (Smolensk, large encirclements) and Stalin’s initial paralysis followed by the Stavka’s reorganisation, and contrast German operational hubris with Soviet manpower and industrial resilience. The conversation addresses the ideological brutality on the Eastern Front, Einsatzgruppen actions and Babi Yar, and how Barbarossa accelerated the Holocaust. They also touch on related operations (Typhoon, Case Blue, Stalingrad) and whether Hitler learned from Napoleon’s 1812 campaign. The episode closes with signposting to further coverage and a forthcoming book on Stalingrad by Ian McGregor.
title: Operation Barbarossa

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook revisit Babylon’s earlier history, answering listener questions about its founding, people and rulers. They locate Babylon on the Euphrates, discuss its relative lateness compared with earlier Mesopotamian cities, and trace its mythical and antiquarian self-image centred on the temple Esegila and the god Marduk. The episode outlines successive phases: memory of Sargon of Akkad and imperial models; the Amorite foundation under Sammu/Summu Abum; Hammurabi’s conquests and his famed law code; periods of decline, Hittite and Elamite sacks, and Kassite rule; and the recurring symbolic theft and return of Marduk’s cult statue. They cover Assyrian interactions — especially Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal — and describe Babylonian literacy, antiquarianism (Ennegaldinana’s museum), and later archaeological recoveries that shaped modern understanding. Throughout the discussion the hosts emphasize cycles of destruction and rebuilding, the city’s cultural centrality, and the strengths and limits of surviving sources such as cuneiform tablets, classical authors and 19th-century excavations.
title: The Birth of Babylon

description:
George Orwell, a love of wildlife, and Raheem Sterling - but what does it mean to be English in the modern world?

In today's episode, Tom and Dominic are joined by the New Statesman editor, Jason Cowley, to discuss England and Englishness in the 20th century.

Jason's new book 'Who Are We Now?' is available at all good book retailers.

Editorial Assistant: Grace Mainwaring
Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Jack Davenport

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Jason Cowley about his book Who Are We Now? Stories of Modern England, using George Orwell's essay The Lion and the Unicorn as a touchstone. The conversation traces continuities and paradoxes in English identity: nostalgia and loss, the legacy of empire and migration, devolution and the rise of Scottish nationalism, and recent political convulsions including the 2014 Scottish referendum, the 2015 election and the 2016 Brexit vote. Cowley and the hosts discuss cultural signifiers — landscape, literature, and especially football — as mirrors of changing Englishness, noting how the national team and figures like Gareth Southgate have reframed national identity. They touch on episodes from history (Blitz, Dunkirk, Spanish Civil War), contemporary crises (Morecambe Bay, EU enlargement), and social tensions (immigration, globalization, urban/rural divides). The episode probes whether Englishness can be progressive and plural within Britishness, stressing the interplay of change and continuity across centuries.
title: England & Englishness

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a survey of French presidents from Charles de Gaulle through Emmanuel Macron, framing the episode as a "French President's Special." They concentrate on personalities, scandals and the evolution of the presidency: François Mitterrand's ambiguous wartime record, his leftward turn and later moderation; Jacques Chirac's long career, corruption scandals and opposition to the 2003 Iraq War; Nicolas Sarkozy's law-and-order posturing and personal flamboyance; François Hollande's unpopularity and personal scandals; and Emmanuel Macron's destruction of the traditional party system and his performance as a modern embodiment of presidential grandeur. The discussion touches on cultural anecdotes (wiretapping of public figures, presidential private lives and culinary eccentricities), and political trends including the rise and adaptation of the Le Pen movement, the persistence of right-wing traditions in France, debates over Islam and immigration, and France's role in international diplomacy (NATO, relations with Putin). The tone mixes historical analysis with humorous anecdote and contemporary electoral concern.
title: French Presidents: 1981-2022

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey the presidents of France’s Fifth Republic, using Charles de Gaulle as the foundational figure whose wartime prestige and constitutional reforms shaped the office. They discuss de Gaulle’s personality, Gaullist exceptionalism, and his role in the creation of a strong executive during the 1958 crisis linked to the Algerian War. The episode then moves through his successors: Georges Pompidou (pragmatic technocrat, cultural projects, TGV and nuclear program), and Valéry Giscard d'Estaing (modernizer with scandals — including the Bokassa diamonds controversy — and social reforms such as legalizing abortion). Along the way they touch on May 1968, the Liberation of Paris, cultural references (Asterix, Tintin), and the interplay between French presidential dignity and personal scandal. The hosts frame this as the first part of a multi-episode look at Fifth Republic presidents, teasing a follow-up covering Mitterrand through Macron, and invite listeners to the paid Rest Is History Club for early access.
title: French Presidents: 1958-1981

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the First Jewish–Roman War (commonly called the Jewish Revolt), focusing on the siege and destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, Josephus's role as a Judean-turned-Flavian client and his problematic testimony, and the capture of remaining strongholds such as Masada. They analyse Titus and Vespasian's objectives, Flavian propaganda (coins, triumphs, monuments) and how the narrative was amplified by Christian and rabbinic traditions. The episode considers contested points — whether the temple’s destruction was deliberate, the fate of cultic treasures, and the reliability of Josephus — and the wider consequences: the reshaping of Jewish religious life (rise of rabbinic Judaism centered on Yavne), Christian theological uses of the event, and modern Israeli appropriation of Masada. Holland and Sandbrook place the revolt in the context of Roman politics (the civil war of 69 CE) and emphasize contingency, propaganda, and later memory in producing the revolt’s outsized historical significance.
title: The Jewish Revolt

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook introduce the origins and early course of the First Jewish–Roman War and the destruction of Jerusalem. They set long-term context, tracing Judean identity from the Babylonian exile, the rebuilding of the temple under Cyrus, Hellenistic influence after Alexander, and the turbulent Roman takeover (Pompey, Herod the Great). They discuss Roman administrative uncertainty in Judea, cultural resistance to Greek/Roman ways, and the mix of messianic expectations and taxation grievances that fed unrest. The revolt of 66 AD is described: the massacre of the Roman garrison, the ambush at Beth-Horon, and Vespasian’s campaign from Galilee after Nero appoints him. Key figures covered include Pontius Pilate, Gessius Florus, Gallus, Vespasian, Nero and Josephus (Yousef). The episode frames the fall of Jerusalem and the incineration of the temple as events with enduring religious and geopolitical significance, and closes indicating a second episode will take listeners into the war’s bloodier climaxes.
title: The Jews Against Rome

summary: In this Easter episode Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland examine crucifixion: its origins, mechanics, social function in the Roman world, and its centrality to Christianity. They survey pre-Roman precedents (Persian and Greek accounts), Alexander the Great's reputed use, and Roman deployment chiefly against rebels and slaves (examples include Spartacus and mass crucifixions along the Appian Way). Archaeological finds (a nailed heel bone near Jerusalem and a British burial) and literary sources (gospels, Paul’s letters, Josephus, Pliny, Seneca) inform discussion of how crucifixion actually worked and why it was deliberately humiliating. They argue the historicity of Jesus’ crucifixion is well attested and consider how the cross transformed from a mark of shame into Christianity’s principal symbol after Constantine, later diverging in Eastern (triumphant Christ) and Western (suffering Christ) art and theology. They close by noting crucifixion’s persistence in later legal/religious traditions and its reappearance in modern extremist contexts.
title: Crucifixion

description:
Richard II, Prince Charles, and Tony Blair. From Merlin, to the middle ages to the modern day, the mysterious world of magic, necromancy and the occult has had a notable presence in the lives of British monarchs, politicians and members of high society. 

Tom and Dominic are joined by Francis Young, author of 'Magic in Merlin's Realm: A History of Occult Politics in Britain' to discuss this infinitely interesting and entertaining topic.
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Dr. Francis Young about his book Magic in Merlin's Realm: A History of Occult Politics in Britain. The conversation traces how occult ideas, prophecy and learned magical practices influenced rulers and politics from medieval Britain through the early modern period and into the twentieth century. Young discusses the literary origins of Merlin in Geoffrey of Monmouth and earlier Welsh traditions, the adoption of occult learning by medieval and Tudor courts (Roger Bacon, John Dee), and the political uses and misuses of prophecy (Richard II, Joan of Arc). The pair also cover the English Civil Wars' supernatural accusations (Prince Rupert's dog Boy, accusations against Cromwell), the late Stuart period (Monmouth, James II and the Glorious Revolution), and a surprising wartime case in WWII when medium Helen Duncan was prosecuted amid security concerns. The episode situates occult beliefs within broader cultural and political contexts rather than treating them as mere superstition.
title: Merlin, Magic and the British

description: China's Cultural Revolution under Chairman Mao was one of the most staggeringly brutal events in recent human history. Tom and Dominic are joined by historian Rana Mitter, who specialises in the history of Republican China.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Professor Rana Mitter about the Chinese Cultural Revolution. They set the scene from the posters in August 1966 and the Red Guards’ attacks on the “four olds,” moving through the preceding decades: foreign incursions, the war with Japan, civil war and the Communist victory in 1949, and the catastrophic Great Leap Forward. Mitter explains Mao Zedong’s motivations — ideological conviction, fear of revisionism after Khrushchev’s denunciation of Stalin, and the desire to reassert his authority — and how the movement quickly escalated from a youth-led initiative into nationwide turmoil. The conversation covers mass mobilization, ritualized Mao worship (including the mango anecdote), factionalism, the army’s eventual intervention, the Gang of Four, and the Cultural Revolution’s legacies, including impacts on later leaders such as Xi Jinping. The episode cites several works and scholars and offers a broad, humane assessment of the period’s violence and long-term political consequences.
title: Chairman Mao and the Cultural Revolution

summary: This is the final episode of the hosts' Falklands War series. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the immediate political and cultural consequences of the 1982 conflict: Thatcher’s boosted popularity and short-lived cross-party goodwill; parliamentary reactions; controversy over a thanksgiving service at St. Paul’s (Archbishop Robert Runcie’s sermon and tabloid criticism); and celebratory military parades. They assess electoral effects (1983 general election), arguing the war accelerated a Conservative recovery that may have already been underway. The pair examine Argentina’s rapid political fallout and Galtieri’s removal, Cold War implications (limited), and the broader significance for British national identity — a rekindled “we are ourselves again” sentiment tied to naval and WWII iconography that the speakers link to later phenomena such as Brexit. Dominic promotes his book Who Dares Wins and they touch on cultural tangents (novels by Malcolm Price, writers like Alan Bennett), closing by reaffirming the series’ value and recommending further reading.
title: The Falklands War: Afterlife (Ep 4)

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (part of the hosts' Falkland series) examines the climactic phase of the 1982 Falklands War. Holland and Sandbrook discuss the political theatre around Margaret Thatcher's public response after South Georgia, the highly contested sinking of the Argentine cruiser Belgrano by HMS Conqueror, and the ensuing international and domestic outrage (including sensational tabloid coverage by The Sun). They cover subsequent British ship losses such as HMS Sheffield and Coventry, pressure for compromise (including a Peruvian peace proposal), and the decisive amphibious landings at San Carlos. The hosts describe the tense, D-Day–style landings, early actions like the Battle of Goose Green (and the death of Colonel H Jones), the Bluff Cove tragedy (Sir Galahad) and the series of night assaults on positions (Mount Longdon, Two Sisters, Mount Harriet, Wireless Ridge, Mount Tumbledown) that led to the Argentine surrender at Port Stanley. The episode closes by previewing a final installment on the war’s aftermath and broader impact.
title: The Falklands War: Battle for the Islands (Ep 3)

description:
In the second episode of our Falklands War mini-series, Britain is faced with an Argentine occupation and prepares to go to war.

Margaret Thatcher discovers her inner Winston Churchill - but faces a titanic showdown in Parliament, which sits on a Saturday for the first time since Suez.

The Task Force eventually sails - to huge public support - while the US, France and Chile all lend a hand. 

Come for Tom's Iron Lady impression, stay for his Tony Benn as Dominic talks us through the second instalment in this epic four-parter.

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producers: Jack Davenport & Tony Pastor

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: This episode continues the hosts' multi-part series on the Falklands War. Using the immediate aftermath of the Argentine invasion (2 April 1982) as its starting point, the discussion covers Governor Sir Rex Hunt's surrender and Margaret Thatcher’s reaction in government — the Cabinet debate, her growing determination, and the shift in public opinion. The hosts examine the political responses in Britain (notably Michael Foot’s backing and Tony Ben's opposition), press and literary reactions, and the mobilisation of the British task force (carriers Hermes and Invincible, requisitioned liners, staging at Ascension). The episode places the conflict in international context: UN action (Resolution 502), covert Chilean assistance, French technical support and diplomatic backing from François Mitterrand, and divisions within the US Reagan administration (Jean Kirkpatrick vs. Caspar Weinberger, Al Haig’s shuttle diplomacy). Early military actions — the South Georgia operation and the contrasting diplomatic attempts at compromise — are covered, and the episode ends on the retake of South Georgia as a pivotal morale boost and a cliffhanger for subsequent episodes.
title: The Falklands War: The Task Force Sails (Ep 2)

summary: This episode, the first of a four-part Falklands War series, examines the origins and early days of the 1982 conflict. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook set the scene with the islands' contested colonial history, early visits and settlements, and the development of competing British and Argentine claims. They trace Argentina's escalating domestic crisis under Perón-era turmoil and the 1970s junta, including General Galtieri and Operation Condor, and explain why the military believed a swift seizure might succeed. On the British side they outline Margaret Thatcher's embattled government, John Nott's defence cuts (including plans to scrap the ice patrol ship Endurance), and diplomatic attempts to negotiate sovereignty arrangements. Anecdotes about the scrap-metal incident at South Georgia, Nicholas Ridley’s failed diplomacy, and Governor Rex Hunt’s reaction bring the narrative to the Argentine landing on 2 April 1982. The hosts frame the war as both tragic and darkly comic while previewing the next episode on the fall of the islands and London’s response.
title: The Falklands War: Countdown to Invasion (Ep 1)

description:
PART 2.

Tom and Dominic are back with Helen Thompson for a second episode on the history of oil, its impact and how it shapes geopolitics.

Tune in to hear about the impact of oil production on US Politics, its importance to the history and current situation in Ukraine and what we can learn about oil from the exploits of J. R. Ewing in the TV show 'Dallas'.

The pod also looks to the future, examining China's explosive growth and advantageous position with Green Energy, whether Putin's recent actions have shifted the basis of his geopolitical power and if Britain is on track for Net Zero by 2050...

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Jack Davenport

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory

@dcsandbrook

summary: This episode is the second Rest Is History instalment focused on oil, featuring Helen Thompson, Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge. Thompson and the hosts (Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) examine oil's political and geopolitical influence across the twentieth and twenty-first centuries: how US oil shaped domestic politics (notably Texas and figures like Lyndon B. Johnson), cultural reflections in shows like Dallas, and the role of oil in both Gulf Wars. They discuss Europe's failed bids for energy independence, Germany's policy choices (including Gerhard Schröder and Nord Stream), and Ukraine's centrality as a transit state since the post‑Suez era. Thompson situates contemporary crises — Russia's actions in Georgia, Crimea and Ukraine, the shifting Russia–Europe–Asia energy dynamics, and China's rising demand — within long‑term energy continuities. She argues we are likely to see a multi‑energy world where fossil fuels remain geopolitically important even as green technologies grow, with transitions shaped by technological constraints, supply dynamics, and geopolitics. Her book Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century is promoted at the end.
title: Oil: Conflict, Chaos and Climate Change

description:
PART 1.

Tom and Dominic are joined by Helen Thompson, Professor of Political Economy at the University of Cambridge, to talk about the incredible influence of oil over the last couple of centuries.

Discussion covers the first oil well ever drilled, how it's hard to overestimate Hitler's obsession with oil, and the formation of OPEC in the aftermath of the Suez Crisis.

Helen's new book 'Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century' is out now.

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Jack Davenport

@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Helen Thompson about the central role of oil in modern geopolitics. They trace awareness of petroleum from ancient authors (Herodotus, Pliny) through 19th-century kerosene and the rise of US producers (Standard Oil) to the strategic anxieties of Britain and Germany before World War I, with particular emphasis on Baku and Persia. Thompson argues oil reshaped both world wars' geostrategic calculations, influenced British imperial policy (Suez) and postwar American engagement, and contributed to the rise of OPEC. The conversation examines mid-20th-century dynamics — Soviet and American oil power, the 1970s crises, the Iranian Revolution and the Iran–Iraq War — and the role of oil-price shocks in undermining the Soviet economy in the 1980s. The episode ends by announcing a follow-up installment to cover later episodes including the Gulf Wars, Nord Stream and contemporary energy-politics in Ukraine.
title: Oil: The Making of the Modern World

summary: This episode is the second instalment on Genghis Khan, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Ali Ansari. The conversation surveys Genghis Khan's early aims (uniting nomads and raiding China for plunder), his declaration as Khan in 1206, and his subsequent campaigns in northern China and Central Asia. The hosts and Ali discuss major episodes of violence — notably the invasions of Khorasan/Khwarazm, and the sacks of Bukhara, Merv and Nishapur — weighing contemporary Persian accounts against archaeological evidence and later exaggeration of casualty figures. They examine Mongol military practice (including Subutai's extraordinary reconnaissance-in-force into the west), administrative character (tribal confederacy versus emerging empire), and debates over Genghis as lawgiver or ‘enlightened’ ruler. The episode also touches on scientific debates: Genghis’s genetic legacy, ecological interpretations of Mongol conquests, and a hypothesis linking Mongol movements to the spread of plague via marmots. The episode closes by situating the Mongol success within the wider steppe/settled-world tension and teasing later episodes on the successors and European campaigns.
title: Genghis Khan: Lord of the Mongols

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Professor Ali Ansari (St Andrews) to discuss the origins and early life of Genghis Khan (Temujin). They focus on source problems — especially the role of The Secret History and Persian historians — and trace Temujin's difficult childhood, his family (including his father Yussegai and wife Börte), his captivity and escape, and the rivalries with figures such as Jamukha and Toghrul. Ali explains the political innovations that enabled Temujin to weld disparate nomadic tribes into a fighting force: blood-brother ties, a decimal military organization (tumens), and meritocratic promotion. They also discuss Mongol military strengths (composite bow, mobility), weaknesses (initial siegecraft), ecological context of the steppe, and the significance of 1206 when Temujin took the title Genghis Khan. The episode ends noting this is the first part, with the campaign phase to follow in the next episode.
title: The Rise of Genghis Khan

description:
Happy St. Patrick's Day! 

No, Tom isn't turning Brixton's River Effra green, nor is Dominic distributing shamrocks throughout the Oxfordshire countryside, but they're here anyway with a very special pod on the mysterious Apostle of Ireland. 

When was St. Patrick alive? Where was he really born? Why was he kidnapped by pirates? And did he really banish the snakes from Ireland?

All this and more on today's episode of The Rest Is History.

Producer: Dom Johnson

Exec Producer: Jack Davenport

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the historicity and legend of Saint Patrick. They foreground Patrick's two surviving writings (the Confessio and a letter to Caroticus), use them to trace his social background in Roman Britain, and debate his birthplace and dates. They review theories about his alleged kidnapping, including Roy Fletchner's thesis that Patrick might have been a tax exile rather than a slave, and discuss the possible existence of multiple Patricks and the contemporary figure Palladius (sent in 431). The episode surveys later hagiography (druid confrontations, snakes, shamrock) and how these motifs developed centuries after Patrick's life, including medieval purgatory legends. The hosts place Patrick in the wider context of late antiquity missionary innovation and the Irish missionary tradition (Columbanus, Columba), and close by considering St Patrick's Day's modern transformations, especially its role in Irish-American identity and nationalist appropriations.
title: Saint Patrick

summary: This episode features historian Edward Shawcross discussing his book The Last Emperor of Mexico with hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook. They trace the improbable episode in which Archduke Ferdinand Maximilian of the Habsburgs, backed by Napoleon III, becomes Emperor Maximilian I of Mexico during the French intervention (1861–1867). The conversation covers Mexico's unstable 19th-century politics, the Reform War, Benito Juárez's liberal government, European financial pressure and Napoleon III's geopolitical aims while the United States was distracted by the Civil War. Shawcross explores Maximilian and Empress Carlota's personalities, the cultural incongruities of their court, military defeats (notably Puebla/Cinco de Mayo), the withdrawal of French support after the Civil War, Carlota's mental collapse in Europe, Maximilian's capture at Querétaro, and his 1867 execution alongside conservative Mexican leaders. The hosts consider legacy, memory in Mexico (Benito Juárez's prominence), and the broader diplomatic consequences for France and the Americas.
title: The Last Emperor of Mexico

'In the noughties, Russian democracy becomes a form of show business'

In the final instalment of our Russia mini-series, Tom and Dominic reach the climax of Putin’s rise to power, charting how a former KGB agent managed to climb from relative obscurity to become the uncrowned Tsar of Russia.

The episode also touches on his relationship with oligarchs such as Roman Abramovich, the hall of mirrors he's created, and a look at how his character has changed over the course of his presidency.

summary: This is the fourth and final episode of a four-episode Rest Is History series on recent Russian history. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Vladimir Putin's rise to the presidency after the 2000 election, the political effects of the Second Chechen War and the 2004 Beslan school siege, and the installation of Ramzan Kadyrov in Chechnya. They examine Putin's crackdown on oligarchs (Boris Berezovsky, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Roman Abramovich) and the ascendancy of security-service elites. The hosts discuss media manipulation and hybrid warfare, referencing Peter Pomerantsev's Nothing Is True and Everything Is Possible and David Remnick's Lenin's Tomb and Resurrection. They trace the pattern of Russian interventions from Georgia (2008) to Crimea and Donbass (2014) and consider comparisons with Augustan propaganda. The episode ends with concern over Putin's escalation in Ukraine, his use of disinformation, and the attendant risks, including nuclear rhetoric and the potential consequences for Ukraine and Putin's regime.
title: Putin's Russia (Episode 4)

summary: This episode — the third in a mini-series on recent Russian history — traces the chaotic 1990s that produced Vladimir Putin's rise. Using Robert Harris's novel Archangel as a prompt, the hosts compare post-Soviet Russia to the Weimar Republic and explain how economic shock therapy, mass privatization (voucher schemes) and the making of the oligarchs produced social collapse, hyperinflation and acute inequality. They recount Yeltsin's political struggles, the 1993 constitutional crisis when tanks shelled parliament, the 1996 re-election and the 1998 ruble crash, and describe the brutality of the First and Second Chechen Wars. The episode charts Putin's career from St. Petersburg fixer to FSB-linked power broker, the 1999 apartment bombings and Yeltsin's surprise resignation on 31 December 1999 that handed the premiership (and then the presidency) to Putin. The hosts also place these developments alongside NATO's post‑Cold War expansion and Western relations with Russia, showing how the 1990s' turmoil seeded modern Russian politics.
title: Yeltsin, Economic Chaos and President Putin (Episode 3)

description:
[Episode 2 of 4]

This episode of The Rest Is History marks the second instalment in our four part series on the Soviet Union, Russia and the rise of Vladimir Putin.

From the 70th anniversary of the Russian Revolution in 1987 to the fall of the Soviet Union on Christmas Day 1991, this episode is jam-packed full of late Soviet drama. 

Tune in now to hear about the abuse Yeltsin received after his attempted suicide, the failed Soviet coup of 1991 and Putin's return from East Germany. 

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producers: Tony Pastor & Jack Davenport

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the collapse of the Soviet Union, tracing developments from the late 1980s through 1991. They examine Mikhail Gorbachev’s dilemmas between reformers and hardliners, and the rise of Boris Yeltsin as a populist rival. The hosts describe economic breakdown, shortages, and the social disorientation produced by glasnost and perestroika. They recount key episodes: televised Congresses of People’s Deputies, the Vilnius violence, the failed August 1991 coup, and the Belavezha meeting that led to the Commonwealth of Independent States. The episode highlights Yeltsin’s dramatic public stand against the coup, the rapid unraveling of Soviet authority, and Gorbachev’s resignation on 25 December 1991. They touch on Vladimir Putin’s reaction and the geopolitical consequences — a smaller Russian state with many non-Russian populations and displaced Russian speakers. The conversation places personal rivalries and elite self-interest at the center of the Union’s disintegration and previews a follow-up on Yeltsin and Putin’s subsequent trajectories.
title: The Fall of the Soviet Empire (Episode 2)

description:
[Episode 1 of 4]

Welcome to our new four part series on the latter years of the Soviet Union, its fall, Putin's early life and his subsequent rise to power.

Today's episode focuses on Brezhnev, Putin's formative years, his early KGB career and Gorbachev's descent into chaos.

Was Putin a nationalist or a communist? What changed from Brezhnev to Gorbachev? What was Putin doing in East Germany during the Soviet twilight years?

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producers: Tony Pastor & Jack Davenport

summary: This episode is the first of a short multi-part series tracing the late Soviet Union, its collapse and the rise of Vladimir Putin. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook set out the cultural and political background that shaped Putin — his 1952 birth in Leningrad, KGB career and posting to Dresden — and place him in the context of Soviet generations shaped by the Brezhnev era. The hosts discuss key late-Soviet leaders (Andropov, Chernenko) and focus on Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (perestroika and glasnost), arguing that Gorbachev’s rapid political and economic changes, catalysed by crises such as the Chernobyl disaster (1986), unintentionally unleashed nationalisms across the USSR. They reference historians and works (Vladislav Zubok’s Collapse; Robert Service’s history) and play an archival clip of George W. Bush referring to his 2001 meeting with Putin. The episode frames multiple contingencies and alternative paths for Russia while previewing subsequent episodes on the implosion of the Soviet system and the chaotic 1990s.
title: Young Putin, the KGB and the Soviet Union (Episode 1)

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Alison Matthews-David, author and fashion historian, to discuss her book Fashion Victims: The Dangers of Dress, Past and Present. The conversation surveys lethal and harmful fashions across history: theatre tutus and mass-produced bobbinet that contributed to devastating stage fires; steel-hooped crinolines that acted like chimneys and caused burn deaths; hobble skirts that restricted movement and caused accidents; the global histories of foot-binding and narrow European footwear; and dangerous hatmaking practices that used mercury. They also examine poisonous dyes and cosmetics — including arsenical greens used on fabrics and artificial flowers, and lead- and mercury-containing whitening cosmetics — and the occupational toll on garment, dye and hat workers. The discussion ties these historical cases to class, gender and technology, notes examples of public health responses and partial regulation, and draws parallels with contemporary garment-industry and cosmetic hazards.
title: Killer Fashion

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multipart discussion about when — and how — the Roman Empire ended. They examine the late antique and medieval transitions around Heraclius, the Persian wars, the Arab conquests (including the Battle of Yarmouk, August 636) and the consequent territorial and cultural contraction of Constantinople's empire. They debate key punctuation points (1204, 1453, 1461) and the persistence of Roman identity in Byzantium. The conversation then surveys later claimants to Roman legitimacy: the Carolingian/Holy Roman tradition (Charlemagne), the Ottoman claim under Mehmed II, and Muscovy’s “Third Rome” doctrine (Philotheus writing to Vasili, links to Constantine XI). They discuss modern resonances — Catherine the Great’s Crimea annexation, Soviet and Russian uses of Byzantine symbolism, and ISIS’s invocation of Roman/Byzantine motifs — and end with a playful argument about Roman identity surviving in medieval Wales and even in the title Prince of Wales.
title: Byzantium and the Ghosts of Rome (Part 2)

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook debate when — and whether — the Roman Empire actually fell, arguing that no single date adequately captures the Empire's complex decline. They begin with Edward Gibbon’s landmark work and move through candidate dates: Augustus’s establishment of the imperial system, the foundation of Constantinople (330), Constantine and the Christianization of the Empire, Theodosius’s death and the east/west division (395), the Battle of Adrianople (378), the sack of Rome by Alaric (410), and the traditional deposition of Romulus Augustulus (476). They highlight structural issues such as the Crisis of the Third Century, frontier pressures, the rise of military emperors, barbarian settlement, and the economic and political fragmentation of the West. The hosts argue that later events — Justinian’s reconquests and the gradual transformation of the eastern Roman state — complicate any tidy end-date. The episode concludes that Rome’s “fall” is a protracted, uneven process with multiple plausible punctuation points rather than a single definitive moment.
title: When did the Roman Empire fall? (Part 1)

description: With eastern Europe apparently on the brink of war and Vladimir Putin citing history as pretext, what exactly is Ukraine? Is it distinct from Russia, and how long has it existed? Tom and Dominic run through a brutal and fractured history, from the Viking conquest and Kyivan Rus', to the ever-shifting landscape in the early modern period, to the incredibly complicated Russian Civil War, right up to the modern day.
summary: This special edition episode is a rapid historical sweep through Ukrainian history prompted by recent Russian actions. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the region from ancient mentions in Herodotus, through the Viking-founded Kievan Rus and its Christianization, to Mongol devastation and the later rival poles of Muscovy and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. They cover Cossack autonomy and Bohdan Khmelnytsky's 1654 agreement with Moscow, the chaos of the Ruin, Mazepa and Poltava, imperial annexations (including Catherine the Great's Novorossiya), 19th-century Russification and the rise of Ukrainian cultural figures such as Taras Shevchenko. The 20th century discussion emphasises the convoluted 1917–22 struggles, the Holodomor, Stalinist repression, wartime occupation and colossal WWII losses, Soviet-era dynamics (including Chernobyl) and late-20th-century moves to independence. They end by connecting these layers to post‑1991 politics, NATO/Budapest discussions, Euromaidan, Crimea 2014 and current tensions over Donetsk and Luhansk, arguing that Ukrainian nationhood long predates Bolshevik policies.
title: Ukraine and Russia

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook compile and discuss a listener-sourced top ten of history's most disastrous parties. They open with contemporary Partygate references, then move through a wide chronological survey: an ill-fated 1908 hunting party in Baden-Württemberg; the modern Fyre Festival debacle; Peter the Great's riotous, destructive stay in Deptford; the bloody Blood Feast of Roskilde; Muhammad Ali Pasha's 1811 massacre of the Mamluks in Cairo; the legendary excesses (and likely embellished anecdotes) surrounding the emperor Elagabalus; the Black Dinner in 1440 and the Abergavenny massacre; the Bal des Ardents that harmed Charles VI and contributed to his mental decline; Nicholas II's coronation festivities that resulted in the Khodynka stampede; and, as their top entry, Alexander the Great's burning of Persepolis and the Shah of Iran's 1971 Persepolis celebrations that later symbolised regal hubris. Throughout they reflect on how disastrous parties often reveal deeper social and political fractures, and they cite sources and listener suggestions while keeping a humorous tone.
title: The Most Disastrous Party in History

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Professor Andrew Preston to discuss the role of religion in American history and foreign policy across the 20th and early 21st centuries. Preston traces persistent religiosity in the United States to institutional features like separation of church and state and a competitive 'marketplace of faith,' and shows how that religiosity shaped American exceptionalism. He connects Franklin D. Roosevelt's invocation of a Judeo-Christian heritage in the run-up to World War II to the Cold War framing of the USSR as an atheistic threat, and follows the theme through Truman's recognition of Israel, Eisenhower's civil-religious era, Nixon, Reagan's alliance with evangelicals and his “evil empire” rhetoric, and post-9/11 evangelical-inflected rhetoric under George W. Bush. They discuss liberal pluralist strains (e.g., Obama’s Cairo speech), the ambivalent religious posture of leaders like Trump, and how religious language and institutions have been both a sword and a shield in American diplomacy. The episode draws on Preston’s book Sword of the Spirit, Shield of Faith and wider Cold War history.
title: God and the American Empire

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Professor Andrew Preston (Cambridge) for a wide-ranging discussion about the role of Christianity in American foreign policy and warfare. Using early New England (including the 1637 massacre of Pequots and John Winthrop's 'city on a hill') as a starting point, they trace religious ideas — providential mission, crusading mentalities, and reformist/pacifist strains like Quakerism — through major moments: the French and Indian War, the Revolution, Manifest Destiny, the Civil War, 19th-century imperial ventures (Mexico, Cuba, the Philippines), and into 20th- and 21st-century conflicts. Preston argues that religion frequently shaped motives and rhetoric (e.g., Lincoln's moral language, McKinley's prayer about the Philippines) and that Americans often oscillate between claiming anti-imperial virtue and exercising imperial power. The episode ends by announcing a follow-up covering the 20th century through the post-9/11 era and contemporary politics.
title: American Crusades

summary: This Valentine's Day special of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) traces the complex origins and cultural evolution of Valentine’s Day. The hosts survey early hagiography and multiple Saint Valentines, Roman festivals such as Lupercalia and medieval literary sources (notably Chaucer and Gower) that linked 14 February with courtly love. They follow the English emergence of Valentine traditions through the later Middle Ages, Tudor reforms, Georgian and Victorian practices, and the boom in printed cards from the 18th–19th centuries, highlighting the penny post (1840) and commercial manufacture of valentines. The episode also explores vinegar valentines—anonymous insulting cards popular in the 19th century—and touches on related incidents that occurred on 14 February, including the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre (1929) and other historical anniversaries. Throughout the discussion the hosts reference relevant books, scholars and primary texts and close with examples of genuinely coarse Victorian valentines to illustrate how ambivalent and varied historical celebrations of love have been.
title: Valentine's Day

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host novelist Alex Preston to examine the history and myths of smuggling in Britain. The conversation contrasts popular fictional images (Moonfleet, Jamaica Inn, Poldark) with archival reality: smuggling began as wool export evasion ("owling") and later shifted to importing taxed luxuries—tea, spirits, lace—after mid-17th-century excise duties. Preston locates the golden age on the south-east coast (Kent and Sussex), describes highly organised and violent gangs such as the Hawkhurst/Hawke's Gang and the Mayfield Gang, and cites episodes like the Poole Custom House raid and the Battle of Goudhurst (1747). He also discusses political links (Jacobitism), enforcement measures (Act of Indemnity 1736, Gazetting Act 1746), and the eventual decline of the 18th-century gang system. The episode closes by connecting past and present: modern people-smuggling, migrant routes into Britain, and contemporary charity work supporting unaccompanied minors, while reflecting on how literature has romanticised criminality.
title: Smuggling

summary: This episode is the second part of a mini-series focused on the Vikings in the East and the origins of Kievan Rus. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the foundational legends (Rurik and his brothers, Askold and Dir) and examine how Norse traders and warriors established forts and trading posts that evolved into political power in Novgorod and Kiev. They discuss key early rulers—Oleg, Igor, Olga, Sviatoslav, Vladimir/Volodymyr—and their interactions with Byzantium, including treaties, raids on Constantinople, the Varangian Guard, and the cultural pull of Byzantine Christianity leading to Vladimir’s conversion. The hosts address the mixture of myth and source material (notably the Russian Primary Chronicle), violent and theatrical death-stories from the chronicles, and the later careers of eastern-bound Vikings such as Harald Hardrada, who made his fortune in Byzantium before returning to Norway and dying in 1066. The episode emphasizes the fluid identities of the period and notes the modern political sensitivities around Kievan Rus’ legacy in Russia and Ukraine.
title: The Birth of Russia

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the Vikings in the East, tracing Scandinavian river routes into the lands of the Volga, Dnieper and Black Sea and exploring why Norsemen travelled east to Byzantium and the Abbasid Caliphate. They discuss staging points such as Gotland, Birka and Staraya Ladoga; the economics of fur, silver and the slave trade; and how Viking technology enabled long river voyages. The hosts consider political controversies over origins (citing Vladimir Putin's essay and Soviet/Nazi ideological reactions), literary and archaeological sources—including Ibn Fadlan's eyewitness account of a Viking ship burial on the Volga—and secondary works by Neil Price, Tom Shippey, Michael McCormick and others. The episode ends as a first part, promising a follow-up to cover the Dnieper, the founding of Kiev and the conversion of the Rus to Christianity, and notes a members-only debate about reactions to a previous Charles I episode.
title: The Vikings Go East

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Kyle Harper about his panoramic history of disease, focusing on the Columbian Exchange and the global impact of pathogens. Harper discusses the demographic collapse in central Mexico in the 16th century, the variety of Old World diseases introduced to the Americas (including unexpected bacterial outbreaks in the 1540s), and pre-Columbian presence and later replacement of tuberculosis strains. He explains how the transatlantic slave trade and plantation ecologies amplified tropical diseases (yellow fever, malaria) and why Europeans struggled to settle parts of West Africa. The conversation moves to the 18th–19th centuries: Edward Jenner’s vaccination (1798), miasma thinking and the sanitary movement, and the emergence and global spread of cholera from 1817. Harper compares the 1918–19 influenza pandemic with COVID-19 and frames disease as an ecological consequence of globalization and technological progress, arguing that interconnectedness both advances civilization and creates new opportunities for pathogens.
title: Disease, the New World and modern pandemics (Part 2)

description:
The way we die has been utterly transformed.

There have been around 10,000 generations of human beings, but only in the last 3 or 4 have infectious diseases not been an expected and accepted cause of death.

What drove the most deadly infectious diseases? Was technological progress and globalisation one of the key causes for its spread over the course of history?

Tom and Dominic are joined by Professor Kyle Harper from the University of Oklahoma to discuss the fascinating history of disease and how shifts in the way we die have changed our world completely.

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Tony Pastor

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: This episode is an interview with historian Kyle Harper about his book Plagues Upon the Earth. Harper traces the deep history of infectious disease from early hominins through the rise of agriculture, urbanization, empire and up to COVID-19. He argues that disease is central to human history, shaping migration, demography, technology and social change. Topics include the role of fire and human ecological expansion in creating a unique human disease pool, the health consequences of sedentism and early farming (especially diarrheal disease), comparisons between hunter-gatherer and urban mortality, and major pandemics such as the Black Death and the Justinianic Plague. Harper also discusses the global reach of pandemics, the Columbian Exchange, and links between Mongol-era connectivity and plague diffusion. The conversation highlights how disease transforms societies and why understanding pathogen history matters for interpreting past and present human change.
title: Disease vs. the rise of civilisation (Part 1)

summary: This Rest Is History episode is a wide-ranging discussion of Babylon, concentrating on its most famous period from Nebuchadnezzar II onward. Tom Holland (who wrote Persian Fire) and Dominic Sandbrook describe Babylon’s monumental architecture — walls, the Ishtar Gate, the great ziggurat (Etemenanki) — and the city’s reputation as a cosmopolitan, wealthy, and morally ambivalent center. They discuss Herodotus’ accounts, the debated reality and provenance of the Hanging Gardens (mentioning Stephanie Dalley’s argument), and Babylon’s relationship with the Judean people: the sieges of Jerusalem, the exile, and the biblical portrayals in Genesis, Daniel and Jeremiah. The hosts consider how those biblical images shaped later receptions of Babylon (Book of Revelation, Rastafarianism, Protestant iconography) and trace Babylon’s afterlife under Persian, Hellenistic and Roman rule, its archaeological decline and modern political appropriation (Saddam Hussein, damage after the Iraq War). The episode blends material culture, ancient texts and reception across millennia to explain why Babylon remains a potent symbol of imperial wealth, hubris and eventual downfall.
title: Babylon

summary: This episode is Part 2 of The Rest Is History’s deep dive into the trial and execution of Charles I, featuring Professor Ted Vannance (Roehampton). The conversation reconstructs the atmosphere of the trial (opening 20 January 1649), the role of John Bradshaw as president and the silent commissioners, and vivid courtroom moments (Charles’s cane, his refusal to recognise the court, and his clear, composed defence). Vannance explains the legal reasoning relied on — notably laws of war and command responsibility — and how concessions made during the Treaty of Newport were used against the king. The hosts and guest describe the logistics and symbolism of the execution at the Banqueting House (30 January 1649), public reaction, and contemporary print and pamphlet culture (Eikon Basilike, Milton’s response). The episode closes by weighing short-term and long-term consequences: the Commonwealth’s legitimacy problems, pursuit of regicides after the 1660 Restoration, and the execution’s enduring international and republican influence.
title: The Trial of Charles I Part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the trial and execution of Charles I with guest Professor Ted Vallance. The episode situates Charles's downfall in the broader context of religious tensions after the English Reformation, his Personal Rule (1629–1640), fiscal measures like ship money, and court culture that alarmed Puritans. Vallance outlines how political, religious and constitutional conflicts produced the First and then the Second Civil War, highlighting key moments: Naseby (1645), Charles’s flight and imprisonment (Carisbrooke), the Engagement with the Scots, the New Model Army’s radicalisation, the Putney Debates, and the Remonstrance that led to Pride’s Purge. The discussion covers the legal and political innovations used to establish a High Court of Justice, the public staging of the trial in Westminster Hall, and attitudes within the army and parliament that made execution conceivable. The hosts and guest assess Charles’s character and decisions, army leadership dynamics (including Cromwell), and the revolution’s broader revolutionary — and theatrical — implications for monarchy and political legitimacy.
title: The Trial of Charles I Part 1

summary: This episode (part two of a special) examines the career and legacy of General Charles Gordon (Gordon of Khartoum). Holland and Sandbrook trace Gordon's evangelical anti-slavery mission in Equatoria and the wider Sudan, his brief, unhappy spell as private secretary in India, and the approaches from Leopold II over the Congo. They discuss W.T. Stead's publicity that helped send Gordon to Sudan, the complex British political context under Gladstone, and divisions over intervention. The hosts narrate Gordon's arrival in Khartoum, his refusal to evacuate, the rise of Muhammad Ahmad (the Mahdi), the delayed Wolseley relief expedition, and the bloody fall of Khartoum in January 1885. The episode ends by considering Gordon's posthumous myth-making, contemporary critiques (notably Lytton Strachey), later British revenge at Omdurman (1898), and the ambiguous legacy tying anti-slavery motives to imperial violence and Victorian martyrdom.
title: General Gordon and the Siege of Khartoum

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life and contested reputation of General Charles George Gordon up to his famed role in China. They trace Gordon’s early military career — Crimea, surveying on the Danube, service in Armenia — and focus on his emergence as “Chinese Gordon” commanding the Ever Victorious Army during the Taiping Rebellion. The hosts examine Gordon’s intense Protestant Christianity, recurrent religious awakenings, philanthropy (notably his work with “ragged boys” at Gravesend), eccentricities and accusations about his sexuality and temperament, and how writers such as Lytton Strachey and later biographers have shaped his posthumous image. They reference primary cultural touchstones (William McGonagall’s verse, John Pollock’s biography) and situate Gordon in broader nineteenth-century imperial conflicts (Second Opium War, Burning of the Summer Palace). The episode ends by previewing a follow-up focused on Gordon’s Sudanese career and the siege of Khartoum, with a membership plug for the Rest Is History Club.
title: General Gordon: The Ultimate Victorian Hero

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian and author Dan Jackson about the origins, technology and cultural impact of railways, with special emphasis on Britain and the North East. The discussion traces early trackways from antiquity and German mining wagonways to wooden wagonways and the first iron rails, then follows the alignment of rail tracks with steam-power advances (Newcomen, Watt) and coal-driven demands. Key engineers—Matthew Murray, William Hedley, George Stephenson and his son Robert—are discussed, together with milestones like the Stockton & Darlington Railway (1825), the Rainhill Trials (1829) and the Liverpool–Manchester opening (1830). They cover civil-engineering feats, differing gauges (Brunel's broad gauge vs narrow gauge), the financing and corruption of railway promotion, Railway Mania, and wider social consequences: standardised time, mass spectator events, commuter suburbs, W. H. Smith and the nationalisation debates. The episode ends by noting remaining global stories for a proposed Railways Part Two.
title: The Birth of the Railways

description:
Who killed the Princes in the Tower? The inspiration behind Shakespeare's Richard III, their murder remains one of the greatest mysteries in English history. 

In the second of two episodes, all eyes turn to Richard III, prime suspect in the disappearance of Edward IV's sons. 

Tom and Dominic discuss whether Richard likely did kill his nephews, potential other suspects, and whether it was a matter of survival for him to do so.

Plus, the greatest question of our time: was Richard III more Raul Castro, Robert Kennedy, or James Callaghan?

Producer: Dom Johnson
Exec Producer: Tony Pastor

Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook

Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: This episode is the second part of The Rest Is History’s examination of the Princes in the Tower. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace events after Edward IV’s death in April 1483: the accession of Edward V, factional manoeuvring between the Woodvilles and Richard of Gloucester, the removal of Edward into the Tower, and the swift consolidation of Richard’s power culminating in his coronation on 6 July 1483. The hosts discuss key characters—Elizabeth Woodville, Anthony Woodville (Lord Rivers), Hastings, Buckingham—and the charges used to declare the princes illegitimate. They weigh competing theories about the boys’ disappearance and likely murder, assessing candidates including Richard III, the Duke of Buckingham and more speculative proposals. Archaeological finds (bones in the Tower, discoveries at Windsor, and recent Devon claims) and their limitations are reviewed. The episode reflects on reasons the mystery endures—political stakes, Shakespearean portrayals, later pretenders (Lambert Simnel, Perkin Warbeck)—and concludes both hosts find Richard the most probable culprit while acknowledging definitive proof remains impossible.
title: The Princes in the Tower Part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook introduce the story of the Princes in the Tower, concentrating on the family and political dynamics that produced Edward V and his brother Richard of Shrewsbury. They set out Edward V’s birth in sanctuary (2 November 1470), explain Edward IV’s rise and character, and show how his marriage to Elizabeth Woodville fractured the Yorkist faction, angering Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick. The episode traces the factional swings, Warwick’s brief defection, Edward IV’s exile and restoration (Barnet, Tewkesbury), and the consolidation of Yorkist power. The hosts profile Richard, Duke of Gloucester, Anthony Woodville and other key figures, discuss the killing of Henry VI in the Tower, and outline how Edward IV’s sudden death (9 April 1483) left his young sons vulnerable. The episode ends as a cliffhanger: the princes are born and alive, but with key protectors absent, the political contest over the boy king is unresolved and promised to continue in part two.
title: The Princes in the Tower Part 1

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their multi-part tour of 1922, surveying political, cultural and geopolitical shifts that helped shape the modern world. They open with Winston Churchill’s Dundee speech and move through the cultural explosion of the 1920s — Hollywood, Chaplin, Hitchcock, Disney — and the mass-media phenomenon sparked by Howard Carter’s discovery of Tutankhamen’s tomb. The episode tracks technological and institutional milestones such as the first regular broadcasts that led to the BBC, and the Washington Naval Conference’s reordering of naval power. Domestically and internationally, 1922 is shown as a year of violent transition: Ireland’s contested Anglo-Irish settlement, the assassination of Sir Henry Wilson, the Four Courts episode and the ensuing Irish Civil War; and the collapse of Ottoman order in Anatolia with Mustafa Kemal’s victories and the burning of Smyrna. They conclude by reflecting on how these events reconfigured empires, politics and culture and on whether the ‘‘modern world’’ they delineate continued past mid-century.
title: 1922: The Birth of the Modern World Part 2

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines 1922 as a pivotal year marking the emergence of modernity in culture and politics. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss landmark cultural works — notably James Joyce's Ulysses and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land — and position them against the broader post–First World War context: the disintegration of empires, economic collapse, political violence and the rise of mass movements. They survey developments across Germany (Weimar instability and hyperinflation), Italy (social unrest and Mussolini’s March on Rome), and Russia (the tail end of the Civil War, famine and the formal creation of the USSR with Stalin's growing power). The hosts also touch on how fear of Bolshevism energized right-wing paramilitaries, the lingering effects of Spanish flu, and cultural reflections of the period in film and popular fiction. The episode is the first of two on 1922, setting the scene for a follow-up focused on Britain, Ireland, the Levant and America.
title: 1922: The Birth of the Modern World Part 1

description: Julius Caesar upended the Roman Republic on this day (maybe) over 2000 years ago. Tom explains everything that led up to the moment and what made Caesar's decision to march his legion back into Italy so seismic.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Julius Caesar's decision to cross the Rubicon and the wider collapse of the late Roman Republic. Holland situates the moment in the context of the Republic's constitutional norms, the professionalization of the legions under Gaius Marius, and Sulla's precedent of using armies for political ends. They trace Caesar's rise via the Gallic campaigns, his use of commentaries to shape reputation, and the political maneuvering of the Pompey–Crassus–Caesar alliance (the informal triumvirate). The conversation covers key episodes — Alesia, the extension of Caesar's command, Crassus' defeat in Parthia, Julia's death, and the final breakdown that produced the 49 BC crossing. They debate whether the Rubicon moment made the Republic's end inevitable, reflect on famous sayings associated with the crossing, and consider the differing legacies of Caesar and Augustus. The episode blends military, constitutional and cultural perspectives to explain why the Rubicon endures as a symbolic political dividing line.
title: Crossing the Rubicon

description: A key battle in the history of England and a forgotten uprising in 17th century London round off our 12 (13) Days of Christmas. Back with to our regular schedule next Monday 10th January.
summary: This episode, the final instalment of the hosts' 12 Days of Christmas special, pairs two historical vignettes. First, Tom and Dominic recount Alfred the Great's Near-Death and comeback: the 878 Chippenham ambush by Vikings, Alfred's refuge on Athelney, the burning-of-the-cakes legend, and his decisive victory at Edington that led to Guthrum's conversion and treaties that secured London and parts of Mercia. The discussion covers the wider Great Heathen Army campaign (from 865) and subsequent Anglo-Saxon recovery under Alfred's family. The second segment shifts to 1661, where they read Samuel Pepys' diary describing the Fifth Monarchists' uprising led by Thomas Venner in January. They outline the group's millenarian beliefs, street fighting in London, Venner's capture and execution, and the event's place in the aftermath of the Civil Wars and the Restoration. The hosts also reference cultural portrayals (The Last Kingdom), doctrinal sources (Book of Daniel), and wider comparisons to later popular unrest and terror attacks.
title: 6 Jan: Alfred the Great and Pepys' 'Fanatiques'

description: The catalyst for the upheaval of 1066 and one of the most controversial episodes in French history happened on this day in history.
summary: This episode (broadcast around 5 January as part of the hosts' seasonal "12 Days of Christmas" series) pairs two sombre historical vignettes. Tom Holland discusses the death of Edward the Confessor on 5 January 1066, explaining the fragile succession politics—Æthelred's descendants, the Godwin family, Harold Godwinson, Edgar the Ætheling and competing claims from William of Normandy—that set the stage for the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings later that year. Dominic Sandbrook then recounts the public humiliation and exile of Captain Alfred Dreyfus (the "degradation" on 5 January 1895), outlining the bordereau discovery, anti‑Semitism, forged evidence, the role of Émile Zola (J'Accuse) and the affair's long political and cultural repercussions in France, including Dreyfus's eventual pardon and later exoneration. The hosts also reference literary and cultural treatments of these events, recommend Robert Harris's novel An Officer and a Spy, and note modern echoes of the affair in contemporary French politics.
title: 5 Jan: Death of Edward the Confessor and the Dreyfus Affair

description: Tom analyses the historical importance of Solomon Northup's story, made famous by Steve McQueen's '12 Years A Slave'. Then, Dominic delves into the death of French philosopher and author Albert Camus. Tune in to also hear about the travails of Monsieur Sandbrook, the 21-year-old Provence-based English language assistant.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook mark 4 January in two historical vignettes. First they recount Solomon Northup's kidnapping and restoration to freedom on 4 January 1853, the story told in his memoir Twelve Years a Slave; they discuss his owners (William Prince Ford, John Tibbote, Edwin Epps), the role of Samuel Bass in securing Northup's release, and the memoir’s importance to Northern abolitionist sentiment. They connect Northup’s narrative to other works that moved white audiences, notably Black Like Me and Uncle Tom's Cabin. In the second segment they turn to 4 January 1960, the fatal car crash that killed Albert Camus and publisher Michel Gallimard, destroying the manuscript of Le Premier Homme. They consider Camus’s Algerian background, his war-time profile, Nobel recognition, political stance during the Algerian conflict, and several of his works (The Plague, The Myth of Sisyphus, Les Justes). The episode blends literary and political context with light banter and cultural references.
title: 4 Jan: Solomon Northup and Albert Camus

description: Luther's excommunication from the Catholic church and the birth of the author of Lord of the Rings happened on this day.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (3 January) is part of the hosts' multi-day anniversary series. Tom Holland opens discussing Martin Luther and the escalation of his conflict with the papacy: the papal bull Exsurge Domine (15 June 1520), Luther's public burning of canon law and the bull (10 December 1520), and his formal excommunication on 3 January 1521. They outline Luther's theological challenges to Catholic doctrine and note attempts at negotiation, the protection of the Elector of Saxony, and later ecumenical gestures.
