The second half celebrates J.R.R. Tolkien's birthday (3 January 1892). The hosts trace Tolkien's family origins, childhood in England, Catholicism, and the Shire's roots in Worcestershire/Birmingham. They argue Lord of the Rings reflects 20th-century concerns — World Wars, industrialization, and Christian themes — and note Tolkien's statement that certain narrative moments evoke divine grace. The episode mentions related historical touchpoints and signals future episodes on Tolkien and other themes.
title: 3 Jan: Martin Luther and J.R.R. Tolkien

description: The conquest of the kingdom of Grenada by Christian forces reclaimed southern Spain from the Moors, and the forgotten monarchs of Hawaii.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (a 12 Days of Christmas special, Day 2) is split into two main segments. First, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the fall of Granada on 2 January 1492, describing the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil) to Ferdinand and Isabella and situating the event alongside Christopher Columbus's presence and the wider 1492 conjuncture: Granada's fall, Columbus's voyage, and the expulsion of the Jews. They debate interpretations of the Reconquista and reference scholarship (Fernando Cervantes's Conquistadores) on the motives of Spaniards in the New World. The second segment turns to the Hawaiian monarchy: the rise of Kamehameha I, 19th-century Anglophone influence, Kamehameha IV, and Queen Emma (her English connections, philanthropy, and loss in the 1874 election). They outline missionary influence, British-American tensions, and the eventual toppling of the monarchy. The hosts close by previewing the next episode on J. R. R. Tolkien.
title: 2 Jan: Reconquest of Spain and the Old Queen of Hawaii

description: In a distinctly Roman start to 2022, Tom sets the scene for Rome's "Year of the four Emperors", while Dominic recounts a battle which was the beginning of the end for the Byzantine Empire.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook mark New Year’s Day with a two-part Roman-themed discussion. Tom opens with events around 1 January AD 69: Nero’s ominous New Year rituals, the mutiny of Rhine legions, and how unrest there contributed to the Year of the Four Emperors (Galba, Otho, Vitellius, Vespasian). He explains legionary politics, local grievances, and how troop loyalty shaped imperial succession. Tom also briefly previews his forthcoming book work covering the period after Nero, including the Flavian dynasty and the two Jewish revolts. Dominic’s segment moves to Byzantium: Romanus IV Diogenes’s accession on 1 January 1068, his military background, marriage into the imperial family, and the disastrous Battle of Manzikert (1071) against the Seljuk Turks under Alp Arslan. They describe Romanus’s capture, ransom, subsequent blinding, death in exile, and the broader consequences for Byzantine control of Anatolia. The episode links frontier armies, political ambition and military defeats across both Western and Eastern Roman traditions.
title: 1 Jan: Nero's succession and the fall of the Byzantine Empire

description: It's New Year's Eve - switch off the Hootenanny and tune in to hear Dominic recount extraordinary tales of coups, cousins and the rise of an emperor in the Central African Republic. Later on in the podcast, Tom questions whether the current pandemic will have a more prominent role in the history books than the often disregarded Spanish flu.
summary: In this year-end episode (31 December 2021) Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their "12 Days of Christmas" mini-series with two historical dates. Dominic recounts the rise and rule of Jean-Bédel Bokassa: his military service with France, the 1965 coup that brought him to power in the Central African Republic, his modernization efforts and atrocities, the extravagant Napoleonic-style coronation in 1977, and his removal in 1979 — including the scandal over diamonds linked to Valéry Giscard d'Estaing. Tom chooses the origin point for the COVID-19 pandemic, noting the WHO alert from Wuhan on 31 December 2019, and situates COVID historically by comparing it to the Spanish Flu, discussing government responses, societal impacts, and how the pandemic may shape memory and policy in the long term. The hosts reference related figures and events — Dien Bien Phu, decolonization, and public reactions — and reflect on how COVID accelerated technological and governmental changes. They close by wishing listeners a happy new year and noting the series will continue.
title: 31 Dec: Jean-Bédel Bokassa and the memory of pandemics

description: Tom dissects the Battle of Wakefield and the subsequent fall of Richard, Duke of York, while Dominic talks us through the last ‘great’ Habsburg emperor, Karl I of Austria.
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their "12 Days of Christmas" mini-series by marking anniversaries on December 30. Tom discusses the Wars of the Roses, focusing on Richard, Duke of York and the Battle of Wakefield (30 December 1460): dynastic rivalry, the breakdown of Henry VI's rule, key engagements (St Albans, Northampton), and Shakespeare's shaping of the narrative in the Henry VI plays and Richard III. Dominic covers the coronation of Karl I (Charles I) as King of Hungary on 30 December 1916 amid the First World War, describing the weakening Austro-Hungarian Empire, Franz Joseph's dynasty troubles, the Holy Crown of Hungary, Karl's character and reform attempts, his failed postwar comeback bids in 1921, exile and death. The hosts compare the two figures — Richard of York and Karl I — and reflect on monarchy, sacral kingship, and how dramatic portrayals influence historical memory. The episode mixes military, dynastic and cultural perspectives across medieval and twentieth-century Europe.
title: 30 Dec: The Battle of Wakefield and Emperor Karl I

description: Tom takes us through the murder of Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, while Dominic looks at one of the United States' most tragic massacres: the 1890 Battle of Wounded Knee.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (a special from the hosts' '12 Days of Christmas / 13 days of Christmas' series) examines two violent, emblematic moments that fall on 29 December. First, Tom and Dominic recount the life and martyrdom of Thomas Becket (murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170), describing his transformation from royal chancellor to archbishop, the quarrel with Henry II of England, the four knights who killed him, and the long cultural legacy of his shrine. After a break, they shift to the American plains and the Wounded Knee Massacre (29 December 1890), situating it amid the collapse of the bison economy, the rise of the Ghost Dance movement, the killing of Sitting Bull, and the deadly interception of fleeing Lakota by the U.S. Seventh Cavalry. The hosts compare the sacral power of martyrdom in both episodes, cite related literature (T. S. Eliot, Jean Anouilh, Dee Brown), and reflect on historical memory and delayed acknowledgment of atrocity.
title: 29 Dec: The Murder of Thomas Becket and the Wounded Knee Massacre

description: In a suitably festive edition, Tom recounts the biblical story of King Herod's massacre of babies in Jerusalem, and Dominic remembers a rail disaster from 1879 and the hilariously bad poetry it inspired.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (day four of the hosts' 12 Days of Christmas marathon) examines two anniversaries for December 28. First, Tom and Dominic discuss the Massacre of the Innocents as told in the Gospel of St. Matthew: they question its historicity, note its echo of the Exodus narrative and Moses, and place King Herod the Great in the wider Judean memory that later contributed to the Great Jewish Revolt and the destruction of the temple. The conversation touches on Josephus, Herod's reputation and patronage projects, and related liturgical commemorations (Childermass, St. Stephen). The second half recounts the Tay Bridge disaster (28 December 1879) — the collapse of Sir Thomas Bouch's railway bridge — and the famously inept poetic response by William McGonagall, including anecdotes about McGonagall's life, his poem "The Tay Bridge Disaster, 1880," and its cultural afterlife. The hosts also mention Camus' The Fall and tease future episodes.
title: 28 Dec: Massacre of the Innocents and the Tay Bridge disaster

description: How the English's fondness for Portuguese fortified wine began, and the unlikely story of the voyage which inspired Charles Darwin's natural philosophy.
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook continue their seasonal "12 (or 13) Days of Christmas" run (27 December). Dominic examines the origins of England's love of port, centered on the Methuen Treaty of 1703 which favoured Portuguese wines and encouraged the growth of the port trade in England. They discuss early English engagement with Portuguese wine regions, the commercial effects of lowered duties, and cultural details like the 18th-century "three-bottle man." Tom's anniversary choice is Charles Darwin’s departure on HMS Beagle in 1831. They recount Darwin’s background, his selection as the Beagle’s gentleman companion under Captain Robert FitzRoy, the fraught preparations, severe seasickness in the Bay of Biscay, and the five-year voyage that produced crucial specimens and ideas leading toward evolutionary theory. The hosts reference relevant books (Lyell's Principles of Geology; a biography of Darwin by Adrian Desmond and James Moore) and flag the voyage and its political and personal tensions as topics worthy of a future full episode.
title: 27 Dec: Port wine and Darwin sets sail

description: Was Wenceslas good? Was he a king? And Dominic remembers the popular Victorian light opera maestros' first production 'Thespis'.
summary: In this Boxing Day episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present two light musical-themed items as part of their seasonal "12 Days of Christmas" series (they note they are doing 13 days). First, they trace the origins of the carol "Good King Wenceslas": lyrics written in 1853 by John Mason Neill and set to a 13th-century Easter hymn (Tempus ad est floridum). They discuss the historical Wenceslaus (c. 921–935), his saintly reputation, his murder in a dynastic coup (implicating his brother Bollislaus), and his later legendary status and posthumous elevation by Otto the Great. The second segment covers the first Gilbert and Sullivan collaboration, Thespis, which opened on Boxing Day 1871 at the Gaiety Theatre (a run of 63 performances). They outline the plot (gods and actors swapping places), note contemporary mixed reviews, lament that the music is lost, and situate it within the later, hugely successful Gilbert and Sullivan repertoire (Trial by Jury, Pirates of Penzance, The Mikado). They recommend the film Topsy-Turvy for context and close with seasonal good wishes.
title: 26 Dec: Good King Wenceslas and the first Gilbert & Sullivan

description: To kick off our 12 Days of Christmas mini-series, Tom and Dominic remember the birth of the Holy Roman Empire and Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation
summary: This Christmas Day episode of The Rest Is History (the first of a 12 Days of Christmas mini-series) features Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discussing two landmark events that occurred on 25 December: the coronation of Charlemagne in Rome (AD 800) and the formal end of the Soviet Union (25 December 1991). Holland outlines the political and ecclesiastical background to Charlemagne’s elevation by Pope Leo III, the role of the Carolingians, Einhard’s biography, Byzantine intrigues under Empress Irene, and the longer-term consequences leading toward the Holy Roman Empire. Sandbrook then narrates the chaotic final months of the USSR under Mikhail Gorbachev: economic decline, the August 1991 coup, Boris Yeltsin’s emergence, the Ukraine referendum, the Belavezha agreements, and Gorbachev’s televised resignation. The hosts reflect on the divergent receptions of these moments — the birth and death of empires — and their long-term impact on figures like Putin and Xi Jinping. The episode sets up the daily run of subsequent festive instalments.
title: 25 Dec: Coronation of Charlemagne and the collapse of the Soviet Union

description: Fan favourite Rachel Morley from Friends of Friendless Churches is back to count down her top ten churches with a festive connection
summary: This festive episode of The Rest Is History (the second of two holiday specials) features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Rachel Morley (director of Friends of Friendless Churches). Morley presents a timed “top 10” of British churches and church-related Christmas traditions: anecdotes about church music and composers, Victorian and medieval ghost-story associations (M. R. James), Dickensian sites linked to A Christmas Carol, the origins and practice of Boxing Day almsgiving, medieval wall paintings and nativity scenes, unusual artefacts (donation boxes, a medieval dominical dial), and folklore such as the Green Knight/Green Chapel candidates. The episode also touches on secular Christmas history — Saint Nicholas traditions, the Scottish and English bans on Christmas in the 16th–17th centuries, Henry Jones’s invention of self-raising flour and its military adoption via Florence Nightingale, and the history of tinsel production. The show blends site recommendations, material-culture details, and light historical commentary, closing with seasonal wishes and a note about an upcoming 12 Days of Christmas mini-series.
title: Christmas churches

summary: In this festive on-location episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk the streets of the City of London discussing Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol. They visit likely sites for Scrooge’s counting house, tavern and home around Cornhill, Bengal Court, White Lion Court, St Michael’s Cornhill, St Peter upon Cornhill and Leadenhall Market, using Dickens’s text to link place and passage. The hosts explore Dickens’s creative energy, his 1842 American trip, his interest in poverty and death, and the story’s mix of supernatural terror and sentimental moralism. They discuss characters (Jacob Marley, Bob Cratchit, Tiny Tim, Mr Fezziwig, Fred), the book’s immediate impact (charitable responses), its conservative/individualist solutions to social problems, and its adaptability—from the Muppets to film and parodies. They situate A Christmas Carol within Victorian Christmas traditions and reflect on why the story remains culturally dominant at Christmas.
title: A Christmas Carol

summary: This episode is a live members' discussion of the 1960s, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook. The pair debate whether the 1960s were a clean break or continuation of earlier trends, touching on economics, youth culture, technology, and the Cold War. They consider defining events — the Cuban Missile Crisis, Vietnam, Prague Spring, Apollo moon landings — and cultural phenomena from Beatlemania and the Maharishi visit to hippie free-love rhetoric and its sexist abuses. The conversation assesses social changes (civil rights, feminism, sexual liberation), institutional decline, and reactions such as Mary Whitehouse and emergent conservative movements. Global perspectives (China's Cultural Revolution, decolonization) and the decade's two-phase arc — optimistic early 1960s and darker late 1960s/early 1970s — are discussed. The hosts underline the ambivalent legacy: widened individualism and liberties alongside social costs and backlash, and they recommend further readings and future guest episodes to explore topics omitted here.
title: RIHC: The 1960s (Livestream)

description: Now mostly overlooked by history, Burgundy was a major political and cultural power in western Europe during the Middle Ages, rivalling France and England. How did the kingdom gain such prominence, and why did it disappear? Bart van Loo, author of "The Burgundians", joins Dominic and Tom to explain.
summary: This episode is an extended interview with Bart (van Leeuw) about the Dukes of Burgundy and the rise and fall of the Burgundian polity in the late medieval Low Countries. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss how Burgundian state‑building stitched together wealthy Flemish towns and territories between France and the Holy Roman Empire, creating a glittering court culture of feasts, tournaments and the Order of the Golden Fleece. Bart traces the dynasty from Philip the Bold through John the Fearless, Philip the Good and Charles the Bold, linking Burgundian policy to key episodes of the Hundred Years' War (Poitiers, Agincourt, the Treaty of Troyes), Joan of Arc's capture and the 1435 Burgundian reconciliation with France. He explains cultural achievements (Jan van Eyck, artists and sculptors) and economic shifts (Bruges to Antwerp). The conversation closes with Charles the Bold's defeat at Nancy, the Habsburg inheritance via Mary of Burgundy and the long-term legacy for the Low Countries and later European politics.
title: Burgundy: Europe's forgotten superpower

description: From their origins in the 1930's running parallel to the rise of fascism in Europe, to the Adam West-era camp of the 60's, to the gritty modern reboots - what has made superheroes a cultural phenomenon, and what mirror does it hold up to society?
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the cultural and historical origins of superheroes. Beginning with a quotation from Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Grant Morrison's Supergods, they trace the rise of comics from 1930s printing innovations through the Golden and Silver Ages. They discuss pioneering creators (Jerry Siegel, Joe Shuster, Bob Kane/Bill Finger) and landmark characters (Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman) and explore antecedents such as the Scarlet Pimpernel and Zorro. The episode addresses creators' backgrounds, immigrant themes in Superman, William Moulton Marston's ideological influence on Wonder Woman, and the 1950s moral panic led by Fredric Wertham. Moving to Marvel’s Silver Age, they highlight Stan Lee, Jack Kirby and Steve Ditko and explain Spider-Man’s teenage focus. Finally, they cover later, darker reinterpretations (Alan Moore's Watchmen, Frank Miller), how comics mirror US social anxieties (race, war, politics), and the modern blockbuster era’s cultural dominance and possible exhaustion.
title: Superheroes

description: How did a game played by peasants in the English countryside as early as the 17th century evolve into one of the most popular sports in the world? Jon Hotten, author of 'The Meaning of Cricket', joins Tom and Dominic to discuss the origins of the game, its Victorian transformation and the inextricable link with Empire.
summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host a wide-ranging episode on the history and cultural meaning of cricket, with guest John Houghton (author of The Meaning of Cricket). They trace cricket's murky origins in rural England, its Victorian regularisation around figures like W. G. Grace, and its statistical and social codification (Wisden). The discussion moves to cricket’s internationalisation — early matches in North America, the Aboriginal Australian tour of 1868, and the birth of The Ashes after Australia’s early victories. They cover flashpoints such as the Bodyline crisis of 1932–33 (Douglas Jardine’s tactics vs. Don Bradman) and cricket’s role across the Empire: West Indies fast-bowling traditions, the symbolic power of West Indies teams in the 1970s, and India’s emergence as the sport’s financial and cultural centre (including the 1983 World Cup and the India–Pakistan rivalry). The episode balances cricket’s pastoral imagery and moral rhetoric with its imperial, class and racial histories, and closes on amateur cricket and contemporary reflections.
title: Cricket

summary: This bonus episode — the inaugural Rest Is History Club instalment for paying members — explores the history and cultural role of clubs from antiquity to the modern day. The hosts trace clubs from ancient convivial groups (Mark Antony and Cleopatra are discussed) and Roman collegia through medieval chivalric orders (Order of the Garter) to the coffeehouses and tavern sodalities of 17th–18th century England. They discuss famous London clubs such as the Kit-Cat Club, White's, Brooks's, the Hellfire Club and Freemasonry, noting notable members (e.g., Charles James Fox, Edward Gibbon, Sir Francis Dashwood) and the clubs’ influence on politics, literature and sport (e.g., the origins of Lord's and the Marylebone Cricket Club). The episode also covers clubs' cultural afterlives — from P. G. Wodehouse’s Drones Club to modern Soho House — and explains the format and aims of the new weekly club episodes and associated Discord/live events for members.
title: RIHC: History's greatest clubs

description: The peasant who became one of the most influential figures in the final days of the Russian Empire is an unbelievable story. But how much of the gossip, rumour and scandal that surrounded Grigori Rasputin is true? Dominic and Tom discuss, and somehow manage not to get too sidetracked by Boney M.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the life, influence and legend of Grigoriy Efimovich Rasputin. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace his origins in rural Siberia, his religious pilgrimage and rise as a charismatic holy man in St. Petersburg, and his intimate relationship with Nicholas II's family—particularly Alexandra and the hemophiliac heir Alexei. The hosts separate documented fact from lurid rumor: Rasputin’s pastoral religiosity and calming effect on the imperial family contrasted with allegations of sexual misconduct and political manipulation. They discuss the spread of obscene pamphlets and foreign intrigue in the pre‑revolutionary climate, Rasputin’s repeated targeting by rivals, and his murder in December 1916 by a group including Prince Felix Yusupov. The episode reflects on historiography, contemporary sources (including polemical memoirs), and how Rasputin became a symbol of late‑imperial Russia’s instability, ultimately linked to the broader crises of World War I and the Russian Revolution.
title: Rasputin

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Chris Stringer (Natural History Museum) about Neanderthals and their place in human prehistory. Drawing on recent archaeology and genetics, Stringer traces the discovery and naming of Neanderthals in the 19th century, evolving scientific views (from brutish 'missing link' portrayals to recognition of cultural complexity), and evidence for burial, ornamentation, cave use (including Bruniquel), and pigment use. The discussion covers interbreeding with Homo sapiens, the geographic overlap during Late Pleistocene dispersals, possible causes of Neanderthal decline (climate stress, low population/low diversity, demographic absorption), and the ongoing influence of Neanderthal DNA on modern immune responses. Cultural representations (Golding, Wells) and contested interpretations (Shanidar flower burials, cannibalism, ritual behaviour) are examined. The episode situates Neanderthals as another viable model of “being human” rather than an evolutionary ladder and underscores how scientific and political contexts shape interpretations of the past.
title: Neanderthals

description: “God is too late, you have begun, now I will finish it.” Swash-buckling hero or sacrilegious tyrant? Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore Napoleon’s campaign in Egypt, his dream of becoming the next Alexander the Great, and the complicated history between France and Islam.
summary: This episode examines Napoleon's Egyptian expedition of the late 1790s — its military drama, cultural consequences and longer-term global significance. Holland and Sandbrook narrate Napoleon's meteoric rise, the strategic aims of striking at Egypt to threaten British routes to India, and the dramatic clashes: the Battle of the Pyramids and the Royal Navy's crushing victory at Aboukir (the Battle of the Nile). They discuss the expedition's odd mixture of Enlightenment science and colonial violence: the 151 savants, hot-air balloons and printing presses alongside brutal repression of uprisings. The hosts trace how the campaign catalysed Egyptology — the Rosetta Stone's discovery, the Institut d'Égypte, the multi-volume Description de l'Égypte and Champollion's decipherment — and how European antiquarian enthusiasm reshaped Western imaginaries. They also address the campaign's legacy in modern politics and culture: tensions over secular French universalism, Edward Said's critique of Orientalism, Muhammad Ali's modernization of Egypt, and the episode's role in early global encounters between Europe and the Islamic world.
title: Napoleon in Egypt

description: America's Central Intelligence Agency is a mysterious organisation which has used covert methods to assassinate enemies, influence governments and tip whole countries into revolution - or so countless films, TV series and books would have us believe. How much of it is true? Hugh Wilford, professor of history at California State University, Long Beach, and author of four books, including The Mighty Wurlitzer: How the CIA Played America, joins Tom and Dominic to discuss.
summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host a wide-ranging interview with Professor Hugh Wilford on the history, culture and controversies of the Central Intelligence Agency. Wilford traces the CIA’s lineage from the OSS in World War II through its official creation in 1947, explaining early Anglo‑American influences and the patrician, Ivy League character of many founding officers. He examines major covert operations — notably the 1953 Iran coup, Guatemala 1954, and repeated attempts against Fidel Castro including Operation Mongoose and the Bay of Pigs — and discusses successes and failures in intelligence and covert action. The conversation addresses cultural Cold War activities (the CIA’s covert sponsorship of the Congress for Cultural Freedom and artistic promotion), cinematic portrayals, congressional inquiries in the 1970s, and later technological and cyber challenges. They consider moral balances, catastrophic outcomes (Indonesia, Congo, Guatemala) and intelligence achievements (Cuban Missile Crisis intelligence, Afghan support), ending with reflections on secrecy, public perception and the agency’s evolving role in the modern era.
title: The CIA

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History runs through the hosts' "World Cup of Kings and Queens of England," recapping the earlier rounds and debating quarterfinal, semifinal and final matchups. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook evaluate monarchs' reputations and legacies — Henry V, Henry VIII, Charles II, Edward III, Athelstan, William I, Elizabeth I and Elizabeth II figure prominently — weighing martial success, political consequence and cultural iconography. They discuss how Shakespeare and later literature shaped perceptions (especially of Henry V and Richard III), the costs and consequences of continental wars, and the seismic impact of the Reformation and dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII. The pair also cover Stuart-era events (the Restoration, plague, Great Fire, Exclusion Crisis) and medieval high points (Crécy, Poitiers, the Black Death). The episode blends serious historical argument with lighter banter, literary references (Wolf Hall, Conan Doyle), and reflections on why certain monarchs remain emblematic of English identity.
title: World Cup of Kings & Queens - Part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Rest Is History "Kings and Queens of England World Cup," focusing on the notable figures who were eliminated in the first round. They review short portraits and popular perceptions of monarchs and rulers including Edward I, Henry II, Henry VII, Cnut (Canute), Richard I, Oliver Cromwell, Victoria, George V, and Henry VIII, mixing biographical detail, anecdotes and historiographical asides. Themes include the changing nature of kingship, regional and modern reactions to historical reputations (e.g., Irish or Scottish perspectives), and how media and public voting reshaped the contest. The episode references related works and previous episodes (including a podcast on Athelstan and a prior Cromwell episode) and previews the quarterfinal matchups and a follow-up episode on monarchy and historiography.
title: World Cup of Kings & Queens - Part 1

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook celebrate their podcast-run "World Cup of the Kings and Queens of England" after the surprising victory of Athelstan. The episode is a wide-ranging discussion of Athelstan's life and significance in the early 10th century: his upbringing under Alfredian influence, time at Athelflæd's Mercian court, the military and diplomatic moves that led to the annexation of York, and his crowning at Kingston upon Thames as ruler of Mercians and West Saxons. The hosts examine his legal and economic reforms (burhs, coinage, law codes), his Christian kingship and continental connections (marriages and fosterage), and his victory at Brunanburh. They explore reasons Athelstan is less known today despite forging a durable English polity, and touch on cultural afterlives (Michael Wood's work, Last Kingdom, possible literary echoes). The tone mixes serious historical analysis with light banter about media reaction to their tournament.
title: Æthelstan: OFFICIALLY England's Greatest Monarch

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host David Hunt to survey Australian history from its deep prehistory to early European contact. Hunt reviews archaeological and genetic evidence for human arrival (~60–65,000 years ago), discusses Australian megafauna and their contested extinction (~40–44,000 BP), and explains Aboriginal Dreamtime, songlines and cultural diversity. The conversation moves to external contacts: Lapita/Polynesian influences (dingoes), Macassan trepang fisheries from Sulawesi, and debunked theories of early Chinese discovery (Gavin Menzies). Hunt outlines early European sightings — Dutch contacts from 1606, Abel Tasman (1642), Dirk Hartog, and the formation of the VOC — and why Australia was not colonised earlier. He also covers Cook’s Endeavour voyage and the 1769 transit of Venus mission, Joseph Banks’s initial negative assessment, and the eventual British choice of New South Wales as a convict destination. The episode ends with plans for a part two on the founding of the colony and further discussion of convict-era Australia.
title: Australia Before Cook

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the 1973 energy crisis, tracing its immediate trigger in the Yom Kippur War (6 October 1973) and the simultaneous OPEC meetings that transformed bargaining power in the global oil market. They discuss the retreat of European colonial influence in the Middle East, the emergence of Saudi and other Gulf producers as geopolitical actors, and the mechanics of the OPEC price hikes and embargoes. The conversation ranges from US policy choices — Nixon, Kissinger, the airlift Operation Nickel Grass — to consequences at home: the US petrol queues, Nixon-era energy measures, and in Britain the miners' disputes, the imposition of the Three-Day Week, and Edward Heath’s political misfortunes. Broader long-term effects are considered: acceleration of environmental thinking, debates over energy independence (Nixon, Carter), shifts in global power, and how later events (Iranian Revolution, Gulf conflicts) were shaped by 1973. They reference key books (Daniel Yergin's The Prize; E.F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful) and Dominic’s own book on Heath.
title: The Oil Weapon

summary: The hosts launch The Rest Is History's playful "World Cup of Kings and Queens," outlining a 16-contender tournament to provoke discussion about monarchy and what counts as a "king of England." They explain eligibility criteria (rulers of England, Great Britain, or the United Kingdom), seeded contestants and qualifiers, and the rationale behind including controversial entrants such as Oliver Cromwell and Cnut. Key seeds include Elizabeth I, Henry VIII, Henry V, William the Conqueror, Victoria, Edward III, Charles II and Elizabeth II. They debate borderline cases (Athelstan vs Alfred the Great), historical continuity of the monarchy from sacral coronation rites to the modern constitutional role, and the political and cultural lenses fans might use to vote. The episode previews the Super 16 draw (prepared by Jonathan Wilson), highlights fan reactions and expert input from Tracy Borman (her book Crown and Scepter), and offers predictions for which monarchs might advance.
title: World Cup of Kings & Queens Preview

summary: This Remembrance Day episode examines how the end of the First World War was commemorated and how those rituals — armistice timing, graves policy, the Unknown Warrior, the cenotaph, the two-minute silence and the poppy — were invented and institutionalized. Holland and Sandbrook discuss the last hours of fighting and specific last casualties, the political collapse in Germany leading to the 11 November 1918 armistice, and the emergence of the Imperial War Graves Commission under Fabian Ware with architects (Lutyens, Blomfield, Baker) and Rudyard Kipling shaping language and memorial design. They tell the story of Reverend David Railton’s Unknown Warrior proposal and its dramatic selection and burial in 1920, the poppy’s origins in John McCrae’s poem and campaigners like Moina Michael and Anna Gerard, and wider cultural tensions (Christian ritual, Greek precedents, pacifist white poppies). The hosts conclude by reflecting on the ritual’s sacred status, its evolution across the twentieth century, and its contemporary contested meanings.
title: End of the First World War & Remembrance

summary: This episode, the second in The Rest Is History's series on Alexander, follows Alexander the Great from Gaugamela through the conquest of Persia, the burning of Persepolis, the pursuit and death of Darius III, and the arduous campaigns in Bactria, Afghanistan and India. Holland and Sandbrook debate motives and sources: whether actions like the burning of Persepolis were revenge, political theatre, or later embellishment. They discuss Alexander's Persianizing policies (marriages, dress, proskynesis), internal dissent and executions (Parmenion, Philotus/Philotas, Calisthenes), the mutinies at the Hyphasis and Opis, the hydaspes encounter with King Porus, the disastrous Gedrosian desert march, and Alexander's death in Babylon in 323 BC. The hosts examine the late and fragmentary nature of primary sources (Arrian, Curtius, Plutarch, etc.), Alexander's legacy in the Hellenistic world and later religions, and whether his empire could have endured. Dom Sandbrook also plugs his children's book on Alexander and a separate book on the First World War.
title: Alexander the Great - Part 2

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin a multi-part treatment of Alexander the Great, explaining why his life is one of history's great adventure narratives and discussing the ambivalent modern reception of Alexander. They cover his Macedonian origins, Philip II's military reforms (the sarissa, phalanx, companion cavalry), Alexander's education under Aristotle, his taming of Bucephalus, and early actions including the suppression of Thebes and Philip's assassination. The episode follows Alexander's crossing of the Hellespont, the victory at the River Granicus, the march through Asia Minor, the cutting of the Gordian knot, and the campaign down the Phoenician coast culminating in the long siege and harsh sack of Tyre. They describe Alexander's entry to Egypt, founding of Alexandria, and journey to the Siwa oracle — debating whether Alexander believed himself divine. Throughout they note limits of sources, Persian perspectives, and recent scholarship reframing Alexander as influenced by Achaemenid kingship rather than only mythic heroism.
title: Alexander the Great - Part 1

summary: This episode is a Guy Fawkes / Bonfire Night special. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook narrate the background, planning and aftermath of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot: the religious tensions after the Reformation, the role of Robert Catesby and his circle, Thomas Percy’s access to Parliament, and Guy Fawkes as the gunpowder expert. They discuss the plot’s discovery (the so-called Monteagle/Montagle letter), the murky questions about Robert Cecil’s involvement, Fawkes’s torture and the conspirators’ trials and executions in 1606. The hosts assess counterfactuals (what might have followed had the plot succeeded) and trace how the event was commemorated: the establishment of annual thanksgiving services, the evolution of bonfire traditions, export to America (Pope Day), 19th-century popularisation of Guy Fawkes as an anti-hero, and modern cultural afterlives (V for Vendetta, Anonymous masks, Guido Fawkes website). The episode closes with reflections on contemporary attitudes to Bonfire Night and lighter asides about hedgehog safety and effigy-burning traditions.
title: The Gunpowder Plot

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Ronald Hutton (University of Bristol) about paganism across time and place. Hutton argues the term "pagan" is a Christian category useful for describing pre-Christian, local rooted religions and stresses varying evidential quality: rich written sources in the classical Mediterranean versus fragmentary material remains for northern Europe. Topics include Roman and medieval encounters with paganism, survival and absorption of pagan motifs into Christianity (e.g., saints replacing gods, church architecture, folk customs), medieval survivals at Haran and in Lithuania, Renaissance attempts to reintegrate pagan deities, and British prehistoric religion. Specific subjects covered are druids, Romano-British votive practices, enigmatic monuments such as Stonehenge, Sheela-na-gig and green man iconography, and the Paviland "Red Lady" burial. Hutton emphasizes the limits of certainty for prehistoric belief while valuing the imaginative and cultural continuities that shaped later revivals and modern paganism.
title: Stonehenge, Ancient Ritual and the Origins of Paganism

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Ronald Hutton about paganism and its modern revivals. The conversation begins with the origins of Halloween and the Gaelic festival Sawin, tracing medieval Christian overlays such as All Hallows and the later Irish influence that exported Halloween to America. Hutton maps strands linking ancient ritual, seasonal customs and classical literature to modern pagan practice, while distinguishing genuine continuities from 19th–20th-century inventions. They discuss key texts and figures: Leland's Aradia, Margaret Murray's witchcraft hypotheses, Gerald Gardner's role in founding modern Wicca, and cultural manifestations in literature and festivals. Hutton rejects deep links between Nazism and mainstream pagan revival, describes the sociological profile of many pagans, and addresses tensions between claims of ancient continuity and deliberate modern reconstruction. The episode closes noting paganism's cultural leakage (festivals, music, environmentalism) and proposes a follow-up to explore medieval and prehistoric strands in more depth.
title: Halloween and Modern Paganism

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host historian Seb Falk to discuss medieval science and to challenge the stereotype of the Middle Ages as a ‘dark’ period. Drawing on Falk's book The Light Ages, they examine how medieval practitioners—monks, astronomers and instrument makers—kept and developed knowledge via devices (astrolabes, equatoria, early mechanical clocks), manuscript scholarship, and cross-cultural transmission from Byzantium and the Islamic world. Falk profiles John of Westwick, a 14th-century monk who built an equatorium, and discusses figures and texts (Aristotle, Sacrobosco, Ptolemy, Copernicus) and the role of institutions such as monasteries. The conversation emphasizes continuity with ancient and Islamic science, the theological contexts shaping inquiry, and the gradual intellectual shifts that culminated in early modern astronomy. They highlight the medieval focus on precision, tinkering, and incremental innovation rather than a single linear progress narrative.
title: Medieval Science

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the idea of 'golden ages': what defines them, whether the concept is legitimate, and how nostalgia and politics shape which eras are remembered as golden. They trace the idea to classical models—Periclean Athens and the Augustan age of Rome—using Virgil and Thucydides to show how prosperity and cultural achievement are often mythologized even as conflict or decline follow. They survey examples (Spanish and Dutch golden ages, Elizabethan England, the Antonine 'peace') and stress that golden ages are retrospective constructs, frequently invoked by political movements. The hosts consider modern candidates (1950s, 1960s, 1990s), national perspectives (Western primacy, China, the US) and moral complications—how cultural brilliance often rests on exploitation. They conclude that golden ages are both imaginative and political, useful for identity and nostalgia but rarely unambiguous or universally experienced.
title: Golden Ages

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome Aparna Andare, an Indian curator and architectural historian, to deliver a sweep through the subcontinent’s history using ten buildings as touchstones. Aparna moves chronologically from Mohenjodaro (Indus Valley Civilisation) and Mauryan rock-cut Barabar Caves, through Gupta-period Udayagiri, early mosques in Kerala, Chola and Vijayanagara temples in the south, to Delhi’s Qutub Minar and Mughal gardens including the Taj Mahal. She discusses later developments — Jaipur’s planned city, Indo-Saracenic colonial architecture such as Mumbai’s Gateway of India — and ends with 20th-century debates over modernist monuments, notably the demolition of New Delhi’s Hall of Nations and the contested legacy of partition. The episode links art and architecture to religion, power, trade, and memory while touching on iconoclasm, cultural encounters, and the politics of preservation.
title: History of India in 10 Buildings

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the cultural and scientific history of dinosaurs: how people first interpreted large fossils in antiquity, the 18th–19th century breakthroughs (Buckland, Mantell, Owen), and the Crystal Palace displays. They examine Mary Anning’s pioneering fossil work (marine reptiles), the mid‑Victorian intersection of geology and Christianity (Ussher, Buckland, Darwinism), and the transatlantic boom of American paleontology (Cope, Marsh, Barnum Brown) including Carnegie’s Diplodocus casts. The episode traces shifting scientific views — from ponderous cold‑blooded reptiles to active, bird‑related creatures (Bakker, John Ostrom/dinonychus — as discussed) — and the Alvarez asteroid hypothesis for the end‑Cretaceous extinction. They also touch on dinosaurs as metaphors in culture (Crystal Palace, Jurassic Park, Soviet imagery), the technological and geopolitical shifts in paleontological leadership (Britain → U.S. → China), and the modern resonance of dinosaurs for ideas about extinction and climate. The conversation mixes scientific history with cultural readings, anecdotes, and listener questions.
title: Dinosaurs

description: Did the industrial revolution really improve people’s lives? And why was Britain first to industrialise? Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Emma Griffin, professor of modern history and author of Liberty's Dawn: A People's History of the Industrial Revolution.
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Emma Griffin (professor of modern British history and president of the Royal Historical Society) about the Industrial Revolution. Griffin argues the Industrial Revolution is a genuine turning point — socially, economically and environmentally — and explains why it began in Britain in the late 18th/early 19th century rather than elsewhere. She discusses factors such as commercial culture, empire and access to raw materials, the role of coal and technical innovation, and the necessity of capital, skilled labour and institutions that supported risk-taking. The conversation moves from high-level causes to lived experience: pollution, Dickensian imagery, changing opportunities for men, the ambivalent effects on women, the catastrophic impact on many children, and the rise of working-class politics including Chartism and the intellectual ferment that influenced Marx and Engels. They close by reflecting on Britain’s mixed national memory of industrialization and on teaching the period more engagingly in schools.
title: The Industrial Revolution

summary: This is the second part of a two-part Rest Is History series on the Watergate scandal. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the unraveling of Richard Nixon's presidency after the June 1972 break-in, focusing on the cover-up, the role of John Dean and the Washington Post investigations, and the crucial revelation of the Oval Office taping system by Alexander Butterfield. The episode covers the fight over the tapes with special prosecutor Archibald Cox, the October 1973 'Saturday Night Massacre', the release of tapes (including the 18½-minute gap), and the Supreme Court decision forcing surrender. The smoking-gun tape made Nixon's complicity clear, prompting impeachment votes and his August 1974 resignation. The hosts then discuss Gerald Ford's pardon, the broader foreign-policy context (Yom Kippur War, 1973 oil shock), cultural portrayals, and Watergate's long-term effects on public trust, partisan politics, and the rule of law in the United States.
title: Watergate - Part 2

summary: This episode (part 1 of a two-part discussion) examines Richard Nixon’s background, character and the origins of the Watergate scandal. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace Nixon’s upbringing, outsider sensibility, political rise and policy achievements — including détente and opening relations with China — while emphasising his psychological grievances and paranoia. They outline the Nixon White House inner circle (H. R. Haldeman, John Ehrlichman, Charles Colson, Henry Kissinger) and the “plumbers” unit (E. Howard Hunt, G. Gordon Liddy). The hosts set the 1970s context of domestic turmoil, the Pentagon Papers leak and escalating Vietnam protests, then narrate the June 17, 1972 break‑in at the Democratic National Committee in the Watergate complex, the bumbling initial burglary arrests, and how the administration sought to obstruct the FBI — culminating in the “smoking gun” tape strategy. The episode ends promising a follow-up that will cover the cover-up, revelations and aftermath.
title: Watergate - Part 1

description: The world’s most famous classicist, Professor Mary Beard, joins Tom and Dominic to discuss how the legacy of classical Greece and Rome has been interpreted and re-interpreted over the past millennium and a half. They range from Dante’s Satan snacking on Julius Caesar’s assassins in Hell to recent demands in the United States that Classics itself should be cancelled.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Mary Beard about the long reception and cultural afterlife of the classical world. Drawing on her new book The Twelve Caesars, Beard explores why images and stories of Roman emperors persist across centuries — from Dante's use of Virgil to Renaissance humanism, Christian appropriation of Roman narratives, and the populist uses of classical tropes in modern politics and empire. The discussion covers how classics became associated with elite education in Britain, the ambivalent uses of Roman models (for both imperialist and revolutionary purposes), and problems such as glossing over slavery and violence in classical sources. They address modern controversies about the discipline’s role in Eurocentrism, the value of language-based study, and the future of classics in public life. The episode ends with playful historiographical questions (e.g. who would win, Alexander or Caesar) while underscoring the continuing relevance and complexity of engaging with ancient Greece and Rome.
title: Classics

summary: This short bonus episode is a spoiler-heavy discussion of No Time to Die. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook analyze how the film reflects contemporary British anxieties and the evolving James Bond myth: retirement, domestic ties (a daughter and significant other), and the replacement of 007 with a Black woman. They examine continuities with Ian Fleming’s Cold War origins, the film’s viral/nanobot threat that eerily predates COVID, and its Indo-Pacific geopolitical framing. They debate the film’s tone—its Nolan-like darkness versus classic Roger Moore lightness—criticize Rami Malek’s villain and the film’s use of physical deformity as moral signifier, and consider whether Bond’s on-screen death signals franchise rebooting or a return to lighter iterations. The episode also promotes a live Rest Is History event and closes with a Jack London quote. Overall, the hosts place the film in cultural context rather than treating it purely as cinema.
title: Bonus: No Time to Die

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the real history behind Shakespeare's Macbeth, contrasting the effective 11th-century king Macbeth of Moray with the murderous dramatized tyrant. They map early medieval Scotland's patchwork of Pictish, Gaelic (Dalriadan), Brittonic (Strathclyde) and Northumbrian territories, the impact of Viking attacks, and the dynastic complexities from Kenneth MacAlpin through Malcolm II and Duncan. The hosts trace Macbeth's rise, rule, pilgrimage to Rome and eventual defeat and honorable burial, then move to Shakespeare's 1606 play: its James I patronage, the influence of Holinshed's chronicle, reactions to the Gunpowder Plot and contemporary beliefs in witchcraft (James's Demonology). They discuss theatre lore (the so‑called Macbeth curse), notable productions — including Orson Welles's 1936 Voodoo Macbeth and Shostakovich-related adaptations — and how Lady Macbeth shaped cultural views of ambitious women. The episode blends political, religious and theatrical contexts to explain why history and drama produced such different Macbethi.
title: Macbeth

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Eleanor Rosamond Barraclough to discuss Viking voyages, the Icelandic sagas and how later medieval Icelanders recorded their world. Barraclough outlines the settlement of Iceland around the late ninth century, archaeological dating tied to a volcanic eruption circa 870–871, and the mix of Norwegian and British Isles ancestry among early settlers. The conversation covers Greenland’s settlement (c. 985), the Vinland voyages around AD 1000 and the L'Anse aux Meadows archaeological evidence (referred to in the episode as Lance Meadows). They explore saga literature — Egil’s Saga, the Vinland sagas, the Prose and Poetic Eddas — and problems of transmission, Christian influence and oral performance. Barraclough highlights prominent saga characters (Gudrid, Freydis) and the 1000 AD conversion of Iceland, plus the later 13th-century political context when Snorri Sturluson wrote. The episode closes with reading recommendations and a plug for Barraclough’s book, Beyond the Northlands.
title: The Norse Sagas

description: As Angela Merkel bows out of German politics, Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland explore the surprisingly colourful world of Germany’s Chancellors since the Second World War. It’s a story of rebels, exiles, Nazis, chain-smokers, the colossal bulk of Helmut Kohl and the East German youth of the future Frau Merkel. And to Tom’s relief, there’s lots of Christianity.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the history of post‑war German democracy by running through successive West German and German chancellors up to Angela Merkel. They open with the devastation of 1945 and the mixed idea of Stunde Null, then discuss Konrad Adenauer’s pragmatic rebuilding and early Cold War choices, Ludwig Erhard’s technocratic economic role, and the controversy around Kurt Georg Kiesinger’s Nazi past. Willy Brandt’s Ostpolitik and symbolic gestures are covered, as are Helmut Schmidt’s steady crisis management and Helmut Kohl’s decisive role in German reunification. They examine Gerhard Schröder’s post‑office ties to Russia and then focus on Merkel — her East German upbringing, Lutheran background, scientific training, cautious pragmatism, energy policy (nuclear phase‑out) and relationship with Russia (including Nord Stream). Themes include German political “boringness” as intentional, the weight of 20th‑century history on German politics, coalition government, and differing international perspectives on Merkel’s legacy.
title: Germany from Adenauer to Angela

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the creation, character and cultural legacy of James Bond prompted by the release of No Time to Die. They trace Ian Fleming's biography — family background, wartime service, and literary origins — and examine the novels' tone, misogyny, racism and wish-fulfilment. Fleming's inspirations (John Buchan's Richard Hannay, Bulldog Drummond, Fu Manchu-style villains) and recurring villain tropes are considered. The conversation contrasts Fleming's novels with the film franchise, assessing how cinematic portrayals (Connery, Moore, Dalton, Brosnan, Craig) shaped global perceptions of Britishness, masculinity and consumerist aspiration. They debate casting, gender and race questions (e.g., Idris Elba), and identify Skyfall as a high point. Dominic recommends his book The Great British Dream Factory for readers who want more. Overall the episode situates Bond as both symptom and driver of post-war British identity while acknowledging the difficulty of reconciling Fleming's reactionary elements with modern values.
title: James Bond

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook talk with guest Tom O'Alade about African decolonisation, opening with Frantz Fanon's role and writings (notably The Wretched of the Earth). They survey the uneven pace of independence across the continent — Ghana's 1957 breakthrough under Kwame Nkrumah, the earlier exits of Tunisia and Morocco, and the long continuities of European rule — and the differing colonial models used by Britain, France and Belgium. The conversation examines elite networks formed in Western universities and Pan‑African intellectual exchanges, the political mobilisation of urban workers, and the role of the Second World War in undermining European prestige. They then turn to violent decolonisation, highlighting Algeria and Kenya, and devote significant time to the chaos of Belgian Congo's transition: Patrice Lumumba's brief premiership, foreign intervention, his assassination, and the rise of Joseph‑Désiré Mobutu. The episode closes by reflecting on post‑colonial governance challenges and contemporary debates about China’s growing role in Africa.
title: Decolonising Africa

summary: This episode continues a multipart Rest Is History treatment of the Greco-Persian Wars, with Tom Holland narrating the climax: the aftermath of Thermopylae and the naval struggle leading to Salamis. Dominic Sandbrook moderates and asks listener questions throughout. Holland recounts the Spartan last stand led by Leonidas I, the betrayal by Ephialtes, and the storm-damaged Persian fleet at Artemisium. He then narrates Themistocles' intelligence manoeuvres and deception that drew Xerxes' fleet into the narrow straits of Salamis, where the Greek triremes prevailed. The episode includes Q&A on troop composition, tactics, numbers, and the myth-making around Thermopylae, plus discussion of sources (Herodotus, Aeschylus, Plutarch). Holland and Sandbrook debate counterfactuals about Persian victory and wider cultural consequences (Athenian democracy, later philosophy, and Hellenistic outcomes). The tone mixes dramatic storytelling, close reading of ancient evidence, and reflections on legacy and historical interpretation.
title: Thermopylae & Salamis - Part 2

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History sets the scene for Thermopylae and Salamis by explaining the broader context of the Greco‑Persian Wars. The hosts discuss Herodotus as the primary Greek source, the scale and nature of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, and why Persia moved against the fractious Greek city‑states. They cover the Ionian Revolt, the Athenian victory at Marathon (490 BC), and Themistocles' naval policy after the Laurion silver discovery and the ostracism of Aristides. The episode describes Xerxes' succession and vast preparations for 480 BC — the Hellespont crossing, the Athos canal and pontoon bridges — and reviews Greek political divisions, Delphi's oracles, and strategies. It ends with Spartan king Leonidas marching to Thermopylae with his contingent and the Greek fleet deploying toward Artemisium/Salamis, leaving the actual battle narrative for the next episode.
title: Thermopylae & Salamis - Part 1

summary: Recorded live at a podcast festival with Dominic Sandbrook absent (quarantining with COVID), Tom Holland is joined by Professor Ali Ansari to present “Top 10 Mistresses in History.” The hosts frame mistresses as figures who, often from humble or precarious positions, could exert intimate political influence. They run a countdown from number ten (a Persian dancing concubine called the Nightingale/Tuti linked to Fath-Ali Shah) through notable cases including Cleopatra VII, Piers Gaveston (a male favourite of Edward II), Emma Hamilton and Horatio Nelson, Nell Gwynn, Lily Langtry, Madame de Pompadour, and Aspasia of Miletus. Marie Woleska (Marie Walewska) is discussed for her link to Napoleon and Polish hopes, and the list tops with La Malinche (Malintzin / Doña Marina) as number one for her decisive role as interpreter, intermediary and alliance-builder during Hernán Cortés’s conquest of the Aztec Empire. The episode mixes biographical detail, political consequences, and cultural legacies while returning to themes of gender, patronage and power.
title: Top Ten Mistresses

description:
There are estimated to be around 16 thousand churches in England alone. But which are the finest in the UK? Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by the director of Friends of Friendless Churches, Rachel Morley, to decide a top ten. They also discuss some of the listeners’ favourites. Just remember: cathedrals not allowed!
8
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by Rachel Morley, director of the Friends of Friendless Churches, for a lively tour of lesser‑known but historically rich churches across Britain (and one Irish example added at the end). Rachel presents an idiosyncratic top‑ten of unobvious churches, weaving vivid anecdotes — Robert Cadman's fatal rope slide (1739) at St Mary’s Shrewsbury, miracle stories around St Bainall, the 1888 burial dispute at Llanfrothen that launched David Lloyd George’s career, Stanley Spencer’s painted Sandham Memorial Chapel memorialising Salonika and hospital scenes, and surprising local links like the first English turkeys at Boynton. She highlights Saxon sundials, medieval wall‑paintings, Norse kirk remains on Aunhallow, and literary connections (Charlotte Brontë and Jane Eyre at Hathersage). The episode closes with a short overview of the Friends of Friendless Churches, their mission and how listeners can help.
title: The UK’s Best Churches

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History marks the 20th anniversary of the September 11 attacks. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the symbolism, origins and long-term consequences of 9/11: the visual spectacle of the strikes, Osama bin Laden's motives and al‑Qaeda’s internationalist recruitment, and the Cold War and 1990s context (globalisation, Fukuyama's 'end of history', Benjamin Barber’s Jihad vs. McWorld). They trace bin Laden’s background from the anti‑Soviet jihad in Afghanistan to grievances over US troops in Arabia and US support for Israel. The hosts debate the US response under George W. Bush — the shift from policing to a global “war on terror,” the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, and institutions like Guantánamo and Abu Ghraib — and how both sides damaged their reputations. They consider cultural factors (Hollywood imagery, Baudrillard’s critique) and whether 9/11 was a decisive turning point or part of longer trends (American overreach, China’s rise). The conversation closes with reflections on long-term damage to Western and Islamic reputations and the unintended global consequences of the post‑9/11 era.

In this second part of a two-part series on the history of Silicon Valley, hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Mark Andreessen about the internet’s historical significance and future impact. Andreessen discusses the filter-bubble debate, comparing the internet’s cultural effects to the printing press and earlier technological shifts. He expands on his essay “How Software is Eating the World,” framing software as a lever that transforms real-world institutions and economies. The conversation covers politics (the internet’s role in populism and polarization), economic consequences and productivity gains accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, Silicon Valley’s ideological composition, and geopolitical concerns around China and cyberwarfare. Andreessen also examines online movements—both commercial and social—such as Bitcoin, Tesla fandom, QAnon and the GameStop episode, arguing the internet acts as a catalyst for modern movements or cults. They close by reflecting on unpredictability of technological consequences and the irreversible nature of major innovations.
title: Silicon Valley Part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Mark Andreessen about the history and development of Silicon Valley and the internet. The conversation traces roots from military R&D between the world wars, through Stanford’s unique entrepreneurial culture and Hewlett-Packard’s early role, to the chip revolution (Intel) that made personal computing affordable. They discuss archetypal founders (e.g., Philo Farnsworth, Robert Noyce), the Homebrew Computer Club and Apple’s cultural synthesis, and the ‘Hungarian mafia’ influx of engineering talent. Andreessen explains the technical origins of the internet (packet switching, ARPANET/NSFNET), the commercialization wave of the early 1990s, and his role with Mosaic/Netscape in packaging web access for consumers. They cover cultural shifts—Eternal September (1993), the move from pseudonymous online culture to real-name networks (Facebook), and the subsequent rise of social media. The episode ends by setting up a part two to explore social media, “software eating the world,” and broader historical parallels.
title: Silicon Valley Part 1

summary: On November 8 1983 the world teetered on the brink of nuclear annihilation, though few realized it at the time. Historian Taylor Downing joins Dominic and Tom to explain how a chilling war‑game was averted and why Tom, living near Salisbury—once third on the Soviet nuclear hit list—was in particular danger.
title: Nuclear Weapons

summary: Recorded live at the Chalk Valley History Festival, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook debate the Beatles' status as historical actors rather than merely musicians. They situate the group in post-war Britain—born during WWII, shaped by austerity, national service debates and full employment—and trace their development from Liverpool and Hamburg to global fame. Topics include Beatlemania, their 1964 U.S. impact after Kennedy's assassination, racial and imperial implications of exporting American black music, and controversies such as John Lennon's "bigger than Jesus" remark and the MBE backlash. The discussion addresses spirituality (the Maharishi, Hindu influence, Yoko Ono), celebrity and wealth, hypocrisy in public moralizing, and the band's lasting cultural effects on youth, language and political sensibilities. Audience questions touch on Dylan's role, the Beatles' future legacy, and parallels with earlier cultural revolutions like the Reformation. The episode blends cultural history with biographical detail and a live Q&A.
title: The Beatles

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Professor Gary Sheffield about the Western Front and the prevailing myths surrounding the First World War. Sheffield explains how the static trench system emerged from failed German attempts to win quickly in 1914, the revolution in firepower, and the difficulty attackers faced in exploiting breaches. The conversation covers soldiers' lived experience — the mix of horror, comradeship and routine behind the lines — and the role of faith and morale. Sheffield challenges the "lions led by donkeys" caricature, situating it in interwar and post‑1945 cultural contexts, and argues the British army learned and improved substantially, culminating in the effective 1918 offensives. He also assesses German strategic choices, the 1918 Spring Offensive (Kaiserschlacht), and why Germany did not achieve a decisive victory. The episode balances operational detail, cultural memory, and historiography, asserting that the Western Front was neither simply senseless waste nor straightforward triumph but a complex theatre of adaptation and political constraint.
title: The Western Front

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a themed episode listing ten ways weather and climate altered history. They open with deep-time effects — the Quaternary Ice Age enabling settled British habitation and the Holocene birth of urbanism — then move through major climate episodes: the Late Antique Cooling (6th century volcanic dust veil) linked to famine, plague and geopolitical shifts; the Little Ice Age and the 17th-century "Global Crisis"; and the Great Frost of 1709 shaping the outcome of the Great Northern War and Poltava. They discuss meteorological moments that reshaped battles (mud at Agincourt, storms that scattered Xerxes and the Spanish Armada, kamikaze typhoons repelling Mongol invasions of Japan), and modern examples: the critical D-Day forecast by James Stagg, and the Mount Tambora eruption/Year Without a Summer (1816) inspiring works like Frankenstein and inventions such as an early bicycle. They close with the UK Winter of Discontent (1978–79), where severe weather amplified political crisis. The episode mixes climate science, literature and political history to show weather's outsized role in human affairs.
title: Climate & Weather

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Willie Dalrymple about the First Anglo-Afghan War, guided by Dalrymple's book The Return of a King (noted as part of his Company Quartet). The conversation traces the spy-driven origins of the conflict, the sighting of Russian agents by George Rawlinson, East India Company paranoia, and the bungled British expedition via the Punjab and Baluchi Desert. Dalrymple narrates the occupation of Kabul, social life of the British there, the personal incidents that triggered the uprising (notably Alexander Burns' indiscretions), and the catastrophic winter retreat from Kabul in January 1842 that left few survivors — with Dr. William Brydon the most famous. They discuss aftermaths: Dost/Dos Muhammad's return to power, Shah Shuja's fate, and long-term tribal faultlines that echo into modern Afghanistan. The episode ends by drawing explicit parallels with later interventions (Soviet and American) and recent events in Kabul, considering how small personal acts and cultural misunderstandings shaped larger historical outcomes.
title: The First Anglo-Afghan War

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook provide a wide-ranging survey of Afghan history, opening with geography and ethnic composition to explain why the region has been both crossroads and crucible for empires. They trace Afghan history from Achaemenid Persian rule through Alexander the Great and the Greco-Bactrian kingdoms, to Buddhist centers such as Bamiyan, Islamic conquest, Timur and the Timurid renaissance, and the Mughal link to India. The hosts chart the emergence of an Afghan polity under Ahmad Shah Durrani, then the 19th-century Great Game, the Anglo-Afghan wars and the Durand Line. They outline 20th-century modernization attempts under Amanullah and Zahir Shah, the 1973 coup by Daoud, communist rule, and the Soviet invasion. They discuss the U.S./Pakistani-backed mujahideen, ensuing civil wars, the Taliban's rise and the dynamics that made them durable, and conclude with reflections on Western interventionism — its motives, limits and legacy — setting up a follow-up episode with William Dalrymple on the First Anglo-Afghan War.
title: Afghanistan

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Enlightenment: its dates, key figures, geographic variations and cultural consequences. They debate whether the Enlightenment represented a decisive break from Christianity or a mutation within Christian Europe, and situate it in the late 17th to 18th centuries (c. 1660 onward), citing Spinoza, Newton, Voltaire, Diderot, Rousseau and others. Topics include coffeehouses, Freemasonry, science as a worldview, the republic of letters, the Scottish and English contributions, and the movement’s universalist claims—both its liberal legacies and its darker links to colonialism, scientific racism and the slave trade. They compare the Enlightenment with the Reformation and Renaissance, discuss continental versus Anglo-Scottish varieties, and touch on related episodes such as Napoleon in Egypt. The episode mixes scholarly points with anecdote and listener questions, finishing with personal likes and dislikes among Enlightenment thinkers (Diderot praised, Rousseau criticized).
title: The Enlightenment

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the Sherlock Holmes phenomenon: its literary origins, cultural impact, and the life of Arthur Conan Doyle. They trace Doyle's medical training under Joseph Bell as the inspiration for Holmes, discuss the stories' publication in The Strand and their shaping of popular images of late Victorian London and empire, and place Holmes within the emergence of modern detection and forensic science. The conversation ranges across Doyle's other historical novels, his sporting life (notably cricket), spiritualist beliefs, and his campaigning on miscarriages of justice (George Adalji/Arthur & George and Oscar Slater). They cover famous Holmes tales and motifs (e.g., The Speckled Band, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Reichenbach Falls), Holmes's global afterlife in pastiches and adaptations (Lupin, modern TV versions), the Piltdown Man hoax near Doyle's home, and the formation of Sherlockian fandom. The episode reflects on how Holmes both reflected and shaped anxieties about empire, science, and modernity.
title: Sherlock Holmes

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the long history and politics of examinations. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by educationalist Daisy Christodlou, founder of No More Marking, who explains comparative judgment as an alternative to rubric marking. The discussion traces exams from early standardized civil-service tests in seventh-century China and Matteo Ricci’s reports to Western observers, through the Taiping Rebellion (linked to failed exam aspirants such as Hong Xiuquan), to Prussian and British nineteenth-century reforms (including university local exams from 1858 and the abolition of purchase of commissions). The hosts and guest consider tensions between standardization, validity and scalability, cite comparative research on changing grade meanings (Chris Weeden’s work), and debate pandemic-era teacher assessment versus exams. Themes include elite overproduction (Peter Turchin), meritocracy (Michael Young), social mobility, and possible reforms to ensure fairness and relevance of examinations.
title: Exams

summary: This episode examines the history and human impact of the Berlin Wall with guest Ian McGregor, author of Checkpoint Charlie. Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook set the context in the aftermath of the Second World War, the Potsdam agreements, and the emergence of the Cold War. McGregor traces the buildup to the Wall—mass emigration from the GDR, pressures on Walter Ulbricht and Khrushchev, and the decision to close borders in August 1961 (Operation Rose). The conversation covers daily life in a divided Berlin, the evolving physical barrier and escape attempts (roughly 10,000 attempts with several thousand successes and ~200 deaths), the 1961 Checkpoint Charlie confrontation, cultural pressure from Western music and concerts, and the growing peace and protest movements of the 1980s that preceded the Wall’s collapse in 1989. The episode mixes military, political and personal perspectives, drawing on first-hand interviews and archival research to explain how a symbol of division became an emblem of the Cold War’s end.
title: The Berlin Wall

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Sparta: its origins, social structure, myths, and lasting reputation. Holland outlines Spartan geography, the conquest of Messenia, the establishment of helotage, and the Lycurgan-inspired militarised constitution that produced the agoge and the Krypteia. They cover Spartan institutions (two kings, ephors, gerousia), the role and treatment of helots, female education and freedoms, and famous individuals including Cleomenes, Leonidas and Epaminondas. The hosts examine key conflicts — Thermopylae, Plataea, the Persian Wars and the Peloponnesian War — and Sparta’s decline after Leuctra and Mantinea. They consider Sparta’s reception through history (Victorian public school culture, Nazi appropriation, Renaissance admiration) and critique modern portrayals such as Frank Miller’s 300. The episode emphasises the difficulty of Spartan historiography, the mixture of myth and fragmentary evidence, and Sparta’s enduring appeal as a bundle of paradoxes: austere yet admired, militaristic yet offering relative freedoms to women, and both inspiring and troubling to later audiences.
title: Sparta

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History continues the hosts' modern Olympics series, tracing how the Games moved from austere post‑war London (1948) into a Cold War battleground of spectacle, state planning and propaganda. The discussion covers the Soviet sporting machine, state doping (notably East Germany), and defining Cold War moments such as the 1956 “Blood in the Water” water polo match and the 1980 “Miracle on Ice.” The hosts examine politicisation and boycotts (Moscow 1980, Los Angeles 1984), high‑profile scandals (Ben Johnson, doping), and tragic episodes: Mexico 1968’s student massacre and the Munich hostage crisis (1972). They survey the economic and social costs of hosting — Montreal, Atlanta, Athens, Rio — versus successes like Barcelona, and reflect on the Olympics’ continuing capacity to inspire amid darker undercurrents. The episode mixes anecdotes about athletes (Daley Thompson, Sebastian Coe, Derek Redmond) with cultural asides and commentary on media and national pride.
title: Modern Olympics - Part 2

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the origins and early history of the modern Olympic movement. Drawing on David Goldblatt's The Games, they trace precursors from English local festivals such as the 1612 Cotswold events and the Much Wenlock Olympian Games founded by William Penny Brookes, to the influence of Pierre de Coubertin, who synthesized Victorian ideals of muscular Christianity and internationalism into a revived Olympic model. They recount eccentric episodes from early Olympiads — the amateur chaos of Athens (1896) and Paris (1900), the disastrous St. Louis marathon, and the farcical and heroic moments of London 1908 and 1924 (as dramatised in Chariots of Fire). The conversation examines how the interwar period and the 1936 Berlin Games transformed the Olympics into a global spectacle and a tool of state propaganda. Along the way they highlight notable athletes, oddities (golf winners unaware they’d won Olympic gold), and the persistent entanglement of sport and politics. They conclude by splitting the story: this episode covers up to WWII, with a promised follow-up covering the postwar to contemporary Games.
title: Modern Olympics - Part 1

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the ancient Olympic Games, exploring origins, mythic founders and the festival’s sacral character. They link the conventional founding date (776 BC) to literary sources, discuss mythic founders such as Pelops, Zeus and Heracles, and explain how athletic victory conferred lasting fame. The episode covers practicalities of the festival — procession, sacrifices, naked competition, the stadium and events (chariot racing, pentathlon, wrestling, boxing, pancration) — and the political dimensions: the Olympic truce, eligibility rules, city-state rivalries, and high-profile entrants like Alcibiades. They describe famous ancient victors (Milo of Croton, Theagones, Cleomedes) and the often violent, dark aspects of heroism in Greek culture. The conversation continues into the Roman period, Sulla’s plundering of Olympia, imperial participation (Nero, Hadrian) and the eventual decline and suppression of the games in the late fourth century as Christianity rose. Throughout they contrast ancient and modern Olympics, noting shared prestige but very different meanings and contexts.
title: Ancient Olympics

summary: This is the third episode of a Rest Is History special tour of central London’s statues, recorded in Parliament Square and around Westminster. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk listeners through the contested meanings of public monuments — from Winston Churchill’s iconic plinth to statues of Lloyd George, Jan Christian Smuts, Palmerston, Disraeli, Millicent Fawcett, Gandhi, Lincoln and Nelson Mandela. They debate why figures are commemorated, whether Parliament Square functions as an imperial pantheon, and whether non-British figures can be “appropriated” by placement in the imperial capital. The hosts also contrast secular civic statues with Westminster Abbey’s 20th-century Christian martyrs (Martin Luther King Jr., Oscar Romero, Maximilian Kolbe, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, etc.), discuss creative anachronism in commemorative culture, and finish at the equestrian Richard I and Oliver Cromwell statues. The episode frames the statue debate as both political theater and public pedagogy, weighing arguments for keeping, rebalancing or removing monuments while reflecting on how context shapes historical memory.
title: Statues: Parliament Square

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk down Whitehall and around central London examining statues, debating whether to "keep or cancel" each monument. They discuss a wide array of figures — from Prince George, Duke of Cambridge and Spencer Compton to First and Second World War generals (Douglas Haig, William Slim, Alan Brooke, Bernard Montgomery) — weighing historical significance, controversies and public meaning. They reflect on the women of WWII memorial and the Cenotaph’s uniquely communal commemoration, and linger on the paradoxical Boudicca statue by Westminster Bridge as an imperial and anti-imperial symbol.
