The conversation touches on nation-building through public art, literary associations with Dickens and Chaucer, and how monuments can both memorialize and raise difficult questions about imperialism, rehabilitation, and human frailty. The episode closes by promising a third instalment focused on Parliament Square and its major statues.
title: Statues: Whitehall

summary: On location in Trafalgar Square, Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the politics and meanings of public statues, asking whether particular monuments should be 'kept or cancelled.' Walking the square they discuss Charles I and the Eleanor Cross, James II in Roman dress, Nelson's Column, George IV, Victorian generals (Charles James Napier and Henry Havelock), and the empty fourth plinth. They explore origins of statuary in Renaissance imitation of Rome, Christian anxieties about graven images, and the role of public subscription in Victorian memorial culture. Debates over Nelson's relationship to slavery, the multicultural readings of battle scenes, and proposals to replace some statues (for example with Edward Jenner) are considered. They also look beyond Trafalgar to Parliament Square and discuss the contested nature of commemoration, the differing messages statues can carry, and promise a follow-up episode walking down Whitehall to continue the conversation.
title: Statues: Trafalgar Square

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian William Dalrymple about the rise, power and eventual fall of the East India Company. Dalrymple traces the company's origins in 1599 as a private, profit-driven joint-stock venture that initially sought spices in the East Indies before shifting to India's textile trade. He explains how a fragmented, post‑Mughal political order, the interventions of figures such as Nadir Shah and the rise of regional powers (Marathas, Shivaji), and opportunistic Anglo‑Indian alliances enabled Company expansion. Key episodes discussed include the Black Hole of Calcutta, Robert Clive's actions at Plassey backed by Indian bankers, the Bengal famine and asset stripping, and the shift from private corporation to increasingly state‑regulated rule after the Regulating Act. Dalrymple ends with the 1857 uprising and the 1858 transfer of power, emphasising that for roughly 250 years India was governed largely by a commercial corporation rather than directly by the British state.
title: The East India Company

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Henry VIII and his six wives, weaving biographical sketches with political and religious context. They open with Anne Boleyn’s alleged last lines and stress Henry’s charisma, insecurity stemming from the Wars of the Roses, and rivalry with Francis I and Charles V. The discussion follows each wife: Catherine of Aragon’s Spanish pedigree and fall-out over succession; Anne Boleyn’s rise and role in triggering England’s break with Rome; Jane Seymour’s brief marriage and motherhood; Anne of Cleves’ diplomatic match and amicable settlement; Catherine Howard’s youthful downfall; and Catherine Parr’s survival and later marriages. Key figures (Thomas Cromwell, Thomas More, Cranmer) and influences (Tyndale, Fish, Holbein) are considered alongside events such as the Pope’s captivity, the English Reformation and the Dissolution of the Monasteries. The hosts mix serious historiography with anecdotes and modern parallels, ending with a playful Love Island thought experiment about which wife would succeed in contemporary reality TV.
title: The Six Wives of Henry VIII

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine England's long, tangled relationship with Italy, moving from Roman encounters and Anglo-Saxon imaginings of Rome through medieval papal politics, Renaissance cultural exchange, the Grand Tour and macaroni fashions, to the Risorgimento and Garibaldi's celebrated reception in Britain. They discuss literary connections (Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton), scientific controversies (Galileo), and the complicated political relations of the early modern and modern periods — including the Reformation, Jacobite exiles in Rome, Italian unification, and the two World Wars. Lighter cultural themes — Italian food, fashion, opera, football and biscuits (notably the Garibaldi) — thread through the conversation, illustrating shifts in British admiration, mockery and eventual respect. They close with reflections on postwar Italian resurgence and a friendly football prediction for an England v Italy match.
title: England v Italy

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Professor Andrew Preston (Cambridge) for a wide-ranging episode on the Vietnam War. They survey the conflict’s roots in French colonialism, the First Indochina War and Dien Bien Phu, and the US decision to take over the French role amid Cold War anxieties. Preston stresses the civil‑war dimension inside Vietnam and challenges common misconceptions about iconic images (Kim Phuc, the self‑immolating monk, the rooftop evacuation). They discuss international responses (de Gaulle, British advice from Malaya), key policy choices by US presidents (Kennedy, Lyndon B. Johnson, Nixon), debates over whether the war could have been won, and the domestic anti‑war movement’s composition and impact. The episode also covers media access to combat, the scale of bombing in Indochina (noting Laos), racial disparities in US draft and casualty rates, and Vietnam in popular culture and film. Throughout, the hosts reference historians and books (Fred Logevall’s Choosing War, Michael Lin’s Vietnam, The Necessary War) and reflect on moral and strategic legacies.
title: The Vietnam War

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, traces Anglo‑Danish relations from the Viking Age to the 20th century, framing the discussion around an England vs Denmark Euro 2020 match. The hosts open with the 1003 sack of Wilton and the raid on Lindisfarne (793), then explore the Great Heathen Army, the making of the Danelaw, and figures such as Alfred the Great, Æthelflæd, Guthrum and Cnut. They move to the early modern period—Anne of Denmark’s fraught marriage to James VI and I, Christian IV’s state visit, and cultural links to Shakespeare—and touch on Charles I seeking Danish aid during the Civil War. The conversation advances to the Napoleonic era, recounting Nelson’s Baltic actions in 1801 and the 1807 bombardment of Copenhagen, then to 19th‑century Schleswig‑Holstein and 20th‑century wartime ties when Danish ships joined the Allies in WWII. Interwoven are literary and cultural anecdotes (Beowulf, Bernard Cornwell, Hans Christian Andersen, Dickens) that underline centuries of rivalry, kinship and shared history.
title: England v Denmark

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discussing how to write and teach history for children. Sandbrook promotes two new children’s titles in his Adventures in Time series — books on the Second World War and the six wives of Henry VIII — and explains his approach to narrative, characterisation and factual detail for readers aged roughly eight to twelve. They debate the balance between gripping storytelling and sober presentation of difficult subjects, including how to handle violence and the Holocaust for young audiences (framing chapters around figures like Anne Frank, and including stories of rescuers such as Nicholas Winton and the Danish rescue). The hosts revisit childhood touchstones — Ladybird books, Plantagenet Somerset Fry’s A History of the World, and Peter Connolly’s illustrated military histories — and take listener questions about propaganda, multiple perspectives, and what history should be taught in schools. The conversation ranges across Roman, medieval and modern examples as they consider myths, debunking, and the ethics of presenting the past to children.
title: Children’s History

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook record a special episode on Anglo–Ukrainian relations prompted by an England–Ukraine match. They trace Ukraine’s deep and tangled past from Kievan Rus and Viking/Varangian connections to Byzantium, to Crimea’s baptismal significance and later Russian claims exemplified by Potemkin and Catherine the Great. The conversation moves to the Crimean War — its battles (Sevastopol, the Charge of the Light Brigade), cultural legacies, and figures such as Florence Nightingale and Mary Seacole. They then discuss Donetsk’s founding as Hughesovka by Welsh engineer John Hughes and the Donbass’s industrial role, before covering 20th-century catastrophes including the Holodomor and the chaotic post–First World War period, highlighting journalist Gareth Jones and hostile coverage by Walter Durante. The episode mixes historical analysis with light football banter about contemporary players and the morale stakes of a Ukraine victory, concluding with reflections on history’s emotional resonance and a wish for a good match.
title: England v Ukraine

summary: Hosts Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland interview Satnam Sanghera about his book Empireland. The conversation explores the complexity and contested nature of the British Empire — its mixture of greed, missionary zeal, culture, violence and bureaucracy — and the difficulty of reducing it to a simple moral balance sheet. Sanghera describes the hostile and at times racist reaction he's received, and discusses his personal perspective as a Sikh from Wolverhampton, including how the British classified certain groups as 'martial races' and the ambivalent British attitudes toward conquest. The trio touch on specific examples (the Tasmanian genocide, the Indian Mutiny, Opium Wars, Mau Mau), literary responses (Wells, Conrad, Orwell), and the long shadow of scientific racism. They debate whether broader education can produce a more nuanced public conversation, consider national memory and political uses of empire, and conclude that the topic resists neat conclusions — what is needed is continued, measured conversation rather than polarized argument.
title: The British Empire

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey Anglo‑German relations across the centuries, prompted by a contemporary England–Germany football tie. They trace imagined kinship from Bede’s account of the Angles and early missionaries such as Augustine and Saint Boniface, move through medieval interactions (Hanseatic trade, Richard of Cornwall), and to the Reformation and Tudor entanglements. The conversation emphasizes the Thirty Years' War’s impact on English Puritanism and figures like Prince Rupert, then the dynastic Hanoverian link (Sophia of Hanover, George I/II) and cultural exchange (Handel). The pair discuss 19th‑century German unification under Bismarck and industrial competition, the build‑up to and propaganda of the world wars, differing British perceptions of Germans (from demonisation to postwar admiration), and the Cold War role of a strong West Germany. They end by reflecting on late‑20th century reunification, the Franco‑German axis in Europe, Brexit-era tensions, and a lingering British admiration for German modernity and seriousness.
title: England v Germany

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host Roger Clark, author of Ghosts, a Natural History, 500 Years of Searching for Proof. The conversation surveys the cultural history of ghosts from classical antiquity through medieval and early modern Britain to contemporary digital-era apparitions. Clark argues that ghost stories evolve to mirror religious change (Reformation, Catholic resurgence), class anxieties and national characteristics. They discuss notable cases (Hinton-Ampner, the Cock Lane ghost, Borley Rectory), the role of witnesses and class, and prominent writers—M. R. James and Henry James—whose fiction both reflects and shapes hauntings. The episode examines the interplay between technology and the supernatural (magic lanterns, photography, X-rays, cinema, radio), media amplification of hauntings, and the persistence of poltergeist narratives. Clark also touches on Methodism, medieval precedents, and modern forms of haunting (Zoom/phone-based ghost stories). The tone is analytical rather than credulous: ghosts serve as a window onto past beliefs and social tensions, regardless of ontological commitments.
title: Ghosts

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History examines the Jeremy Thorpe scandal: the rise of Thorpe as leader of the Liberal Party, his clandestine relationships with men (notably Norman Scott), and the slow-unfolding allegations that he conspired to have Scott killed. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace the relationship from a meeting at a stable in the early 1960s through Scott's persistent demands and letters, the suggested murder plots (including an Everglades/alligator scheme), the Autumn 1975 attempted killing of Scott and the death of his dog Rinker, and the subsequent press revelations and trial. The hosts situate the scandal within 1970s Britain—party politics, the stigma around homosexuality (decriminalised in 1967), Fleet Street’s feeding frenzy, and the era’s political decay that helped shape the Thatcherite ascendance. They discuss key participants, witness credibility, the legal outcome (acquittal after the Old Bailey trial), and the cultural reverberations of the affair.
title: A Very British Scandal

summary: In this episode (Hitler — part two) hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook speak with Sir Ian Kershaw about Adolf Hitler's rise, methods and later years. Kershaw explains how Hitler combined demagogy with organized violence, recounting near-failures such as the November 1923 putsch and his early imprisonment, and describes how Hitler set broad directives while civil servants, industry and the military filled in details. The conversation covers radicalization, plans like Generalplan Ost and genocidal policy culminating in the Holocaust, key wartime turning points (Stalingrad, North Africa, the Fall of France), and Hitler’s refusal to accept defeat until late 1944. They discuss the regime’s final days in the bunker, the persistence of Nazi structures, postwar denazification, and how Hitler was mythologized as the embodiment of evil. An Al Murray appeal for DKMS is included. The episode interrogates whether Hitler was “mad” or strategically driven and considers how historical memory of such figures changes over time.
title: Hitler, with Ian Kershaw - part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview Sir Ian Kershaw about Adolf Hitler, focusing on historiographical issues and Hitler’s early development. Kershaw rejects simple labels like "great" or merely "evil" as analytical tools, arguing instead to assess Hitler’s impact within political and social contexts. He traces Hitler’s transformation from an obscure, marginal figure into a central leader between 1919 and 1923 — especially during Munich’s postwar turmoil and the 1919 Councils (Bavarian Soviet Republic) — when Hitler discovered his demagogic talent. Kershaw outlines the evolution of Hitler’s ideas (anti-Semitism, Lebensraum, anti-Bolshevism), distinguishes early rhetoric from later genocidal policy, and stresses long-term processes leading to the Holocaust rather than instantaneous intention. The episode foregrounds questions about individual agency versus structural forces and ends with plans for a second part addressing World War II, Hitler’s mental state, suicide, and Germany’s postwar reckoning.
title: Hitler, with Ian Kershaw - part 1

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Magna Carta with guest Ted Vallance, Professor of History at Roehampton and author of A Radical History of Britain. The conversation covers King John’s failures (loss of Normandy, taxation, reputed cruelties), the immediate context of the Runnymede settlement in June 1215, and key clauses of the charter (church liberties, protections for London, clauses on arrest/imprisonment and justice). Vallance situates Magna Carta among European precedents, highlights the detailed, pragmatic nature of its clauses (forests, fish weirs, labour obligations), and explains why it was reissued in the 13th century and thereafter. The episode traces Magna Carta’s evolving afterlife: its reinvention in the 17th century by common-law jurists and radicals (Sir Edward Cook, John Lilburn), its rhetorical use by later reformers, its influence on American and other constitutions, and modern invocations (lockdown debates, Brexit). The hosts and guest emphasize both the document’s medieval specificity and its long-standing symbolic power in constitutional discourse.
title: Magna Carta

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the longue durée and myth-making of California, tracing its name to the early Spanish romance Deeds of Esplandian and noting prehistoric remains from the La Brea tar pits. They cover early European contact (Francis Drake), Spanish and Jesuit missions, Mexican rule and the effects of Mexican independence, then the chaotic American takeover around the Mexican–American War and the explosive population shift of the 1848 Gold Rush. The episode examines demographic change — including Native American dispossession, Chinese labor on railroads, Russian Fort Ross, Hispanic continuity — and economic transformations from refrigerated railcars to huge agribusiness, Hollywood's rise, water politics (Owens Valley/LA aqueduct), mid-20th-century racial tensions (Zoot Suit Riots, Japanese internment), the 1960s counterculture, and California's pivot from Republican to Democratic politics. They end by discussing Silicon Valley, social inequality, homelessness, seismic risk, and California's dual status as both utopian imagination and dystopian warning.
title: California

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the life of Muhammad and the problems historians face reconstructing early Islam. They outline the traditional narrative—Muhammad's life in Mecca, revelations via Gabriel, the Hijra to Yathrib/Medina, the establishment of a community/state, and the subsequent Arab conquests—and then probe the sources: late narrative biographies (Ibn Ishaq redacted by Ibn Hissam), contemporaneous non-Muslim references (e.g. Doctrina Jacobi), and early Quranic fragments (Birmingham, Tübingen). They survey historiographical debates from radical sceptics (who questioned the Quran's early formation) to contextualizing approaches that place Muhammad in late antiquity amid the plague, the Byzantine–Sasanian wars, and shifting frontier dynamics. The episode examines how political actors (notably figures in the late 7th century such as Ibn al-Zubayyah and Abdul Malik) shaped the emerging Muslim polity, shrine locations, and the public status of Muhammad. The hosts emphasize the tension between faith-based and secular historical explanations and recommend cautious, contextual reconstruction of early Islamic origins.
title: Muhammad

summary: This episode (part two of the "World Cup of Gods" coverage) features Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook taking listeners through the quarter-finals, semi-finals and final of a Twitter-run tournament pitting deities against one another. They discuss matchups (Zeus v Athena, Mithras v Dionysus, Anubis v Isis, Apollo v Odin), interpret myths and cult practices, and weigh each god's cultural resonance, origins and later reception. Topics include Roman–Greek syncretism (Jupiter vs Zeus), the secretive Roman Mithraic cult and its mithraea, Egyptian myth cycles around Osiris, Isis and Anubis, Dionysian ecstasy and its social anxieties, and Odin’s shamanic imagery and later appropriation. They reference classical authors, modern scholars and several books while debating why Athena ultimately wins. Broader themes are the diversity and adaptability of ancient religion, how later cultures reframe gods (from Ptolemaic syncretism to Christian-era decline), and modern cultural afterlives of mythic figures.
title: The World Cup of Gods - Part 2

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present a light-hearted themed episode built around a Twitter-run "World Cup of Gods," explaining eligibility (defunct gods only) and reviewing the round-of-16 eliminations. They discuss each knocked-out deity in turn—Moloch and its contested textual/archaeological evidence; Xipe Totec and Aztec sacrificial rites; Ishtar/Inanna and her long Mesopotamian cultic profile; St. Brigid/Bridget and debates over saint-versus-goddess continuity in Ireland; Augustus and Roman imperial deification; Loki and Norse myth; Cybele and the cult of the Galli (self-castrating priests); plus the modern cargo-cult worship of Prince Philip on Tanna. Throughout they weave literary, archaeological and comparative-religion observations, reference classical and modern texts (e.g., Paradise Lost, The Second Sex, Epic of Gilgamesh), and flag cultural transmission, syncretism and the roles of ritual, sacrifice and gender in ancient cults. The episode closes promising a follow-up covering the remaining eight contestants and the tournament winner.
title: The World Cup of Gods - Part 1

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome French journalist Agnès Prairie for a wide-ranging, whistle-stop history of Paris. The discussion begins with the symbolic power of Notre-Dame and Prairie's personal account of the 2019 fire, then surveys Paris’s long continuity from Roman Lutetia through its medieval boom, the intellectual life of the University of Paris, and the ferment that produced the French Revolution. They explore recurring themes: Paris as idea versus reality, its status as political and cultural magnet (from St Bartholomew’s Day to the Dreyfus Affair), and the city’s habit of protest exemplified by the Commune, student movements and modern demonstrations. Haussmann’s 19th-century remodelling, the Belle Époque, the sewers and catacombs, and Paris under occupation and liberation in 1944 (with anecdotes about de Gaulle, Leclerc and Hemingway) are covered. The episode closes reflecting on Paris’s postwar intellectual prominence and its changing international influence.
title: Paris

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) examines the life, reign and reputation of the Roman emperor Nero. The hosts discuss Nero’s background in the Julio-Claudian dynasty, his early tutelage under Agrippina and Seneca, and the dramatic rupture with his mother. They explore Nero’s theatrical self-presentation — singing, acting and staging public spectacles — and debate how much later literary invective (principally from senatorial authors and Christian writers) shaped the ‘monster’ image. Key episodes covered include the Great Fire of Rome (AD 64) and the subsequent persecution of Christians, the murder/poisoning narratives around Britannicus and Agrippina, Nero’s artistic ambitions and personal relationships (Acte, Poppaea, Sporus), and his downfall leading to suicide and the Year of the Four Emperors. The conversation balances ancient sources, archaeological evidence and modern scholarship to argue Nero was a charismatic, performative ruler whose notoriety fused genuine deeds, propaganda and hostile posthumous portrayals.
title: Nero

description:
It promises to be the biggest event of the summer - The Rest is History World Cup of Gods.

Sixteen competitors, but there can be only one winner. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook preview all the runners and riders.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook launch a playful "World Cup of Gods" tournament, explaining the rules (no currently widely worshipped deities) and presenting the 16 contestants. They run through the unseeded entrants — including Anubis, Augustus Caesar, "Bridget", Kibbele, Ishtar/Inanna, Moloch, Prince Philip and "Chippy Totec" — then introduce the seeded heavyweights such as Mithras, Zeus, Odin, Isis, Dionysian/party god (ambiguous in transcript), Apollo, Balder, Loki and top-seed Athena. The hosts debate pedigrees, histories and likely outcomes, referencing related historical topics (Roman imperial cult, Aztec sacrifice, the Euro 1992 upset involving Yugoslavia) and note promotional material featuring pundits like Mary Beard. They explain how listeners can vote via Twitter, outline the draw and match schedule (draw/by Jonathan Wilson on the morning of Saturday the 22nd; tournament culminating with a final and a recorded highlights feature on the 27th), and encourage participation in the crowd-voted, bracket-style competition.
title: The World Cup of Gods - Preview

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, examines Oliver Cromwell and the decade of the British Republic between the execution of Charles I and the Restoration. Their guest, Paul (Hay/Lay), editor of History Today and author of Providence Lost, guides discussion on Cromwell's military career, religious convictions, political role in the Protectorate, and contentious actions in Ireland (notably Drogheda and Wexford). The conversation addresses constitutional experiments such as Barebone's Parliament and the Instrument of Government, the power of the New Model Army, and the Levellers' democratic critique. They consider Cromwell's ambiguous legacy — embraced by different political traditions and mythologised across centuries — and how memory of him resurfaces in later debates (Victorian politics, Brexit). The episode references primary battles (Marston Moor, Naseby), key figures (Charles I, Charles II, John Milton) and recent scholarship, concluding that Cromwell's era reshaped British and Irish history but remains contested and often misunderstood.
title: Cromwell and the Protectorate

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine Game of Thrones as a cultural phenomenon and a lens on popular understandings of the medieval past. They trace George R.R. Martin's influences — from Shakespeare, Tolkien and medieval literature to Roman, Renaissance and modern events — and assess the series' historical resonances (Hadrian's Wall, Wars of the Roses, Viking and Anglo-Saxon material) and anachronisms. Topics include dragons as a symbol of modern aerial power, the White Walkers as a climate-change/eschatological motif, religion and the High Sparrow (Savonarola analogue), representations of violence and sex, and historical precedents such as the Black Dinner and sack of Rome. They debate whether Martin's gritty sensibility is more "realistic" than Tolkien's moral framework and discuss political analogies (Daenerys compared to Galla Placidia and Tony Blair). The episode intersperses listener questions, medieval anecdotes (toilet deaths, hospitality breaches/Red Wedding parallels) and reflections on Game of Thrones' impact on places like Dubrovnik.
title: Game of Thrones

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Camilla Townsend about her book The Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs. Townsend reframes common myths: the Aztecs did not generally think the Spaniards were gods nor foresee an imminent apocalypse at first contact. She explains Aztec origins as migrant Nahua/Mexica groups, their political rise in the Basin of Mexico, and the urban complexity of Tenochtitlan. The conversation covers religious beliefs and rituals—human sacrifice in social, political and cosmological context; ritual self‑bleeding; gods such as Tlaloc and Xipe Totec; and ancestor myths like Nana Huatzin. Townsend discusses technological and agricultural differences between Old and New Worlds, the role of European diseases in the collapse, and colonial and post‑colonial effects on indigenous peoples, noting later 19th‑century and revolutionary upheavals. The episode balances appreciation of Aztec cultural achievements (poetry, markets, urban planning) with candid discussion of violence and its uses within empire.
title: Aztecs

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the historical origins and evolution of the teenager. They begin with ancient practices — Roman and Greek coming-of-age rituals, patria potestas, adoption and generational divides — then trace a modern genealogy: Victorian boarding-school culture, the late-19th/early-20th-century pre-history of adolescent identity, and the coalescence of a distinct teenager in 1940s America (magazine 17, spending power). They discuss the centrality of girls in early youth consumer culture, the rise of mass youth movements (swing kids in 1930s Germany, Beatlemania, mods vs rockers, punk), and recurring moral panics. The hosts consider why contemporary teenage tribes are more fragmented, whether teenagers remain a distinct social category, and whether modern figures such as Greta Thunberg represent a politicized new model of youth. The episode mixes cultural history, examples from antiquity to the 20th century, listener questions, and reflections on economics, style, and idealism.
title: Teenagers

summary: In this episode Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland host Pen Vogler to discuss the history of British food and its relationship to class, using Vogler's book Skoff: A History of Food and Class as a guide. They trace attitudes to foreign foods (potatoes, tomatoes, curry) and reflect on how social aspirations and French culinary fashions altered English tastes from the long 18th century into the 19th. Vogler discusses medieval spicing, the influence of Puritanism, the effects of enclosures and industrialisation, and the role of literature (Dickens, Austen) in shaping food rituals such as the Christmas turkey. The conversation covers practical topics—pies, pasties, the full English breakfast, tea, sandwiches—and broader imperial links that brought curry and tea into British life, touching on the Raj and political episodes tied to tea. The tone is informal and anecdotal, mixing culinary trivia with social and economic context to explain why Britain eats what it does today.
title: Food Glorious Food

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the causes, course and legacy of the French Revolution. They outline the structural problems (demographic pressure, fiscal crisis, bad harvests), the convocation of the Estates-General, the Tennis Court Oath, and the popular unrest culminating in the Storming of the Bastille. The conversation moves to the radical phase — the Terror — and profiles leading figures (Robespierre, Saint-Just, Danton), debates over motivations and responsibility for violence, and the particularly brutal treatment of notable women (Marie Antoinette, Madame Roland, Olympe de Gouges). They examine civil conflict in the Vendée, the global consequences (Haitian Revolution), and Napoleon’s emergence. The hosts also touch on cultural memory and historiography (Burke’s critique, Simon Sharma’s Citizens), symbolic acts (calendar reform, metric system) and how the Revolution reshaped modern politics and the left-right divide. The episode balances vivid anecdotes, moral questions about revolutionary violence, and discussion of the Revolution’s enduring global significance.
title: The French Revolution

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interviewing Dan Snow about the Seven Years' War. The conversation surveys the global conflict (commonly dated 1756–1763) across North America, India and Europe, highlighting pivotal 1759 victories — Wolfe's capture of Quebec, Hawke's naval victory at Quiberon Bay, and Clive's success at Plassey — and the fiscal-military state that enabled British global operations. They discuss the European dimension: Frederick II of Prussia's central role, the diplomatic realignments (the Diplomatic Revolution), and Maria Theresa's efforts against Prussia. The hosts explore consequences: the rise of British imperial power, its economic underpinnings (sugar, slavery, and mercantilism), and the war's links to later events like Pontiac's Revolt and the American Revolution. The episode interrogates celebratory national memory versus modern critiques of empire, and emphasises how 18th-century military, financial and naval developments shaped the anglophone global order.
title: The Seven Years' War

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the long historical roots and character of "culture wars," debating whether the phenomenon is essentially modern (coined in Bismarckian Germany) or as old as history. They trace continuities from Late Antiquity—examining the Altar of Victory dispute, Ambrose versus Symmachus and the rise of Christian universalism—through Byzantine iconoclasm, the Reformation and 18th-century statue culture, to modern Americanized culture wars. They argue Christianity reshaped the terms of debate by introducing ideas of universal identity and progress, which later secular movements inherit without recognizing their theological origins. The conversation covers Britain’s Whig–Tory roots, the transmission of conflicts to America, the civil rights movement’s Christian rhetoric, the role of universities and generational change, and tactics for "winning" culture wars (top-down enforcement versus cultural change). The episode ends by noting upcoming episodes on the Seven Years' War and the French Revolution.
title: Culture Wars

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History is a themed "Top 10" on eunuchs. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook survey examples across time and space, from ancient Persia and Rome through Byzantium, Ming China, early modern North Africa and Russia, to eccentric modern cases. They discuss Bagoas (the Persian eunuch associated with Alexander the Great), Sporus (a boy castrated for Nero and presented as a wife), the self-castrator Boston Corbett (who killed John Wilkes Booth), and Samson Rowley (an Englishman turned treasurer in Algiers). Tom highlights Narses and Zheng He as powerful eunuch state actors; Dominic covers commercial castrati like Farinelli, the tragic Abelard, and the mass castration movement of the Russian Skoptsy led by Kondrati Selivanov. The hosts explore motives behind castration—political loyalty, religious fervor, economic gain, punishment and sexual dynamics—while reflecting on cultural attitudes and the ethical distance of discussing these practices today.
title: Top Ten Eunuchs

summary: In this episode Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss 1066 and the Norman Conquest, treating it as both a dramatic story and a decisive pivot in English history. They narrate the three-way contest between Harold Godwinson, Harald Hardrada and William of Normandy, cover Stamford Bridge and the Battle of Hastings, and explain how Norman military (castles and cavalry) and papal support (a papal banner and the broader Gregorian Reform) changed England's political and ecclesiastical landscape. The hosts answer listener questions about rightful succession (Edgar Ætheling), long-term social consequences (decline of slavery, shifts in elite landholding and class perceptions), the Varangian Guard and English exiles, and the contested accounts of King Harold’s death (eye versus later grisly narratives). They also consider myth-making around the Norman yoke, cultural assimilation (language and identity), and whether England might instead have oriented toward Scandinavia. The episode blends narrative, source critique, and popular memory of 1066.

This episode of The Rest Is History brings James Holland (guest) to discuss the pivotal year 1940. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interrogate popular myths and trace the arc from the Phoney War through the German offensives of April–May 1940, the collapse of France, and the evacuation at Dunkirk (Operation Dynamo). They examine the political drama in London — Chamberlain's fall, the Halifax–Churchill dispute and the Five Days in May — and argue why Churchill insisted Britain must fight on. Militarily they analyse Blitzkrieg innovations (radios, Panzer divisions, close air support), the halt before Dunkirk, and why Operation Sea Lion was unrealistic. The conversation covers the Battle of Britain, the strategic consequences of Germany failing to subdue Britain, and how that failure pushed Germany toward Barbarossa. They also touch on the Blitz, Royal Navy and Empire strengths, and the wider geopolitical stakes that made 1940 a strategic turning point.

Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the history and myth of the American Wild West, balancing romanticised popular culture with the brutal realities of westward expansion. They trace the era's drivers—economic motives, railroads, gold rushes and post–Civil War chaos—and consider the role of religion, media and celebrity (dime novels, Wild West shows, photography) in shaping the myth. Key episodes and figures are examined, including George Armstrong Custer, Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse and Buffalo Bill, alongside works of literature and film that constructed and transmitted the legend (Owen Wister's The Virginian, Cormac McCarthy's Blood Meridian, Jack London's novels). The hosts assess myths — cowboy life, Cowboys vs Indians, and the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner — and confront the environmental and human costs, notably the slaughter of bison and the catastrophic decline of Native populations. Comparative frontiers (Canada, Russia) and the persistence of Western tropes in global popular culture are also considered.
title: The Wild West

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome Ali Ansari, professor of Iranian studies, to argue for Persia/Iran's outsized influence on world history. Ansari explains the continuity between Persia and Iran, outlines pre-Islamic Persian empires (Achaemenid, Parthian, Sassanian), and contends Persia contributed foundational elements to empire, religion, and culture. He highlights Zoroastrian influences on Jewish and Christian texts, Persian roles in Islam’s development, and the Persian origin of the walled garden/paradise concept. The discussion ranges across Persian garden design, cavalry and possible stirrup diffusion, fashions (trousers, coats, high heels), leisure (polo, refinement of board games), administrative models adopted by the Mughals and then the British Raj, and claims linking algebra/science and even noodles to Persian transmission. The hosts probe why strong Persian polities sometimes fell (political fragmentation, decadence). The episode blends scholarly claims, cultural anecdotes, and light provocation to stress Persia’s deep, often underappreciated, impact on the West and Asia.
title: Persia

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sambrook discuss how history functions as entertainment across reenactments, theme parks, board games and video games. They examine ancient Roman spectacles (including staged naval battles and gladiatorial types), medieval and Victorian tournament revivals, and modern historical theme parks like Puy-du-Fou, noting political inflections in their presentations. The conversation covers controversies around reenacting morally fraught pasts (Nazi uniforms, Confederate reenactments, plantation tours and the National Trust debate) and the ethical limits of spectacle (e.g., Jack the Ripper tourism). They move on to games: Monopoly’s Georgist origins (Henry George), Risk, Diplomacy, Campaign for North Africa, Kingmaker, Civilization, Europa Universalis, Assassin’s Creed and war games, debating pedagogical value, Eurocentrism, counterfactual play and how games simplify or reproduce strategic dilemmas of statecraft. The episode ends by flagging taste and politics in historical entertainment and noting upcoming topics (Persia).
title: History as Entertainment

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Tracy Boorman about Elizabeth I, exploring how the queen’s image, politics and personal history produced enduring fame. Boorman argues Elizabeth’s mastery of public presentation, pragmatism on religion and careful use of patronage underpinned the stability and cultural flowering of her reign. The conversation addresses rumours about Elizabeth’s virginity (Boorman supports the virgin-queen interpretation), the trauma of Thomas Seymour’s conduct, Elizabeth’s smallpox bout in 1562, and her relationship to parents Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn. They discuss the threat posed by the Spanish Armada and the Tilbury speech, the role of advisers such as William Cecil and Francis Walsingham (including surveillance networks), and the fraught succession, including Mary, Queen of Scots and James VI. Boorman also comments on screen portrayals of Elizabeth and recommends further reading. The episode balances myth-busting with appreciation of Elizabeth’s political skill and cultural impact.
title: Elizabeth I

description:
It was one of the great political ideologies of the 20th century, vying with capitalism for supremacy.
Now communism has retreated from the political mainstream having failed to create the utopia of a classless society.
Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss the origins of communism as a theory and the frequently repressive attempts to govern by its principles.

summary: Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss the origins, evolution and legacy of communism. They trace proto-communist ideas from early Christianity, Thomas More and radical Reformation movements (Hussites, Anabaptists, the Diggers) to Marx and Engels in mid-19th-century industrial Britain. The hosts debate whether Marxism functions like a political religion and assess Marx’s scientific pretensions versus its theological resonances. They move on to Lenin’s adaptation (vanguard party, democratic centralism) and the emergence of violent, centralized regimes under Stalin, asking whether totalitarianism is inherent to communism. China, North Korea and post‑war Soviet conservatism are examined, with references to collectivization, famines in Ukraine, Stalinist purges and debates over inevitability and historical failure. Audience questions cover Mensheviks vs Bolsheviks, whether a non-communist Russia could have defeated Nazi Germany, and long-term technological futures. The episode cites key texts and historians while reflecting on communism’s continuing cultural and intellectual influence.
title: Communism

description:
History is littered with stories of espionage and its capacity to change the course of events. But does spying truly matter and has the human operative finally been replaced by the computer?
Ben MacIntyre, author of books including Agent Zigzag and The Spy and the Traitor, joins Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook to discuss the history of spying.

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian and author Ben McIntyre about the real history of espionage and its interplay with fiction. McIntyre discusses famous deception operations from the Second World War — notably the dead-body ruse used in Operation Mincemeat and the D-Day deception (Fortitude) that used double agents — and how such operations materially influenced Allied strategy. The conversation then moves to Cold War spying, focusing on Oleg Gordievsky's impact on Western perceptions of the USSR and on near-misses such as Able Archer 1983. McIntyre contrasts ideological motivators (rare) with other drivers of espionage like money, ambition and the “drug” of secrecy, and highlights female spies via Agent Sonya (Ursula). He argues that modern intelligence now combines signals intelligence (GCHQ) with human intelligence, and warns that declassification practices and ephemeral digital records will make future intelligence history harder to recover.
title: Spies, with Ben MacIntyre

summary: This episode is the second special covering the Rest Is History Prime Minister's World Cup, a Twitter knockout tournament pitting British prime ministers against each other. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook review the quarterfinals, semifinals and build-up to the Gladstone–Attlee final, recapping notable matches such as Benjamin Disraeli vs William Gladstone and Lloyd George vs Clement Attlee. They discuss voters' reactions, cultural archetypes that shape historical reputations (the flamboyant Disraeli vs the pious Gladstone), and how public memory and modern politics affect perceptions of historical figures. The hosts examine each contender’s achievements and controversies — civil service and army reforms, the creation of modern political campaigning, the NHS, wartime leadership, scandals like the Marconi affair, and moral reputations — and reflect on how myth and history collide (especially around Winston Churchill). The episode closes with reflections on the tournament’s popularity, planned future themed World Cups, and upcoming guests on the regular podcast feed.
title: Our Greatest Prime Minister

description:
Who is the greatest British Prime Minister of them all? The bookmakers have Winston Churchill favourite to lift the crown, but William Gladstone and Maggie Thatcher won’t give up the fight without a struggle. And who’s this coming up quietly on the left-hand rail? Why, it’s Clement Attlee, who looks a real threat to the horses on his right. Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland debate the runners and riders in our inaugural Rest is History World Cup.

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook present and review the "Rest Is History" Prime Ministerial World Cup, a Twitter-run knockout tournament to find the most popular British prime minister among their listeners. They explain how Dominic seeded a 16-player field (including Churchill, Walpole, Disraeli, Gladstone, Pitt the Younger, Attlee, Lloyd George and Thatcher) and discuss early-round results: Disraeli over Salisbury, Gladstone over Tony Blair, Churchill over Palmerston, Pitt the Younger over Pitt the Elder, Attlee trouncing Lord Liverpool, Asquith beating Thatcher, Peel defeating Walpole, and Lloyd George besting Harold Wilson. Alongside match recaps they debate reputation versus historical achievement, noting cultural memory, scandals, and policy legacies (e.g., Corn Laws, Peterloo, Seven Years' War, Napoleonic conflicts, MI5 suspicions). They flag a follow-up episode covering quarterfinals onward and reference related works such as Spycatcher and The Beggar's Opera while previewing an upcoming espionage episode with Ben McIntyre.
title: The Prime Ministers’ World Cup

summary: This special episode of The Rest Is History is devoted to St Cuthbert. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Cuthbert’s seventh-century life in Northumbria, his asceticism, miraculous powers (healing, control of wind, communion with animals) and his connection to Lindisfarne and St Aidan. They cite early sources, notably Bede’s life of Cuthbert, and consider how saints’ lives blend personal memory and hagiographic formula. The hosts trace Cuthbert’s powerful posthumous career: a miraculously preserved corpse, a major pilgrimage cult, Viking attention culminating in the 793 sack of Lindisfarne, the monks’ carrying of the relics (875), and the political use of the saint by figures such as Guthred and Athelstan. Comparisons are made to other relics and preserved bodies (Alexander, Lenin), and the episode covers the shrine’s survival through the Reformation and Cromwell’s agents, concluding with modern anecdotes (an alleged WWII fog protecting Newcastle) and a light-hearted proposal to adopt Cuthbert as England’s patron saint.
title: St Cuthbert’s Day

description:

Sports journalist and author Jonathan Wilson joins Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland to look at the history of the game and how it became Britain’s most successful export.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook host football writer and historian Jonathan Wilson in a wide-ranging episode tracing football’s evolution from mob games and public-school codification to a global cultural phenomenon. Wilson outlines the 1863 rules meetings at Freemasons' Tavern and the late 19th-century tensions between elite codifiers and working-class clubs, noting professionalism's legalization in 1885 and the Football League's 1888 founding. The discussion follows football’s spread beyond Britain — particularly to Argentina, where the sport helped forge national identity — and surveys 20th-century developments: industrial roots, the Factory Act’s role in creating Saturday spectatorship, the export of clubs by industrialists, and continental national styles. They examine 1980s–90s crises (Bradford, Heysel, Hillsborough), subsequent safety reforms and commercialization, the Bosman ruling, skyrocketing player wages, globalization of the Premier League, and worries about accessibility and youth engagement. The episode ends on women’s football, recounting the early prominence of teams like Dick, Kerr Ladies, the 1921 FA ban and its late reversal, and the modern rise of the women’s professional game.
title: The Beautiful Game

description:
Counterfactuals are the great what ifs of history.
Imagine the Nazis winning World War 2, or the Roman Empire never falling.
Is this a valid form of historical enquiry? Or is it simply game-playing?
Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss what might have been.

A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History, hosted by Dominic Samrook and Tom Holland, explores counterfactual history — the what-ifs of the past — weighing its value as serious inquiry against its tendency toward fantasy. The hosts discuss methodological distinctions (limited, evidence‑based counterfactuals versus sprawling wish‑fulfilment scenarios), referencing Herodotus and key hinge moments like Marathon, Salamis, Marathon’s broader consequences, and May 1940. They debate whether individuals or deeper structural forces drive change, using examples such as Margaret Thatcher, Hitler, Churchill (and the taxi incident hypothetical), Franz Ferdinand, Hannibal, Cortés, and technological what-ifs (Roman or Alexandrian steam power). The conversation cites several works on counterfactuals and alternative histories (Fatherland; Altered Paths; The Difference Engine) and touches on literary/TV examples (SSGB; The Man in the High Castle). Listener questions prompt discussions on dystopian tendencies in alternative history and whether major 20th‑century wars were inevitable. The hosts generally emphasise structural forces over simple great‑man contingencies while acknowledging a few decisive choke points.
title: What If?

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Katja Heuer about Prussia, the emergence of Germany and the formation of the Second Reich. Heuer outlines Prussia's complex geography and ethno-linguistic patchwork, traces origins from the Baltic Prussians and the Teutonic Knights, and stresses the decisive nineteenth-century processes—Napoleonic disruption, volunteer militias, and the three wars (against Denmark, Austria and France) that enabled unification in 1871. The conversation explores competing strands in German identity: militarism and state-building under Otto von Bismarck versus philosophical and cultural currents (Hegel, Kant, the Brothers Grimm), the ambiguous role of Austria, and the long shadow cast by the World Wars. Heuer argues Germany’s creation relied on "blood and iron" yet was also shaped by liberal and economic forces, and discusses how later regimes (including Nazi appropriation of Prussian symbols) have complicated modern German memory and commemoration of the 1871 foundation.
title: The Second Reich

summary: This special edition of The Rest Is History (hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook) reacts to the high-profile interview with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. The hosts place the episode in broader historical context: comparing Meghan's entry into the British monarchy with past examples such as the 1936 abdication crisis (Wallis Simpson and Edward VIII), Diana's public struggles, and earlier dynastic conflicts. They discuss themes raised by the interview—racism, mental health, generational divides, and the clash between American celebrity culture and British royal tradition—arguing the story touches on British national identity and the monarchy's symbolic role in the Commonwealth. Historical analogies range from George IV's coronation spectacle and Elizabeth Woodville's fraught marriage to medieval and Viking-era father–son conflicts (Harald Bluetooth, Sweyn Forkbeard, Cnut). The episode closes by flagging related forthcoming Rest Is History episodes (including a podcast on the Second Reich).
title: A Royal Row

description:
Has America taken over the world? Did the dollar and Hollywood enable the US to replace the British empire as the dominant international influencer? And is that power now waning?
Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss Americanisation on the Rest is History.

A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com

See acast.com/privacy for privacy and opt-out information.
summary: This episode of The Rest Is History explores the history and dynamics of Americanisation, tracing its linguistic, cultural and political roots from the 19th century into the present. The hosts discuss early commentators such as W. T. Stead, cultural moments like Buffalo Bill’s Wild West shows and the impact of sound film (The Jazz Singer, 1927) on British exposure to American accents. They examine the post‑World War II rise of American soft power via Hollywood, MTV, Silicon Valley and the internet, and consider how language, shared Protestant intellectual traditions and consumer markets aided American influence. The conversation addresses shifting political alignments around Americanisation, the export of American cultural battles (statue removals, identity politics), sport’s relative resistance to American export, and comparisons with rising Chinese influence. Religious narratives (American exceptionalism and the “city on a hill” motif) and their role in shaping both pride and self‑critique are discussed, along with questions about whether other cultures might undergo similar processes in future decades.
title: Americanisation

description:
Comedian Al Murray joins Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook to discuss the history of comedy as well as the funny side of history.
Has comedy changed through time? When and why are we not allowed to laugh at events?
Al Murray has made a living out of making people laugh, while also frequently placing history at the heart of his humour.

A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Harry Lineker
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by comedian Al Murray to discuss the intersection of comedy and history. They trace comic treatment of historical subjects from medieval jesters and court fools through Spike Milligan, the Goon Show and mid‑20th century British satire to modern television and film (Blackadder, Life of Brian). The conversation examines how comedy can shape popular understandings of events such as the First World War, the role of satire as safety valve or social critique, changing tastes and censorship, and difficulties in re-broadcasting dated material. They also discuss how media fragmentation and shared experiences (e.g., lockdown) affect national comedic culture. Historical examples and sources (1066 and All That; Looking at History; The Wipers Times) are used to illustrate how humor functions across status hierarchies, wartime contexts and evolving public sensibilities.
title: The Kings of Comedy

summary: Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss the enduring allure of Tutankhamun, tracing it from Howard Carter's dramatic 1922 discovery of an intact royal tomb to the wider, stranger politics of the Amarna period. They outline Carter's career, the Carnarvon partnership and the popular 'curse' mythology, then pivot to Akhenaten (Amenhotep IV) and his radical Aten monotheism: the founding of Akhetaten (Amarna), the unusual artistic style, Nefertiti's prominence and the violent rollback after Akhenaten's death that erased names from king lists. They address contested issues — the identity of mummies (KV55), theories on Tutankhamun's death, Freud's speculation in Moses and Monotheism, Jan Asman’s work linking memories of Atenism to later traditions, and twentieth-century cultural projections (including Nazi interest in Nefertiti). The episode closes with listener questions on murder, chariots, gender-fluid imagery in Amarna art, Velikovsky-style hypotheses and the impulse to map ancient religious change onto later monotheisms.
title: Tutankhamun

summary: This episode of The Rest Is History features hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook with guest Susanna (Susie) Lipscomb, Professor of History, discussing witches and witchcraft from antiquity through the early modern period and into modern echoes. Lipscomb traces witch beliefs from ancient Greek cases (Theoris of Lemnos) to the intensification of prosecutions in the late 15th–17th centuries, noting the role of texts like Malleus Maleficarum and James VI/I's Demonology in framing witchcraft as diabolic heresy. They examine geography (England, Scotland, Germany, the Americas), gender patterns (predominantly older women but important male and child cases), social causes (poverty, famine, neighborhood quarrels), and evidence practices (confessions, spectral evidence). The discussion covers famous outbreaks (North Berwick, Pendle, Salem, Würzburg), the decline of legal executions by the late 17th/early 18th centuries, and modern parallels in scapegoating and social-media “witch hunts.” The episode balances scholarly literature, folklore, and contemporary relevance.
title: Witches

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook conduct a wide-ranging discussion of 'empire': what it means, how empires form, and whether they can be morally defended. They trace imperium from Roman etymology and Augustus to early Near Eastern imperialism (Sargon, Assyria) and the Persian model of moral legitimation (Cyrus the Great). The episode contrasts imperial violence and terror with infrastructure, law, and cultural attraction (Greek, Roman, Islamic examples), and examines classical and biblical inheritances that shape modern anti-imperial sentiment. They discuss European distinctiveness, attitudes toward the British Empire, and modern manifestations of empire (United States, China, Russia), plus commercial and digital forms. Listener questions prompt conversations on longevity of empires, assimilation versus federalization, and whether people were better off inside empires. The episode references books and authors (Tom Holland's Persian Fire; John Darwin; C.L.R. James) and flags many future podcast directions while concluding that empire remains central to world history and contemporary politics.
title: Empires

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian and author Halle Rubenhold about sex, sexuality and sex work in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. Rubenhold discusses her novel Mistress of My Fate and explains her research methods—diaries, memoirs and letters—highlighting sources such as Boswell, William Hickey and popular confessionals. The conversation covers the geography of prostitution in London, distinctions between courtesans and street sex workers, class dynamics, famed courtesans (Kitty Fisher, Cora Pearl), and how men used mistresses as status symbols. Rubenhold addresses pregnancy and abortifacients, the prevalence of home remedies and early abortive medicines, and changing sexual ideologies from Georgian libertinism to Victorian ideals of purity. They debate moral panics—criminal conversation suits and anxieties about homosexuality—and discuss figures like Rousseau, Byron and Dickens in shaping sexual attitudes. The episode emphasizes nuance: public rhetoric versus private behavior, class-based differences, and continuities and changes across two centuries.
title: Sex in the City

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss how historians should treat recent history while taking the 1990s as their focus. They debate when a period becomes "history," the effects of proximity on perspective, and contrast nostalgic, upbeat memories (Britpop, club culture, rising tech) with darker global events (Rwanda, the breakup of Yugoslavia, Russia’s post-Soviet collapse). They consider defining 1990s themes: the end of the Cold War, the rise of the internet and digital culture, the ascent of China, and political moments such as Tony Blair’s 1997 victory and Princess Diana’s death. Cultural flashpoints — Oasis vs. Blur, ecstasy culture, Hollywood’s uncritical Americanism — are weighed alongside longer-term consequences (European integration, not joining the euro). Tom plugs his book Dominion in a discussion about religion’s underestimated resilience. The episode mixes anecdote, listener questions, and broad analysis about whether the 1990s were a golden age, a seedbed of later problems, or both.
title: The 90s

summary: Hosts Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland present a themed episode surveying ten “weird” or unusual wars from antiquity to the twentieth century. Each host picks five conflicts, ranging from the First Sacred War (c. 590 BC) — notable for a siege and alleged use of poisonous plants at Kirra — to the 1932 Australian Emu War, where farmers and soldiers spectacularly failed to stop emu crop raids. Other selections include the War of Canudos in Brazil, the Umayyad–Berber resistance led by the prophetess Al-Kahina, the British 1867–68 expedition to Abyssinia, the 955 clash between Hungarians and Otto’s forces at the Lech, the far-flung Dutch–Portuguese global trading wars, the horrific Paraguayan War (Triple Alliance), the War of Jenkins’s Ear and its Portobello episode, and the vast Russian Civil War (with the Czech Legion highlighted). They reference literature (Mario Vargas Llosa, James Meek) and historians (Margaret Macmillan) while reflecting on the human cost and oddities of each conflict.
title: Weird Wars

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the history of thinking about the future: prophecies, oracles, apocalyptic religion and scientific projections. They contrast ancient and medieval horizons (Delphic and Sibylline oracles, Croesus, Philip of Macedon, Herodotus) with modern technological and environmental imaginings (Huxley, Orwell, Gibson, Philip K. Dick). The discussion ranges from practical uses of prophecy in antiquity (Delphi, Siwa, Sibylline Books) to cultural drivers of apocalyptic thinking (sixth-century climate shocks, the Little Ice Age) and modern dystopias focused on computing or climate catastrophe. They address Nostradamus, Mother Shipton, Halley's Comet (1066), Oswald Spengler and late-20th-century geopolitical theses (Huntington, Fukuyama). The episode is largely a question-and-answer format with listener queries about oracles, prophetic credibility, and whether literary visions such as 1984 or Brave New World have been borne out. The tone mixes historical analysis with cultural critique and some light banter.
title: The History of the Future

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook interview historian Michael Wood for a sweeping one-hour survey of Chinese history. They discuss the sense of cultural continuity in China — the role of emperors, the central bureaucracy, Confucian ethics and legalist ideas — and why China has tended toward large centralized states. Wood highlights periods Chinese people celebrate (the Tang) and painful turning points (the Opium Wars and the 'century of humiliation'), the Taiping Rebellion, the Long March and the Japanese invasion. They examine why China, despite early maritime prowess under Zheng He, turned inward rather than pursuing overseas empire, and touch on the causes of the Communist victory in 1949. The conversation closes by considering Mao's legacy, Deng Xiaoping's opening up in 1978–79, and President Xi's contemporary use of historical narrative and Confucian themes to legitimize the regime. The episode references books and primary sources and proposes a follow-up episode focused on Communist-era China.
title: China

description:
It remains the most romantic historical story of all time, but is the legend of King Arthur a myth? Was he even English? And will he rise again when the country needs him most?
Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook take their places at the round table.


A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor

@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com

summary: Hosts Dominic Samuruk and Tom Holland debate the historicity and cultural afterlife of King Arthur. They evaluate early sources (Gildas, Nennius), medieval constructions—especially Geoffrey of Monmouth’s History of the Kings of Britain—and archaeological and genetic evidence about post-Roman Britain and Anglo-Saxon settlement. The conversation covers the emergence of Arthurian motifs (Merlin, the 12 battles, Battle of Badon), regional claims (Tintagel, Cornwall, Dunbarton), and medieval and later appropriations by figures such as Edward I, Henry VII and Henry VIII. They discuss Tintagel archaeology, Glastonbury’s claimed tomb, the Grail and Joseph of Arimathea, and the political and commercial uses of Arthurian legend. The episode also surveys literary and cultural adaptations (Malory, T. H. White, Rosemary Sutcliff, Bernard Cornwell, T. S. Eliot, film Excalibur, and pop-culture echoes like Lord of the Rings and Star Wars), concluding that Arthur’s uncertain historicity is part of his enduring appeal.
title: King Arthur

description:
England has long been divided by an invisible line somewhere north of Watford and south of the Mersey.


But do northerners really have more in common with Scots and Welsh people than their fellow Englishmen in London?


Dan Jackson, author of The Northumbrians and a former advisor to Cheryl Cole, joins southerner Tom Holland and midlander Dominic Sandbrook to try and decide if we should eat lunch then dinner, or dinner then tea.


A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com

See acast.com/privacy for privacy and opt-out information.
summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by historian Dan Jackson (author of The Northumbrians) for a wide-ranging discussion of regional identity in England. The episode interrogates the north–south divide, arguing geography and geology (rivers, hills, marshes) as long-term determinants shaping distinct economies, dialects and cultures. They trace roots from Roman provincial divisions through Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria), the Danelaw, and the medieval northern frontier (Battle of Carham), to the industrial heyday when coal and manufacturing briefly inverted regional power. Political and cultural consequences are considered — from Chartism, Peterloo and the Harrying of the North to 20th-century class identities, sports affiliations (rugby league/union, football, cricket) and the Brexit aftermath. Comparative remarks consider Italy, France and the US (Scots-Irish migration, American North/South). The conversation also touches on the centralising pull of London, the making of a national English culture, and how modern communications have reshaped regional alignments.
title: The North South Divide

description:
What is fascism and where did it come from? No one admits to being a fascist yet it continues to be a term of abuse hurled on a regular basis. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the history of this most unacceptable of political models.


A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com

Episode Website
summary: Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland discuss the nature, origins and appeal of fascism. They argue fascism is primarily a product of specific post–First World War conditions — national humiliation, revolutionary aspiration and violent modernism — rather than a timeless temperament. Key topics include Benito Mussolini and his Roman iconography (fasces), Gabriele D'Annunzio's proto‑fascist role at Fiume, and Adolf Hitler's racialized reading of antiquity fused with distorted Darwinism. They examine aesthetics (uniforms, blackshirts), modernist cultural appeal, philosophical influences (Friedrich Nietzsche), and contrasts with authoritarian rulers such as Salazar and Franco. The hosts debate distinctions between fascism, authoritarianism and communism, the latter’s differing moral reception, and historians' roles in myth‑making. The episode closes by noting contemporary analogies (e.g., Vladimir Putin) are imperfect, and promoting an upcoming episode featuring Dan Jackson on the North–South divide in Britain and his book The Definitive History of Northumbria.
title: Fascism

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook are joined by archaeologist Sophie Hay to discuss Pompeii and Herculaneum. They cover how the sites were preserved by the Vesuvius eruption, the value of Pliny the Younger's eyewitness account, and the ongoing archaeological work (about one third of Pompeii remains unexcavated). Sophie highlights recent excavations and notable finds—a bar with pots containing animal remains that change ideas about food and fast-food practices—and the importance of multidisciplinary analyses. They debate the eruption date (traditional 24 August from Pliny's letters versus autumnal evidence such as pomegranates and graffiti dated in October), discuss daily life (diet, sanitation, baths), the ubiquity of erotic imagery and its ethical display, the lives of slaves, and how Pompeii’s rediscovery and excavation were shaped by politics (Bourbons, later national narratives). They stress that much of Pompeii’s story is pieced together fragmentarily from graffiti, inscriptions and small finds.
title: Pompeii

summary: In this episode of 'The Rest Is History', Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore the historical significance of walls and borders. They discuss well-known walls such as the Berlin Wall, Hadrian's Wall, and the Great Wall of China, analyzing their purposes and effectiveness. The hosts cover the ambiguity of walls, questioning whether they symbolize strength or weakness. They delve into the political motives behind constructing walls, such as Donald Trump's border wall with Mexico, and examine historical examples of border disputes and agreements like the Treaty of Westphalia and the Treaty of Tordesillas. Additionally, they touch on modern issues of digital borders like the Great Firewall of China, and the impact of technological advancements on border security and migration. The episode concludes with listener questions about borders and enclaves, as well as discussions about the philosophical and practical implications of these man-made divides.
title: Walls and Borders

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the nature, purpose and influence of historical fiction. They debate whether historical novels should prioritise accuracy or narrative, and whether fiction serves as a gateway to serious history. The conversation ranges across children’s classics (Ladybird histories, Rosemary Sutcliff), sea and military fiction (Patrick O'Brian, C.S. Forester, Arthur Conan Doyle), modern prizewinning works (Hilary Mantel, Tolstoy’s War and Peace) and speculative/counterfactual fiction (Game of Thrones, Kim Stanley Robinson, Philip K. Dick, Robert Harris). They consider how novels shape popular memory of events — Dickens’ A Tale of Two Cities influencing Anglophone views of the French Revolution, Scott shaping medieval England, Gone with the Wind mythologising the antebellum South — and discuss how changing moral standards affect which older historical novels remain acceptable. They answer listener tweets about earliest historical novels, first-person narration, alternate histories and recommend books they’d leave to future generations.
title: Historical Fiction

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook welcome their first-ever guest, Stephen Fry, to discuss Greek mythology with a focus on the Trojan War. Fry, whose latest book (the third in his myth cycle) treats Troy and its aftermath, reflects on the transition in Greek myth from elemental gods to richly characterized deities and humans. The conversation ranges over Homeric narrative techniques, the difficulty of translating ancient codes of honour and violence for modern readers (including children), and the interplay between mythology and historicity — from Hesiod and Homer through nineteenth-century excavations of Troy to modern retellings. They debate the role of gods as symbolic or active agents, Odysseus as archetypal trickster, and why myth endures, with references to later adaptations (Dan Simmons' Ilium) and storytelling lessons drawn from film and literature. The episode blends literary criticism, classical scholarship, and reflections on contemporary readership and cultural transmission.
title: Stephen Fry and Troy

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss conspiracy theories across history and how they both reflect and shape their times. They examine modern examples (QAnon, vaccine conspiracies, moon-landing denials, JFK theories), and trace parallels to historical episodes including Watergate, the Popish Plot, medieval blood libels (William of Norwich, Hugh of Lincoln), and the Albigensian/Cathar crisis in southern France. They consider the persistence of anti-Semitic conspiracies (Protocols of the Elders of Zion, Dreyfus) and how conspiracy narratives can be politically weaponized — from Nixon's paranoia to Nazism. Cultural manifestations (books like Foucault's Pendulum, popular fiction, and films) and internet-era phenomena (Finland-doesn't-exist meme) are discussed as ways conspiracies spread and become industries. The hosts emphasize that conspiracies often mix grains of truth with fabrication, fill social needs for explanation, and can produce measurable political and social consequences.
title: Conspiracy Theories

summary: In this episode Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland survey a range of historical parallels that have been invoked in debates about Brexit. They present a playful "Top 10 Brexits" spanning millennia — from the submergence of Doggerland and the end of Roman Britain, through medieval episodes such as King John’s disputes with Pope Innocent III, the English Reformation under Henry VIII, and the Cromwellian Protectorate, to modern touchstones like the Seven Years' War, Napoleonic exclusion, late‑Victorian "splendid isolation," Irish independence, and Dunkirk. The hosts stress that most parallels are tendentious but argue some illuminate how geography, religion, empire and wartime experience shaped British distinctiveness. They pick Doggerland, the Reformation and Dunkirk as particularly revealing comparisons and reflect on how mythmaking and selective memory amplify historical analogies in contemporary politics. The conversation remains deliberately non‑partisan and episodic, aimed at historical perspective rather than policy advocacy.
title: Brexit

summary: Hosts Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the history and evolution of Christmas, from questions over the historical Nativity narratives to the festival's pagan and seasonal resonances (Saturnalia, Solstice, Yule). They examine dating difficulties in the Gospels, how early Christians adopted a 25 December birthdate, and medieval and Anglo‑Saxon practices (including an Æthelstan charter tying hospitality to Christmas). The episode traces Puritan opposition and the 17th‑century Parliamentary attempts to suppress popular festivities, the Restoration, and the long 19th‑century reinvention of Christmas—highlighting Washington Irving, Clement Clarke Moore, Prince Albert, and Charles Dickens (A Christmas Carol, 1843) as key influences in domesticating and commercializing the festival. They contrast Father Christmas and Saint Nicholas/Santa Claus origins and finish with wartime Christmases, including the 1914 Christmas Truce and an anecdote from the eastern front (Siege of Przemyśl). The tone mixes historical analysis with cultural commentary on generosity, commercialization, and continuity of themes.
title: Christmas

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook examine the causes of the First World War, weighing contingent moments against structural forces. They narrate the immediate Sarajevo trigger — the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand by Gavrilo Princip — and trace how alliance systems, mobilization timetables and prestige politics pulled powers into a general war. Topics include British decision-making (honour, protecting the empire and the channel), the Anglo–German naval race, Russian mobilization and the Balkan and Ottoman context. Sandbrook discusses counterfactuals (Britain staying out or allying with Germany), revisionist debates (Christopher Clarke, Neil Ferguson) and cultural responses: invasion fiction, Blackadder, war poets and Oh What a Lovely War. They stress that many policymakers understood the likely devastation yet chose what they perceived as the least worst option. The episode balances military-diplomatic explanations with imperial, social and cultural considerations, concluding that fear, prestige and contingent choices combined to produce catastrophe.
title: Causes of the First World War

description:
Social media has colonised the world but is it really a new phenomenon? Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook debate the effects of technical innovations from the printing press to Twitter. Do they really make a difference?
Or was Swift right when he said: “It is the folly of too many, to mistake the echo of a London coffee-house for the voice of the kingdom.”

Produced by Jack Davenport
