summary: This episode examines whether modern social media is genuinely novel by tracing historical precedents for rapid, divisive public debate. The hosts argue that technologies from the printing press to coffeehouses similarly amplified minority voices and fuelled culture wars — citing Martin Luther's pamphleteering and John Calvin's Geneva as early social-media analogues. They discuss how polemic, abuse and ‘viral’ short-form messaging have long affected politics and religion, from Roman trolling (Cicero) and Athenian ostracism to anti-popery campaigns, the Reformation's pamphlet explosion, and the press-driven 18th-century public sphere. Listener questions prompt comparisons (Socrates/Plato on writing; Aristides and ostracism) and highlight how rapid cultural change often stems from educated minorities but requires broader societal receptivity. The episode connects historical examples (German Peasants' War, Thirty Years' War, Great Fire of London, Act of Union) with contemporary phenomena like cancel culture and online campaigning, concluding that while media change accelerates debate, the dynamics of cultural conflict are longstanding.
title: The Echo of a Coffee House

description:
Can we truly learn from history? And if we can - do we?
It’s one of the big questions this week as Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook roam through the centuries in search of certainty.
Never get involved in a land war in Asia. That’s our starter for ten.

A Goalhanger Films & Left Peg Media production
Produced by Jack Davenport
Exec Producer Tony Pastor
Twitter:
@TheRestHistory
@holland_tom
@dcsandbrook
Email: restishistorypod@gmail.com
summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook debate whether history yields usable lessons. They interrogate classical models—from Thucydides, Herodotus and Ibn Khaldun—to modern attempts to systematize the past (Peter Turchin, Jared Diamond, Asimov’s fictional predictive model). They challenge the idea of fixed rules, arguing lessons are often cherry-picked to support present prejudices; examples include misuses of the appeasement analogy (Munich), Cold War and post‑9/11 decisions (Vietnam, Iraq), and Suez (1956). Geography and material conditions (Britain’s relation to continental Europe, Belgium/Lotharingia, Russia/Ukraine) are asserted as powerful constraints. The hosts also consider recurring patterns (revolutionary dynamics, hubris in invasions of Russia) and the limits of predictive history. Listener comments fuel topics from human nature and historical method to cultural specificity, concluding that while history offers perspective and recurring patterns, it rarely furnishes simple, universal prescriptions for action.
title: The Lessons of History

description:
It’s been described as the most legendary story ever told. But did the Trojan War actually happen? And was it really fought over a beautiful woman? Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss an enduring tale that still resonates to this day.

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the Trojan War: its mythic narrative, archaeological evidence, and cultural afterlives. They summarise Homeric plotlines (Helen's abduction by Paris, the decade-long siege, the wooden horse) and consider ancient and modern attempts to historicize the tale — from Homer, Herodotus and Thucydides to Heinrich Schliemann's 19th-century excavations at Hisarlik. They evaluate Hittite textual evidence (Wilusa, Ahiwawa) that may connect to Trojan traditions, and debate whether the conflict was about honour, wealth or control of trade. The episode examines later receptions — Roman identification with Troy via Aeneas, medieval claims of Trojan descent, Greek tragedy (Euripides' Trojan Women) and modern portrayals in film (Troy, 300). They also consider which modern wars occupy Trojan-like mythic status (WWI/WWII) and how audiences empathize with Trojans or Greeks. The hosts touch on themes of heroism, suffering, rape in wartime, and the Christianized sensibility that shapes modern sympathies.
title: Troy

description:
As a new series of The Crown arrives on Netflix, returning viewers to the 1980s, we look back at the year many Britons consider the worst in living memory.
Rocketing unemployment, riots in major cities and a country governed by the most divisive prime minister in post-war British history made 1981 a year to forget.
Amidst the gloom was the wedding of Prince Charles to Lady Diana and the greatest Ashes fightback England cricket fans had ever seen.
So what can we learn from a closer analysis of 1981?

summary: In this episode Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the recent past through the prism of The Crown's return to Netflix, focusing on Britain around 1981. They situate the royal wedding and Diana's mythic status against a backdrop of recession, mass unemployment, race riots (notably Brixton), the Maze hunger strikes and political polarization under Margaret Thatcher. The hosts consider how music, sport (especially Ian Botham's Headingley heroics) and pop culture act as a collective memory and national narrative, comparing those mythic threads with political and economic forces. They debate Thatcher's role as symptom versus cause of deep structural change, how younger generations perceive Thatcher and Diana, and the way mythic figures shape historical understanding. The episode ranges across examples from ancient sources (Cicero) and literature (Hardy) to contemporary TV, arguing that the mythic qualities of public figures are historically significant in themselves. The conversation closes with plans for further episodes on 1981's unresolved topics.

summary: This special edition of The Rest Is History, hosted by Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook, responds to the networks declaring Joe Biden the 46th President and surveys historical parallels for Donald Trump's conduct. The hosts compare Trump to modern and ancient figures — especially Richard Nixon and various Roman leaders (Julius Caesar, Nero, Caligula) — drawing on themes such as the mos maiorum, Cincinnatus/Washington as the reluctant leader, the imperial presidency, and populism versus establishment politics. They discuss Nixon’s Watergate, Caesar’s legal jeopardy and the Rubicon, and Roman popularist tactics, using these to illuminate contemporary Republican dynamics, Trump’s media-style governance, and his post-election behaviour (including the Giuliani “Four Seasons Total Landscaping” episode). They consider the likely historical memory of Trump relative to Nixon, the prospects for prosecution, and the durability of political legacies and constituencies shaped by figures like Nixon and Reagan.
title: Is Trump Caesar or Nixon?

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook explore parallels and contrasts between the tumultuous 17th century and the present. They sketch the period's key episodes — Elizabeth I's death, the accession of James VI/I, the English Civil Wars, the execution of Charles I, Cromwell's Protectorate, the Restoration, the 1665 plague and 1666 Great Fire, and the Glorious Revolution — and link them to modern concerns: pandemic lockdowns, climate-driven crises, information revolutions, political polarisation and cultural witch-hunts. They discuss how new media (pamphlets and early newspapers) inflamed divisions then as social media does today, and note the role of religious belief in shaping politics. The hosts touch on regional echoes in Scotland and the mapping of civil-war loyalties onto recent Brexit voting patterns. They also recommend reading: Geoffrey Parker's Global Crisis, Paul Lay's Providence Lost, Christopher Hill's God's Englishman, Samuel Pepys' diary, Robert Toomes' The English and Their History, and the novel Instance of the Fingerpost.
title: We’re All So 17th Century

summary: In this inaugural episode Dominic Sandbrook and Tom Holland debate the concept of "greatness" in history: its origins, meanings and modern relevance. They trace the idea back to Persian and Hellenistic exemplars and show how Roman and Victorian historiography canonized figures as "the great". The hosts contrast classical, martial models (Alexander, Frederick the Great, Peter and Catherine) with moral or saint-like modern figures (Nelson Mandela, Martin Luther King, Gandhi). They discuss republican and communist tensions about celebrating individuals, citing George Washington, Lenin, Stalin and Mao, and touch on contested modern icons such as Winston Churchill. Contemporary leaders (Putin, Trump, Merkel, Macron) are considered as potential future candidates for greatness, with attention to how political culture shapes commemoration. The conversation ranges across monuments, biographies and children's histories, probing whether the modern world still produces figures who fit older notions of greatness.
title: Greatness

summary: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook discuss the causes, warning signs and historical patterns of civil wars, drawing on examples from antiquity to the present. They compare Julius Caesar's Rubicon moment and personal ambition with mass, ideologically driven conflicts like the Spanish Civil War and the Yugoslav wars. The hosts explore how history, identity, religion and political radicalization can fuel dehumanization and violence, citing Northern Ireland, 1968 France, the 1984–85 UK miners' strike and contemporary US polarization. They debate triggers for modern breakdowns of order—weapon availability, politicized militaries, delegitimization of democratic processes (with reference to Donald Trump) and potential future drivers such as climate and migration. While agreeing that outright conventional civil war in stable Western states is unlikely, they warn about lower-intensity violence, paramilitary activity and localized unrest. The episode ends ambivalently: modern democracies have safeguards, but political polarization and armed populations make certain forms of domestic violence plausible in coming decades.
title: Civil War
